☆ ʻĀKALA

Vol I · scan p. 9 · book p. 2

Rubus hawaiensis, syn. R. sandwicensis, syn. R. damienii. ☆ Outstanding species.

EDIBILITIES: Deep purple, red, or sometimes yellow berries ~1" to 2" {2.5- 5mm} long. Flavor varies from sweetish to sometimes bitter. Edible fresh it. ‘ raw, in pies, or jams & preserves.

MATURITY: spring through summer. aight Wy ay eH DYE..;... oy 4 oh

FIBER: stems sometimes pounded to KAPA. oo vo.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES. ee

DESCRIPTION: Thornless, perennial, Endemic shrub. Stems can grow to 15' le a - OP {4.5m} long. Trailing or upright, sprawling habit. Sometimes prickly, but - a IN usually unarmed. Often deciduous. Flowers rose, pink, or occasionally My ait - oS white. Fast growing.

ORIGIN: Hawaiʻi. Found in forests on the islands of Name 7 Lp Hawaiʻi, Moloka‘i, Maui, & Kauai. Although this species was formerly seen down to 2000' {600m}, now it's usually found only above 4000' {£1200m} elevation.

CULTURE: prefers moist soil, acid pH, & full sun.

ADVERSARIES: susceptible to insects introduced as bio-control in attempts to control weedy alien Rubus spectes., as well as grazing animals.

PROPAGATION: cuttings, layering, & divisions. Cuttings: semi-ripe, hard-wood, or leaf-buds. Thirsty in youth.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh& VeryHigh, WetMesic

⚠️ ʻĀKALA Rare

Vol I · scan p. 9 · book p. 2

ʻĀKALA, KALA, ~AKALAKALA, Macrae's Raspberry. Rubus macraei.

⚠️ NOTE: PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB ANY NATURAL STANDS OF THIS SPECIES.

EDIBILITIES: Berries 1" to 2" {2.5-5mm} long, blue-black, deep red to purple, juicy & tart or bitter.

MATURITY: summer through fall. Now too rare to eat.

APPLICATIONS:

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Endemic perennial shrub. Sprawling & creeping. Young growth is prickly. Flowers rose to pink.

ORIGIN: Hawaiʻi. Much less common than R. hawaiiensis. This ʻĀKALA is Rare & a Species-of-Concem; few plants remain. Sometimes found in shrub lands, forests, rocky areas, bog edges, foggy areas of Hawaiʻi & Maui. Typically grows in montane areas, where people rarely live.

Elevation / Rainfall: High& VeryHigh, WetMesic

ʻAʻALIʻI (continued — its first page is not in the scan)

Vol I · scan p. 10 · book p. 2

wauumuvu sui, Most any pH, & full sun. Quick to establish & easy to grow. Does not require much space, water Or nutrients.

— scan page 10 —

TOLERATES: harsh weather, drought, & many soils, including poor ones, most elevations, coastal conditions, some salt, & gale winds. Inflammable but, somewhat fire tolerant as seeds will germinate & plants can ungulates are excluded.

INTOLERANT OF: heavy clay soil & poor-drainage.

ADVERSARIES: basically free of pests & diseases, except scale if over-fed. SEX: dioecious.

POLLINATION: insects & wind.

PROPAGATION: seeds, cuttings, & air-layering. Seeds can be scarified with sandpaper, or lightly boiled water can be poured over seeds, allowing them to soak 1 day. Sown in sterile potting soil & watered daily. Germination: 2 to 4 weeks. Transplanted into larger containers when 4 true leaves have grown. Pot-binding should be avoided. ʻAʻALIʻI is planted out only when well-established.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh & VeryHigh, MesicDry

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Bacopa monnieria, syn. B. monnieri.

FAMILY: Scrophulariaceae {FIGWORT}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: Herpestis, Rau dang.

EDIBILITIES: Leaves can be eaten in mixed salads, cooked as greens, fried, in soups stews, or pickled.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING.

EROSION CONTROL. ——

GROUND-COVER.

LANDSCAPING: wet-lands, shallow ponds, etc.. f

☆☠️ ʻAWA / KAVA Polynesian Introduction

Vol I · scan p. 11 · book p. 8

Polynesian Introduction ☆ Outstanding species. Attractive, multipurpose shrub with important ritual & ceremonial applications.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Piper methysticum, syn. P. methisticum. Many forms, cultivars, & varieties exist.

FAMILY: Piperaceae {PEPPER}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: “AVA, KAWA, KAVA Pepper, PU-AWA.

MAJOR APPLICATION: Bitter, relaxing beverage for ceremony & sacrament. Stems, leaves &/or thick woody roots, fresh or dried, are ground, pounded or chewed, then placed in a bowl, stirred & warmed with COCONUTwater or water, & finally strained. Purification, prayer & other ritual often accompany each phase of planting, digging, processing, to consumption. Roots have highest potency, with oldest being strongest. Saliva from chewing helps convert carbohydrates into sugars. Unpleasant flavor can be moderated with water, SUGAR CANE, BANANA, SWEET POTATO, fish or pork.

☠️ TOXICITY: ʻAWA is addictive & can be noxious. More dangerous for those with liver conditions. Continual indulgence affects eyes, skin, mind, alertness, & coordination. {AUMIKI NONI is a reported remedy for adverse reactions. }

OTHER APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: specimen, screen, etc. a - MEDICINAL, SACRED, &

CEREMONIAL QUALITIES: applications vary depending upon specific variety.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen shrub. Early Polynesian introduction. Can grow 4' to 15' {1.2-4.5m} tall. Prominent stem-joints, Attractive, heart-shaped leaves. Inconspicuous male flowers. Does not seem to fruit in Hawaiʻi. Slowgrowing. Wood-like rootstock.

ORIGIN: Islands of the Pacific.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics.

HAWATFI LOCATION: previously rare here, but now being planted more frequently. Occasionally found wild on or near wet cliffs, forest edges & clearings, or stream banks.

CULTURE: prefers rich, moist, fertile soil, shade or part shade in lower elevations & full sun in mid elevations.

INTOLERANT OF: dryness, intense sun, & coral atoll conditions.

ASSOCIATES: grown on upper edges of KALO or WAUKE plantings.

WEEDY: sometimes escapes & naturalizes, but not considered a problem. SEX: dioecious.

PROPAGATION: cuttings; 1' {30cm} sections, set in ground, & gradually hilled up with humusy mulch with growth.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, WetMesic

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, woody, climbing shrub. Polynesian introduction. Can grow quite tall, but usually kept under 12' {3.6m}. Related to ʻAWA. Clings by adhering aerial roots. Fragrant leaves.

LIFE-SPAN: 50 years possible.

ORIGIN: Indio-Malaysia.

HAWAIʻI LOCATION: occasionally grown in Hawaiʻi.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: warm Tropical rain-forests.

CULTURE: prefers moist, fertile, heavy soil, & shade. Responds to care & amending with manure. Needs protection from wind.

TOLERATES: clay soil.

INTOLERANT OF: dry conditions.

TRAINING: requires support, trellis, stakes, nitrogen-fixing tree, or a NIOJ-PEKELA to climb.

ADVERSARIES: susceptible to mildew, foot-rot, & requires careful pest management.

⚠️ CAUTION: bio-cides {herbicides, pesticides} render the leaves toxic. SEX: generally dioecious.

PROPAGATION: cuttings. Vertical stem-tips 1.5' {45cm} long; directly or to transplant, with at least 2 nodes buried & several remaining above soil level. Can be planted densely in mounds or pits.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics.

CULTURE: prefers high humidity, steady ample water, loose fertile humusy soil, & shade. Responds to light feeding; fishenoulsion & other liquid- or time-release fertilizer in dilute quantities. Easy to grow in appropriate conditions.

TOLERATES: handles more salt-spray & harsher conditions than the introduced MAIDENHAIR FERN.

INTOLERANT OF: heat & dryness, wind, & full sun. Can “die back" during summer, after flourishing in a wetter winter.

PRUNING: cut back hard & watered well for regeneration.

ADVERSARIES: basically free of pests & diseases, except for mollusks. {“Sluggo"m}

PROPAGATION: divisions & spores. Deserves to be planted more often. Sometimes available in nurseries.

☆ Outstanding species. Attractive, ancient, multi-purpose evergreen tree.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Pandanus tectorius & P. odoratissimus. Many types, varieties, clones, & cultivars exist, including edible & smooth-leaved varieties.

FAMILY: Pandanaceae {SCREW PINE}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: Screw Pine, Pandanus, Nicobar Breadfruit, Walking Trees, Pineapple Tree, Balawa, Sabotan, “Ara, Aggag, Fara, Laufala.

PRINCIPLE APPLICATION: FIBER - Leaves {LAU HALA} provide a strong lasting fiber for weaving & plaiting, hats, mats {for floors, beds, & tables}, baskets & sacks, shelters, roof-thatching, beds, sails & kites, clothing, sandals, decoration, fans, umbrellas, cordage, sacking & much more. Processing: leaves are dried, spines scraped off, beaten, & briefly soaked in sea water before being sun bleached. Leaves are slit lengthwise, as needed. Dried keys as brushes for KAPA decoration. Male flower-spike bracts can provide fiber for matting. Aerial prop-roots can be beaten for paint brushes. Roots can be retted for cordage.

EDIBILITIES: Minor food applications. Pulp of inner part of fruit-segments can be sweet, starchy, high in vitamin C, & can be eaten as a scarcity food, but SEE: TOXICITY, following. Eaten fresh raw, or cooked & mashed for a flour for flat-cakes, preserved, dried, & beverage. While most do not, some Hawaiian HALA varieties have few of the crystals typically found in Hawaiian HALA, with some cultivars being much better than others. Leaf-base: white flesh at the bases of young, tender Jeaves can serve as a scarcity food fresh raw, boiled, or baked in an IMU. Terminal bud has been eaten similarly to PALM-cabbage {kills the tip, but new buds arise.} Seeds are tedious to remove from their hard shells, but tasty & edible if carefully processed. (how?) Tips of aerial prop-roots though reportedly not palatable, are rich in B vitamins & are edible cooked or made into a drink. Aromatic male flower-spikes {HINANO} have edible bracts when boiled until tender. Pollen is eaten mixed in various dishes, or as a COCONUT-oil scent, & is reportedly aphrodisiacal.

☠️ TOXICITY: Hawaiian HALA fruit are usually too high in calcium oxalate crystals to eat raw, but o.k. as dried, cooked flour.

BEARING: Begins to fruit 10 years of age.

APPLICATIONS:

BARRIER PLANT: large & formidable.

BEE FORAGE.

CONTAINER-GROWING. DYE: leaves & roots.

EROSION CONTROL: binds soil well.

FIBER: SEE: PRINCIPLE APPLICATION, ABOVE.

LANDSCAPING: accent, specimen, hedges & edges. SEE: DISADVANTAGES, FOLLOWING. LEI: leaf & fragrant, unripe fruit segment tips can be strung.

LIVING FENCE: large & aggressive.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: numerous applications.

PERFUME: male flowers {HINANO} are the source of the flavoring scent "Kewda attar" or the oil “Keora."

Female trees have been hollowed as pipes for water. Prop-roots can be split for house walls.

Female flowers mature into large PINEAPPLE-like fruits. Fragrant male flowers hor, are white & form a long, well-bracted, pollen-rich spike. Shallow, lateral root system. so

GROWTH-SPEED: fairly fast-growing.

LIFE-SPAN: long-lived. uo

ORIGIN: Pacific Polynesian islands, N Australia, S Asia & surrounds.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics. Adapted to various climates, but prefers the wetter coasts, Tolerates hot conditions, drought, salty wind, & wet regions.

HAWATPI LOCATION: Commonly found on sandy & rocky sea-sides, ocean cliffs, seaward edges of coastal forests, atolls & lowlands, though can grow to mid elevations.

CULTURE: HALA prefers rich, moist, well-drained soil, acid pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: various soils, including salty & sandy, high water-tables & very light shade.

INTOLERANT OF: water-logging & intense shade.

ASSOCIATES: ĀULU, HAU, KAMANI, KOA, KUKUI, NIU, NELEAU, Ptsonia species, etc.

ADVERSARIES: Basically disease & pest free, but may be susceptible to mealy bugs & scale. Readily killed by fire.

DISADVANTAGES: HALA is large & prickly. Attracts rats who eat the fruit {removing brown leaves discourages rats from nesting.} SEX: Dioecious.

POLLINATION: Reportedly pollinated by wind, possibly assisted by insects.

PROPAGATION: Grown by cuttings, basal suckers, offsets & seeds. Cuttings: large branch ends can be started in good sized containers or planted directly in soil. Fresh seeds: soaked overnight & placed 1/2 buried in potting soil. Easy to germinate. Small, self-sown plants transplant easily. Seeds can survive long ocean voyages.

NOTE: Many other Pandanus species exist & are often planted in Hawaiʻi as omamentals. Some have edible & flavoring applications. Some have striped or variegated leaves. The Variety Pandanus tectorius v. laevis is valued for is unarmed leaves. It is sterile, although it can bear male flowers when older.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

IN CENERAL: Small, attractive, evergreen trees or shrubs. Endemic or Indigenous. Can grow 3' to 40'.9- 12m} tall {depending on species & location.} Glossy leaves. Fragrant white, red, orange, yellow flowers {depending on species.} Blossoms generally form on new wood. Slow-growing. Non-aggressive roots.

ORIGIN: Hawaiʻi. All species are depleted & a number are Endangered. Recently coming more into cultivation. Found in forests on Molokai, Kaua‘i, Maui, O° ahu, & Hawaf‘i.

CULTURE: prefers airy conditions, moist, light, well-drained, humusy soil, slightly acid pH, & full sun. Easy to grow in appropriate environment. Need protection from strong winds. Under- or over-watering, or over-feeding should be avoided; excess fertilizer can create abundant, succulent foliage, which is tempting to pests & also can cause the plant to lodge.

TOLERATE: dry conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: salt, excess moisture, strong winds, & poor drainage.

ADVERSARIES: several pests, including ants & ROSE-beetles, virus, blight, feral grazers. The seeds are eaten by rats. Resistant to HIBISCUS blister-mite. Like most Hawaiian species, HAWATIAN HIBISCUS are very sensitive to biocides. PROPAGATION,

IN GENERAL: air-layering, cuttings, grafting, & seeds {variable}. Cuttings: 4"-6" {10-15cm} of tip & stem, ~1/4th" {6mm} thick, each having at least 3 nodes. Dipped in rooting-hormone, placed in a vermiculite/perlite/potting-soil medium & kept misted. Transplanted into small pots ~3 months. Seeds: fresh clean seed sown in starting mix, kept shaded watered. Germination: 3 to 9 days. Transplanted into small pots when 2 to 4 leaves have grown. Kept shaded & moist, then transplanted when 4" to 6" {10-15mm} tall, into 1 gallon pots or directly into soil. Plants can be purchased from a nursery, or a friend may have cuttings, but please DO NOT TAKE CUTTINGS FROM WILD PLANTS due to likelihood of spreading disease. Nursery propagation has saved some of these plants from Extinction. Local species should be planted.

☆🌿 IPU / HUE / PŌHUE / GOURD Polynesian Introduction

Vol I · scan p. 26 · book p. 32

☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Lagenaria siceraria, syn. L. vulgaris, syn. L. longissima, syn. L. ro leucantha. Many varieties & cultivars exist.

FAMILY: Cucurbitaceae {GOURD}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: Calabash Gourd, Container Gourd, Bushel Gourd, White- Flowered Gourd, Trumpet Gourd, Ugao, LAUKI. Three varieties grown by the ancient Hawaiian: 'TPU NUL,' Great Gourd, *

UMEKE PŌHUE: Large IPU with thick, hard rind. ‘TIPU MANALO,' Sweet Gourd: Small IPU that are edible when harvested immature. YPU “AWA‘AWA,' LAU HUE, Bitter Gourd: Small, poisonous IPU, diluted for their medicinal qualities.

PRINCIPLE APPLICATION: Dried gourds. Ancient, important, & wide-spread crop. Large fruit from 4" to 3' {10-90cm} or longer, with a thick cortex. Shell becomes hard when dried, making the fruit hollow & durable. Forms are highly variable in size & shape, thickness & hardness of rind, & degree of edibility. GOURDS are made into containers, jars, flasks, bowls, spoons, ladles, kitchen utensils, musical instruments, ornaments, helmets, floats, bird houses, seed containers, planters, pipes, flow-forms, baskets, & storage vessels for water, POI, clothing, KAPA, & feather LEI, etc. GOURDS are sometimes carved or decorated; designs can be dyed, carved, scrapped, or burt into surface.

PROCESSING: After harvest, the GOURD is wiped free of moisture, cut open at neck, & pulp scooped out as thoroughly as possible. After pulp is removed, water can be poured into the GOURD for a brief time to soften remnants & ease final scraping before curing. Amount of time needed to cure GOURDS varies from 1 to 6 months, or longer. Cleaned GOURD can be dried over smoky fires, turning regularly. Surface mold can be scraped off. Shells are not washed nor disinfected. Shells can be steel-woolled or lightly sanded to eliminate outer skin, then lacquered, shellacked, varnished, enameled, waxed, or rubbed to a fine surface. The medicinal IPU “AWA*AWA' are processed in their own special way.

EDIBILITIES: Although GOURDS of most cultivars are too bitter to be eaten, certain select cultivars are excellent. Young fruit can be boiled or steamed & eaten as a vegetable similar to summer SQUASH, also in soups & stews, curries, fried, frittered, or pickled. Tender young leaves & shoots are cooked as greens. Seeds are high in protein & oil & can be cooked, ground, roasted, chewed, in soups, extracted for a tofu-like food, or as an edible oil. The sweet 'IPU MANALO' is cleaned & utilized immediately. For eating purposes, young fruits are picked when still tender, or 1/3rd mature size. £70 OxICITY: Despite the yariety IPU *AWA*AWA' being considered poisonous, this species is generally harmless. Pulp around seeds iS purgative.

— scan page 27 · book page 33 —

BEARING: Fruiting can begin in 3 months. 90 to 180 days to matutity, depending on variety & conditions.

MATURITY: For containers, the fruits are left on the vine as long as possible, preferably until full ripeness. Maturity is noted when skin color changes from green to beige & fruit-stem dries & withers.

HARVESTING: GOURDS are cut from the vine with a knife or clippers, retaining a few inches of stem.

STORING: The fruits have a short shelf-life & do not store well.

SHIPPING: Immature fruits are soft & easily damaged in transport.

APPLICATIONS: see also: PRINCIPLE APPLICATION, above.

CEREMONIAL: seeds.

LANDSCAPING: excellent candidate, although temporary.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: TPU*AWA*AWA:'

NURSE PLANT: when grown on trellis or arbor, the plant can offer valuable shade for tender plants.

SACRED: the Hawaiian culture have specific rituals & myths concerming ‘IPU NUT.’

XERISCAPING.

LEFE-SPAN: 6 to 10 months.

ORIGIN: Eastem rr rn “;. Hemisphere Tropics, most likely Africa, India, or Asia. a ag f. 1: a ey 4

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics, Subtropics &, during hot summers, 4 a a] a fae the Temperate regions. Needs a very long growing season. gt en v be Pa Sr Requires hot weather & normal rainfall. More or less tolerant of., fe o. intense heat, drought, or excess rain. Best yields result when; ni ka " rainfall is low at the end of the growing cycle. Intolerant of frost. so ST bese: eit full sun. IPU & ʻUALA {SWEET POTATO} thrive under similar a oA i

CULTURE: IPU prefer rich, light, well-drained, humusy soil, pH 6.0- ee conditions. Although plant responds to soil amended with aged- 7S a z| it al ie i manure or compost, excess nitrogen stimulates greenery at the on oT ys sinh ‘ih Lf i eile expense of fruit. Shallow roots are easily damaged by cultivation. ‘ides.

TOLERATES: various soils, including soil less rich than needed by " g MELONS or SQUASH.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding.

TRAINING / SHAPING: The vines need a sturdy trellis, tree, arbor, fence, or roof to climb. If touching the ground, any pebbles under developing fruit should be removed. GOURDS can be rested on mulch, kept clean, & tumed regularly to prevent mold & discoloration. The fruits can be carefully suspended on a tripod & supported upright to facilitate a well rounded, self-standing shape. The developing fruit can also be shaped by tying with string, cloth, tape, or by frequent hand-bending.

ASSOCIATES: IPU grown on trellis or arbor can provide light shade for plants underneath.

ADVERSARIES: A wide variety of insect & disease problems are possible, but when GOURDS are grown on a small scale, rotated with other crops, these are normally not serious. Pest-resistant cultivars exist. WEEDY?: The spreading vine occasionally escapes, but is not hard to control. IPU & ʻULU {BREADFRUIT} are two ancient Polynesian plants that have apparently not naturalized.

REMARKS: Can be harvested continuously to prolong fruiting period. SEX: Monoecious, with unisexual flowers.

POLLINATION: Bees & other insects, or by hand.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds have remained viable even after GOURDS have floated in the ocean over half a year. They are believed to have drifted to S America from N Africa.

ISOLATION: for home gardening, varieties need to be separated by at least 1/8 mile {.2k}. For pure seed, 1/4th to 1 mile {.4-1.6k} separation is needed, depending on size of plot. Blossoms can also be hand-pollinated & bagged.

PROPAGATION: Seeds. {IPU & KUKUI are among the few Polynesian plants which are propagated by seeds.} Often 3 to 5 seeds are sown directly on mounds, thinned to 1 to 3 seedlings, or grown in 6" {15cm} pots to transplant. Seeds are sown 1/2" to 1" {1.25-2.5em} deep. Germination: 2-3 weeks. Sown at beginning of spring rains, or preferably a few months before a hot, dry season so the end of the cycle will be drier for IPU production.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, MesicDry

☆☠️ KALO / TARO Polynesian Introduction

Vol I · scan p. 28 · book p. 35

ALO /vT ARO aye ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Colocasia esculenta, prev. Caladium colocasia, prev. Caladium esculentum. Many varieties & cultivars exist. Boot

ALSO KNOWN AS: Eddoe, Aba, Old Coco-yam, Gabi, Dasheen. ere Shea

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed staple. With suitable preparations, the entire plant OS a is edible. Rich in minerals, especially calcium, phosphorus, as well as iron, bee: carbohydrates, & protein {although low in amino acids cystine & methionine.} Moderate. in vitamin B's & C, & low in A. Cooked KALO, & Pol especially, are highly digestible, hypo-allergenic, & good as infant or invalid food. Corms are steamed,: boiled, baked, cooked soups & stews, roasted, IMU baked, or made into KALO chips, Te wg pudding {KULOLO}, dumplings, chilled for salads, dried & ground into flour, KALO Looe Rive bread, extracted for starch, or mixed with a touch of water & fermented to POI. ne) Unfurled & very young tender leaves of al] varieties are cooked as greens, LUAU &.

LAULAU. Mature leaves & stems of some varieties have less calcium oxalate than others. Midrib & largest veins are removed before cooked. Depending on variety, cooking water may need several changes. Leaves are high in vitamins A, C, B, & K, calcium, iron, & protein. Leaf-stalks {petioles}, although low in nutritional value, can be peeled & cooked as greens or a soup-thickener. Cylindrical flower spadix can be cooked as a gourmet dish or baked with other foods.

☠️ TOXICITY: Sharp crystals of calcium oxalate are contained in all raw plant parts, although amount depends on type. Parent corm, oldest leaves & veins are highest in these raphides. To avoid the irritating affect, a thorough cooking is typically required, sometimes with several changes of water, &/or cooking with a fatty meat or fish.

FIRST-AID: affected areas can be rinsed with water, LEMON or other acid fruit juice, or ice.

MATURITY: KALO is ready in 6 to 18 months, depending on cultivar, planting system, location, & conditions, especially on amount of water. Grows quickly in sunny, warm, wet, humid lowlands. As maturity nears, new leaves grow smailer & slower. Wetland KALO needs to grow for a prolong time before harvesting, but yields heavier corms. UPLAND KALO is mature in 8 to 10 months, noted when leaf-stems become shortened & slim, & leaves yellow. Harvest period can last nearly a month.

HARVESTING: Rather than harvesting whole patch at once, larger corms can be gathered as needed, allowing KEIKI to continue {ratoon}. A week or so before harvest the desired comms can be loosened to lessen the separation shock for remaining corms. HULI is cut off to replant before comm is cleaned & dried. When harvesting the leaves, the 2nd & 3rd leaves can be cut when the plant is vigorously growing, taking care not to damage the newest leaf. Harvesting the leaves reduces corm quality.

STORING: Cultivars vary in storability, but corms tend to have a short shelf-life, especially POI KALO types. Large corms do not keep very well after harvest: 2 months maximum. Smail corms last a little longer, therefore the larger ones should be eaten first. Refrigeration extends storage. Steamed corms can be sliced & sun-dried for ionger storage. Cooked, pounded KALO can be made into POI, or it can be air-dried or freeze-dried, & later reconstituted by steaming & re-pounding. Cooked KALO or POI can also be canned for baby food. KALO flour is long-lasting & can be baked into many items. Freezing cooked conms a day reduces their sticky consistency, making shredding or drying easier.

SHIPPING: Handles transport well when fresh, if air is not too moist.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY CROPPING: many KALO cultivars are planted in multiple cropping systems.

ANIMAL FEED: corms, second scrapings & stems are often eaten by livestock, especially pigs. Cooked corms for dogs.

CANOE-ROLLERS: formerly, some enormous varieties which grew 6' {1.8m} long & 2' {60cm} wide, were utilized in moving canoes.

COMPOST: peelings, stems, & leaves are good additions to the compost.

CONTAINER-GROWING. DYE: red KAPA dye.

EROSION CONTROL: some varieties can be planted as a quick, temporary, rainy season ground-cover.

FERTILIZER: first scrapings, stems & leafs can be incorporated back into the soil.

LANDSCAPING: accent, fill, edges, etc. Ornamental varieties exist.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: KALO has many important healing properties.

SACRED: ritual & ceremonial plant.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous perennial, usually grown as an annual. Introduced by the ancient Polynesians & continuing as an important food crop. Plant can grow 1' to 7' {.3-2m} tall, depending on variety & growing conditions. KALO typically has a central, basal corm, & smaller side corms. Large, heart-shaped leaves on long petioles, with leaf-tips pointing downward. Fragrant yellow-white, JACK-IN-THE-PULPIT-type flower followed only very rarely by seeds. Hundreds of distinct forms exist based on differences in color of leaf & corm, size & shape, varying in the amount of water needed, time to maturity, & in the quality & quantity of corms produced. Fast-growing. Shallow fibrous roots.

ORIGINS: Tropical India & Eastern Hemisphere.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics. KALO is best adapted to hot, humid, lowland conditions during its long growing period, yet many varieties also grow in moist, higher elevations. Prefers consistent rain. In old Hawaiʻi, there were numerous varieties well adapted to all the various climates & elevations. WETLAND KALO is grown in paddy culture along streams, in marshes, water-logged soil, or in shallow irrigated terraces {LO'I KALO.} UPLAND KALO {a.ka.: "Dry" KALO} is planted in non-flooded, rain-fed conditions. Although "dry" KALO is sometimes called “dry-land" KALO, it cannot stand dry soil. “Dry" KALO needs at least 2" {5em} of water weekly. Even though many edry." Tolerates a range of "dry" i i iti iti le jeties can be growh ¥; eee eee a et cacy ay conditions, harsh Winds & fos.

CULTURE: WETLAND KALO prefers deep, heavy or medium textured, flooded, humusy soil, pH 5.5-6.5, & full sun. Requires ample nutrients. Needs protection from harsh, leaf-tearing winds. Prior to planting, the ancient Hawaiians enriched the soj| by stomping into the mud leaves & branches of HAU, KUKUI, CASTORBEAN, KOHEKOHE, Eleocharis Species, non-invasive GRASSES, weeds, & old KALO leaves & stalks. Excessively acid soil can be sweetened with lime or dolomite {dolomite Provides needed magnesium.} Needs to be kept well weeded, although hoeing, or other deep cultivation can damage the shallow roots of KALO. For the healthiest LO‘I plants, cool, fresh running water is best.

INTOLERANT OF: warm, stagnant LO'l, or dry, light soil. UPLAND KALO prefers deep, moist, adequately rich, well-drained, clayey or loamy soil. Can be grown on level ground, trenches, hills or ridges. depending on conditions. An organic mulch preserves moisture, retards weeds, reduces erosion & supplies nutrients. Possible mulch materials include dried, brown fronds of FERNS, or leaves of GINGER, MAT A {BANANA}, KI, {TI}, KO {SUGARCANE}, NIU {COCONUT}, non-seedy GRASSES, weed trash, etc. Responds to being side-dressed every 2 to months, depending on soil analysis, with fertilization ending 6 months of age. Benefits from being hilled up as corms tend to form high on the mother-corm.

TOLERATES: a wide range of soils {depending on variety}, extended flooding, poordrainage & shade. For detailed growing information, consult the U of H's Co-op Extension Service CTAHR information Notes.

INTOLERANT OF: rocky soil creates misshapen corms.

PRUNING: Spent flowers & dead or damaged leaves may be removed, taking care not to damage the newest, unfurled leaf.

ASSOCIATES: MATA {BANANA}, ʻUALA {SWEET POTATO}, KI {TI}, PIʻA, KO {SUGARCANE}, WAUKE, NIU {COCONUT}, etc., can be grown on edges of Lo’. Fish can be raised in the water, i.e.: mullet, “AMA’AMA, etc. In small gardens, short-season vegetables can be interplanted between young KALO, harvested before the corms grows large. can be caused by

ADVERSARIES: Needle-like raphides protect the plant from many pests, including herbivores. Root-rot “— careless propagation techniques, as in cutting the HULI too close, but is mostly the result of infertile soil. This is more of a problem in flooded terraces than in "dry" KALO plantings. UPLAND KALO can be attacked by phytophora leaf-blight, leafspot, dry-rot, root-aphids, & leaf-hoppers. Leaf-blight tends to be more severe in rainy weather. All KALO are intolerant of competition from weeds, especially in the first few months. Rocks in the soil can deform the roots. Although heavy sulfuric vog burns KALO leaves, the plant recovers.

ORGANIC CULTURE: Excellent candidate with well-prepared soil, the right cultivars, nght techniques, & careful management; the better the care, the fewer the problems. Root-rot prevention: fertilizing & resting the LO'I. WEEDY?: KALO can be persistent, but is neither rampant, nor hard to control. Wild KALO occurring along stream edges & in forests is thought to be food for spirits, therefore only eaten in times of famine, never taking all the plants, & always replanting in times of abundance. Generally wild KALO require more cooking.

REMARKS: While TARO is one of the great foods of the Pacific, DASHEEN is preferred in most of the world. DASHEEN & CHINESE TARO are now common in Hawaiʻi & easy to grow. SEE: SOME NOTABLE VARIETIES & CULTIVARS, following.} SEX: Hermaphroditic, but male & female flowers open at different times.

POLLINATION: most likely by flies.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds usually infertile or variable, producing off-type or weak plants, but valued for breeding.

PROPAGATION: Grown from HULI {"setts"}, cormels, side tubers, dormant buds, seeds, & tissue culture.

HULI: a crown-cutting consisting of 1/4" to 1/2" {6-13mm} of the upper part of the corm. TS is to 10" {20-25cm} of the leaf-stalk, containing its unfurled leave. HULI can be bundled, co AES placed in a shaded spot & covered with a light mulch to root a week or so. These cuttings are; on sturdy & will keep months in a damp spot. There are many ways to plant KALO. Consult: - Native Planters in Old wai i, by Handy, Handy, & Pukui, for complete descriptions.;

IN GENERAL: HULI or cormels can be placed into a hole 3" to 6" {7.5-15cm} deep, straightened, t oO back-filled, firmed, & finished with mulch. Planting one HULI in a hole will give bigger corms: planting 2 or 3 will give more offshoots. In areas with year-round rain, planting may be done in any season. Otherwise, KALO is planted at the beginning of a rainy season. Consalt: the Hawaiʻi Fishing & Farming Calendar.

DESCRIPTION: Graceful, attractive, evergreen shrub. Green KI was probably introduced by the ancient Polynesians, or is Indigenous & now quite common. Can grow 3' to 20' {.9-6m} tall. Trunk diameter can reach 6" {15cm}. One or more principal upright trunks. Only occasionally branching naturally. Shiny narrow leaves to 2' {60cm} long, grow spirally up stem forming a rosette on top, leaving circular scar-rings as they shed. Open, pendant inflorescence to 1' {30cm} long, with spikes of small, fragrant, lilac flowers in springtime, rarely followed by red berries ~1/4" {6mm} wide. Horticultural varieties are more likely to produce berries than the green form. KI can be confused with plants in the Genus Dracaena. Fairly fast-growing. Long, thick, tuberous tap-root, with short suckers; non-aggressive.

LIFE-SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: Probably India & the Himalayas, spreading eastward to Australia, SE Asia, & Oceania.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics. Although KI is well suited to open, warm, humid, low elevation, wet & mesic forests & forest edges, it is also found in a wide range of habitats. Tolerates hurricanes {grows back from root}, periodic flooding & drought. Intolerant of frost & continual harsh winds. ROU ive

INTOLERANT OF: sand, coral soil & brackish water.

New seedlings resemble thin GRASS leaves. Can be fed with dilute liquid fertilizer. Benefits from being transplanted to larger containers before final planting out. ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Saccharum officinarum, syn. S. officinale.

FAMILY: Poaceae {GRASS}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: To, Noble Cane.

EDIBILITIES: A principle source of extracted sugar world-wide. Fresh, sweet, raw stalk is peeled & chewed {fiber discarded,} The sugar in young stalks is glucose & fructose, while in mature ones, it has changed to sucrose. Mature stalks are the source of cane-juice, a sweetener for various foods, medicines, & beverages. Cane-juice can be extracted in a crushing mill. Or, ‘| on home level, canes can be pounded in a trough, or cut into pieces & hammered on a cutting i |. board, scraped in a pan with water just covering, & cooked very slowly; fiber strained, then the liquid can be cooked slowly to desired thickness. Cane-juice can be evaporated to molasses, / ‘0 which then can be refined to sugar, cane-syrup, golden syrup, or fermented &/or distilled into various drinks. Unrefined sugar {"raw sugar"} is a bit more nutritious, but not as long-lasting as white sugar. Most "Brown Sugar" is often just refined "white sugar" with molasses added for. color. Unfolded leaf is edible cooked. Stem-cores as grilling-skewers.

☠️ CAUTION: Leaves have sharp, cutting edges.

— scan page 34 · book page 41 —

BEARING: Nine months to 2 years, or longer, depending on elevation, climate & cultivar. Typically 2 years in Hawaiʻi. Maturity is stimulated when lack of water or nitrogen, or cooler temperatures, slow the plant's growth-rate. Canes should be at least 5‘ {1.5m} tall before harvesting. Ratoon {regrowth} crops mature 1 year Jater.

MATURITY: Typically ready to harvest just before flowering commences around November. Commercially, sucrose content of canes is randomly tested every week or so in order to harvest at highest levels. Sweetness is concentrated in the lower sections of the stalk. Flowering depletes energy, consumes sucrose, & may cause pithy areas in stems.

HARVESTING: KO canes are cut close to, or just below soil-level. Commercially they are hauled or floated to a mill for processing. Commercial fields are typically bummed to reduce leaf-bulk. Several ratoon crops are usually allowed to mature before the field is replanted.

STORING: Fresh cane-juice should be stored in a covered jar in a refrigerator. Refined white sugar has a very long shelf-life, if kept dry & cool. Fresh stalks are best if processed within a few days after cutting.

SHIPPING: Refined sugar, brown sugar, & molasses all transport well.

APPLICATIONS:

ALCOHOL: ethyl alcohol, acetone, & butanol are processed from molasses.

ANIMAL FEED: cattle relish the sweet stalks. Cane-tops for fodder. Molasses can be fed as is, or added to other feeds, to tops, or to bagasse-pith for livestock.

BIOMASS: bagasse is the fibrous residue from sugar extraction. Utilized for mulch, green-manure, compost, plastics, etc.

CEREMONIAL. s

COMPOST MATERIAL: green waste, bagasse, & filter press-cake {"cachaza."} DYE: leaf & stem.

EROSION CONTROL: fast-growing protection for eroded or otherwise damaged land.

FERTILIZER: filter press-cake & filter-mud residue from cane processing is high in phosphates, nitrogen, & calcium carbonate; utilized as fertilizer after composting.

FIBER: dried leaves & stalks as inferior thatching; interior applications. Flower-stalk fiber, or leaf-midrib for hat braiding. Bagasse as paper, cardboard, as well as fiber-board.

FUEL: dried bagasse. LEI: flower.

LIVING-FENCE: rapidly established hedge or barrier, with the more upright varieties usually being desirable.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: many applications, especially regarding several ancient Hawaiian varieties. Reportedly KO is aphrodisiacal.

MOLASSES: source of food, animal feed, silage ingredient, brewer's- & baker's-yeast, alcohol, & fertilizer.

MULCH: bagasse, leaves, & tops.

SCREEN: good candidate. WAX: extracted from stalks.

WINDBREAK: tall, thick plants can act as a wind-buffer for ʻUALA {SWEET POTATO} & KALO fields or LO‘, etc.

WOOD: particle-board, plastic, or wall-board from bagasse: “Canec,” "Celotex."

🌿 DESCRIPTION: KO is a tail, perennial, jointed GRASS. Many varieties were introduced by the ancient Polynesians; most are now Extinct. Can grow 20! {6m} or taller. Monocot. Rhizomatic clumper. Typically has an upright habit, though some varieties & older stems tend to lean. Heavy, segmented, v unbranched stalks vary in color from green, yellow-green, yellow, red, purple,. to almost black, or variegated & are 3/4th" to 2 1/2" {2-6cm} thick, depending on variety. Long GRASS-like leaves, with most varieties having sharp, saw- - / toothed edges. Plume-like inflorescence {"arrow"} consists of thousands of tiny flowers. Typically blossoms in November or December. Flowering in mature KO is stimulated by short days. Tendency to flower differs markedly with cultivar. Flowering can be retarded by withholding water & providing a nitrogen fertilizer. Seeds can be produced, depending on cultivar & conditions. Although slow-growing in youth, towards maturity, as well as in adverse conditions, KO is fast-growing during its "boom" stage. Growth-rate is also related to hours of sun, temperature, amount of nutrients, moisture, weed competition, strength of winds, & inherent nature of cultivar. Rhizomatic roots form fibrous adventitious roots, which are mainly active in the upper 1' {30cm} of soil. Ratoon crops form their own shallower roots. Cane bases form supporting buttress-roots.

LIFE-SPAN: indefinite, but > productive life typically does not exceed 6 years.

ORIGIN: Probably New Guinea.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Hot Tropical conditions. Thrives with long, warm, moist, sunny weather. Ideally ripens during a cooler, drier, but aiso sunny season. Requires @ least 60" {1500mm} annual rain. Hybrids & varieties exist which tolerate dry conditions or higher elevations. Species S. spontaneum, S. sinense, barberi can accept colder climates. KO tolerates very heavy rainfall, as well as some drought & some frost. Intolerant of hurricanes & freezing conditions.

HAWAIILOCATION: Best adapted to moist lowlands, but will grow well as high as 2800' {840m} elevation on leeward slopes 1800' {540m} on the windward side. Varieties exist which can tolerate the highlands. KO was important to the ancient Hawaiian people, with many varieties & numerous applications. Later it became a major agri-business in Hawaiʻi, with vigorous & resistant imported varieties being planted. Although KO has currently declined m commercial importance, it is well adapted to small-scale, organic poly-cultures.

CULTURE: KO is a heavy feeder & needs ample room. Prefers deep, moist, fertile, dense well-drained, soil, somewhat acid pH, full sun. Needs to be kept weeded & mulched. As the plant grows, it benefits from soil being mounded up around its est to assist in the accumulation of juice in 42 gs, seas raised beds, banks, or drains can roots. ORGANIC GROWING: Healthy, fentle, well-prepared soil & careful culture sneer nen, greater Tesistance: Select disease: & ealthy, ferule, well-prepar soi carer culture enco ea! 1 pest-free “setts" from varieties suitable to your locale. Cutting knifes should be ect cleat Weeds controlled with mule, "Tilapia," a herbivorous fish from Africa, can control water weeds in ditches & canals.

WEEDY: Persistent, but apparently not naturalized. Underground stems can be invasive. A solid 2' {60cm} deep barrier may contain KO roots, but the plant can still expand by leaning & rooting.

DISADVANTAGES: The world history of large-scale, commercial SUGARCANE production has been inseparably linked with Slavery, indentured labor, & environmental degradation.

REMARKS: Heavy machinery, common on commercial fields has created serious hardpan & irreparable soil-structure damage. Hardpan can be loosened by knifing, chiseling, disking &/or crop rotation with appropriate species. SEX: Hermaphroditic flowers.

POLLINATION: Wind.

SEED-SAVING: SUGARCANE is typically only grown from seed for breeding purposes. Seed life-span is short, but can be lengthened by storing in a deep-freeze or desiccated. Sown on top of sterilized compost {needs light to germinate}, & kept very humid. Germination: 2 to 5 days. Transplantable @ 1 1/2 months.

PROPAGATION: Grown by stem-pieces, called "setts:” 1' {30cm} long pieces from top 1/3rd of stalk, each having at least 2 to 3 budded nodes. Cut from fresh, healthy, 6-month to one-year-old canes. To direct energy to buds, canes can be topped several days before cutting. "Setts” are buried either horizontally, or at a45 degree angle, in moist trenches 6” to 1 1/2" {15- 45cm} deep. Covered with 1" to 2" {2.5-5cm} of soil {or more in dry conditions}, mulched, & watered. As sprouts grow, the trenches are gradually filled in, until the "sett" is eventually buried 1' to 1 1/2' {30-45cm} deep. Shallow trenches are better in heavy soil or cooler areas, deep trenches in lighter, drier soil. Sprouting: usually occurs in 7 to 12 days. Ideal temperature is between 90F - 100F {32-38C,} Growth slows or stops @ 70F {21C} or under. "Setts" are sown anytime warmth & moisture will be available for a long duration. CoastalLowMid/High{occasionally}, WetMiesic

NOTABLE CULTIVARS: SOME The innumerable commercial varieties are complex hybrids of Saccharum officinarum & WILD SUGARCANES, S. spontaneum, S. robustum, & others. Elaborate crossing & back-crossing has occurred in a sustained effort to increase yields & keep ahead of the proliferation of pests & diseases inherent in mono-cropping. S$. spontaneum has provided most of the disease-resistant genes.

LANDSCAPING: large attractive specimen, shade tree, or in groves.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: leaves & bark.

REFORESTATION: good choice if correct locale variety is selected for locale.

SACRED: protected by KUPULUPULU, god of the KOA forests. HULA altar offering.

SHADE TREE: provides light cover, but often suckers.

TANNING: bark.

WEED SUPPRESSION: reportedly KOA can shade out & suppress GORSE. KOA is possibly allelopathic & thus retardant to some plants, though not to GRASSES & many other aggressive aliens species.

WOOD: old trees provide an attractive, long-lasting, red-brown hardwood, which is moderately coarse, medium in density, variable in figure, easily worked, stable, with a low shrinking-rate, taking a high polish. Susceptible to termites. Utilized for canoes & paddies, house timbers, interior work, furniture, cabinet-making, turnery, calabashes, tools, bearing poles, surfboards, spears & other weapons, musical instruments, ceremonial images, carving, etc. This species typically only forms tall, straight, clear trunks if grown in dense, highland KOA forests. Wood from slow growing KOA in drier regions tends to be more beautiful.

⚠️ CAUTION: food stored in KOA containers takes on a disagreeable taste & can cause an allergic reaction.

XERISCAPING: some local varieties.

— scan page 36 · book page 43 —

🌳 DESCRIPTION: KOA is an handsome, Endemic, evergreen, nitrogen-fixing tree. Can grow 30' to over 100' {9-30m} tall. The largest Hawaiian tree. A pioneer species passing as a climax tree. Trunk diameter 10' {3m} or thicker. Wide-crown. Unarmed. Produces two types of foliage; leaves of seedlings, juvenile branches & root-sprouts are pinnately compound, composed of many small leaflets, whereas the leathery "leaves" of mature trees are modified, flattened, crescent-shaped petioles called phyllodes. Springtime clusters of compact, spherical, light lemon-yellow flowers mature into flattened pods containing 5 - 8 or more seeds.

GROWTH-SPEED: fast-growing in youth. Deep roots, as well as wide spread, shallow roots. Can sucker tenaciously. Possibly allelopathic due to substances in leaves.

LIFE-SPAN: very long-lived.

ORIGIN: Endemic to Hawaiʻi. KOA ancestors evolved in arid Australia. Related species also found in the S Pacific & SE Asia.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: found in wet, mesic, dry or humid highland forests. a aay, j dei) Tolerates heavy rain, vog & some wind, but susceptible to salt bum. a a ae

HAWATLI LOCATION: KOA is adapted to most Hawaiian environments; can grow from low to very high elevations, but thrives in cool, moist, windward highlands. Second only to the ʻŌHIʻA tree, in numbers.

CULTURE: prefers deep, rich, moist, well-drained soil, somewhat acid pH, & full sun. Responds to regular feeding. Easy.

TOLERATES: acid soil & fields.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding, water-logging, salt, & shade.

PRUNING: Although KOA resents being coppiced or pruned, the trees benefit from dead, diseased, or pest-ridden wood being removed. Pruning wounds treated with ALOE gel. Infected wood should be bummed.

ASSOCIATES: ʻĀKIA, ʻAMAʻU, ĀULU, HALA, HĀPUʻU, HAU, KAMANT, KŌLEA, KUKUI, MAMANI, NAIO, NELEAU, NIU {COCONUT}, ʻŌHIʻA, ʻŌLAPA, etc. KOA hosts epiphytic HAWAIIAN FERNS, LOBELIA Clermontia & ʻŌLAPA, etc.

ADVERSARIES: Widely destroyed by ranching, logging, weedy alien plants, feral pigs, & grazers including cattle, goats & sheep. "Cattle are the great enemy of the Koa." J. Rock, 1913. Even fully mature trees cannot handle root-trampling. Forests of KOA can be revitalized by removing livestock. KOA are also attacked by COFFEE twig-borer, black twig-borer, & seed-pests. Rust attacks misplaced varieties & can spread to healthy KOA & other species. Highland trees tend to have fewer adversaries. Trunk is sensitive to fire & although KOA can regrow from root-suckers & seedlings after a burn, tenacious weeds such as CLIDEMIA & alien GRASSES often take over instead.

ORGANIC GROWING: Excellent candidate, with suitable variety & location.

REMARKS: "

E OLE KOA live with "the health, wealth, & well-being of a koa tree!" KOA is synonymous with boldness & courage.

PLANTATION GROWING: A plantation of KOA can never replace the nourishing, protective irreplaceable guild created by the birds, insects, soil organisms, & other species typically found in a natural KOA forest.

DISADVANTAGES: Rampant root-suckers difficult to contain & rob nutrients from a wide area. Leaves may be allelopathic. SEX: Monoecious, with hermaphroditic flowers.

POLLINATION: Insects.

SEED-SAVING: Dried seeds keep well in reasonably cool, dry conditions.

PROPAGATION: Seeds. Scarified by nicking or soaking in hot-water. Planted in deep, narrow containers. Germination: 2-3 weeks @ 70F-80F {21-27C}. Seedlings need to be planted out before pot-binding occurs.

INOCULATION: beneficial.

NOTABLE VARIETIES: Many locally adapted varieties exist, differing in size & shape of phyllodes, & placement of flowers, & especially in climatic adaptatio”” CoastalLowMidHigh& VeryHigh {thrives in highlands}, WetMesicDry

🌳 DESCRIPTION: KUKUI is an attractive, mid to large evergreen tree. Most likely an early Polynesian introduction, though possibly Indigenous. Can grow 90' {27m}, or taller in ideal conditions, but usually seen under 1/2 that. Trunk diameter can reach 3' {9m}. Upright, dense, wide- to narrow crown. Large, pale, gray-green leaves vary in shape, but are typically palmately lobed. Large, whitish, terminal flower panicles mature into green, indehiscent fruits nearly 2" {5cm} wide, containing 1 or 2 oily seeds ~1" {2.5em} wide. Fairly rapid-growing. Deep tap-root & large lateral-roots; non-aggressive, does not sucker.

LIFE-SPAN: moderately long lived.

ORIGIN: Probably Malaysia.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics. Often found in lowland gulches & slopes on all larger Hawaiian islands, with except perhaps Kaho olawe, to date. From coastal forests to ~2200' {660m} in wet or moist areas, or drier climates where ground-moisture is available. Tolerates coastal conditions, some wind & some salt. Intolerant of dry, windy conditions.

HAWATFI LOCATION: Often grown here & widely seen, especially along windward gulches.

CULTURE: Easy. Prefers moist, fertile, well-drained soil, somewhat acid pH & full- or part-shade or full sun.

TOLERATES: varied conditions, including poor soils & some drought.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Accepts pruning well.

ASSOCIATES: MAILE, PALAPALAI. Few plants can grow under the dense, damp shade of KUKUI, though early Hawaiian people grew KALO in its clearings, planted in heaped piles of KUKUI-leaf compost. KUKUI can be intercropped with PAPAYA, the KUKUI closing in & coming into bearing as the PAPAYA ends its productive life.

ADVERSARIES: Very few in Hawaiʻi. Wood is often invaded by boring insects.

ORGANIC GROWING: Excellent candidate. WEEDY?: Thoroughly naturalized, but not considered a weed. Spread by fallen & feral pig-borne seeds.

DISADVANTAGES: Fallen nuts & leaves can be messy. {

SEE ALSO: TOXICITIES, above.}

ATA / BANANA & PLANTAIN ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAME: M usa species. Several Species, subspecies & hybrids exist, incld. numerous varieties, cultivars, & omamentals.

FAMELY: Musaceae {BANANA}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: Fruit of Paradise, Fruit of Knowledge, Adam's Fig.

PARTIAL LISTING: wo COMMON BANANA, Plantain: Musa x paradisiaca, syn. M. acuminata x M. balbisiana, syn. xq. wg sapientum, syn. M. rubra. ee CHINESE BANANA, Dwarf Banana: Musa x nana, syn. M. acuminata, syn. M. cavendish. gy 8 7 FE'I, Fehi: Musa troglodytarum. From Polynesia. Starchy, thin skinned fruit are sometimes seeded, but --; tasty cooked. Upright bunches. Wide-leaved ornamental. Can grow 36' {11m} tall. Often planted here. ¥

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed ancient fruit. Staple food for many cultures, especially the cooking

BANANAS {PLANTAIN}. Size, shape, quantity, color, edibility, texture & flavor differ with species, cultivar, & environment. Varies from sweet & fragrant to somewhat tart. Ripe fruit are eaten fresh raw, cooked, roasted, fried, jams, mashed for bakery goods, dried, or pureed & dried to grind as a flour or powder {often made into infant or invalid food}, BANANA-butter, extracted for starch, or fermented to vinegar, wine, beer, or alcohol. High in carbohydrates, iron, with a fair amount of vitamins A, B,C, & G, protein, & a few major minerals such as potassium. In some BANANA Varieties, parts of the trunk, leave buds {heart}, inflorescence, & even rhizomes are prepared as food. To eat the flower-bud, the tough outer bracts are removed, saving the smaller inner flower; this tender bud is sliced thinly & soaked in salted water up to an hour; squeezed repeatedly to remove the bitter sap & rinsed, then boiled or sautéed with fish or shrimp. There is also a form of BANANA with carbohydrate rich subterranean stems.

PLANTAINS: "cooking BANANAS" or unripe BANANAS, are eaten fried, boiled, baked, broiled, roasted, IMU baked, diced for stews or omelettes, mashed for POI, or dried & ground into flour. PLANTAINS are richer in starch, potassium & vitamin A, with less sugar. Most of the original Hawaiian varieties are more palatable when cooked.

BEARING: In ideal conditions MAT A may bear in 9, or as long as 18 months, otherwise. Clump may bear 5-20 years.

MATURITY: For highest quality, fruit are harvested when fully mature, but not yet npe; maturity is noted when fruit turn light green & their angular edges have rounded. To delay ripening, the hands can be cut off from the top progressively. If clump is left on tree, fruit can begin to crack open & are more likely to be attacked by fruit-flies, rats, birds, etc.

HARVESTING: The entire stalk can be harvested. Since fruiting occurs but once per trunk, the entire trunk is cut to the ground after harvesting. With tall cultivars, the trunk can be carefully nicked with a cutting tool on a long handle until the bunch slowly lowers enough to catch & cut. An assistant may be needed. Bunches need careful handling to avoid bruising or rubbing fruit. Bunches can be cushioned with BANANA leaves, etc. Kept in the shade in a cool, airy spot. Individual hands can be cut from stalk with a thin-bladed knife.

RIPENING: Unlike most fruit, BANANAS have the ability to ripen after harvest at various stages, even when only a few inches long. Most varieties turn from green to yellow, then to a rich golden color. Fruit develop flavor & nutrients well @ 59F to 68F {15-20C}. Excess heat, 72F {22C} & over, causes mushy flesh even though skin can remain green.

STORING: Fruit store well when cut green if they are fully developed. Entire bunches are best stored for home consumption by hanging in a cool, shaded spot. Refrigeration can hold ripe fruit over, but cold darkens the skin. Discoloration may be prevented by wrapping fruit gently in newspaper & placing them in warmest part of refrigerator, with 61F {16C} being ideal. Refrigerated green fruit won't ripen later. Fruit keeps well dried as chips, slices or whole fruit. Fruit pulp can be frozen or made into BANANA-bread. Frozen fruit darken & turn mushy at thawing {LEMON juice reduces discoloration.} Frozen fruit in ice-cream, milk shakes, smoothies, cakes, etc. BANANA-bread freezes well. Also canned, or processed as BANANA-butter.

SHIPPING: To prolong the green stage for lengthy transport, bunches can be harvested before fruit become fully expanded. Storage @ 53F to 58F {depending on cultivar} delays ripening & permits longer travel. Lower temperatures will damage fruit. 85% humidity reduces water loss.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: occasionally grown for this purpose.

ANIMAL FEED: leaves, green- or ripe fruits, as well as chopped trunks, flower stalks, & peels as animal fodder.

BANANA CIRCLES: planted in an arc around a pit for an outdoor shower enclosure, compost heap, family tua, etc, BANANAS thrive on the extra water & nutrients.

BEE FORAGE: if bell is left on.

CEREMONY: many ritual applications for leaf & stem.

COMPOST MATERIAL: trunks & peels are rich in potash, phosphorus, nitrogen, & compost-activating bacteria.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Dwarfs & miniatures for greenhouses, atriums, lanai, etc. DYE: sap stains a lasting brown.

EROSION CONTROL: good, fast growing plant to bind bare, burned, or eroded earth.

FIBER: leaves are valued for house-roofing, wrapping, umbrellas, cigarette papers, plates, & as sources of fiber for thatching, packing, etc. Trunk: source of paper-making pulp, etc. Leaf-sheath: plaited fabric, thatching, screens, cordage. Petiole fiber: cloth & cordage. IMU: trunk can be mashed & placed in an IMU to create steam. Layers of MAI A leaves protect food.

LANDSCAPING: dramatic foliage as hedges, barriers, groupings, privacy screens, & by pools or ponds. Ornamental & flowering species & varieties exist, including SUMATRAN, PINK-FRUITED, RED-FLOWERING BANANA, & the variegated cultivar ʻAE ʻAE LEL leaf.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: roots, fruit, stem, sap,& flowers are all valued.

MULCH: trunk {split or cut into chunks} & leaves as biomass or mulch.

NURSE-CROP: for COFFEE, CACAO, NUTMEG, etc.

TERRACING: trunks can be lain on contours, though they disintegrate quickly. 23.

— scan page 45 · book page 54 —

DESCRIPTION: MAT A is an attractive, herbaceous evergreen perennial. Height can range from to 40' {.6-12m} tall {depending on species & variety.} Monocot. Several stems arise to form a es L clump. Succulent trunk is made up of closely packed leaf-bases. Huge leaves. Each trunk my f bears a large inflorescence followed by finger-like fruits. Not day-length sensitive. Fast- y* EP? growing. Tends to be surface rooted, with an immense underground corm. An ancient plant, MATA was introduced to Hawaiʻi by the early Polynesians. Unfortunately, these early varieties have proven susceptible to subsequently introduced diseases. Many of the original 50 to 70 Polynesian varieties are now Extinct.

ORIGINS: Most from Tropical SE Asia. Others: India, Africa, Australia, China, Java, Mexico, New Guinea, Malaysia, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Viet Nam, E & W Indies, & elsewhere.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics. BANANAS are best adapted to the hot, humid, low- to mid-elevations in Hawaiʻi. Temperature range of 70F to 85F {21-29c}. When temperatures rise reach too far into the 80’sF {27+ C}, proper coloring is impeded. Most prefer yearly rainfall of 80" to 100" {2.4-3m}, evenly distributed. BANANAS tolerate a variety of conditions, including periodic flooding. Although temperatures below 50F {10C} slow growth, a few varieties can tolerate the highlands. Intolerant of frost, drought, & strong winds. Even though there are cultivars that resist drought, this is not the norm. As much as light wind-tearing of leaves does not seriously hurt the plant, excessive tearing reduces production & trunks readily blow over in severe winds; strong wind is said to be especially detrimental to Hawaiian varieties.

CULTURE: BANANA need ample space & consistent feeding. They prefer rich, constantly moist, well-drained, heavy, clay-loam with ample humus, pH 5.0-7.0, & full sun. A few varieties favor partial shade. Although sheltered sites or gulches can offer wind protection, good air-circulation is also important. Very heavy feeder, BANANAS respond well to heavy fertilization, mulch, & ample water. For good fruiting, BANANAS need abundant potassium {K}, minerals, some nitrogen {N}, but only little phosphorus {P}. {NPK: 10-5-40} Minor elements such as calcium, magnesium, zinc, & copper may also be needed. Fertilized several times a year, with many lighter applications being more beneficial than a few heavy ones. A thick mulch retards weeds, provides nutrients, & preserves moisture. Cultivation should be avoided, as it disturbs the plant's shallow roots.

TOLERATES: a variety of soils, from clay to rocky. Some varieties tolerate temporary flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: salt spray, & sandy, alkaline or saline soil, poor drainage, & root competition, especially from GRASSES.

PRUNING: BANANAS sucker plentifully & benefit from pruning {depending on conditions & cultivar.} During the first year, all but to suckers {preferably on opposite sides of the mother plant} are cut off. The following years, 3 to 5 suckers may be allowed to grow each year. Some diseases can be prevented by removing the small, brown, dried flowers on tips of the maturing fruit. After the last sizable hand of fruit has set, the flower-bud {the "bell"} can be cut off. {Although this practice reportedly increases ultimate weight of the bunch, & can decrease damage by birds, there may be reason to leave it on due to its beneficial hormones & as bee nectar source.} Support is usually provided to prop up the heavy fruit stalk.

ASSOCIATES: AVOCADO, NIU, PAPAYA, PALMS, other fruit trees, & some nitrogen-fixing ground-covers. MATA can be planted on KALO LO’! banks.

ADVERSARIES: BANANA have specific problems that are often important locally. Pests include Oriental fruit-fly, various nematodes, red-banded thrip, & BANANA-skipper. Diseases include Panama wilt, Bunchy Top, Black Leaf Streak {a.k.a. Black Sigatoka}, Cigar-tip rot {a-k.a. Cigar-end disease, or Blossom rot}, & Freckle. Many problems are brought in with infected planting- materials, -soil, -tools, -equipment, or in contaminated irrigation water. Black Leaf Streak is carried largely by wind. BANANA plants are very vulnerable to hormonal herbicides. Banchy Top Virus, spread by the BANANA-aphid, is a very serious problem. Symptoms include: dark green, broken streaks on undersides of mid-rib, shorter, narrowed leaves, & leaves that grow erect rather than spreading, progressing on to stunted, brittle leaves & suckers with wavy edges & a bunchy top appearance. Later the bunches becomes choked or twisted. If you see BANANAS with this problem, contact an University Extension agent for advice on destroying the plant. Resistant varieties include: ‘Dwarf Brazilian’ & perhaps Red.' Susceptible varieties include: ‘Cavandish' & 'Chinese.' Panama Wilt is a fungus, AKA: Panama Disease or Banana Wilt, Panama Wilt disease spreads more readily in very acid soils & is transported on equipment, wind, & water. A cover-crop or 6 months of flooding has helped. Resistant varieties include: 'Brazilian,’ ‘Chinese’ {‘Cavendish‘ cultivars}, ‘Lactan,' Williams’ & perhaps ‘Red.’ Susceptible varieties include: 'Bluefield’ & 'Silk.'

ORGANIC GROWING: Excellent candidates for organic culture, especially in polycultures. Problems can be reduced with resistant cultivars, clean propagation material, clean culture, crop-rotation, good nutrition, ample water, bagging fruit, & clean field hygiene. Some disease can be prevented by cleaning the fruit-clump of bracts & flower residues, cutting dead leaves off the trunk & keeping the ground weed-free with mulch. Rhizomes can be cleansed by thorough trimming & soaking for 10 to 20 minutes in 122F to 131F {50-55C} water, or a 1:5 solution of chlorine bleach & water.

WEEDY: Persistent & sparsely naturalized. BANANAS are often seen wild in gulches, on forest edges, & elsewhere.

CAUTION: an established clump of BANANAS is not easy to eliminate.

DISADVANTAGES: BANANA can harbor rats & the water in petiole bases can host mosquitoes.

REMARKS: Originally "PLANTAIN" was the term for certain relatives of BANANAS which are starchy & usually require cooking. PLANTAINS are a staple for many peoples & are hardier than true BANANAS. Now, PLANTAINS are often lumped under the term BANANA. SEX: Inflorescences bear female, male, & sometimes hermaphroditic flowers, though most edible BANANA are female sterile, producing seedless, edible fruit without needing pollination through parthenogenesis.

POLLINATION: Bats, large insects including bees & wasps, ants, & birds are possible pollinators for wild BANANA.

PROPAGATION: Because few edible BANANA have viable seeds, they are usually propagated from suckers {side-shoots/ KEIKI}, from pieces of rhizome {"bits"}, or by tissue culture. The best KEIKI are the taller, vigorous shoots, 2 to 8 months old, 1' to {30-90cm} tall, preferably with thick conical trunks & narrow leaves. Removed from mother plant with a machete or mattock, suckers should be exposed to the air for a day before planting. Most MAMA varieties can retain their leaves. Planted in a deep, narrow hole, placing corm deeply, with sucker at original soil level. Back-filled with a mix of compost or aged-manure & soil. Planting the corms deeply helps prevent suckers from rising too quickly & provides better plant anchorage. "Bits" with two or more buds, can also be removed & replanted immediately, with no drying period. Propagated year-round, but winter or early spring is often best, depending on locale. LowMi ly }High

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree, or tree-like shrub. Possibly Indigenous, but probably an early Polynesian import. Can grow 40' {12m} or occasionally taller, but more often seen 1/2 that. Quite similar to HAU, but does not form tangled thickets. Trunk can grow 2' {60cm} wide. Thick bark corrugated. Heart-shaped, POPLAR-like leaves. Large, showy, light yellow flowers with purple hearts, which change to purple-pink, & twist closed as the day passes. Blossoms nearly yearround. Flowers mature into thick, woody, green, disk-shaped fruit-capsules over 1" {2.5cm} wide containing several woolly seeds. Widespread roots. Mid- to fast growing.

ORIGIN: Africa to high Islands of the Pacific.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Tropics & Subtropics.

HAWAIʻI LOCATION: was once very common, but has been often destroyed for its various applications. Found on coastal wetlands, strands, beaches, old house-sites, MANGROVE swamps, estuary edges, & other protected sea-side sites, sometimes inland as well. Typically not a forest tree.

CULTURE: prefers light, sandy, well-drained, loose soil or sand, & full sun or light shade.

TOLERATES: hot coastal conditions, including salt, wind, some drought, as well as heavy rain.

INTOLERANT OF: prolonged drought.

ASSOCIATES: various Hawaiian beach-side GRASSES, many herbaceous Hawaiian plant & trees, including WILIWILI.

ADVERSARIES: practically none, except for humans.

WEEDY: naturalized & occasionally found wild by the sea, but not a nuisance & not considered a weed. SEX: hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: self-pollinated or crossed by insects.

PROPAGATION: seeds & cuttings. Cuttings: root slowly. Seeds: store well & tolerate prolonged ocean travel. Seeds can be sown any time of the year. Able to sprout even in baking sand.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow, WetMesic

Flowers: can be cooked as a vegetable. pytised spathe of undertree-tip is eaten raw as “Millionaires' salad" or PALM-cabbage, but this destroys the tree. Sap: developed flower is tapped for a fresh beverage, boiled to sugar, or fermented as a toddy, beer, wine, liquor, or vinegar + though this process destroys the crop of nuts that would have developed. Sap can also be obtained by tapping the trunk, but this can introduce disease into the tree & is an emergency practice only. BEARING: A healthy ‘Jamaican Tall' can begin to fruit in 5 to 8 years & then bear to ~70 years of age, though the tree can live longer. ‘Malayan Dwarf" generally bear in 3 to 4 years, & produce ~30. wWater” stage at 6 to

MATURITY: “Spoon meat" stage depends on variety, but generally starts to form at 4 to 6 monthsmonths, Nut ripens fully in 9 to 12 months. Year-round harvest. b

HARVESTING: Fallen nuts can be gathered. Experienced climbers can harvest less mature nuts. Of they can be cut down with a pole-knife. Flavor is improved by heaping young green nuts in a pile & allowing them to age a month.

APPLICATIONS: {A plant with a thousand or more utilizations.}

ALLEY-CROPPING: and on berms....

ANIMAL FEED: fresh nut-meat is eaten by many animals, including poultry & pigs. Oil-cake residue, after pressing as livestock feed, including cattle & poultry...:

ANIMAL SHELTER: trunks or leaf-stalks can be made into shelters for various animals.

AVENUE & PARK TREE: but dangerous unless heavy nuts & leaf-stalks are removed.

BARRIER: a neglected PALM jungle is a formidable barrier. Seedlings & young trees make passage difficult.

BEE PLANT: a major source of nectar & pollen.

CEREMONY: many ceremonial applications. NIU was originally the designated "tree of the territory” of Hawaiʻi.

CHARCOAL: an important source of charcoal from nut hulls & husks.

FIBER: fronds can be woven or plaited into mats for floors, walls, house thatching {temporary}, baskets, shade-screens, hats, bags, etc. "Coir" is the husk, which is retted, washed, separated, beaten, & made into a coarse yarn for weaving mats, rough cloth, sennit, sacks, rugs, twine, cordage, rope, fill, furniture stuffing, etc. The stiffer fibers can be made into brooms, brushes, in ORCHID cultivation, or for kindling. Nutshells: household items, including cups, ladles, bowls & other vessels, tools, carving, rattles, buttons, gas-mask charcoal, & automobile fuel. Cloth-like fiber at leaf bases as strainers, sandals, shoe fabric, etc. Leaf-stalk {petiole} for construction of crude fences, walls, cages, including fish-cages, etc. Mid-rib of leaves for flower-arranging, LEI stringers, or for KUKUI nut lamps.

FUEL: old leaves are readily available. Can be cut to manageable lengths & dried. Other parts for tinder.

LANDSCAPING: sea-sides, boundaries, courtyards, etc. Omamental varieties exist.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: many applications. OIL: cosmetics, body- & hair- oil, soap-making, illumination & candles, lubrication, & industrial applications.

SHADE TREE: light shade for people, animals, & various crops grown below.

WINDBREAK: can be planted to buffer harsh winds.

WOOD: "Porcupine wood" from the trunks' outer layer is hard & resistant to moisture decay; an inferior, but appreciated lumber source for construction, furniture, cabinet-making, posts, pilings, fish-spears, carvings, drums, planks, etc. In construction, trunks are strongest whole.

XERISCAPING: excellent candidate if ground-water is available.

DESCRIPTION: Graceful evergreen tree. Most varieties of the "tall" COCONUTS can grow 100' {30m}. “Dwarfs” grow 30' {9m} tall. Original strains were brought by ancient Polynesians, but most varieties are of more recent introduction. Single trunk. Usually leans with age. Unarmed. Pinnately feathered spreading fronds to 20' {6m} or longer. Large cluster of small yellow to whitish flowers mature into the large, tough, thick-husked fruits. Fast-growing in youth. Strong shallow roots can be extensive if soil conditions permit, but typically growing only 5' {1.5m} deep & ~20' {6m} long. Roots have no hairs. In a hurricane trunk may break or entire tree & root mass can blow over. 'Talls' can live 70 to 100 years.

ORIGIN: Not known with certainty, but probably from Malaysia, then taken to the Islands of the Pacific, Melanesia, & into the Indian Ocean. Widely distributed in the world Tropics since ancient times.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: COCONUT are suited to hot, humid, or sub-humid Tropics & especially to coastal strand conditions. Tolerates many conditions, including light frost, some drought, & salt spray. Intolerant of strong winds, until well established, & prolonged drought, unless ground-water is reachable by roots.

HAWATILOCATION: Widely grown here. Often seen by the sea & inland, though generally no higher than ~2000' {600m}.

CULTURE: NIU prefer deep, well-drained, well-aerated, light or sandy soil, pH 5.0 - 8.0, & full sun. The trees thrive with constant fresh ground-water. Heavy feeders, especially after maturity. Growing trees need regular weeding or mulching & yearly application of fertilizer. Supplied with organic fertilizer, aged-manure, or compost. Analysis of soil, leaf, or COCONUT-milk can determine if potassium or other elemental nutrients are needed. Additions of lime to strongly acid soils may help lower level of toxic soil alumium.

TOLERATES: many soils, including volcanic, clay, peat, sand, limey or saline soil, salt water, & temporary flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: poorly-drained or poor-aerated soil. 'Malayan Dwarfs’ are more Sensitive to stressful conditions. Deep cultivation is “enritaee cn a re avoided, as it is damaging to roots. “f ne pRUNING: Self-pruning. Dead leaves are often left beneath the - nr re tree as mulch. 7 ‘3 bY fe ait

ASSOCIATES: NIU is often grown with BANANA on the bunds of re sae brat KALO LO’I or RICE paddies. Polycultured with BREADFRUIT, { a BE tet be CACAO, CASHEW, CITRUS, MANGO, PINEAPPLE &/or A G a pasture GRASSES, leguminous green-manures or cover-crops, ' etc. Ground-covers can be slashed, grazed, or turned-in oe ny de es Boge shallowly to keep reduce competition to the tree. Young trees “4 = Pd i oo need to be protected from grazers. {

NOTE: pasturing animals 4 among NIU can impede roots due to soil compaction.} Until trees begin to bear, catch-crops can be planted such as BANANA, SWEET POTATO, CASSAVA, RICE, MILLET, CORN, TOMATOES, etc. These should be at least 3' {.9m} away from young trees. When nut-harvest is the principle goal, green-manure is preferred.

ADVERSARIES: COCONUTS have a few specific pests & diseases, the control of which is important. Lightening can kill several trees at once. Susceptible to hurricane damage. Rat infestation can be prevented with metal trunk-guards. Lethal yellowing disease {LY}: can become epidemic. LY is transmitted by insects as wel! as contaminated tools during trimming. Symptoms of LY: 1. nuts falling prematurely. 2. death of flowers. 3. “flag-leaf." 4. yellowing of leaves from lowest upward. 5. "spear-leaf" turns yellow & rots. 6. tree death in 3 to 6 months from 1st symptom. ‘Jamaican Tall’ are highly susceptible to LY, as is 'King.' Resistant varieties include the especially healthy 'Malayan Dwarf & a cross of ‘Malayan Dwarf / ‘Panama Tall.'

ORGANIC GROWING: Problems are prevented with clean-culture & tools, careful management & quick treatment of wounds.

⚠️ CAUTION / DISADVANTAGES: Location should be planned carefully to avoid the very real danger of falling nuts.

REMARKS: One of the world's most important plants. In some countries, the COCONUT PALM is so valued that cutting one down is a serious crime. Most cultures fee] that even trimming the fronds is a sacrilege. SEX: Each panicle has female & male flowers. 'Talls' usually cross with a neighbor, while ‘Malayan Dwarfs' self-pollinate.

POLLINATION: Insects, including bees, ants, flies, & possibly by wind.

SEED-SAVING: The light, waterproof, buoyant husks can keep a nut alive almost 4 months at sea. For propagation, undamaged fruit are selected from a high quality, prolific tree, preferably with a dry husk, containing adequate "water." Stored in a cool airy spot until planting.

PROPAGATION: Nuts are sown in moist, well-drained, humusy soil, in part shade. The whole ripe nuts can be placed horizontally with 1/2 to 3/4ths of their husk buried, longest side on top & eyes tumed slightly up. Sprout usually comes out of the eye on this longest side of the husk or from the biggest, softest eye. Germination: 2 to 7 months in ‘talls' & 1 to 5 months in 'dwarfs.' The most vigorous seedlings are chosen. Transplanted when fully sprouted, or when there are 3 to 4 leaves, preferably before plant reaches ~18" {45cm} tall {~6 - 9 months}. At this point, husk is covered completely, with center bud remaining above soil-line. Seedlings need protection from animals & weed competition. Propagation can occur year-round, or at start of a wet season in areas where water may be scarce. COCONUT trees transplant well, even when quite mature. Older, productive trees can be rejuvenated by air-layering, but this is an awkward, expensive practice & done only to preserve exceptional trees.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic & Dry {only if ground water is available}

SEE ALSO: PALMS; DOUBLE COCONUT, Coco-de-mer. Lodoicea maldivica. In Encyclopedia.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, Endemic, evergreen shrub or tree. Attributes vary richly. Presumed to be Nitrogen-fixing. Varieties can grow from several inches to 100' {30m} tall, in ideal conditions. Rough, greyish bark. Largest recorded trun, diameter ~18' {5.4m}. Important successional pioneer, as well as a dominant forest species. Can begin life as an epiphyte especially on HĀPUʻU. Flowers are typically red, but varieties can be golden-yellow, orange, red-orange or very pale yellow.

GROWTH-SPEED: moderately fast-growing.

LIFE-SPAN: very long lived. Appears to go through a natural cycle of die-off & regeneration.

ORIGIN: Hawaiʻi. Common & found in rain-forests, bogs, on lava flows, windy cliffs, & dry sea-side slopes on all of the larger Hawaiian islands, excluding perhaps Kaho olawe & Nr ihau.

CULTURE: prefers deep, moist, fertile, well-drained soil, pH tolerant, & full sun. Easy to grow. Smooth-leaved forms grow better with some shade. Fuzzy-leaved forms can handle drier, sunnier conditions. Responds to light fertilization.

TOLERATES: extremes; scant or acid soil, bogs, wet feet, drought, wind, & salt-mist {depending on variety.} Fire-resistant; susceptibility depends on fire intensity. Often resprouts from root-crown, but only rarely recovers by seeds, if fire was not too hot.

INTOLERANT OF: severe drought & severe wind.

ASSOCIATES: HĀPUʻU, KOA, LAMA, ʻŌHELO, UKI, etc. Branches host a variety of species including FERNS, MOSSES, LICHENS, LIVERWORTS & some herbaceous plants. Flower nectar feeds bees, various butterflies, -APAPANE, etc.

ADVERSARIES: Chinese Rose-beetles sometimes chew tender new growth, ants can carry in aphids & scales, etc., thrips, & over-zealous LEI-pickers have been stripping some trees.

SEED-SAVING: seed-capsules can be gathered before they have opened, placed in a paper bag & kept in a dry spot. Seeds are so small they took like sawdust. Wind-dispersed.

PROPAGATION: usually by seeds. Air-layering & cuttings have also been successful, but requires great skill. Seeds: fresh seeds readily sprout, sown on surface of sterile, moist, well-drained medium. Light is required for germination. Placed in a shaded spot & watered gently every day. Germination: 1-3 months. Transplanted into containers of rich, humusy soil when seedlings have grown at least 4-6 pairs of true leaves. Watered every day. Fed monthly with a dilute foliar spray. Potbinding severely retards growth. Plants should be transplanted into the next sized container, or in final location, as soon as strong enough & at least 6" {15cm} tall. Young plants are kept moist until well established, then watered only occasionally during dry spells. When purchasing plants, request local varieties. Cuttings: stems or tips ~1/4" {6mm} thick & ~5" {12.5em} long; lower leaves are removed, stem end dipped in root-hormone, placed in sterile medium. Constantly misted or watered several times a day, until established. aj CoastalLowMidHigh& VeryHigh, WetMesicDry

PROPAGATION: KI is easily & often planted from cuttings, also from air-layers, suckers, & seeds. Can also be rooted in water 1" {2.5em} deep, changing water regularly to prevent rot. Planting the cutting vertically produces one plant, while planting horizontally {leaving 1/2 of diameter uncovered} can produce several sprouts. Air-layering: speeds up propagation time; 8" to 10" {20-25cm} tip-layers. Seeds: sown 1/4" {6mm} deep, kept warm, & moist. Germination: 1-3 months @ 70F-75F {21-24C}. New seedlings resemble thin GRASS leaves. Can be fed with dilute liquid fertilizer. SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Saccharum officinarum, syn. S. officinale.

FAMILY: Poaceae {GRASS}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: To, Noble Cane.

EDIBILITIES: A principle source of extracted sugar world-wide. Fresh, sweet, raw stalk is peeled & chewed {fiber discarded.} The sugar in young stalks is glucose & fructose, while in mature ones, it has changed to sucrose. Mature stalks are the source of cane-juice, a sweetener for various foods, medicines, & beverages. Cane-juice can be extracted in a crushing mill. Or, Va on home level, canes can be pounded in a trough, or cut into pieces & hammered on a cutting Ly board, scraped in a pan with water just covering, & cooked very slowly; fiber strained, then the \, liquid can be cooked slowly to desired thickness. Cane-juice can be evaporated to molasses, wh which then can be refined to sugar, cane-syrup, golden syrup, or fermented &/or distilled into various drinks. Unrefined sugar {"raw sugar"} is a bit more nutritious, but not as long-lasting as white sugar. Most “Brown Sugar” is often just refined "white sugar" with molasses added for color. Unfolded leaf is edible cooked. Stem-cores as grilling-skewers.

☠️ CAUTION: Leaves have sharp, cutting edges.
