☆🌿☠️ ʻUALA / SWEET POTATO Polynesian Introduction

Vol I · scan p. 66 · book p. 86

🌿 Polynesian Introduction ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAME: Ipomoea batatas. Varieties differ greatly in adaptability & all other characteristics:

FAMILY: Convolvulaceae {MORNING GLORY}.

ALSO KNOWN AS: KUMALA, ʻUALA, Camoti, Camote, Kamote, Kumara, Kumar.

TWO TYPES: Drier, coarser, light yellow, white, or purple fleshed types are typically called SWEET POTATOES & are usually boiled or fried. - The smoother, moister, orange fleshed types for baking are often called YAMS, but true YAM are in another Genus & Family. SEE: UHI. } ad

EDIBILITIES: Tuberous roots are an important, productive staple. Shape, color, texture, OS, flavor, nutrition, yield, timing, leaf form, & ease of processing all differ significantly with variety. Tubers: cleaned, peeled or not, roasted, steamed, boiled, cooked in an IMU, baked, fried, battered, as a breakfast cereal, candied, mashed, pureed, or as POI {fermented or not.} — “Se. Cooked tubers can be mashed & added to WHEAT flour for breads, flat-breads, pancakes, Pact és fritters, puddings, pies, cakes, & cookies. To make SWEET POTATO-flour, tubers are roe ~; os at peeled, finely shredded, soaked in a couple changes of water, drained & dried in shade. 7 then in the sun or an oven. These brittle shreds are then easily blended to be added to. ad other flours or extracted for a long-lasting starch {"Brazilian Arrowroot."} Also can be itamin A dar fermented for an alcoholic drink, including POTATO-beer. Tubers are high in carbohydrates, vitamin A precursors {darker varieties}, Vitamin C, with some vitamin B1, iron, & a bit of protein. Foliage: young, tender leaves & growing stem-tips are edible & nutritious as cooked greens, cooled for mixed salads, or in soups & fish dishes. Leaves are higher in protein & vitamins, helping fill the nutritional gap left by eating principally the starchy, protein-poor tubers. Leaves are not eaten raw.

☠️ TOXICITY: SWEET POTATO tubers contain a trypsin inhibitor that must be cooked to deactivate. Insect infested & diseased tuberous roots are usually poisonous & should be carefully trimmed off before eating, also discarding discolored areas that appear on tubers after being cooked. Oxalic acid in leaves also requires deactivation by cooking.

MATURITY: Tubers mature in 10 weeks to 10 months, depending on variety, climate, & treatment, with 3 to 5 months being typical. Maturity is reached when leaves yellow or flowers form. Cool, highland conditions or winter can lengthen the time to maturity. There is no perfect time for harvesting SWEET POTATOES. Early harvest results in less yield, smaller roots, less insect damage, less cracking, milder flavor, & poor storability. Late harvest results in the opposite. Harvesting leaves can begin in 2 to 3 months, gathering new tips while the plants are rapidly growing.

HARVESTING: Main cluster of tubers grow just under center of plant. Varieties range in depth of tuber, but usually no deeper than 10" {25cm}. After vines are cut, tubers are dug with care to avoid cutting or bruising. Tubers can be rested in a shady spot to dry a few hours. If soil is hard to remove, tubers are not washed but dried in shade & brushed. Typical yield is ~10 tubers per plant. Sorting: quality roots are chosen for curing & storing, damaged tubers for processing or immediate cooking, small tubers for livestock. Harvesting "as needed" can continue for months. if no insect damage is occurring.

CURING: To cure, tubers are held @ 85F-95F {29-35C} with 80-90% relative humidity, for 5 to 10 days or up to 3 weeks. As well as sweetening some of the starch, curing helps heal harvest damage & extends storage life. In warm humid areas of Hawaiʻi, tubers can simply be cured in an airy, rodent-proof shed for a few weeks, inspecting regularly.

STORING & SHIPPING: In the hot Tropics only short storage is possible. Undamaged roots last up to 2 months if kept cool. Although cured roots can last a while between 55F & 70F {13-21C}, when stored @ 50F to 55F {10-13C} with a humidity level of 75-80%, they can last a year. Above 70F {21C} tubers tend to shrink & sprout. Chill injury occurs below 50F {10C}. Cured tubers can be pressure-canned, frozen, or made into a lasting starch or flour. SWEET POTATO-flour is storable for 6 months when sealed. Fully cooked tubers can be sliced & dried, but this is questionable due to subsequent enzyme problems unless they are suitably conditioned & pasteurized; research recommended.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: excellent feed. Tubers, leaves & vines are relished as feed by most farm animals. Stored tubers should be cooked before feeding to pigs. Rabbits are especially fond of raw tubers..

COMPOST BIOMASS: although spent vines can be put into the compost, they tend to sprout unless dried first.

GROUND-COVER: covers ground, but SWEET POTATOES can host rats & insects if not harvested regularly. In orchards or around trees, the climbing vines must be regularly turned back.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: leaf & root, although doses & applications are controversial.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous, perennial vine, usually grown as an annual. ʻUALA is considered to be a Polynesian introduction. Stems can grow 3' to 16' {.9-Sm}. Although generally a trailing, ground-hugging vine, many forms readily climb by twining. A few varieties have a bush habit. Latexy sap. Leaf shape & color varies. Purplish-pink, funnel-shaped flowers are stimulated to bloom during short days & long nights {daylength of 11 hours or less.} Rarely forms seeds. Fastgrowing. Fibrous, wide-spread adventitious roots. Stems typically root at nodes.

LIFE-SPAN: plant will persist for years.

ORIGIN: American Tropics.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Thrives with hot, sunny days & cool nights; Tropical, Subtropical, or summers in Temperate regions. Prefers 75F {24C} or higher as an average daily temperature & 68F {20C} at nights. Grows best with evenly distributed rainfall in the annual range of 30" to 50" {75-125cm}. Tolerant of heat. Accepts drought after well rooted & can handle fairly severe drought after 4 months. Intolerant of frost.

— scan page 67 · book page 87 —

CULTURE: ʻUALA are easy to grow. They prefer well-drained, well-aerated, medium loam, with clay subsoil, pH 5.0-6.7, & full sun. Even though the plants need ample space, if given more than 1 sq. yard {1 sq.m} the roots tend to become large irregular "lunkers." Responds well to soil amended with compost. Ridges, mounds, raised-beds, or terraces can help drain & aerate heavier soil; in drier, lighter soil, cuttings can be planted on flat ground or in furrow-bottoms. Mulched or kept thoroughly weeded until the vines themselves can shade the soil. After plants are well established they are watered only at noticeable wilting. Needs abundant potassium, ample phosphorus, but only moderate nitrogen; excess nitrogen or excess water encourages foliage rather than tubers. Excess nitrogen can also create ridges on tubers. Fresh manure is typically avoided due to the chance of disease contagion to new roots.

TOLERATES: sandy, poor, or heavy soil, & most varieties can grow in crushed porous lava. INTOLERANT OF; shade, water-logged &/or non-aerated soil, though some Tropical varieties can tolerate short periods of flooding. Excessively dense or rocky soil can deform roots, or reduce size.

PRUNING: Vines can be flipped back into the center of the plant to discourage spreading & divert energy back to tubers.

ASSOCIATES: SWEET POTATOES do not combine well with any plant that shades them.

ADVERSARIES: Generally pest & disease free, except for SWEET POTATO-weevil, vine-borer, root-knot nematodes & spidermites, Drip irrigation reducea water-splash bome fungus. Eaten by pigs, cattle, rats, wild pheasant, etc.

ORGANIC GROWING: Many varieties have excellent pest- & disease-resistance. Potential problems are reduced by planting clean cuttings of resistant varieties, practicing crop-rotation & thoroughly removing plant-residue & all tubers. New site should be far from previous ones & from all SWEET POTATO relatives, including MORNING GLORY.

DISADVANTAGES: Trailing vines can spread over large areas.

SEE ALSO:

APPLICATIONS: GROUND-COVER, prior. WEEDY?: Persistent, & though rarely found escaping, the climbing vines can get unruly. Occasionally found wild near dumpsites & old home sites.

REMARKS: ʻUALA is a tasty, nutritious & productive staple food, High variability encourages planters to test varieties. sEX: Hermaphroditic. Self- & cross-compatibilities vary.

POLLINATION: Mostly by bees.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds are rare, highly variable & generally sown only for breeding purposes. Seeds are scarified &/or soaked in warm water for 2 days. Germination: 2-10 days @ 70F-75F {21-24C}.

PROPAGATION: Most often by tip-cuttings & slips. Slips are new root-sprouts. Tip-cuttings are green stem pieces, preferably from 2 to 3 month old plants, cut 12" to 18" {30-45cem} long. Shorter cuttings are possible if nodes are closely spaced. Vigorous, healthy, leafy vines are chosen, which are neither too soft & succulent, nor too hard & old. Cuttings from older vines tend to produce fewer tubers. All but 2 to 4 leaves at the tip are taken off {or not}, & the end placed 2/3rds of its length into prepared soil or medium, vertically or better, at an angle. Cuttings are best taken early in the moming. To stimulate rooting, cuttings can be tied in bundles, wrapped in KI leaves or burlap, & kept moist in the shade afew days. Newly planted cuttings require shade, protection from harsh wind & pounding rain & frequent watering for 4 to 8 weeks, or until they are well established. Can be planted anytime rain is eminent, preferably on a damp, cloudy afternoon. various leaf-forms of ʻUALA

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesic

Good substitute for IRISH POTATO for warm areas. Does not tolerate cold. ‘Viola’ - Purple-skinned, sweet, white-fleshed tuber. Grows well at low or high elevations. EDIBILITIES: Important & esteemed food. Size, shape, &.color of tuber depend upon cultivar.; Underground or sometimes aerial tubers are an excellent starchy vegetable, moderate in protein & - vitamin C. Higher in nutrients than CASSAVA or SWEET POTATO {ʻUALA.} Always eaten cooked; either boiled, baked, roasted, fried {pre-boiled}, mashed, in stews, chips, extracted for starch, dried & z ground into flour, or as a soup-thickener. Not suitable for Pol. Peel & areas that quickly darken are 1 a discarded. Tender tips of vines are eaten stir-fried or steamed.

☠️ TOXICITY: Aithough raw tubers may be poisonous & can cause vomiting, cooking destroys any antinutrients. Since some other species of YAM are poisonous, proper identification is required.

BEARING: 7 to 10 months, depending on cultivar.

MATURITY: After the foliage has died back, during the short winter days, tubers continue to mature. Best time to harvest is a few weeks after vine dies & from then until new sprouts appear. Early tubers can be carefully cut from root crown allowing more tubers to form. -

HARVESTING: Deep tubers are laboriously dug. Tubers destined for storage should not be bruised, cut, or otherwise damaged. Vine tips for cooking purposes are harvested while plant-growth is vigorous.

STORING: Roots are tender & readily rot if damaged, thus need careful handling during storage. Sound tubers can be stored 3 to months before sprouting begins. Some cultivars store better than others. UHI store better than ʻUALA. Tubers can be tied & hung in an airy, shady place. Inspected regularly for pests. Chill injury occurs at temperatures lower than SOF {10C}. For longer storage, cooked tubers can be ground finely, dried, & sieved to a flour.

SHIPPING: Tubers tolerate transport well if handled with care.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: with fast-growing nitrogen-fixing trees, such as MOTHER OF CACAO, etc.; YAMS are planted at tree bases & when the tubers start to form, the tree is ring-barked ~16" {40cm} from ground-level. This releases the tree's root-nitrogen, causes its leaves to drop, allows sun to reach the YAM'S leaves. After tuber harvest, upper part of tree can be cut for firewood, with the strongest sucker being left to grow, renewing the tree.

ANIMAL FEED: although animals will eat raw tubers, they can show digestive problems-afterwards; tubers need cooking.

EROSION CONTROL: some varieties are good for temporary, dense ground-covers, & will root at nodes on moist soil.

GROUND-COVER: dense, but temporary.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: several Dioscorea species have important health properties. Diosgenin {steroidal sapogenins} for oral contraceptives & other hormonal applications is often collected from wild plants & is not yet sustainable. Cultivating wild species has been shown to be profitable as early as 3 to 4 years. Species Dioscorea floribunda is highly promising, since it yields as much as 10% diosgenin, based on dry weight. Seeds of FENUGREEK, Trigonella foenumgraecum, are also a diosgenin source.

NURSE PLANT: trellised shade & protection for young COLA plants, etc.

SHADE: excellent when trellised & trained as summer shade.

XERISCAPING: marginal. SEE: CLIMATIC ADAPTION, following.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive perennial vine with annual stems. Introduced by ancient Polynesians. Can climb 7' {2m} or taller. Monocot. Right twining habit. Vine in cross-section is square, winged. Simple, heart-shaped leaves with parallel vines. Foliage dies back during shorter days of autumn. Possibly day-length sensitive; long-days seem to encourage vine growth, while tubers seem to be stimulated by short days. Female plants occasionally produce clusters of tiny flowers maturing into winged seed-capsules. Underground & occasionally aerial tubers. YAM has relatively weak roots, With some cultivars being shallow rooted, while others being quite deep.

Polynesian Introduction ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAMES: Artocarpus altilis, syn. A. incisa! incisus, syn. A. communis. Many varieties cultivars exist. Ce soos

FAMILY: Moraceae {FIG} Family. - oO:,

ALSO KNOWN AS: Fruta Pao, Pakak, Rima, Maiore, Aeiore, Uto, “Uru. ytd

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, staple food. Large, round or oblong, multi-faceted yellowish fruit 6" to. 12" {15-30cm} wide, weighing up to 10 Ibs. {4.5kg}. Size & shape depend upon variety, with the «5 original Hawaiian variety being quite small. Fruit has a somewhat rough rind {with some cultivars having short spines}, is typically seedless & contains white to light yellow, mild, moist, mealy brothers? pulp, surrounding a hard, inedible core. Food applications can differ with variety. High in carbohydrates, proteins, with a wide range of amino acids, including fysine, moderate in vitamins A & B, & calcium. Whole, under-ripe fruit can be cooked as a vegetable, baked, boiled, roasted, steamed in an IMU, or fried. Fruit can also be peeled & cut into sections or slices for baking, boiling, steaming, sautéing, frying, deep-frying {pre-cooked}, stir-fries, soups stews, mashing, marinating, creaming, or as a puree. Cooked pulp can be beaten & made into cakes, batter-fried, puddings & pies, or frozen, & occasionally pounded & fermented as a POI {POPOI.} Soft, sweet ripe fruit can be eaten raw, roasted for dessert, or spooned in to a frying pan & like a pancake, made into a baked pudding, or baked whole over a smal} amount of water. Male flowers can be cooked as a vegetable.

☠️ TOXICITY: Though a few varieties can be eaten raw, most raw BREADFRUIT are said to be purgative.

NOTE: can be cooked in changes of water to prevent stomach gas.

BEARING: Trees propagated by root-suckers can start to fruit in 3 to 7 years. Tree tends towards alternate beanng.

MATURITY: Around 2 to 3 months from flower to fruit. While fruit can be harvested green, it is generally harvested when small white droplets of latex form on rind & rind itself turns tannish-green, but before the fruit softens, Fruit generally ripen in summer, but harvest can extend through late winter, 3 to 5 months or longer. Fruit softens in 1 to 2 days after picking, as its carbohydrates become sugars.

HARVESTING: Fruits can be separated from the tree with a long forked stick & caught with care. A strong picker-pole with a cutting edge & bag is helpful. Beware of sticky, staining sap.

STORING: Because the fruit tends to be abundant in season & ripe fruits last only a few days at room temperatures, preservation is desirable. BREADFRUIT can be refrigerated @ 54F {12C}. Chill-injury is likely at lower temperatures. Fruit can also be pickled, canned, candied, or stored under water. BREADFRUIT pulp can be dried, powdered, & utilized like a flour, or sliced, cooked, mashed, & dried as a leather. BREADFRUITS can be fermented in pits & stored; ʻULU POPOI can last as long as KALO poi, but reportedly makes stomach gas. Ripe fruit can also be made into a better POPO! with COCONUTmilk & baked in KI leaves & eaten or dried as slices.

SHIPPING: Packed carefully in cartons with separating dividers.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: ripe raw or cooked under-ripe ʻULU make excellent livestock feed. O.K. as a poultry feed, if supplemented. Leaves for fodder.

CEREMONY: fruit. DYE.

FIBER: fibrous inner bark can be made into KAPA, but is not easy to extract. Male flowers mixed with WAUKE-fiber was made into KAPA.

FUEL: wood is inferior fuel, but dried spikes of male flowers are good tinder.

LANDSCAPING: edible ornamental, but massive with age unless pruned & falling fruit are dangerously heavy.

LATEX: sticky sap as caulking for canoes & boats, or as a chewing gum.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: entire tree has numerous applications.

SANDPAPER: dried, rough leaves or flower-sheaths can be utilized to sand & polish KUKUI nuts, calabashes, etc.

SHADE: handsome, dense-shade tree, but dangerous falling fruit.

WINDBREAK: closely planted, ʻULU can make a good windbreak.

WOOD: coarse textured, soft, strong, lasting, light-weight, easily worked, with low shrinkage. Some varieties are more valuable than others. For timber, house construction, furniture, doors, carving, calabashes, canoe-making, surf-boards, drums, kapa tools, POI boards, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 30' to 85' {9-26m} tall, with a trunk 2' to 6' {.6-1.8m} wide {depending on variety.} The first types of ʻULU were introduced to Hawaiʻi by the early Polynesians. Round crown. Frequently buttressed. Large, lobed leathery leaves. Thick flower spikes, with female flower cluster maturing into the fruit. ʻULU is a variant, seedless form of the original BREADNUT. Fast-growing. Forms a mass of surface roots, as well as tap- & lateral-roots.

LIFE-SPAN: productive ~50 years.

ORIGIN: SE Asia, Java, Marquesas & Polynesia.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: ʻULU is best suited to hot, wet, humid Tropics. Temperature range of 70F to 90F {21-32C} preferred. Annual rainfall of 60" to 100” {18-25m} or greater is needed. Tolerates heavy rain, as well as some drought. Tolerances differ with varieties & can include other climates. Intolerant of cool temperatures, frost, & harsh winds.

HAWAIʻI LOCATION: Grown often here, especially on windward coasts, but is widely adapted to all except the driest regions. Found throughout the lowlands & up to mid-elevations.

CULTURE: Easy to grow & highly productive. Prefers deep, moist, rich, well-aerated, well-drained soil, slightly acid or neutral pH, full sun. Flourishes with weed control, mulch, ample water, & regular fertilization.

TOLERATES: various soils, from somewhat light to heavy, or slightly salty ones {depending on variety.}

INTOLERANT OF: poorly aerated or water-logged, sandy, shallow, alkaline, or strongly salty soils.

PRUNING: Since branches that have fruited tend to die-back, they can be judiciously removed to encourage new growth. Large trees can be pruned back severely to conserve space, stimulate new growth, & make fruit more accessible.

— scan page 72 · book page 9 —

ASSOCIATES: ʻŌHIʻA AI {Mt. Apple} & KUKUI. Produces dense shade which few 3 understory crops can withstand, except perhaps ʻŌLENA {Turmeric}.

ADVERSARIES: While remarkably free of pests, ʻULU does have a few serious diseases. It is not advisable to replant where one has died. Growth in young plants is seriously Bas slowed by weeds. 8 ‘

ORGANIC GROWING: Excellent candidate,

NOT WEEDY: This species, plus IPU, are said to be the only two Polynesian introductions not naturalized. oe,

REMARKS: Attractive & valuable. With suitable varieties, ʻULU are among the most easily ot vo i produced staple in the Tropics. Ce gee pISADVANTAGES: Beware when fruits are falling. Hands & knife can be oiled to prevent i i ae sap from sticking. “ r SEX: Monoecious & unisexual flowers. Ls. —

POLLINATION: Probably wind. Hand-pollination creates more plentiful & larger fruit. ee

PROPAGATION: Because ʻULU tend to be seedless, they are propagated from root-shoots, cuttings, root-cuttings, & air-layering. Root-shoots: spontaneous or induced. For greatest success they are pre-separated by root pruning a few times. Later carefully dug with as much root & soil as possible & kept partially shaded until established. Hardened off gradually. Root-shoots are best taken at the beginning of a rainy season. Cuttings: up to 15" {38cm} long & {1cm} thick; dipped in rooting hormone, placed in shade & watered daily. Root-cuttings: up to 10" {25cm} long, & 1/2" to {1.25-Scm} thick, placed in sand horizontally or diagonally. The end of cutting which was previously closest to tree is left protruding from sand by 1" to 2" {2.5-S5cm}. Placed in a shaded spot & misted often. Transplanted when rooted to a container & watered a couple times a day. Grafting: buds can be v-grafted onto BREADNUT or JACKFRUIT.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: Many outstanding Samoan & Tahitian varieties exist. The 'Puero,' a Tahitian cultivar, is highly valued.

☆ WAUKE / PAPER MULBERRY Polynesian Introduction

Vol I · scan p. 73 · book p. 94

Polynesian Introduction ☆ ☆ Outstanding species.

SCIENTIFIC NAME: Broussonetia papyrifera, syn. Papyrius papyrifera, syn. Morus papyrifera. Varieties exist.

FAMILY: Moraceae {MULBERRY }.

ALSO KNOWN AS: Tapa-Cloth Tree, Aute{Polynesia & NZ}, U*a{Samoa}, PO*A‘AHA.

EDIBILITIES: Minor foods. Young leaves are edible cooked. Fruit has some sweet, edible pulp, but is not particularly tasty.

APPLICATIONS:

EROSION CONTROL: Especially for stony slopes. FIBER {PRINCIPLE APPLICATION): Excellent fiber for KAPA cloth: soft, pliable, water-resistant, & warm. Utilized for skirts, loincloths, capes, bed-covers, & ritual, ceremonial & burial purposes, etc. For KAPA-making, WAUKE is cut when 12' to 16’ {3.6- 5m} tall or while trunk is still less than 1.5" {4cm} thick while the bark is still soft, the plant ~1 1/2 to 2 years old. While harvesting, the stems are cut carefully to avoid damaging new nising shoots.

OTHER FIBER APPLICATIONS: Bast fiber is also made into excellent paper, as well as sandals, ropes, cordage, bags & portage nets, wicking, & fish-lines or -nets. Fibers are only 1/2” {1.25cm} long. Leaves can be utilized as sandpaper.

HEDGE: Can form dense barriers by suckering.

LANDSCAPING: Specimen tree, grove, screen, heritage garden, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: WAUKE has medicinal properties. WAUKE MALOLO is a variety that is purely medicinal.

SHADE TREE: When grown alone. Woon: Light, soft, & porous. #304

DESCRIPTION: Small, deciduous tree or shrub. Polynesian introduction. Can grow 30' {9m} or a bit taller, but usually seen 1/2 that. Trunk diameter can reach 1’ {30cm}. Tall, narrow habit when planted closely, or having a broad, dense crown with many branches when grown alone. Rough-surfaced leaves vary in shape; often 3-lobed or heart-shaped. Rarely flowers in Hawaiʻi & apparently does not fruit here. Rapid-growing. Tap-root.

ORIGIN: Pacific Islands, China, Japan, & possibly elsewhere.

CLIMATIC ADAPTION: Prefers moist, cool low- or mid-elevations, wet forests, stream edges, & damp “bottom” lands. Found on all larger Hawaiian islands. Requires constant moisture. Tolerates lower or drier areas {if watered}, adverse climates, including polluted air, as well as heat & drought, deserts, & harsh winds {if not grown for KAPA.} Does not tend to grow on coral atolls. Intolerant of harsh winds & drought if grown for KAPA.

CULTURE: Tough plant. Prefers deep, moist, well-drained, loamy soil, & part-shade. Scars from wind-rubbing can be prevented by planting in sheltered spots. Benefits from moist leaf-mulch & thorough weeding.

TOLERATES: full sun {if watered during prolonged droughts}, sloping Iand, as well as poor or alkaline soil.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage.

PRUNING / TRAINING: Side leaves & buds can be carefully pinched off each week to prevent scars. Leaves on top 2' {60cm} of trunk are left on.

ASSOCIATES: Can be grown on the banks of KALO LO'1.

ADVERSARIES: Generally free from problems.

WEEDY: Surface root-suckers are often prolific, persistent, & come up at great distances from the mother tree, especially along stream edges. Can be difficult to contain, but apparently does not run into forests.

REMARKS: For Hawaiian educational displays, WAUKE is planted closely in the “plantation style." SEX: Dioecious, although it rarely blossoms here.

POLLINATION: Insects.

PROPAGATION: Grown by root-suckers, slips, & stem- or root-cuttings. Root-suckers {HULI} separated from "second growth" plants, leaving several inches of root attached & avoiding damage to the tap-root of mother plant. Shoot is stripped of leaves, leaving tip intact, bundled, wrapped, & placed in water or in a moist, shaded spot, then carefully planted the next day. Propagated late-winter or very early spring. Young, tender plants are watered regularly & provided with shade & wind protection. Planted out when 1'-2' {30-60cm} tall. Setting plant too deeply is avoided.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesicDry

SEE ALSO: MULBERRY. Morus species. In Weed Book.

☆⚠️ ACEROLA

Vol II · scan p. 96

☆ ACEROLA "Barbados Cherry," West Indian Cherry, Cerejeira, Malpi, Shimarucu. Malpighia punicifolia, err. M. glabra. Malpighiaceae (Malpighia) Family. dozen or so varieties exist, varying in appearance, tartness, & vitamin C level. three-seeded fruit higher in vitamin C than 4 to 6-seeded.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed fruits. Having three lobes or none, fruit can grow 1 in. (2.5 cm) wide. Thin, glossy, red or orange-red skin. Looking somewhat like a Cherry or a tiny Apple, with several seeds. Juicy, tasty & refreshingly tart; eaten fresh raw when full ripe, or almost so. Somewhat under-ripe fruit (with seeds removed) can also be stewed or made into jams, jellies, preserves, syrups, tarts, purees, sauces, also dried or as wine. Much of the ascorbic acid is retained in wine. Juice can be pressed, combined with other juices or made into gelatins, sherbets, or dried & ground to a powder. Fresh ACEROLA juice can be squeezed on fruit salads to prevent discoloration. Fruits are very high in vitamin C (especially just before becoming fully ripe), although some of this vitamin is lost by cooking. Fruits are also high in thiamine, niacin, B,, riboflavins, calcium, iron & vitamin A. Abundant copper in some areas of Hawaiʻi reportedly lowers vitamin C content.

⚠️ CAUTION: Plant-hairs may irritate sensitive skin. Seeds are inedible & irritating if consumed in large quantities.

BEARING: ACEROLA can begin bearing in one year, but yields are higher after three.

MATURITY: From flower to fruit in seventeen to thirty days & another month to ripen. Season of fruiting depends largely on weather, but typically occurs during rainy seasons. Picked when fully ripe & slightly soft, before falling. For cooking purposes they can be picked just as color changes. In some areas ACEROLA yields nearly year-round.

HARVESTING: Fruit are plucked from tree, harvesting often to avoid fruit-drop.

STORING & SHIPPING: Soft, ripe fruits are easily damaged & fast to decay. Need to be kept cool to retard loss of vitamin C. Fruit will jast a few days with refrigeration, longer if frozen. Fresh fruit or juice can be canned or dried.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: foliage is a limited forage for ruminants. Pigs eat the fruits.

CONTAINER-GROWING: especially the dwarf variety.

EROSION CONTROL: planted on terraces.

LANDSCAPING: attractive, edible, specimen tree & hedge (pruned or not).

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

SCHOOL-YARD TREE: high in vitamins & well liked by children. (But SEE: CAUTION, above.)

WOOD: hard & dense: suitable for smaller articles.

DESCRIPTION: ACEROLA is an attractive, evergreen shrub or small tree. Can grow 4 to 20 ft. (1.2-6 m) tall & as wide, or smaller, depending on cultivar. Short trunk. Small, waxy, dark green leaves. White, lavender, or pink flowers. Pioneer species. Deep roots.

LIFE SPAN: productive usually around fifteen years, although a hundred plus year old fruiting trees exist in the Caribbean.

ORIGIN: Caribbean, Puerto Rico, West Indies & other parts of tropical South America.

CLIMATE: ACEROLA needs abundant rain. Grows in the lowland tropics & subtropics. Best suited to hot climates with a monsoon season. Mature trees will withstand considerable rain, drought, as well as a brief frost.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: ACEROLA thrives below 2000 ft. (600 m) elevation in Hawaiʻi. Before synthetic vitamin C became available, many acres of ACEROLA were planted in the Puna District on the Big Island, with large amounts of the fruit exported to the continent.

— scan page 97 · book page 2 —

PREFERS: Deep, moist, fertile, well drained soil, pH 5.5 to 6.5 & full sun. Thrives when fertilized twice yearly with adequate nitrogen & potassium. Benefits from thick mulch. Easy to grow.

TOLERATES: most soils, including poor ones, some salt spray pH range of 5.0 to 8.3.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly acid soil, heavy wet clays or flooding.

ASSOCIATES: Often grown alone, although their compact nature could provide some shelter for smaller plants.

ADVERSARIES: Root-knot nematode is ACEROLA's prime enemy. The fruits often suffer insect or damage. Fairly disease resistant, especially when grown in polycultures.

ORG NI GROWINE. Excellent antidote in diverse plantings. For nematode control, mulching, as well as budding or grafting onto other resistant species, such as Malpighia syberosa, have been suggested.

WEEDY: Although ACEROLA has naturalized in some countries, it is not considered to be a serious problem.

REMARKS: ACEROLA is considered a plant of high value, especially for home gardens. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Bees. Nearby hives increase fruit yield. For some reason, either from lack of specific pollinators or possibly excess wind, pollination is not always successful in Hawaiʻi. Isolated plants often do not set fruit.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds are highly variable. Seed life span is short.

PROPAGATED BY: Easily established from 'select' seeds at any time in the tropics. Also propagated by cuttings, air-layering, & grafting or budding. Seedlings are best established in flats in a rich soil mixture, then transplanted to containers when 3 in. (7.5 cm) tall. Vegetative propagation is most productive just after winter. Cuttings: pieces to 10 in. (25 cm) long & up to % in. (1.25 cm) thick, with several top leaves left on, dipped in rooting-hormone & given intermittent mist. Transplanted about two months kept shaded for six to twelve months.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: ‘Dwarf ACEROLA.' Growing 2 ft. (60 cm) tall, this cultivar is suitable for hanging baskets & other containers. Tolerates cooler weather. ‘Manoa Sweet.' Another upright tree, developed in Hawaiʻi, producing abundant, sweet, orange-red fruits.

NOTE: There are several other Malpighia species with edible fruit.

NOTE: The true BARBADOS CHERRY, Malpighia glabra, is a smaller, wild relative.

TOLERATES: many soils. Drought resistant, but better with adequate moisture.

☆🌳☠️ ANNONA

Vol II · scan p. 99

☆ ANNONA Annona species. Annonaceae (Custard Apple) Family. SEE: SOME NOTABLE SPECIES, following. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Highly esteemed. Small to very large fruits having tasty, tender, creamy or juicy pulp. Eaten fresh raw or in fruit salads, juices, frozen, etc. Often chilled, halved & scooped with a spoon, discarding seeds & rind. Course straining of some species can yield a thick, rich juice for fresh beverages, ice-creams, sherbets, & fermented beverages. Under ripe fruit of most species can be cooked as a vegetable.

☠️ TOXICITY: 1. Seeds are somewhat toxic if chewed; always removed before processing. 2. Leaves of some species contain potentially poisonous alkaloids. Seed-juice has caused blindness. BEARING,

IN GENERAL: Can begin in two to five years, depending on species, conditions, & propagation technique. Often yields two major crops yearly.

MATURITY: Fruits mature over several months. Maturity is noted when green color lightens. If gathered at the correct time & held at a favorable temperature, fruits can ripen in two days. Fruit harvested immaturely do not successfully ripen.

HARVESTING: Fruit is clipped or sometimes twisted from tree. Handled with great care to prevent blemishes.

STORING: Ripe fruit are usually soft & deteriorate quickly. Will last several days if refrigerated above 59°F (15°C). Colder temperatures will darken the rind.

SHIPPING: Some species & varieties hold up better than others. Fruit pulp is often processed & transported as nectar.

APPLICATIONS:

☠️ NOT AS ANIMAL FEED: Most animals will not eat the foliage & it is considered poisonous.

INSECTICIDE: Seeds are often crushed for their insecticidal properties (But, SEE: TOXICITY, prior). Other applications are noted under individual listings.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Some.

LANDSCAPING: Small species are often seen in gardens.

🌳 GENERAL ANNONA DESCRIPTION: Small to medium, evergreen or partly deciduous trees. Climax species. Dense canopy can reach ground level. Yellowish flowers. Brittle surface roots.

ORIGIN: Central & South American tropics, unless otherwise noted.

CLIMATE: Tropics to subtropics. Dry or wet, humid, lowland forests, to higher & drier climates, depending on species & variety. PREFERENCES & CULTURE,

IN GENERAL: Most species are fairly easy to grow. ANNONA prefer rich, moist, well drained loam, slightly acid or neutral pH & full sun. Mulching encourages vigor, with 4 in. (10 cm) thickness beneficial. Mulch is kept at least 6 in. (15 cm) away from trunk, replenished as needed. Fertilized regularly to stimulate vigorous growth first three years, then decreased to encourage fruiting.

TOLERATES: sandy or heavy loam.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage.

PRUNING & TRAINING: In their early years, trees are trained to develop a low spreading form with strong, widely spaced lateral branches. Thereafter, only dead wood & awkward branches are removed. To promote good aeration & inner light, entire limbs are trimmed off rather than heading-off branches.

ADVERSARIES: Susceptible to root-rots, scale, fruit fly & anthracnose. Foliage & trunk is very sensitive to herbicides.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate with appropriate, resistant cultivars & attending to factors such as correct feeding (including mineral needs), IPM, wind protection, mulching, proper training, pruning, removal of fallen fruit, etc. Beneficial wasps, ladybugs & lacewings, etc., can help reduce the numbers of pests. WEEDY?: Rarely weedy, although CHERIMOYA has sparsely naturalized in higher, dry regions. Wild fruit is hardly edible. SEX: Hermaphroditic & protogynous: although flowers have both female & male sexual parts, the female parts generally mature before pollen is ready. Hand pollination is often needed.

— scan page 100 · book page 6 —

APPLICATIONS:

FIBER: bark from young, tender twigs.

INSECTICIDE: young fruits, seeds & leaves have insecticidal properties.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: soft, yet fairly dense.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Nearly evergreen tree. Can grow 35 ft. (10.5 m) tall. Fetid smelling leaves. Greenish-yellow flowers. Rapid growing. Largely surface rooted.

ORIGIN: American tropics.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics.

GROWN IN HAWATLT: occasionally.

PREFERS: deep, fertile, fairly moist, well drained soil, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. Grows best with frequent water, humid conditions, mulch & regular fertilizer.

PRUNING: trained to shape.

TOLERATES: pH range of 4.3 to 8.0, dry spells & somewhat harsher conditions than most ANNONA.

INTOLERANT OF: wet feet, extreme drought & wind.

ADVERSARIES: anthracnose is common, especially in highly humid conditions.

WEEDY: has naturalized in many tropical countries. SEX: hermaphroditic, but a pollinator is needed.

POLLINATION: insects & by hand.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds, budding, inarching & grafting. Valued as a strong rootstock for other ANNONA.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic/?

vv ILAMA. Annona diversifolia. Severat cultivars exist, Whiter pulped types are sweeter than reddish ones.

EDIBILITIES: Called the “Cherimoya” of the lowlands; considered to be the best ANNONA for lower elevations. Rosy-pink, or light green fruits to 6 in. (15 cm) long, with low bumps & a harder rind than Cherimoya. Pulp is sweet, delicious, tinted with peach or ivory & ripe enough to eat only when soft. Eaten fresh raw, chilled, or in nectars, beverages, ice-creams & sherbets, etc.

BEARING: seedlings can bear in three to four years. Yields vary from low to moderate.

MATURITY: mid to late summer. Fruit can be gathered just before fully ripe & brought indoors to ripen, or can be picked to eat immediately when starting to split open. Prematurely harvested fruit do not ripen well.

STORING: soft, ripe fruit ferment rapidly; highly perishable.

SHIPPING: difficult.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Smal] evergreen tree. Can grow 25 ft. (7.5 m) tall. Slender trunk. Fragrant bark. Yellowish or reddish flowers-

ORIGIN: Central American tropics.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Adapted to hot, humid lowlands. Does best when heavy rain is preceded by a prolonged dry weather.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: succeeds better at lower altitudes than CHERIMOYA.

PREFERS: loose, deep, moist, fertile loam, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. This species is not easy to grow.

TOLERATES: various soils, a pH range of 5.5 to 8.0, & drought.

INTOLERANT OF: wet feet, high winds.

SOURSOP, Guanabana, Corossol. Annona muricata. Many types & varieties exist; including ones varying from high to low acid, juicy to dryish, & round to oblong. Excellent, creamy-pulped varieties exist, including ‘Cuban Fiberless' & ‘Whitman Fiberless.'

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Seeds are slightly poisonous. 2. Seed-oil is extremely irritating to eyes. 3. Bark is highly poisonous.

EDIBILITIES: Large, yellowish-green, heart-shaped fruit 10 in. (25 cm) or longer, can weigh 10 Ibs (4.5 kg), or more. Has soft fleshy “spines." Fragrant juicy pulp has a pleasant sweet/sour flavor. Fruit are sweeter when ripened in summer or in warmer climates. Because pulp is usually filled with long, indigestible, cotton-wool-like fibers, fruit is often prepared by peeling, removing inner stalk & course sieving for a rich cream. Fruit is eaten fresh raw, in fruit salads, as delicious beverages, nectars, gelatins, custards, jellies, tarts, ices, ice-creams, sorbets, sherbets, nectars, teamed with COCONUT-milk, or canned. High in pectin & vitamins C & B. Under-ripe fruit can be eaten fried, boiled, roasted or in soups. Young, tender, leaf-shoots are aromatic & have good texture when steamed or boiled, but are bland & somewhat bitter. Note: leaves have been brewed as a tea, but this is a questionable practice (SEE: TOXICITIES, prior.)

BEARING: three to five years. Usually not productive due to poor pollination &/or high humidity.

MATURITY: when skin begins to yellow, fruit can soften in less than a week. Fruit tend to fall if allowed to ripen fully on tree. Fruit can ripen nearly year-round, but peaks in mid-summer.

STORING: ripe fruit will last several days in the refrigerator.

SHIPPING: soft skin requires careful handling.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: fruits for livestock.

INSECTICIDE: pounded seeds & leaf decoction kills bedbugs, head lice, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES. SHADE TREE

DESCRIPTION: Smal] evergreen tree. Can grow 12 to 30 ft. 3.6-9 m) tall. Bushy upright habit. May drop foliage during droughts. Odorous leaves. White to yellow flowers. Fast growing. Shallow roots.

ORIGIN: American tropics.

CLIMATE: hot, humid coasts.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: currently higher demand for fruit than is available.

PREFERS: loose, deep, fertile, dryish, well drained loam, pH 5.5 to 6.5 & full sun. Needs protection from intense winds. Responds to regular manure or fertilizer. Benefits from mulch during drought.

TOLERATES: shallow, sandy or compact soils, pH range of 4.3 to 8.0 & prolonged drought.

ARTICHOKE Various Genera & Families. *xw ARTICHOKE, GLOBE ARTICHOKE. Cynara scolymus. Asteraceae (Sunflower) Family. At least fifty varieties exist; many are improved, adaptable &/or colorful.

EDIBILITIES:; Esteemed vegetable. Succulent base of immature flower bracts, fleshy receptacles & stem -pith are delicious steamed, boiled, baked, grilled, stuffed, pickled, or marinated; dipped in melted butter, mayonnaise or other salad dressing. After the ARTICHOKE is washed under cold water, small, tough leafs near the stem are trimmed off, stem is peeled & trimmed, thorn tips can be snipped off; Lemon-juice on the cuts preserves color. Tough leaf-lamina & seed-down are discarded at eating. ARTICHOKES are high in folic acid, vitamin C & magnesium. Small secondary ARTICHOKES are eaten cooked or in omelettes, soups & stews, oil preserved, marinated or pickled. Flowers are a rennet replacement.

BEARING: anywhere from four months to two years from seed to harvest, depending on cultivar. Fastest when propagated by root-divisions.

MATURITY: full-sized heads are cut before they open. Harvested at least twice a week during peak season, March to May. Biggest heads are high on the stalk.

STORING: although best within three days of harvest, unwashed heads can last up to a week refrigerated, altemately they can be frozen, marinated or pickled.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: ormamental, edible hedge, accent, flower borders, background, etc.

MED AL QUALITIES. Degeare Large, attractive, herbaceous perennial. Can grow 3 to 6 ft. (.9-1.8 m) tall. Often spiny, although unarmed cultivars exist. Silver-gray foliage. Large, purple, fragrant, Thistle-like flowers.

LIFE SPAN: around three to four years.

ORIGIN: Mediterranean, Canary Islands.

CLIMATE: thrives in cool, moist, foggy conditions, with an ideal temperature range of 60 to 65°F (15-18°C). GROWN IN HAWAIPl in the cool highlands.

PREFERS: very rich, moist, well drained, humusy, sandy loam soil, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun. Fairly easy to grow. Fast growing-conditions, including a well prepared bed & ample space, enhances production. Benefits from thick mulch, leaving several inches of bare soil near base of stem to reduce the likelihood of crown-rot. Responds to timely feeding of compost or aged manure. Resents disturbance.

TOLERATES: many soils & part shade where hot.

PRUNING: dead leaves should be removed. New evidence suggests that pinching out central bud does not increase yield.

ASSOCIATES: Cosmos.

ADVERSARIES: basically pest free, except for possible slug, snail & aphid damage, & crown-rot if too wet. Heat causes early boiting & toughness.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize. SEX: self-fertile.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are typically variable, but a new, less variable strain of 'Green Globe' has been developed. Seed life span: one year.

PROPAGATED BY: root-divisions, root off-shoots, seeds & cuttings. Sown in fertilized trenches. Germination: two to four weeks, Every few years, plantings can be revitalized by dividing & re-planting.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, WetMesic

🌿Ⓦ ASPARAGUS

Vol II · scan p. 101 · book p. 10

ASPARAGUS Garden Asparagus, Sparrow Grass. Asparagus officinalis var. altilis & others. Alliaceae / Liliaceae (Lily) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed vegetable. Young, tender shoot tips are eaten fresh raw in salads, with a dip, or boiled, steamed, stir-fried, sautéed, etc. Stalks are gently washed, snapping of bases where they break naturally. Tough bases add flavor to soups or stews. High in vitamins A, B & C, moderate protein & other essential nutrients. Seeds can be utilized as a Coffee adulterant. Entire plant contains large amounts of the amino acid, asparagine, which gives ASPARAGUS its name & characteristic odor.

BEARING: Seedling in two to three years; vegetative propaguls in one to two years, depending on initial age of roots.

MATURITY: First spears are harvested over a couple of weeks in the second year. Length of harvest doubles in the succeeding year. Twice yearly harvests are possible. If ASPARAGUS is well tended from the beginning, early production will be the likely outcome. Spears are cut young, before tip-scales begin to open, when they are only 4 to 10 in. (10-25 cm) tall. Only large, thick spears are gathered, allowing thin spears to grow to feed the roots.

HARVESTING: Spears are harvested by slipping a knife (preferably ASPARAGUS-knife) into soil surface at 45° angle, cutting base carefully to avoid damaging developing spear-tips. For freshness, early mornings or cool evenings best. Cut spears are kept out of direct sunlight & chilled quickly. Spears can be harvested every one to three days depending on season.

STORING: Spears can be refrigerated; preferably with tips up, butts in an inch of icy water. Wrapped in plastic in refrigerator, spears can keep three to four days. At 34 to 36°F (1-2°C) they can last three weeks. Freezing, canning or pickling possible.

SHIPPING: ASPARAGUS needs cool temperatures & gentle handling in transport.

APPLICATIONS:

EROSION CONTROL: ASPARAGUS has been planted on the continent to stabilize sandy river banks & dunes.

LANDSCAPING: Background or borders in perennial beds.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Formerly, ASPARAGUS's most important application was as a medicine. il 🌿 aie

— scan page 102 —

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous perennial. Can grow 3 to 6 ft. (.9-1.8 m) tall. Graceful feathery branched stems & delicate, thin “leaves,“ Female plants bear small white to yellowish-green flowers that mature into small red fruits, containing a few seeds. Day-length neutral. Typically vigorous. ASPARAGUS has deep, wide spread, underground rhizomes.

LIFE SPAN: although ASPARAGUS does not seem to live long in Hawaiʻi, thirty plus productive years are possible

ORIGIN: Coasts & river banks of Europe, western Asia & Siberia.

CLIMATE: Suited to the temperate & subtropical zones. Grows best in areas with chilly winters & moderately cool or warm summers. Thrives in a summer temperature range of 60 to 80°F (15.5-27°C). During its growth periods, ASPARAGUS needs plenty of moisture & in dry weather, plants like to be watered once or twice weekly.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: ASPARAGUS is grown successfully in Hawaiʻi in mid & high elevations. Once an important export.

PREFERS: ASPARAGUS needs ample space in a deep, permanent bed. Prefers moist, fertile, humusy, loose, well drained soil, pH to full sun. Responds to deeply worked soil with phosphorus & potash added. Fast-drying, gravely or sandy soils benefit from amending with compost. Heavy soils can be amended with compost or plants can be placed more shallowly. Thrives with an aged manure top-dressing, worked in shallowly two or three times a year & a thick mulch. Mulch reduces maintenance, controls weeds, encourages beneficial soil organisms & maintains needed root coolness. Suitable mulch has a neutral pH & is chopped or granular. In acid conditions lime or dolomite can be added under the mulch.

TOLERATES: excess water.

INTOLERANT OF: wind, shade, flooding & large rocks (produces twisted sprouts).

NOTE: Without a dormant period in the tropics, shoots tend to become quite slender, therefore, culture in warm regions involves simulation of winter. This might be accomplished by keeping the hed well fertilized & watered to encourage growth during the early spring & summer months, then, during the winter season withholding water & renewing mulch.

PRUNING: Old stems can be cut early spring before new growth starts.

ASSOCIATES: Parsley, Basil, Tomato or Rue are frequently planted near ASPARAGUS.

ADVERSARIES: Pest possibilities include stugs, snails & occasionally aphids, thrips & cutworms. Diseased looking, stunted, or crooked spears may be infected by rust; because this serious disease spreads if put into a compost pile, rust-affected stems are cut bumt, or anaerobically composted. ASPARAGUS is burnt by strong sulfuric vog.

ORGANIC-GROWING: To discourage pests: beds cleaned each autumn, disease resistant cultivars chosen (especially rust-resistant), beneficial wasps encouraged, & hens occasionally allowed into plots. Cutworms are toads' favorite food.

WEEDY: Escaped & naturalized worldwide. Fortunately, ASPARAGUS does not tend to displace other plants.

NOTE: The CLIMBING ASPARAGUS FERN, A.K.A. Plumosa, A. sefaceus, syn. A. plumosus 'Baker,' syn. Protasparagus plumosus, is a seriously invasive horticultural weed. And the inedible, ornamental ASPARAGUS FERNS, Asparagus racemosus, A. sprengeri, A. africanus, densifiorus & others exist, also with extreme weed potential. SEX: Piants are either male or female; dioecious.

POLLINATION: Not needed for home gardening.

SEED-SAVING: ASPARAGUS can be grown from seeds, but initial growth is much slower. Seed life span: three years.

PROPAGATED BY: Typically grown from one to three year old roots, or crown division. Roots are set 1 to 2 ft. (0-60 cm) apart, in trenches 4 to 5 ft. (1-1.5 m) apart. Root tops are placed 6 to 10 in. (15-30 cm) below the surface & crowns are covered with 1 to 3 in. om) of manure- or compost-rich soil, then saturated with water. As stalks grow, the trench can be gradually filled in with rich compost & topsoil mix, taking care not to smother plants. Detailed planting instructions often accompany purchased plants. Crown-division is best done during dormancy. Seeds are sown to ¥ in. (,6-1.25 em) deep in sterile seedling medium. Germination: about two to four weeks at 70 to 80°F (21-27°C),

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: Vigorous, prolific, all-male cultivars are available in Hawaiʻi. ‘Jersey Centennial’ & ‘Mary Washington' sirains are highly regarded.

NOTE: There are other edible Asparagus species, but they are much inferior to Asparagus officinalis.

🌳☠️Ⓦ AVOCADO / PEA

Vol II · scan p. 102

AVOCADO / PEA Pear, Alligator Pear, Vegetable Butter, Vegetable Marrow, Abokado, Abacate, Zaboka. Persea americana & varieties, syn. P. drymifolia, syn. P. gratissima, syn. Laurus persea, syn. P. edulis, syn. P. nubigena var. guatemalensis. Lauraceae (Avocado/Laurel) Family. Many varieties & hybrids exist, including some with disease resistance.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed & important staple food for many. Spherical, egg- or pear-shaped fruits with yellowish-green flesh & a single seed. Size of fruit & seed, thickness & color of rind, & quality of flesh all differ greatly with variety, cultivar & conditions. Fruit size can vary from 3 to 12 in. (7.5-30 em) long. Can be buttery, smooth & delicious, or mealy, stringy or watery. Fully ripened, high quality fruit are rich in oil & have a tasty, nutty flavor. Eaten fresh raw in salads, or halved, as guacamole, dips, spreads, soufflés, chilled cream soups, sauces, sandwiches, in tortillas, tacos, or nachos, etc., added to omelettes, chili, stews, ice-creams, sherbets & milk shakes, or frozen (with added Lemon or Lime juice) & can also be pickled. To prevent bitterness when cooking, pieces are added to hot foods just before serving. High in protein, healthy oils, carbohydrates, vitamins A, B's (especially niacin & riboflavin), C, D, E, K, & minerals such as phosphorous, iron, iodine, etc. Contains no cholesterol. Oil extracted from flesh is much like Olive oil. Excellent oil for cooking & salad dressings (long-lasting when refrigerated), or for lighting, soapmaking & a number of cosmetic purposes. Some trees produce vast quantities of small, aborted fruit that can be processed to the delicious cocktail AVO's, called "Kukes" or "Cukes." Although leaves are sometimes brewed as a tea or toasted to flavor stews & other dishes, this may be a questionable practice.

☠️ TOXICITY: All parts of the AVOCADO plant, excluding ripe fruit flesh, are poisonous if eaten in quantity. Raw, under ripe fruits are thought to be toxic.

— scan page 103 · book page 12 —

BEARING: Seedlings can begin to yield in four to twelve years. Vegetatively grown trees fruit much sooner. Nevertheless, until tree is three to four years of age, plucking off developing young fruit is recommended.

MATURITY: From flower to fruit in six to eighteen months, depending on race, variety, location & temperature during fruiting. Time of year depends on variety, but a tree with mature fruit can usually be found somewhere on your island. Even though AVOCADOS have alternating heavy & light years, even light years produce enough for a family. Maturity is noted, in some varieties, when mature fruit begin to fail; then they can all be picked. In others, trial pickings can be home tested & when they've become soft, delicious & buttery about three to four days after picking the tree is ready to harvest en masse. When the fruit nears ripeness, the stem yellows & shrinks where it enters the fruit. Typically the fruit will not soften while hanging on the tree. Mature fruit can be left on the tree several weeks, but extending this too long can reduce the next season's harvest, as well as impair the quality & shelf-life of this season's crop. Immaturely picked fruit can ripen, but tend to shrivel or be rubbery because the oils have not developed.

HARVESTING: Best if clipped from tree leaving a small piece of stem & handled with care. Or picking pole & padded basket.

STORING: It is best to eat AVOCADO fresh, avoiding long storage. Ripe fruit can last in a refrigerator only a few days, preferably wrapped in newspaper to prevent bruising & drying, at 40°F (4.5°C). Left over, halved fruit store better with their seed, in plastic wrap in the refrigerator. Chill-injury occurs at temperatures below 50°F (10°C). Pulp can be blended with Lemon- or Pineapple-juice & frozen, later to be baked in cakes, muffins, breads, etc.

SHIPPING: Pre-cooling advisable. Fruits transport well with refrigeration. Fruit stem can inhibit ripening. Even hard green fruit require careful handling to prevent bruising; fruit are packed for transport in shredded paper in shallow containers.

APPLICATIONS:

NOTE: %6*

TOXICITY: Leaves can

ANIMAL FEED: Excess ripe fruit & oil-pulp residue for livestock, including pigs & chickens-. be deadly as forage or fodder, due to prussic acid. Leaves in ponds can kill fish. Ripe fruit is deadly to canaries.

BEE FORAGE: Nectar & pollen source.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Dwarfs.

COPPICING: Some ability, especially with healthy, vigorous trees. DYE: Seed sap.

FIREWOOD: Fallen branches for fast burning fuel.

LANDSCAPING: Edible ormamental, with constant leaf drop & heavy falling fruits. Dwarfs for shrubs, screens, or containers.

SEE ALSO: DISADVANTAGES, following.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Every part has traditional applications.

SHADE TREE: Dense cover for some shade loving plants.

WOOD: Softish & brittle, with the grain varying from irregular to straight. Although easy to work & takes a smooth polish, AVOCADO wood needs careful curing, is susceptible to termites & is non-lasting, especially when in contact with soil. Utilized in house construction, lumber, furniture, turnery & carving, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive, mostly evergreen tree. Seedling trees can grow 70 ft. (21 m) or taller, graftlings 20 to 50 ft. (6-15 m) & dwarfs as short as 8 ft. (2.4 m) tall. Trunk can reach 2 ft. (60 cm) or wider. Upright or spreading habit. Dense, round or narrow crown. Leathery leaves. Can be briefly deciduous if flowering during a dry period. Clusters of small, fragrant, yellowish-green flowers. In good soil, AVO's are fast growing & strong.

LIFE SPAN: a hundred productive years possible; life often shortened by soil-borne diseases. Most.roots are in top 2 ft. (60 cm) of soil. AVO’S have surface roots, a tap-root, plus large anchor roots, but few hair roots, which limits the trees’ ability to take up water & nutrients.

ORIGIN: Central America & Mexico.

CLIMATE: Subtropical to tropical. The original three races have been highly selected & hybridized, & cultivars suitable for most climates of Hawaiʻi have been created. Although AVOCADO prefers moderate winter temperatures, hot or warm summers & ample rain, they usually need dry weather with 50% relative humidity level, while flowering & setting fruit. Heavy rains, excess humidity, cold weather, or hot, dry winds causes blossom- & fruit-drop. ‘West Indian’ races require higher humidity during flowering & fruiting. Occasionally yields in higher elevations. Intolerant of very hot, very dry, droughty conditions, severe wind & salt spray. Year-round irngation is needed in dry regions.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: AVOCADO need ample space, allowing for their wide spreading branches & roots. Prefer naturally tich, moist, very well drained, humusy soil & pH 6.2 to 6.5. Need uninterrupted sun all day long.

INTOLERANT OF: high water tables; requires at least 7 ft. (2 m) of free drainage. Free moving air is important, but wind protection is also necessary. The trees like calcium & ample humus. Because AVO's have shallow roots, light, frequent watering is best, with periodic heavy irrigation to wash out accumulated salts. Even though AVO's respond to top-dressing from early spring to summer with rich, organic compost or aged manure, encouraging excessive growth before flowering can reduce yield. A cover crop can be planted & cut as mulch. Mulch is maintained, leaving at least a 6 in. (15 cm) ring of bare ground around trunk. Ideally, the mulch is coarse, long lasting & non water-logging. Tree can be fed under the mulch. When chlorosis is apparent, iron chelate & correcting the pH may be helpful.

TOLERATES: many soils, including shallow & rocky ones & a pH range of 5.0 to 8.0. Some cultivars tolerate slightly salty soil,

INTOLERANT OF: heavy, wet, acid or salty soil, in general, as well as flooding & poor drainage. Susceptible to serious root diseases in wet, clayey soil.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Spindly youngsters can be headed back to promote branching. After that, AVO's are only pruned to balance shape, remove dead wood, suckers or awkward branches. Because trunks & branches are easily bumt by sun, lower branches are typically left on. Excessively tali, older trees can be shortened by cutting back. Branches can be propped to avoid breaking under the weight of fruit. Over-bearing varieties benefit from thinning fruit.

ASSOCIATES: Mango, Coconut, Citrus, Papaya, & Banana are often interplanted with AVO's. Cacao alongside.

ADVERSARIES: When the tree is healthy, few insects or diseases will successfully attack. Resistance often depends on cultivar. Intolerant of standing water. AVOCADOS are very susceptible to root-rot (a.k.a.: crown-rot) fungus Phytophthora species, that can kill young & mature trees alike; may make production impossible in some regions. Fruit flies, several other insects & some animals can damage fruit. Some varieties are susceptible to vog damage, causing leaves to yellow & drop.

— scan page 104 · book page 13 —

ORGANIC-CULTURE: Excellent candidate in appropriate locations, with naturally rich, well drained soils, resistant & carefully selected rootstock & clean culture to avoid root-rot. Root-rot might be prevented by providing only pure water, clean planting areas, avoiding diseased soil, maintaining pH level above 6.2 & by increasing soil humus with mulch. Drier areas less likely to have certain pests & fmit-rotting diseases. Aerating treated irrigation water helps remove toxic chlorine. WEEDY?: Escaped & naturalized in Hawaiʻi, but not particularly invasive. Can regrow from stumps. Invasive roots.

DISADVANTAGES: Possible diseases, excessive size & large fruit production.

REMARKS: Finding adapted varieties for your location is advised. SEX: Bisexual (progressively female then male, actually) flowers are either protogynous or protandroeceous. Although most are selffertile, some need a mate nearby. Fruit yield is greatly increased by cross-pollination from different nearby varieties.

POLLINATION: Insects, especially bees. Isolation can hamper pollination.

SEED-SAVING: AVOCADOS typically cannot be trusted to run true & often make inferior fruit. Seed taken from ripe fruit are cleaned & stored in a refrigerator in a perforated plastic bag. Seeds held at room temperatures tend to dry out & only live a couple of weeks. Root-rot may be avoided by planting seeds from tree harvested fruit (not fallen).

PROPAGATION: AVOCADOS are reproduced by grafting, budding, cuttings (some varieties), air-layering, or fresh seeds. Cuttings: leaves left on, under mist. Seeds are soaked in hot water for half an hour then sown with pointed end up, tip just showing, in moist well drained medium. Germination: one to one & a half months at 70 to 75°F (21-24°C); germination is improved by removing seed coat. Vigorous seedlings are transplanted promptly to larger bags in a well drained, fertile medium & fertilized regularly. Young plants need light shade & protection from wind until they become established. CoastalLowMid (& High, depending on variety), WetMesic & Dry (if irrigated) THREE RECOGNIZED RACES,

HYBRIDS & SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: 'Guatemalan.' Persea nubigena var. guatemalensis, Includes cultivars: ‘Edranol,' ‘Hazzard,’ 'Lyon,' ‘Panchoy‘ & dwarfs to 12 ft. (3.6 m).

EDIBILITIES: Large to medium, lighter green fruit with smail seeds. Thick, hard, rough skin, although some have thin skin. Rich flavor. Oil content medium to high. From flowering to ripening about nine months to one year. Late maturing.

DESCRIPTION: Tall vigorous tree. Usually foliage not fragrant. Not as cold hardy as ‘Mexican,’ but more so than West Indian.’ Handles frost to 25°F (-4.5°C).

ORIGIN: Central American highlands. Often grown commercially. ‘Guatemalan’ x 'Mexican.' Includes cultivars: 'Hass,' ‘Hayes,’ 'Fuerte,' 'Sharwil' & 'Lula.'

🌿 GENERAL DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, often nitrogen-fixing annuals & perennials. Twining, climbing, sprawling or bush-like habit. Leaves in three’s. Flat to rounded pods.

ORIGIN: Tropical, to warm temperate western hemisphere, unless otherwise noted.

GENERAL CLIMATE: Most are adapted to warm or hot climates & need drier weather to mature seeds. Most COMMON BEANS require regular watering, especially in youth. General temperate range of 60 to 75°F (15.5-24°C). Most cannot tolerate frost.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: COMMON BEANS, LIMA BEANS, SOYBEAN (vegetable-type), WINGED BEAN & YARD-LONG BEAN are often grown in Hawaiʻi. BEANS for dried seeds are only rarely grown here. PREFERENCES & CULTURE,

IN GENERAL: Depends on species & cultivar. Soil pH 5.5 to 7.0. Although excessive nitrogen stimulates greenery over pod production, monthly feedings (10-30-10) can improve & prolong yield. Most species are widely adapted to soils.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Vining types usually require support to climb. Seedlings begin vining at two or three weeks of age.

ASSOCIATES: Often grown with a support crop such as Corn.

ADVERSARIES: Disease possibilities include rust, anthracnose, bacterial- & halo blight. Diseases are favored by long wet periods. Pest possibilities include white-fly, Chinese Rose-beetle, cutworms, aphids, leaf miners, stink-bugs, pod-borers, French BEANfly, mites, root-knot nematodes, etc. BEANS are very sensitive to pesticide solvents & herbicides.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Many excellent candidates exist.

WEEDY: SEE: individual listings, following.

REMARKS: Generally reliable, although pests & diseases can be a problem. SEX: Hermaphroditic & self-fertile. Often crossing between varieties.

POLLINATION: By bees. PROPAGATION,

IN GENERAL: Almost always by seed, unless otherwise noted. Germination usually requires moisture & warm soil & air, day & night. For longer harvest, they can be successively sown every two to three weeks throughout spring & summer. Seeds are often hard & may need scarification &/or soaking.

INOCULATION: Inoculation with proper bacteria usually increases yield.

NOTABLE SPECIES:

☠️Ⓦ BROAD BEAN

Vol II · scan p. 107 · book p. 17

BROAD BEAN, Fava Bean, Faba Bean, a "Horse Bean,” a "Field B ean," Tick Bean, European Bean, Windsor Bean. aba vulg aris, syn. Vicia faba. Many cultivars exist, varying in seed size (larger seeds being tastier), adaptabilities & include dwarfs.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, esteemed & highly nutritious foods. Mature pods can grow 1 ft. (30 cm) long. Immature seeds, harvested when pods are only 4 to 7 in. (10-17.5 cm) long, are edible fresh raw as an appetizer, but, SEE: TOXICITIES, following. Undried mature seeds, harvested just when pods have become full, are eaten boiled or steamed, mashed, pureed, or sautéed. Dried seeds, harvested when pods have just turned black, are eaten boiled, ground, pickled or fermented to tempeh or soy sauce; high in protein & carbohydrates. Tender, immature pods, harvested when 2 to 3 in. (5-7.5 cm) long, are eaten boiled as a vegetable, or in soups & stews. Young leaves & flowers can be cooked as greens.

MATURITY: eighty-five to one hundred & fifty days, depending on cultivar & temperature.

STORING: seeds of many cultivars freeze weil.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Some people of Mediterranean descent lack a necessary enzyme to digest BROAD BEAN (a.k.a. FAVA BEAN) & can have severe allergic reactions to them & to the pollen. 2. Under developed seeds are thought to be toxic.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: some cultivars are good for hay, silage & fodder for livestock. BEE FORAGE. BIOMASS.

COVER CROP. GREEN MANURE.

LANDSCAPING: backdrop for flower gardens. MULCH MATERIAL.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annual. A large Vetch. Can grow I to 8 ft. (30 cm - 2.4 m) tall, depending on type. Vine or bush habit. Fragrant, white flowers, with central purple blotch. Mostly day-iength neutral. Vigorous. Well anchored with tap-root & lateral-roots.

ORIGIN: Mediterranean region.

CLIMATE: tropical highlands, subtropics & temperate zones. Grows best in cool or warm weather, or in mild winter conditions in hot climates.

PREFERS: moist, average or fertile, well drained loam, near neutral pH & full sun. Responds to lime where needed. Plants can support themselves if rows are planted close together.

TOLERANCES: depend on cultivar, with some accepting occasional flooding, heavy clay, gravely, salty, dry, or acid soils, & heat.

INTOLERANT OF: strong winds, very hot summers, lowland tropics & frost.

☠️ COMMON BEAN

Vol II · scan p. 107 · book p. 17

COMMON BEAN, Garden Bean, Bush Bean, Pole Bean, Green Bean, French Bean, Kidney Bean, Black Bean, Pinto Bean, Wax Bean, Salad Bean, Frijoles. Phaseolus vulgaris & Phaseolus nanus. Hundreds of cultivars exist, including those eaten mainly as DRIED BEANS, SHELL BEANS (syn. SHELLY BEANS), & SNAP BEANS (syn. STRING BEANS). Cultivar Poamoho' was developed for topical areas, resists rust & nematodes. ‘Manoa Wonder’ & ‘Hawaiian Wonder' (flat-podded, pole-types), ‘Kentucky Wonder’ & ‘Blue Lake’ (pole-types), & ‘Greencrop' (flat-podded, bush-type) have all done well in Hawaiʻi.

EDIBILITIES: Important, ancient & esteemed food. Moderate in protein, vitamins A, B, C & G, iron & calcium. Low in.ealories, fat & sodium. Young, tender pods, harvested before seeds are visible, are edible as a fresh raw salad addition, or steamed, boiled sautéed, stir-fried, added to many dishes, soups & stews, pickled, marinated, frozen, or canned. Immature seeds are cooked as a vegetable, or in soups, stews & succotash. Dried seeds are soaked & boiled, or pureed, as baked beans, also in soups & stews, chili, casseroles, dips, sauces, tempeh, canned, or sprouted (PINTO or KIDNEY). Sprouting the seeds makes them more digestible. Young, tender leaves are sometimes cooked as greens.

MATURITY: plants of DRIED BEANS can be gathered when seeds are mature, pods have turned yellow & seeds have shrunken inside their pods. SHELL BEANS are gathered when seeds are full, but not dry, when thin pods have become rubbery, about seventy days. SNAP BEANS are gathered when pods are still young, tender seeds are small, about six weeks after sowing. POLE BEANS need a longer growing season, but produce for a long period & tend to be more flavorful.

HARVESTING: Gathering SNAP BEANS every two to three days prolongs harvest. Entire DRY BEAN plants are pulled up just as seeds start to shatter. The plants can be hung from rafters in bundles of three to four until dry, or the pods can be dried in the sun on trays & turned daily until they are quite brittle.

STORING: dried pods are threshed & seeds stored in sealed containers in a cool, dry spot, or canned.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: straw & foliage for fodder or forage.

ROTATIONAL PLANTING: for heavy feeders. 43s

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annual. Bush cultivars can grow 2 ft. (60 cm) tall, vining types to 10 ft. G m). Lavender, yellowish, pink or white flowers. BUSH BEANS cultivars are day-length neutral, while POLE BEANS are either neutralor short day-length plants. Tap- & lateral-roots.

ORIGIN: western hemisphere.

CLIMATE: tropics, subtropics & temperate zones. Fast growing in warm, moist conditions. In the very hot tropics they may set more pods during winter or at higher elevations.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: BEANS are more often grown for their pods, than for their dried seeds in Hawaiʻi.

PREFERS: rich, moist, well drained, loam, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun. Climbing cultivars need a rough surfaced support at least 8 ft. (22.4 m) tall. Although BEANS sometimes respond to a nitrogen-rich fertilizer, excess nitrogen stimulates greenery over pod production. To avoid damaging surface feeder roots, plants are cultivated only shallowly. Mulch conserves moisture & inhibits weeds.

TOLERATES: most soils, including heavy clay to sandy loam.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly acid soils, weed competition, dry conditions, flooding, frost, & heavy rains during flowering.

ASSOCIATES: Potato, Sweet Potato, Com, Coffee, Cotton, etc.

ADVERSARIES: anthracnose, root-rot, nematodes, mosaic virus, rust & many more; BEANS tend to have more diseases where too wet.

ORGANIC-GROWING: wisdom suggests choosing disease-resistant varieties best suited to your locale. Bush-types, such as 'Greencrop' tend to resist rust. ‘Hawaiian Wonder,' a pole-type, also resists rust. 'Manoa Wonder' resists root-knot nematodes, but is susceptible to rust. To prevent mildew & other diseases, BEANS are watered deeply but infrequently, preferable early in the day. Diseases may be avoided by not walking through BEAN patch, & not cultivating, when plants are wet.

WEEDY: can reseed. SEX: self-fertile.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span can be two to three years when stored at 45 to 60°F (7-15.5°C).

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, ?/Mesic/?

COWPEA & RELATIVES: Vigna unguiculata subspecies. Subspecies, forms & cultivars exist, varying in pod- & seedcolor, -size & -number, plant habit & disease-resistance. See individual subspecies listing, following.. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Important & prolific, especially as pulses (edible seed). Pods from 3 in. to 4 ft. (7.5 cm-1.2 m) long, containing from 8 to 20 seeds, depending on species, subspecies & cultivar. Undried BEAN-like seeds are cooked like SHELLED

BEANS. Dried seeds are high in protein, carbohydrates, vitamins, fiber, iron & potassium. Eaten cooked sike a dried LIMA BEAN; soaked for 24 hours, rinsed & simmered on Jow until quite tender (no soda), then added to soups & stews, ragouts, marinated, ground as a meal for numerous applications, or roasted & ground for a Coffee-replacement. Young tender pods are high in vitamins & are eaten cooked as a SNAP BEAN. Young tender leaves & shoot tips, fresh or dried, have strong cooking odor initially, but mild flavor when done; eaten cooked as greens, mixed vegetables, or chilled & added to salads.

MATURITY: tender green pods can be ready as early as fifty days. Early cultivars for seed-production can bear in one & a half to three months, with later cultivars as long as five months. Ripening staggered; COWPEAS mature over a long period of time, with the pods harvested at the desired stage. Typically gathered when the color of pods is green, before turning yellow.

HARVESTING: large, mature, green pods are picked & seeds removed. Gathering pods regularly prolongs production. Young plants readily regrow when tender leaves & tips are regularly plucked.

STORING: tender pods & fresh seeds are often canned or frozen. Young tender leaves & shoot-tips can be dried.

SHIPPING: only dried seeds ship well.

☠️ TOXICITY: Raw legume seeds tend to be slightly poisonous & are always well cooked.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: climbing varieties, grown on trellis or support plant.

ANIMAL FEED: foliage & pods are relished by livestock as pasturage, hay, straw or silage. Plants cut young can regrow. Hay crop is harvested after the majority of pods are well grown. Seeds for cattle & fowi. Dried crop-residue as cattle fodder.

ANIMAL LITTER: plant-residue as straw.

COVER CROP: especially low-growing cultivars.

EROSION CONTROL: fast growing plants for quickly covering bare soil.

FIBER: one particular COWPEA form produces a sturdy fiber from its flower stalks.

GREEN MANURE: cut young, plants will regrow. Vining types provide the most biomass.

GROUND-COVER: temporary.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: some. MULCH

MATERIAL.

NITROGEN-FIXING: enriches the soil.

PASTURAGE: intercropped with Com, Sorghum, Sudan Grass, etc.

ROTATIONAL PLANTING: with Corn, Cotton, Tobacco, etc.

SHADE: some varieties, trellised, can provide temporary shade.

GENERAL DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annuals. Appearance & height varies with species, subspecies & cultivars. Climbing, upright or prostrate habit. Small clusters of large, whitish or blue flowers. Mostly day-length neutral. Fast growing & vigorous. Long, thick, deep tap-root & many spreading surface roots; large nitrogen-fixing nodules.

LIFE SPAN: short lived.

ORIGIN: African tropics & Asia.

CLIMATE: widely adapted in the tropics, subtropics & sometimes into the temperate zones, with variation within species, subspecies & cultivars. CATJANG COWPEA & YARD-LONG BEANS are probably well adapted to lowland tropics. They tend to thrive during long, hot seasons.

GROWN IN HAWATIYT: although all the COWPEA forms have been introduced to Hawaiʻi, perhaps the best known is the YARD-LONG BEAN. PREFERS,

IN GENERAL: preferences & tolerances differ with the subspecies & their varieties. Prefer moist, rich, well drained, sandy loam, near neutral pH full sun. Plants respond to fertilizing, especially with phosphate. Climbing varieties require a trellis for best yield.

TOLERATES: many soils, including infertile, thin, sandy, clayey or acid ones, some shade & adverse conditions, dryness & drought, in general. COWPEAS are more adapted to hot conditions than most BEANS.

INTOLERANT OF: poor-drainage, cold or frost. Highly acid or alkaline soils can reduce nodulation & result in chlorosis.

ASSOCIATES: often intercropped with Sorghum, Millet & Corn.

ADVERSARIES: pests & diseases vary with subspecies & varieties; could be a limiting factor in some regions & seasons. Susceptible to nematodes, although resistant varieties exist.

REMARKS: important crop plants on small farms in the tropics.

DISADVANTAGES: crops are often lost to insects & disease.

WEEDY: can naturalize. SEX: hermaphroditic. Selffertile, but sometimes readily crosses, depending on conditions, creating fertile hybrids.

POLLINATION: a heavy, larger bug such as a honey- or carpenter bee is needed to push down the keel for pollination.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span of several years is possible.

PROPAGATION: by seeds. Broadcast or drilled. Sown 1 to 1% in. (2.5-4 cm) deep. Germination: reliable, especially in warm soil, at 70°F (21°C) or higher. Usually planted at the start of a hot season. Thinned seedlings can be cooked as greens.

INOCULATION: beneficial when COWPEA is first grown in an area, although some soils contain necessary rhizobia.

THREE NOTABLE SUBSPECIES:

CATJANG COWPEA. Vigna unguiculata subsp. cylindrica. Many cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: The most ancient of the subspecies. Very prolific. Cylinder-shaped pods grow 3 to 5 in. (7.5-12.5 cm) long. Seeds in. (6mm) long. Seeds are eaten as SHELL BEANS. Young tender pods are eaten as SNAP BEANS. 43s

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous annual. Can climb 20 ft. (6 m) tall. Typically a climber, but bush forms exist. Fast growing.

ORIGIN: Africa & Asian tropics.

TOLERATES: drought.

WEEDY: can naturalize.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, MesicDry

GREEN MANURE: particularly those varieties with a ground-covering habit. 43s

ADVERSARIES: resistant cultivars exist.

WEEDY: can naturalize,

YARD-LONG BEAN, Long Bean, Asparagus Bean, Snake Bean, Bodi Bean, Dow Gauk. Vigna unguiculata subsp. Sesquipedalis. Cultivars exist, varying in pod length, color of pods & seeds, including a non-climbing, shade-tolerant dwarf.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed for its tender, under-developed pods. Very high in protein & other nutrients. Prolific, narrow pods can grow to 3 ft. (30-90 cm) or longer, & have a wilted appearance, with seeds to 1/3 to 1/2 in. (8-12 mm) long. Pods are typically harvested when only 1 to 1% ft. (30-45 cm) long, before seeds are full sized & pod is still tender. Eaten fresh raw, chopped & Steamed, boiled, or stir-fried as a SNAP BEAN, sautéed & in Asian cuisine. Seeds, harvested mature & threshed, are small & Widely spaced in their pods, but edible cooked as a DRY BEAN, also can be mashed or sprouted. Young tender leaves & tips can be cooked as greens.

MATURITY: about eighty days. Produces year-round in most of Hawaiʻi.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.
