GARBANZO BEAN, Chick Pea, Gram, Bengal Gram, Egyptian Pea. Cicer arietinum. Many adaptable cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Important food for many. High in fiber, protein, carbohydrates, iron, potassium & the B vitamins thiamine & niacin. Low in fat. One or two large seed per pod. Fresh or dried, whole or split seed are eaten in soups & stews, falafels, fermented into tempeh or miso, parched or toasted & eaten; whole, sprouted, fermented, or roasted & ground as a Coffee-replacement. Seeds can be ground to a meal or flour for soups, sauces, fritters, batters, dumplings, noodles, pancakes, puddings, etc. Tender immature leaves, pods & shoots can be cooked as vegetables. Roots can also be roasted & ground for a Coffee-replacement.

MATURITY: four to six months.

HARVESTING: cut plants are dried & threshed.

STORING: seeds last well if airtight in cool place or can be frozen up to four months.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: dried, threshed foliage & stems as fodder for cattle. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annual. Can grow 2 to 3 ft. (60-90 cm) tall. Upright spreading vine or bush habit. White, pink, greenish or blue flowers. Mostly day-length neutral. Tap- & lateral-roots.

ORIGIN: western Asia.

CLIMATE: temperate zones.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, well drained, light, airy soils, nearly neutral or slightly acid pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: some drought.

INTOLERANT OF: hot, wet tropics, heavy rain & flooding.

ASSOCIATES: grains & other crops.

ADVERSARIES: gram blight, rust & wilt.

WEEDY: probably not invasive. SEX: self-fertile.

POLLINATION: sometimes crossed by bees. Pollination hampered by wet, cloudy weather.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Prefers coarse seedbed. LowMidHigh, WetMesicDry(depending on cultivar)

pw HYACINTH BEAN, Lablab Bean, Bonavista Bean, Bonavist Bean, Egyptian Bean, Indian Bean, Lubia Bean, Seim Bean, Val dal, Parda, Bat-ao, Pi, Bataw, Papapa. Dolichos lablab, syn. D. purpureus, syn. Lablab purpureus, syn. L. vulgaris, syn. niger. Many varieties & several cultivars exist, differing in color of seeds, flowers, foliage, etc., as well as shape & size of pods, although varieties are indistinct as they tend to cross or be crossed. White-seeded forms are preferred for eating.

Seeds are high in protein & carbohydrates, while low in fat. Young tender leaves edible fresh raw, as cooked, or dried. Flowers edible fresh raw, steamed, or in soups & stews. Roots edible cooked.

ANIMAL FEED: some varieties, especially during dry seasons; stay green. Young leaves & stems (green, dried oF as silage), pods & dried seeds are relished by livestock. Temporary forage legume in pastures.

COVER CROP: soil-buildins-

EROSION CONTROL.

GREEN MANURE: slashed before blossoming.

LANDSCAPING: temporary screen. MEDICINAL

QUALITIES.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, short lived, nitrogen-fixing perennial, often grown as an annual or biannual. Vines grow 5 to 25 ft. long. Pioneer species. Possibly an early Polynesian introduction to Hawaiʻi. Twining, trailing, climbing or bush habit. Attractive, lightly fragrant, violet, white, red or pink flowers. Day-length sensitive; short- & long-day cultivars exist. RED LABLAB produces tender pods during short or long days. During long days growth is typically viney.

ORIGIN: Asian & Indian tropics.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Vigorous in warm or hot weather.

PREFERS: garden cultivars need fertile, well drained soil & full sun. Field cultivars are more forgiving.

TOLERATES: acid soil, coarse seedbed, tropical heat, extreme drought (once established), low to high rainfall & shade. Some cultivars, usually field ones, tolerate flooding & others can handle dry conditions. While field varieties are drought resistant, tolerant of poor soil & some frost, garden varieties need better culture.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage & frost.

PRUNING & TRAINING: garden cultivars need support to twine onto. Trellising increases yields.

ASSOCIATES: field cultivars can be intercropped with cereals.

ADVERSARIES: susceptible to root-knot nematode, wilt & occasionally seed-borers.

WEEDY: readily escaping & naturalizing. HYACINTH BEAN can be aggressive & smother surrounding vegetation. Needs to be kept in bounds by grazing, or cutting three or four times a year. Regrows from cut roots. Found wild on disturbed & barren ground, forests, farm-lands, old home- & dump sites, & road- or trail edges. Level of rampancy depends upon variety with D. labiab var. lignosus being a known suspect. SEX: hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: possibly cross-pollinated by insects. Pollination & seed-set is hampered by cold conditions.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: seeds. Soaked for one day & sown 4" (12 mm) deep. Germination: around five to fourteen at 70 to 75°F (21-24°C).

INOCULATION: beneficial.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesicDry

TWO MAIN VARIETIES: Dolichos lablab var. lignosus, syn. Dolichos lignosus. A.K.A.: AUSTRALIAN PEA. Bushy, long lived, odorous perennial, typically grown as an annual field crop & fodder. Dotiches lablab var. lablab, syn. v. typicsus. Grown in gardens for its longer, tasty green pods. Twining, short lived, longer podded perennial.

ADVERSARIES: resistant to yellow BEAN mosaic virus, but several other possibilities exist; this is best resolved by variety trial. WEEDY?: possibly, as it can reseed itself,

SEED-SAVING: for pure seed, varieties require isolation of 1/8 to 1/4 mile (.2-.4k), or for home gardens, 75 to 150 ft. (22.5-45 is adequate.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds or tubers. Tubers for next season are dug in auturon & stored cool for the winter.

Elevation / Rainfall: ?Low/MidHigh, WetMesicDry

COVER CROP: but readily climbs trees with low branches, rough bark, or trunks under 6 in. (15 cm) thick.

ORIGIN: easter hemisphere.

INTOLERANT OF: frost.

☆☠️ SOYBEAN

Vol II · scan p. 112 · book p. 22

☆ SOYBEAN, Soy Bean, Soya, Soja. Glycine max, syn. G. soya, syn. G. hispid®-

SOYBEANS & VEGETABLE SOYBEANS..:..

EDIBOLITIES:

FIELD SOYBEANS: Ancient, versatile pulse, rich in protein, oil, vitamin C& B's, calcium, iron, potassium & soluble fiber. Black-seeded cultivars are typically highest in protein & lowest in oil compared to yellow. Tasty, immature, green seeds are eaten boiled (boiling pods makes shelling easier), shelled & added to many dishes. Mature seeds are strong flavored; this can be improved by pre-boiling with two changes of boiling water. Dried, mature seeds, whole or split, are soaked overnight, pre-boiled simmered until tender (about three hours), then added to many dishes; soups & stews, gumbos, casseroles, grits, paté, flour, or roasted & ground for a Coffee-replacement, & as cheese, curds, tofu, SOY-milk, tempeh, miso, oil, sprouted & soy sauce. (Bill Mollison referred to soy as a “slow growing, toxic bean mostly good for making auto-paint.") SOYBEAN-nuts; pre-boiled seeds are deep-fried for a dozen minutes at 350°F (175°C), then salted. Tofu ("BEAN-cake") is eaten cooked, or added to many foods. SOY-oil is a semi-drying oi] for salads, cooking, margarine or ‘Lecithin.’ Young, tender leaves can be eaten fresh raw or cooked.

MATURITY: two & a half to six & a half months, depending on cultivar.

HARVESTING: pods for dried seeds are gathered mature, after they have ripened & dried, but before they shatter. Plants can be cut at soil level or pulled from ground, dried & threshed.

STORING: seeds are dried to a moisture content of 12%, or less. Dried seeds last well covered in a refrigerator.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Raw seeds contain anti-nutritive properties (although some varieties have less). 2. When grown or dried in wet environments, seeds can be infected by poisonous fungal byproducts.

MORE EDIBILITIES: VEGETABLE SOYBEANS, (AKA: EDIBLE SOYBEANS, or EDAMAME,) have larger seeds than the pulse forms. Delicious steamed or boiled & popped from shells (salt, tamari, Wasabi optional), or added to many dishes. High in protein flavor.

MATURITY: pods are gathered when full, but still green.

HARVESTING: entire plant can be pulled when most of the pods have filled out, or they can be regularly picked, prolonging yield..

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: pasturage (intercropped), hay, fodder, silage & SOYA-meal (residue after oil-extraction). COVER

CROP. GREEN MANURE. OIL: numerous industrial applications, including paint. ROTATIONAL PLANTING.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annual. Can grow 8 in. to 6 ft. (20-180 cm) tall, depending on cultivar. Typically hairy, with an upright, bush habit. Small, insignificant flowers mature into short, hairy pods containing several seeds. Short daylength plant. Fast growing in healthy conditions. Deep tap- & lateral-roots.

ORIGIN: high plateaus of northern China, East Asia.

CLIMATE: temperate (& marginally tropics & subtropics). Will grow where Corn thrives; warm- or hot climates, with ample water during growth period & drier weather during seed-maturation. Narrow range of tolerance. It is important to select an appropriate cultivar, grow it in an appropriate season & variety test for adaptation.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: here, SOYBEANS are grown mostly for their vegetable form, seldom for a dried pulse. Adapted vegetable-type varieties have been developed for the islands. Japanese varieties can grow well here if planted in spring or summer.

PREFERS: deep, rich, moist, loamy soil, near neutral or slightly acid pH (6.0 to 7.0) & full sun. Needs ample space. SOYBEANS are greedy plants, requiring extra fertilization & erosion control. Responds to soil amended with phosphorus, potassium, as well as calcium, where needed.

TOLERATES: most soils, including somewhat acid ones, light drought & frost.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly alkaline or strongly acid soil, dry conditions, flooding, water-logging, excess heat & heavy frost.

ASSOCIATES: interplanted with Corn, or rotated with Com, Millet, Sorghum, Rice, etc.

ADVERSARIES: although SOYBEANS are susceptible to some pests & birds may eat the seedlings, they generally have few diseases. Diseases are more prevalent in wet conditions or in soggy soil.

ORGANIC-GROWING: with resistant cultivars & right growing conditions.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize. SEX: hermaphroditic & self-fertile.

POLLINATION: self-pollinated, with rare crossing by insects.

SEED-SAVING: thoroughly dried seeds are stored in a cool, dry spot. Seed life span is fairly short unless carefully stored.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Needs a moist, well-worked seedbed. Sown 1 to 1% in. (2.5-4 em) deep, on hills or flat. Can be grown at any season, but long day-length varieties will be larger & more productive in summer months. Usually sown spring-time. Germination: five to seven days with soil temperatures above 60°F (155°C).

INOCULATION: SOYBEAN-inoculant, Rhizobium japonicum, is important.

Elevation / Rainfall: ?LowMidHigh, ?MesicDry

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: For the tropics: ‘Duocrop.' of recommendations for Hawaiʻi include 'Kahala' & 'Kailua' (Vegetable-types). Other heirloom EDAMAME cultivars: ‘Butterbeans,' 'Sapporo Midori’ & 'Saya Musume.’ Both 'Kahala' & 'Kailua’ resist root-knot nematodes. New crosses between VEGETABLE & FIELD SOYBEANS have recently been released.

SEE ALSO: GLYCINE. Glycine wighti. In,

Seeds are cooked thirty minutes, water discarded & cooked again until tender. Mature seeds are edible only with prolonged detoxifying cooking in several changes of salted water & removal of seed coat, or made into tempeh. Serious attention by plant breeders could turn this marginal vegetable into a valuable food. Immature pods are boiled as a snap

BEAN. Young tender leaves can be cooked as greens.

TOLERATES: somewhat heavy or water-logged soil.

INTOLERANT OF: dry conditions & flooding.

TEPARY BEAN. Phaseolus acutifolius. Many cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, esteemed, Indigenous-American food. Seeds are sweet & rich in protein. Edible when soaked overnight & cooked a very long time. Also eaten in soups & stews, or parched & coarse ground.

MATURITY: sixty to ninety-five days.

STORING: lasts well with dry conditions. Long storage hardens seeds; longer cooking required.

⚠️ CAUTION: can create painful flatulence & therefore are not recommended for babies under a year,

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: hay & dried pods as fodder, young pods & leaves as forage. CATCH CROP. COVER CROP.

GREEN MANURE. #3s

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous annual. Can grow 10 in. (25 cm) tall. Bush or weakly vining habit with greater vining with more water. Light lavender or white flowers.

ORIGIN: Sonoran Desert.

CLIMATE: temperate & subtropical zones. Adapted only to warm or hot desert conditions. Tends to flower during short days.

PREFERS: needs moisture to germinate, then can grow in sandy, dry, weil drained, alkaline soil, with full sun,

TOLERATES: heat & drought, dry conditions, heavy infrequent rains & somewhat salty or calcareous soils.

INTOLERANT OF: certain salty soils, humid conditions, tropical wetness, water-logged soil, flooding & frost.

ASSOCIATES: Sorghum.

ADVERSARIES: very resistant to bacterial blight (a common Bean disease in tropics), but susceptible to other diseases in unsuitable climates.

WEEDY: can reseed. SEX: probably self-fertile.

☠️ VELVET BEAN

Vol II · scan p. 113 · book p. 23

VELVET BEAN, Florida Velvet Bean, Cowhage, Cowitch, Benguk. Stizolobium deeringianum, syn. Mucuna deeringiana, syn. M. pruriens, syn. M. pruriens var. utilis subspecies deeringianum.

TWO TYPES: Long- & short-day types exist, with short-day being best for the tropics. Cultivars of both exist.

APPLICATIONS: Principie application is as a ground-cover, not as a food. Most parts require special processing to be edible.

EDIBILITIES: Marginal as food. Very young seeds are edible cooked like shelled Peas. Very young pods can be eaten cooked. Young leaves can be cooked as a potherb. Mature seeds are questionable as a food, but have been eaten sprouted & boiled, also in tempeh & miso making, or roasted & ground for a Coffee-replacement.

HARVESTING: seeds are gathered from the ground after vines have died back.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Confusion & unsteadiness have been reported after eating certain varieties. 2. Raw seeds contain several antinutrients & always require cooking. 3. Raw seeds contain a volatile oil that irritates eyes. 4. Ripe pods of some varieties have stiff, highly irritating, air-borne hairs.

APPLICATIONS: ALLEY-CROPPING.

ANIMAL FEED: foliage excellent livestock fodder or forage. BIOMASS.

COVER CROP: mines deep nutrients.

EROSION CONTROL: temporary. GREEN MANURE.

GROUND-COVER: smothers all neighbors, including small trees.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: seeds are a L-Dopamine source. MULCH MATERIAL.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annual. Stems can grow 60 ft. (18 m) long. Climbing or trailing habit. Climbs by tendrils. Purple flower clusters mature into thick velvety pods with large grayish seeds. Vines die back after seeding. Although slow growing at first, the plant is fast & aggressive once established. Sustained by deep roots.

ORIGIN: Asia.

CLIMATE: tropics. Thrives in warm or hot conditions. Although most varieties blossom during short-days, there is a long-day variety with irritating, hairy pods.

PREFERS: average, well drained, sandy soil.

TOLERATES: dense soil, heavy rain, sea-sides, & drought, once established.

INTOLERANT OF: waterlogged soil, pH of 4.5 or lower & cool temperatures.

ASSOCIATES: Com, etc.

ADVERSARIES: slugs & snails.

WEEDY: readily volunteers from fallen seed, thus it is important to harvest or graze before blossoming to prevent regrowth.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: seeds. Sown early spring 1! in. (2.5 cm) deep & kept moist.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesicDry

☆☠️ WINGED BEAN

Vol II · scan p. 113 · book p. 23

☆ WINGED BEAN, Goa Bean, Asparagus Pea, an "Asparagus Bean," Four-angled Bean, Princess Pea, Manila Bean, Pallang, Kabay, Cigarillas, Sigarillas, Segidillas. Psophocarpus tetragonolobus. Varieties & cultivars exist, including: ‘Square,’ ‘Bogor & 'Chimbu.'

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed by many. Plant is entirely edible. Mature, square or flat, winged pods can grow 1% ft. (45cm) long. Very small green pods are edible fresh raw. Young, half-grown pods are cooked like snap Beans. Frequent harvesting promotes higher yield. Immature seeds are eaten in soups & stews, stir-fries, etc. Mature, fresh seeds are edible when cooked like shelled Beans, boiled, steamed, roasted, in soups & stews, vegetable dishes & with fish. Hard dry seeds are very high in protein, containing vitamin E & iron. To soften, seeds can be boiled in water, soaked overnight, & then rinsed, washed & cooked until done. Seeds are also edible parched, roasted, fried, steamed, in soups, pureed, as tempeh, flour, processed for an edible oil, or as Coffee-replacement. Flowers & flower-buds are eaten fresh raw in salads, steamed, battered & fried (reportedly similar to cooked mushrooms). Young tender leaves, shoots & tendrils are rich in vitamin A & eaten cooked. Irregularly shaped, tuber-like roots of some varieties are sweet, nutty & very high in protein. Roots are harvested at seven to eight months & eaten fresh raw, boiled, fried, baked or roasted. Cooked dried seeds & roots are possible protein-rich foods for weaning babies.

— scan page 114 · book page 24 —

☠️ TOXICITY: Raw seeds have several anti-nutrients or toxic substances & must always be cooked.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: can be grown on nurse trees or trellis.

ANIMAL FEED: foliage & spent stems as livestock fodder. COVER CROP. GREEN MANURE.

SHADE: temporary cover when trellised.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, short lived, perennial, nitrogen-fixing vine. Often grown as an annual. Can reach 15 ft. (4.5 m) or taller. Climbing or trailing habit. Climbs by twining. Clusters of white or bluish flowers. Most varieties blossom only during short days, but there are several day-length neutral varieties. Vigorous & fast growing, once established. Well anchored with thick, shallow, tuber-like roots. Large, abundant root nodules.

ORIGIN: Asia & India.

CLIMATE: hot, humid tropics. Although it can tolerate cool weather, temperatures of 40°F (4.5°C) or below would be harmful.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: adapted to the hot, humid, wet regions.

PREFERS: rich, moist, well drained, loamy soil, acid pH & full sun. Easy to grow. Responds to feeding.

TOLERATES: poor soils, very rainy conditions & some flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: dry or water-logged soil & frost.

PRUNING & TRAINING: trellised for greater vigor & yield.

ASSOCIATES: leguminous trees can provide living-trellis.

ADVERSARIES: although WINGED BEANS are resistant to most pests & diseases, they are susceptible to nematodes. SEX: hermaphroditic, self-fertile. Occasionally crossing.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Germination is quickened by scarifying & soaking Over night, but is not necessary. Inoculation is not required. Sown 1 in. (2.5 cm) deep at the start of a rainy season. Germination: one to four weeks. Seedlings require adequate moisture. Slow, fragile, young plants need care & support at first.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

☆🌿☠️ BEET / PIKA

Vol II · scan p. 114 · book p. 24

☆ BEET / PIKA Garden Beet, Table Beet, Mangel, Sugar Beet, Blood Turnip. Beta vulgaris Crassa Group. Chenopodiaceae (Goosefoot) Family. (SEE: SWISS CHARD, following.) There are also many unique cultivars, including striped, golden, white, cylindrical, flattened & miniature BABY BEETS. There are two type of

GARDEN BEETS: Early BEETS, which grow better in cool conditions. Late BEETS, which handle more heat & store well.

EDIBILITIES: Nutritious & highly esteemed foods. Roots are eaten grated raw in salads, as Borscht, cooked & cooled for salads, or boiled, baked in their skins, juiced, fermented as a juice, or pickled. Delicious, nutritious leaves are often steamed as greens, or added to soups, stews, or roasted & braised dishes. Sugar can be extracted from SUGAR BEET root. Some varieties of SUGAR BEET roots are very good to eat when young, plus the greens are edible cooked.

☠️ TOXICITY: As raw leaves contain oxalic acid, BEET greens should not be eaten without being cooked.

MATURITY: GARDEN BEET roots can mature in 45 to 75 days, depending on cultivar. Roots tend to get bitter & may split if grown too large. BABY BEETS, or very young regular BEETS, can be harvested for a gourmet food. SUGAR BEETS mature in eighty to one hundred & twenty days. MANGELS take as long as a hundred to one hundred & twenty days. —

HARVESTING: Mature BEETS destined for storage are preferably harvested when the soil is dry, pulled with their green tops left on. When trimming BEETS for cooking, loss of color can be prevented by leaving 1 in. (2.5 cm) of stem on.

STORING: BEET roots hold up well for four or five months when stored in an evenly cold, dark place at 33 to 48°F (.5 - 9°C), with enough humidity to prevent shrinkage. They may be layered in cold, lightly moisten sand. BEETS can also be canned or pickled. To retain best flavor & texture when freezing, BEETS are cooked & skinned first.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: GARDEN BEET roots & greens are good fodder for rabbits. MANGELS are a large, coarse root-crop typically grown as forage or fodder for livestock: goats, cattle, milk-cows, rabbits & chickens. Their roots grow mostly above ground. Several cultivars exist, varying in shape & color, with some having young roots tender enough to eat. SUGAR BEETS are also grown for fodder, especially sheep, but too sugary for cattle. SUGAR BEET typically grow underground.

LANDSCAPING: Some varieties, such as 'Lutz Green Leaf,' have attractive slender leaves suitable for flower beds or borders.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous biennial, grown as an annual. Can grow 15 in. to 3% ft. G8-100 cm) tall. Day-length neutral. Some BEETS form partially above the soil, others underground. Deep tap-root & fibrous laterals.

ORIGIN: Mediterranean region.

CLIMATE: Tropics, subtropics, to temperate summers. Ideal temperature range is between 60 & 65°F (15.5-18°C). In hot areas BEETS prefer to grow before or after deep summer heat. Hot weather promotes woody, stringy or malformed roots & cause early bolting, but plant may still be valuable for its greens. Tolerates light frost & dry spells. Intolerant of continually dry conditions.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: BEETS prefer cool, moist climates in the mid- or higher elevations here.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Easy to grow. Light feeder. Prefers deep, moist, fertile, well drained, friable, sandy loam, pH 6.0 to full sun. Deeply amending with compost or aged manure improves soil. Mulch helps prevent surface crusting & retains soil moisture. Evenly moist soil & well-balanced fertilizer promotes fast growth, high quality & pest-resistance. Monthly feeding sustains this vigorous growth.

TOLERATES: many soils.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly acid soil.

— scan page 115 · book page 25 —

ASSOCIATES: Brassica Family, including Cabbage & Kohirabi, as well as Lettuce & Onion. Early BEETS can be interplanted among late Potatoes. BEETS can also be planted in rotation before Peanuts,

ADVERSARIES: Basically free, although possible pests include "scab" & leaf miner. BEETS reportedly dislike Pole Beans.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate, especially with right cultivars & conditions. Thinning helps reduce problems & promotes higher production. Keeping soil humus content high & pH around neutral may prevent “scab.” Leaf miner infected leaves are trimmed off. Internal browning or black spots are symptoms of boron deficiency; prevented by maintaining adequate mineral levels with a wide-spectrum supplement such as seaweed.

WEEDY: BEETS can naturalize, but are not considered invasive. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: BEETS are wind-pollinated. Pollen can be carried as far as 1 mile (1.6 k).

SEED-SAVING: To prevent cross-pollination with varieties or other members of this family, plants must be isolated by 1/8 to 1/4 mile (.2-.4 k) for home gardening, or % to 1 mile (.8-1.6 k) for pure seed. Seed life span: up to four years, if dry & cool.

PROPAGATION: “Seeds.” Sown directly 4 to % in. (1.25 - 2 cm) deep (deeper when soil is warmer.) Soil-crusting prevented with a light mulch of compost, aged-manure, vermiculite, etc. Germination: five to fourteen at soil temperature of 50 to 85°F (10-29°C). BEET “seeds” are actually small fruits containing two to six seeds (except for the "mono-germ" types). To loosen & separate the clusters, they can be soaked for twenty-four hours. BEETS benefit from thinning twice by carefully snipping or harvesting small roots until there's 2 to 4 in. (5-10 cm) around each plant. If seeds are sown sparsely, thinnings will be big enough to eat. When sown every one to three weeks, plot could provide continuous supply & enough to store.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, WetMesic

☆🌿☠️ SWISS CHARD

Vol II · scan p. 115 · book p. 25

☆ SWISS CHARD. chard, Silver-Leaf Beet, Spinach Beet, Indian Spinach, Leaf Beet, Perpetual Spinach. Beta vulgaris Cicla Group. Many cultivars exist, including red-veined, white-veined, wide-veined & ornamentals. Varying in resistance to heat, cold, bolting, or diseases. Cultivar 'Lucullus' is good for tropical conditions.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed. High in vitamins A, B, C, minerals such as calcium & phosphorus, & other nutrients. Leaves are more succulent than BEET greens; eaten steamed, boiled, stir-fried or in quiches, soups & as a Spinach-replacement. Stalks need slightly more cooking than the leaves. Leaves are cleaned well before cooking to avoid hidden slugs, snails, etc.

☠️ TOXICITY: Although some cultivars, especially the LEAF BEETS, are occasionally eaten fresh raw in mixed salads, this is a questionable practice due to oxalic acid content.

MATURITY: First harvest as early as four to eight weeks is possible.

HARVESTING: Large outer leaves are cut at base, leaving smaller, inner leaves to continue growing.

STORING: Tolerates freezing well.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Fodder for poultry.

LANDSCAPING: Red forms are attractive in 1 flower gardens.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

SOEL-CONDITIONING & SOIL-BUILDING: Deep roots aerate compacted soil & add beneficial humus.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous biennial. Can grow 3.3 ft. (1 m) tall, although shorter cultivars exist. Fast growing. LIFE

SPAN: two to three years in warm climates. Deep, extensive tap- & lateral-roots.

ORIGIN: Mediterranean region.

CLIMATE: SEE: BEET. Heat- & cold resistant cultivars exist. SWISS CHARD tolerates hotter weather than BEETS & some cultivars can handle drought. Intolerant of intense summer heat in dry regions.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: SWISS CHARD is relatively easy to grow. Similar conditions & culture as BEETS. Thrives in average or nich, moist, humusy, well drained soil, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun. Benefits from mulch.

TOLERATES: salty soil.

ADVERSARIES: basically free from pests & diseases. Red-stemmed varieties tend to be less troubled by insects. Susceptible to root-knot nematodes.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate in good conditions. Foliar seaweed spray keeps plants vigorous & resistant. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Wind.

WEEDY: SWISS CHARD can naturalize.

SEED-SAVING: SEE: BEET. Seed life span: two to four years if stored dry & cool.

PROPAGATION: By seeds. Sown % to % in. (1.25 -2 cm) deep. Germination: about a week. Thinned to 6 to 10 in. (15-25 cm) spacing. SWISS CHARD needs more room than BEETS.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆☠️ BELEMBE / TAHITIAN TARO

Vol II · scan p. 115 · book p. 25

☆ BELEMBE / TAHITIAN TARO Tahitian Spinach, Tanier Spinach. Xanthosoma brasiliense. Araceae (Arum) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Mild, highly palatable vegetable. Considered the "Queen of the Spinach's." Entire leaf & upper stem can be cut up cooked for at least a half hour, changing the water about twenty minutes through the cooking process. The resulting greens are served spiced as desired or splashed with vinegar. High in vitamin A & moderate in vitamin C. Leaf & stem can be cooked separately. Stem & main leaf-vein can be chopped for soups & stews. Corm-like tubers are small, 4 to 1 in. (.6-2.5 cm) in diameter, not very starchy, thus are rarely eaten. Unlike Taro, BELEMBE is traditionally cultivated exclusively for its leaves. High quality, low yield.

☠️ TOXICITY: Because of the calcium oxalate crystals, BELEMBE must always be cooked, changing water at least once.

BEARING: Suitable leaves for harvesting can begin in two to three weeks, but six weeks is needed for leaves to mature.

HARVESTING: The large, mature leaves, unless yellowed or damaged, are harvested in preference to the young leaves. It is always advisable to leave plenty of new foliage for rapid regrowth. Stems are cut at their base, avoiding a stump.

🌳 BO TREE

Vol II · scan p. 116 · book p. 28

BO TREE Bodhi Tree, Peepul, Sacred Tree, Sacred Fig. icus religiosa. Moraceae (Fig) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Immature leaf buds can be eaten cooked as a famine food.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: leaves for fodder.

LANDSCAPING: omamental tree. MEDICINAL QUALITIES. ROADSIDE &

PARKING-LOT TREE.

SACRED: tree of Buddha's enlightenment, Vishnu's birth & Hindu fertility. East Indian saying: “It is better to die a leper than pluck a leaf of a Peepul." SHADE TREE. WINDBREAK.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Large attractive tree. Can grow 60 ft. (18 m) tall. Upright. Open foliage. Elegant, quivering leaves. Can be briefly deciduous during spring. Occasional aerial roots.

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: India.

CLIMATE: hot & wet. GROWN IN

Ⓦ BREADNUT

Vol II · scan p. 117 · book p. 29

BREADNUT Seeded Breadfruit, Chataigne. Artocarpus altilis ‘Seminifera.'’ Moraceae (Fig) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Highly valued food. Fruit are covered with short, soft prickles. Contain scant pulp, but is packed with Chestnutsized seeds ("Pan de pepita.") Seeds are irregularly spherical with a thin brown seed coat. Eaten fried, boiled (retains firm texture), or roasted. Cooked seeds can be peeled as a snack, or combined with other foods. Said to taste like Chestnuts, but having a distinctive flavor alt their own. High in carbohydrates, with some protein & moderate fat. Unripe fruit, with its immature seeds, can be cooked as a vegetable.

BEARING: can fruit in three years.

MATURITY: when fruit-skin turns from green to yellow.

HARVESTING: fruit are usually allowed to ripen & fall. Upon falling, fruit often flatten & seeds can be picked from the pulp.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: fruits as pig food. Seeds can be cooked & fed to chickens.

GLUE: from milky latex sap.

SHADE: dense cover.

WINDBREAK: planted closely for a fast, effective windbreak.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. BREADNUT is the original, seeded form of the variant Breadfruit. Can grow 60 ft. (18 m) tall. Very large, deeply lobed leaves. Greenish-yellow flower spikes. Fast growing. Roots are deep & spreading.

LIFE SPAN: twenty to thirty years.

ORIGIN: Asia.

CLIMATE: tropics. Requires ample rain.

PREFERS: deep, moist, rich, well-aerated, well drained soil, slightly acid or neutral pH & full sun. Flourishes with weed control, mulch, ample water & regular fertilization. Young trees need protection from animals.

TOLERATES: many soils.

INTOLERANT OF: prolonged droughts, cold climates, & alkaline-, strongly salty- or poorly aerated soil.

ASSOCIATES: normally grown as a single tree, or a few together. Produces dense shade very few understory crops can tolerate.

ADVERSARIES: although remarkably free of pests, BREADNUT should never be replanted where one has died.

WEEDY: can naturalize, but not noxious.

DISADVANTAGES: falling fruits. SEX: monoecious, each tree has female & male flowers.

POLLINATION: wind.

SEED-SAVING: seeds quickly die if permitted to dry.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds or vegetatively like Breadfruit. Fresh seed can be planted directly in loosened soil mixed with compost.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SEE ALSO: BREADNUT, RAMON. Brosimum alicastrum. \n Permacopia IIL. the Weed Book.

Ⓦ CABBAGE & RELATIVES / KĀPIKI

Vol II · scan p. 118

CABBAGE & RELATIVES / KĀPIKI Brassica species & others. Apiaceae (previously Brassicaceae) (Mustard) Family. Many species, forms & thousands of varieties in this Genus have been domesticated in both hemisphere. These are grouped together here for convenience, having much in common in spite of differences in appearance. (SEE: INDIVIDUAL LISTINGS FOR DETAILS.) EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Ancient, nutritious & esteemed foods. Rich in calcium, vitamins A & C, & a good source of protein vitamins. Various plant parts, including leaves, flowers, heads & seeds are eaten raw in salads & slaws, or steamed, sautéed, stir-fried, added to stews & soups, sprouted or pickled, etc. Most have a strong distinctive flavor. Cooking with milk & Caraway seed, or with Celery, suppresses the aroma of sulfur. Winter Savory reduces the gas. Sometimes roots such as Rutabaga, are eaten steamed, baked, boiled, mashed, or fried.

MATURITY: Days to maturity varies with cultivar, climate, soil & culture.

HARVESTING: Most Brassicas have a long harvest period. Cut-&-come-again.;

STORING: Many Brassicas can be stored long, unwashed, in a dark, cool place. They can also be frozen, pickled, salted, or processed into sauerkraut, kimchee, etc. APPLICATIONS,

IN GENERAL:

GREEN MANURE: Some species...

LANDSCAPING: There are ornamental varieties with ruffled, colorful, or variegated leaves for edible landscaping.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Most Brassicas are noted for having healing, cancer-fighting qualities. Rich in nutrients.

GENERAL DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous annuals & biennials, usually grown as annuals. Although differing in superficial morphology, all are succulent, herbaceous plants. Racemes of white, yellow, or purple flowers with four petals mature into long, narrow seed-pods. Generally rapid growing. Generally tap-rooted, with numerous fine laterals.

ORIGINS: Eurasia, North America, North temperate region, southwest Asia, depending on species..

GENERAL CLIMATE: These species are best suited to moist, cool climates. These Mustard Family species are some of the most successful temperate greens for the tropics. Preferred general temperature range: 60 to 65°F (15.5-18°C). Many more heattolerant cultivars are needed.

GROWN IN HAWALI: This Family produces abundantly in the moist, higher regions here. With the availability of adapted varieties, they can yield well at lower elevations, too.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Require plenty of sun, air & space. Prefer moist, rich, loose, humusy, sandy loam, pH 5.5 to 8.0 (depending on species & variety), & full sun, or light shade in hot climates. Balancing the pH level improves pest-resistance. Most respond to soil amended with aged-manure or compost, worked in deeply, long before planting. Like to be fed monthly. ARUGULA, COLLARDS, etc., are more succulent & mild when protected under floating row-cover (in the highlands). Mulch is much appreciated by all these species.

TOLERATES: many soils.

ASSOCIATES: This Family likes to grow near aromatic plants & those with profuse blossoms. Some protective herbs include: Dill, Chamomile, Celery, Garlic, Hyssop, Marijuana, Nasturtium, Onion, Peppermint, Rosemary, Sage, Southemwood, Tansy, Thyme Wormwood. Also partial to the proximity of vegetables such as Beets, Lettuce, Onions & Potatoes. Tagetes (Marigold) nearby reportedly repels rot-knot nematodes.

ADVERSARIES: As this Family tends to attract similar pests, such as CABBAGE-moth & aphids, slugs & snails; some protection may be necessary. This Family is also said to dislike the proximity of Pole Beans, Strawberries & Tomatoes.

ORGANIC-GROWING: For the fewest problems, healthy, balanced soil is important, as is a three year rotation, good sanitation & adequate air-flow. Deficiency of lime, phosphorus, or potassium will retard heading. Lack of boron may create heart-rot in

CABBAGE. Crop-rotation is especially needed in the case of root-knot nematodes. Amending soil with crushed coral or eggshell is one deterrent to nematodes, Floating-row-cover protects tender leaves. Aphids farmed by ants can be repelled with water- or hot pepper-spray, dusting with limestone or diatomaceous earth, or interplanting & mulching with non-invasive Mints other ant-repellent plants. Nearby wild Brassicas spp. can host downy mildew. It's smart to plant resistant varieties already known to do well in your area.

DISADVANTAGES: The majority of these species tend to bolt & become bitter during hot weather.

REMARKS: Leafy forms, compared to the heading kinds, are typically higher in nutrition, easier to grow & less troubled by insects. While perennial vegetables may be preferred for ease, these traditional vegetables grow fast, give a high yield & repay the efforts made to cultivate them (& can almost become perennial.) Most varieties are of much better flavor & tendermess than those commercially available. Seeds of most Brassica species are readily available. SEX: Typically hermaphroditic. Usually self-incompatible, though crossing readily occurs. Some spp. & varieties self-fertile.

POLLINATION: Cross-fertilized by insects, especially bees.

— scan page 119 · book page 31 —

SEED-SAVING: If grown for home seed, varieties & cultivars need at least 1/8 to 1/4 mile (.2-.4 k) separation to avoid crossing. For pure seed, a separation of % to 1 mile (.8-1.6 k) is suggested. Or, a ‘select’ cultivar can be caged & bees introduced for pollination. Seed life span: from a few months up to fifteen years, PROPAGATION,

IN GENERAL: By seeds, either sown directly, or in containers to transplant. Sown % to ¥ in. (.6-1.25 cm) deep. Germination: several days at a preferred soil temperature 75°F (24°C) & strong, direct light. Root-ball needs careful handling when transplanting. Seedlings are kept well watered. Planted in spring, summer or fall, with maturity planned to coincide with cool weather. Seedlings benefit from thinning. Harvest can be prolonged by successive sowings, or planting varieties with different maturities.

SOME IMPORTANT SPECIES & VARIETIES: Ww ARUGULA, Rogquette, Rocket Saiad, Garden Rocket, Rocket, Rucola. Eruca sativa, syn. E. vesicaria. slow-bolting cultivar is available.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient esteemed greens. Foliage & tender stems have a nutty to peppery flavor when raw, bland when cooked. Eaten fresh in salads, cooked as mixed greens, sautéed with Olive oil & Garlic, or in casseroles, etc. Older leaves can be pureed for sauces or soups. Leaves are reportedly high in the free amino-acid proline. Flowers can be eaten in mixed salads, or as a gamish. Seeds provide a MUSTARD-replacement & source of "Jamba oil."

MATURITY: under one month from seeding to first harvest. Thinnings can be eaten.

HARVESTING: largest leaves are cut at stem-bases, leaving the plant to keep growing. Continuous harvest prolongs yield,

APPLICATIONS: BEE FORAGE. CATCH CROP.

CONTAINER-GROWING: window sills.

GROUND-COVER: temporary. 23+

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous annual. Foliage can grow 1 ft. G0 cm) tall, then reaching 3 ft. (.9 m) when flowering. Fast growing & easy.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

CLIMATE: thrives in cool, humid weather.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: year-round greens are possible.

PREFERS: moist, rich soil, full sun (part shade in hot conditions).

TOLERATES: cold weather & acidity.

INTOLERANT OF: hot lowlands; bolts in hot weather.

ADVERSARIES: basically free. SEX: hermaphroditic.

WEEDY: readily seeds; can naturalize.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Broadcast & raked in, or drilled % in. (6 mm) deep. Thinned well. L?/MidHigh, WetMesic

☆🌿 BROCCOLI

Vol II · scan p. 119 · book p. 31

☆ BROCCOLI. Brassica oleracea Botrytis Group. Several varictics & many cultivars exist, including: Cultivars for lowland Hawaiʻi: "Blue Ocean,' ‘Copenhagen Market,' "De Ciceo,’ 'Express Corona,’ ‘Golden Acre,’ 'Greenbud,’ ‘Green Comet,’ ‘Sucession' & others. For higher, cooler elevations: ‘Express Corona,’ ‘Atlantic,’ ‘Waltham 29' & ‘Premium Crop.'

EDIBILITIES: Tasty esteemed vegetable. Exceptionally high in vitamins & other nutrients. Immature flower-heads & stems are boiled as a vegetable, served au gratin, in stir-fries, soups, or marinated & pickled. Leaves are higher in nutrients than the heads are delicious cooked as greens.

MATURITY: one & a half to five months, depending on cultivar; main head is best at twothirds its potential size, when buds are still tight & green.

HARVESTING: stem is cut at an angle, low on the stalk to promote subsequent side-shoots. Prolonged harvest season is possible.

STORING: freezes well.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous annual. Can grow 2% to 4 ft. (.75-1.2 m) tall. Branching habit. Although BROCCOLI is fairly deep rooted, side roots are easily damaged with near cultivation.

LIFE SPAN: about one year.

ORIGIN: Europe.

CLIMATE: temperate & subtropical zones. Easy to grow in cool weather, with an ideal temperature range of 60 to 70°F (15.5-. 21°C). Coolness produces tight heads; hot weather promotes early bolting.

PREFERS: moist, deep, rich, well drained, humusy soil, 5.5 to 7.0 pH & full sun. Requires good care & feeding. Responds to deeply dug soil amended with aged-manure or compost. Mulching suppresses weeds, provides steady moisture & cools the soil. BROCCOLI requires steady rapid growth; constant moisture & monthly feedings.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on cultivar & can include hot or cold conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage & hard-pan.

ADVERSARIES: damp, over-crowded conditions can lead to diseases. Possible diseases include downy mildew, black-leg, black-rot & wirestem. Possible pests include CABBAGE-womm, -lopper & -webworm, red spider mites, aphids, slugs & snails.

ORGANIC-GROWENG: floating row-cover controls caterpillar pests (in cooler bighlands). Planting disease-resistant cultivars is beneficial. Water lack can cause hollow stems. Good ventilation can be provided by thinning well.

SEED-SAVING: readily crosses with other B. oleracea varieties. KALE, CABBAGE, CAULIFLOWER, KOHLRABI, etc.: needs isolation of 1/8 mile (.2 k) for home gardening, or 4 to % mile (.4-.8 k) for pure seed.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown in. (1.25 cm) deep, directly, or in containers to transplant. Germination: four to eighteen days. Seedlings can be ready to transplant in one to one & a half months, or when 4 to 6 in, (10-15 cm) tall. Firm soil around transplants well. Over-crowding can be avoided by allowing at least 18 in. (45 cm) between plants. Seedlings need daily water, preferably early in the day, so leaves can dry. LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆ PERENNIAL BROCCOLI. Brassica oleracea Botrytis asparagoides.

DESCRIPTION: A fairly recent British cultivar. Ww SPROUTING BROCCOLI, Cape- or Asparagus Broccoli, Purple Cauliflower. B. oleracea Italica Group. Several cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: An ancient BROCCOLI. Produces multiple florets like tny CAULIFLOWER. Tender under-developed flowerheads & tender stem centers taste & are prepared much like Asparagus. Eaten fresh raw as a salad addition, or boiled, steamed, sautéed, au gratin, tempura, pickled, marinated, or frozen. Leaves can be cooked as greens.

MATURITY: harvested before flowering.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous annual. Can grow 4 ft. (1.2 m) tall. Not as greedy as many Brassica species.

PREFERS: moist, cool conditions & well drained, average soil.

TOLERATES: drier & hotter conditions than CAULIFLOWER & frosts.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on cultivar.

INTOLERANT OF: tropical lowlands (especially in summer), or hot, dry conditions.

ADVERSARIES: slugs, snails & aphids could be problematic, especially when young.

ORGANIC-GROWING: floating row-cover protects plants from CABBAGE-moth, etc. (in the highlands). Iron-phosphate slug-killer like "Sluggo,"™ etc.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, WetMesic

☆ CABBAGE, kapikipiki. Brassica oleracea Capitata Group. Many cultivars exist, including those with varying leaf-forms & colors. Several are adapted to tropical lowlands, some resist splitting, & others are slow-bolting, or disease-resistant.

EDEBILITIES: Nutritious ancient food. Fresh heads are high in calcium, vitamin C, a surprisingly good source of complete protein, as well as vitamins A & B. Eaten raw, or in salads, coleslaw, cooked, soups & stews, pickled, stuffed CABBAGE-rolls, New England boiled dinner with corned beef, or fermented as sauerkraut or kimchee. Sulfur provides its characteristic aroma. Stems, peeled, are excellent boiled or pickled. Seeds can be sprouted.

MATURITY: early types are ready in seven to eight weeks; late types in three to five months, depending on cultivar. Gathered before heads split open.

HARVESTING: stalk is cut at base with a sharp knife.

STORING: most cultivars can last up to six weeks if kept cool.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: various ornamental SAVOY CABBAGES (Kawao), FLOWERING CABBAGES, or miniatures for flower beds, borders, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous biennial, usually grown as an annual. Can grow 1% ft. (45 cm) tall. Yellow flowers. Moderately slow growing. Shallow roots.

ORIGIN: Europe.

CLIMATE: likes cool conditions. Some of the colorful cultivars need frost to deepen their color.

PREFERS: moist, rich, well drained, humusy soil, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun (or part shade in hot weather.) Heavy feeder. Responds to light, regular nitrogen applications. Early harvest is associated with sandy soil, while in clay, yields are higher, though later. Although CABBAGE tends to bolt in hot weather, full-grown heads can be twisted slightly to retard this tendency. Benefits from mulch.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on cultivar, but CABBAGE are generally quite adaptable & many cultivars can withstand a fair amount of heat.

INTOLERANT OF: dry soil & weed competition. CABBAGE rarely heads at very low elevations.

ADVERSARIES: susceptible to nematodes, cutworms, CABBAGE-moth, etc.; resistant cultivars exist.

ORGANIC-GROWING: many problems can be prevented with a three year rotation from other Brassica, & correcting the pH. Toads relish cutworms.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span short in the tropics; can be extended by refrigeration at 45°F (7°C).

PROPAGATED BY: seed. Sown: to % in. (.6-1.25 cm) deep. Generally planted to transplant, although some cultivars can be sown directly. Seedlings need protection from heavy rain. Over-production can be avoided by staggered planting or with early late types.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆ CAULIFLOWER

Vol II · scan p. 120 · book p. 32

☆ CAULIFLOWER, Kapiki pua pua. Brassica oleracea Botrytis Group. Many celtvars exist, including: For tropical lowlands: ‘Sutton's Early Patna' & ‘Puakea.' - For mid-clevations: ‘Snow Queen,' ‘Snow King' & ‘Extra Early Snowball.' For highlands: ‘Early Snowball,’ ‘Super Snowball’ & ‘Perfected Snowball.'

EDIBILITIES: Tasty, nutritious, esteemed vegetable. High in vitamins & other important nutrients. Under-developed flower-heads are eaten fresh raw in salads, with dips, boiled, steamed as a vegetable, served with a cheese sauce, sautéed, stir-fried, braised, soups, casseroles, tempura, or pickled. Can be blanched to protect curds from the sun by bending its leaves up over the heads (some are self-wrapping.) Young tender leaves can be cooked as greens. Seeds can be sprouted.

MATURITY: typically cut when heads are 5 to 8 in. (12.5 -20 cm) wide, depending on cultivar;.before they yellow or become ricey looking.

STORING: lasts a month at 32°F (0°C), & freezes well.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

DESCRIPTION: Typically a biennial, but at least one perennial cultivar exists. Can grow 2 ft. (60 cm) tall. Characteristics & cultural needs are much like BROCCOLL Deep roots.

ORIGIN: Europe.

CLIMATE: thrives if warm when young, then cool & humid during heading.

PREFERS: moist, humusy, rich, well drained, silty or sandy loam, 5.5 to 7.0 pH & full sun. Very heavy feeder & more difficult to grow than most other Brassica spp. Needs its soil deeply amended with aged-manure or rich compost. Fed monthly to maintain constant vigorous growth. Deep cultivation can injure roots. Benefits from mulch.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on cultivar.

INTOLERANT OF: highly acid soil, poor drainage, hard-pan & dry, hot conditions. Not as tolerant of heat as CABBAGE. Will not form good "curds" on poor soil or in hot conditions.

ADVERSARIES: damp, overcrowded conditions can lead to disease; possibilities include downy mildew, black-rot, black-leg & wire-stem. Pest possibilities include CABBAGE-worm, -lopper, -webworm, aphids, cutworms, root-knot nematode & red spider mites. ORGANIC-

GROWING: plants can be protected from many pests with floating-row-cover (highlands), hand-picking, a safe iron-phosphate slug & snail bait, etc. Good ventilation & drainage are important.

SEED-SAVING: four year seed life span is possible.

PROPAGATED BY: seed. Sown directly or to transplant. Germination: three to five days, with an optimal temperature of 85°F (29°C). Seedlings need regular water, preferably early in the day, so foliage can dry quickly. Seedlings can be ready to transplant in one to one & a half months.

Elevation / Rainfall: High, WetMesic

☆🌿 CHINESE CABBAGE

Vol II · scan p. 120 · book p. 32

☆ CHINESE CABBAGE. Brassica rapa, syn. B. chinensis, syn. B. pekinesis. Two varieties exist: (Note: there are cultivars of each variety that tolerate tropical heat). Chinensis Group: non-heading, resembling Swiss Chard with their thick white petioles. They tend to bolt in hot weather. Numerous varieties & cultivars exist, including: ‘Pak Choi,’ "Bok Choy,' ‘Joi Choi,’ Tatsoi,' 'Non-heading Chinese White Cabbage,’ ‘Chinese Celery,’ ‘Cabbage Mustard,’ ‘Mustard Cabbage,’ ‘Chingensai,’ ‘Shadushina,’ etc. Pekinensis Group: either narrow & upright, or short & squat. Numerous varieties & cultivars exist, including heading, loose, leafy & some with heat-resistance. Cultivars include: 'Pe-Tsai,’ ‘Bok Choy,' Wong Bok' (‘Napa’), 'Ming Choi,’ 'Chinese Cabbage,' 'Celery Cabbage' (‘Michihli'), ‘Hakusai,’ ‘Siew Choy,’ ‘Spoon Cabbage,’ ete.

— scan page 121 · book page 33 —

EDIBILITIES: Ancient esteemed vegetables. High in calcium, vitamin A & C & other important nutrients. Leaves, petioles & young flower-stems are eaten fresh raw as salad greens (with Ginger, sesame oil & tamari), coleslaw, on sandwiches, steamed or boiled, stir-fried, chop suey, chow mien, wonton & other soups, braised, marinated, tempera or dried. Seeds can be sprouted for salads & sandwiches, or ground to a MUSTARD.

MATURITY: one & a half to three months, depending on variety & cultivar.

HARVESTING: large, outside leaves can be snapped off at base of stalks, allowing the plant to continue growing, or entire head cut at its base.

STORING: heading types can last two or three months in a cold, well-ventilated spot, although not in plastic bags. Some cultivars hold up better than others. Can also be parboiled & dried, pickled, or fermented & stored in salt as kimchee (Kimchee can last three months in cool conditions).

APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: herbaccous or flowering edges, 🌿 ats

DESCRIPTION: CHINESE CABBAGE are herbaceous biennials, grown as annuals. Can grow 3 to 24 in. (7.5-60 cm) tall, depending on variety & cultivar. Heads are loose, or less compact than the European CABBAGE. Light yellow flowers. Day-length neutral. Fast growing. Relatively short lived.

ORIGIN: East Asia.

CLIMATE: best in cool or warm conditions. Neither group can handle as much heat as Swiss Chard. Excess heat tends to induce flowering & bitterness.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: very successfully.

PREFERS: rich, moist, light, humusy soil, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. Easy to grow. Mulching maintains humidity, soil coolness & suppresses weeds. Side-dressing twice a month is suggested.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on variety & cultivar, but include heavy or light soil (if they are well amended) & light frost.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding or dry conditions. Although moist soil & high humidity is needed for successful harvests, excess water towards harvest time can produce soft-rot in heading types.

ADVERSARIES: less attacked by pests than many Brassicas, although susceptible to root-knot nematodes & slugs or snails.

ORGANIC-GROWING: raised beds help prevent mollusk damage, as do the new, safe iron-phosphate baits. Disease resistant cultivars are important.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown ¥% in. (1.25 cm) deep, directly, or in containers to transplant. Germination: three to six days. Carefully tended until transplanting. Root system sensitive; benefits from good tilth & thoroughly incorporated nutrients. Needs to be well thinned. Usually planted during winter or spring, although summer cultivars exist. Planted successively to prolong harvest.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

BLACK MUSTARD, Short-Podded Mustard, Makeke. Brassica nigra, syn. Sinapis nigra. Two varieties exist.

ADVERSARIES: nematode, mildew & other resistances exist.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown directly. Can be planted towards the end of June for fall harvest.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, WetMesic

🌿 vz TURNIP

Vol II · scan p. 124

vz TURNIP, Stubble Tumip, Fodder Turnip, “Uala Pilau. Brassica rapa Rapifera Group, syn. B. campestris var. rapifera. Many varieties & cultivars exist, including some tolerant of tropics. Besides ROOT TURNIPS of various colors, there are FOLIAGE TURNIPS (syn. “Turnip Greens"). ROOT TURNIPS often have acceptable greens, but roots of FOLIAGE TURNIPS are usually too fibrous to eat.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, esteemed & nutritious vegetable. Size, shape, color & density of root vary with cultivar. Tuberous tap-root is eaten fresh raw in mixed salads (harvested immaturely), or as a cooked vegetable, braised, casseroles, soups & stews, pureed, mashed, scalloped, or pickled. Leaves are highly nutritious; rich in calcium, phosphorus, potassium, as well as vitamins A & C, Eaten fresh raw, as cooked greens & in soups or stews. Seeds can be sprouted.

MATURITY: one to three months for roots, usually harvested when half or two-thirds grown, or less. Roots left too long in ground tend to get bitter & woody. Some cultivars grow largely above ground; ‘Corinthian.’ Greens can begin to be harvested only a few weeks of sowing; cut-&-comeagain.

STORING: most cultivars hold up very well if cool & dry. Roots & leaves, if stored separately in plastic bags, last about a week in a refrigerator. Roots do not hold up well if left in the soil..

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: roots & greens as fodder for livestock.

INSECTICIDE: repoitedly the plants contain a compound detrimental to house flies, aphids & spider mites.

ROTATIONAL PLANTING: grown after heavy feeders.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous biennial. Can grow 18 in. (45 cm) tall. Brilliant yellow flowers. Fast growing & vigorous. Deep, wide-spreading roots.

ORIGIN: south & central Europe.

CLIMATE: thrives in cool conditions. Most varieties are quick to bolt in hot weather.

PREFERS: deep, moist, rich, loose, humusy loam, near neutral pH & full sun. Benefits from amending soil with granite dust, rock phosphate, compost, & only lightly with aged-manure. Benefits from mulch. Roots tend to become more pungent in dry conditions.

TOLERATES: tolerances depend on cultivar, but TURNIP can grow in most soils.

ADVERSARIES: young plants can be lightly dusted with wood ashes for flea-beetle protection. WEEDY?: not.

SEED-SAVING: requires isolation from MUSTARD, CHINESE CABBAGE, RUTABAGA & other TURNIPS, of 600 ft. (180 m) for home gardening, & of 4% to 1 mile (.4 for pure seed.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown % to 1 in. (.6-2.5 cm) deep; directly. Germination: soil temperature range of 60 to 105°F (16-40°C). Can be planted towards end of July for a fall crop.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆☠️ CARROT / KĀLOKE

Vol II · scan p. 125

☆ CARROT / KĀLOKE Daucus carota, syn. D. carota subsp. sativa. Apiaceae (previously Umbellifereae) (Parsley) Family. Numerous cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, esteemed & nutritious roots. Long to short, yellow, orange to reddish, or purplish roots. Eaten fresh raw, grated for salads, in soups & stews, fried, roasted, tempera, casseroles, numerous other dishes, jam, pickled, canned, dehydrated, dried as a flour, chopped & roasted for a Coffee-replacement, or fermented into wine. High in carotene, potassium, soluble fiber vitamin C (raw). Most of the nutrients are in or near the skin. Brighter colored roots have more carotene; this vitamin A precursor is made more digestible when released from its cellulose cell by cooking, finely grating, or juicing. Aromatic seeds can be utilized as a flavoring for soups, stews & chowders, curries, sauces, & as an essential oil for food-flavoring & perfume.

☠️ TOXICITY: Although some have listed young CARROT foliage as edible, they are potentially poisonous (when mature?). Young leaves & roots irritate sensitive skin. All dirt should be washed off roots to rid a dangerous fungi; peeling may be advised.

MATURITY: Two to four months, or when roots are large enough, according to variety. The high-carotene variety matures about a month later than most other varieties.

HARVESTING: CARROTS are pulled from the ground as needed. Roots store well in ground if soil is not too soggy, or pest-ridden, but tend to harden with age.

STORING: Unwashed roots store well in a moist, cool spot. Long lasting in plastic bag in refrigerator. Can also be frozen or dried.

SHIPPING: Unblemished CARROTS transport well when chilled & handled with care.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Foliage & roots for livestock.

BENEFICIAL INSECT HOST: Umbelliferous flowers provide nectar for beneficial insects.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous biennial, grown as an annual. Size depends on cultivar. Can grow 1 to 3 ft. (.3-.9 m) when flowering. White flower umbels. Day-length neutral. Deep tap-root & many fine laterals.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

CLIMATE: Tolerates various climates, but high temperatures can toughen roots. Prefers temperature range of 60 to 70°F (15.5- 21°C). CARROTS tend to be lighter-colored, shorter & stronger tasting at temperatures higher than 75°F (24°C). Typically needs a cool to cold winter for seed production. Established CARROTS tolerate frost. Intolerant of dry conditions. Interruption of water availability can cause cracks, while excess water causes roots to lighten & roughens their skin.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Regularly & well.

— scan page 126 · book page 40 —

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: CARROTS flourish in deep, moist, loose, well drained, light, compost-rich, loam, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. Constant moisture is needed. Responds to being side-dressed after thinning & again a month later. Fresh manure or excess nitrogen can cause hairy, deformed, or forked roots. Rocks, lumps & trash can split or deform roots. Benefits from mulch for moisture conservation, weed control & coolness,

INTOLERANT OF: flooding.

ADVERSARIES: Pest possibilities include aphids, wireworms, mealy bugs, vegetable-weevil & cutworms. Susceptible to root-knot nematodes. Disease possibilities include early- & late-blight, especially where excessively wet. Intolerant of weed competition,

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent. Most pests & diseases can be prevented by crop rotation, & floating row-cover (highlands).

WEEDY: Escaped & naturalized in many countries. Can be a Noxious weed. Re-seeds prolifically where winters are cold. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: By insects and wind.

SEED-SAVING: To prevent crossing, CARROTS require 200 to 1000 ft. (60-300 m) isolation between varieties & between other Umbellifers. Seed life span is two to three years (less in high humidity).

PROPAGATED BY: Seeds. Tiny CARROT seeds can be mixed with sand or Radish-seed to ease sowing & subsequent locating. Sown early spring. Drilled % in. in light soil or % in. (.6-1.25 cm) in heavier soil. Ideal seed bed is deep, well-worked & finely textured. Soil-crusting is avoided by thinly covering bed with sifted compost, vermiculite or other light mulch. Germination: slow & irregular; one to three weeks at 50 to 85°F (10-29°C). Moisture is required. Young seedlings are fragile. Thinned to 2 in. cm) spacing. Planted successively for continuous harvest.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: Numerous varieties, forms & many cultivars exist, being adaptable to most climates. The strain recommended by the U of H are the various 'Nante’ cultivars. In lowland conditions, the long-rooted varieties tend to be irregularly shaped & poorer quality. ‘Danvers Half-long' & ‘Chantenay' produce heavily, but tend to be inferior in quality. Variety ‘A-plus' has a darker color, 50% richer in carotene & tastier than most, but longer to mature. Variety Uberlandia‘ can produce seeds in the tropics.

☆Ⓦ CASSAVA / MANIOKA

Vol II · scan p. 127 · book p. 41

☆ CASSAVA / MANIOKA Tapioca Plant, Manioc, Manihot, Mandioca, Brazilian Arrowroot. Manihot esculenta, syn. M. utilissima, syn. M. aipi, syn. M. palmata, syn. M. dulcis. Euphorbiaceae (Spurge) Family. Many varieties & cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: The huge starchy roots with their hard whitish to yellow flesh, are a staple food for many. SWEET CASSAVA is eaten fresh raw (peeled), or baked, fried, boiled, roasted, as chips, pastries, processed to tapioca, fermented into tempeh, beer, or dried as slices. When young, SWEET CASSAVA roots have little or no HCN (hydrocyanic acid), compared to BITTER CASSAVA. BITTER CASSAVA is peeled, sliced, dried & ground to an Arrowroot-like bread or pastry flour. Tapioca (Pia Monioka), pearls or flour, is eaten as custards, puddings, soups, sauce-thickener, or in dumplings, biscuits & candies. Even though high in calories, vitamin C calcium, roots are actually nutrient deficient. On the other hand young leaves & tender tips are highly nutritious, rich in protein when cooked as greens, or in soups & stews, but SEE: TOXICITIES, following. Leaves are also dried & powdered to add to soups & other foods. When making powdered leaf, the more the cell-wail’s are ruptured with grinding, the more HCN is dispersed.

ROOT-PROCESSING: roots are washed, grated & soaked, then roasted, fermented, or expressed to remove the poisonous glucosides.

BEARING: roots grow to sufficient size in eight to twelve months.

HARVESTING: dug as needed. BITTER CASSAVA holds up longer in the ground than SWEET CASSAVA.

STORING: deteriorates within two to seven days, but can be peeled & frozen, or dried.

NOTE: BITTER CASSAVA is not completely different from SWEET CASSAVA, they are more poles-of-a-continuum. Selecting low- HCN cultivars is critical.

TOXICITIES: 1. A thorough processing of roots of most varieties is required to remove the HCN (hydrocyanic acid). 2. Greens must be boiled at least fifteen minutes to deactivate the poison & even then there is evidence suggesting avoidance of long & regular consumption.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: processed leaves are excellent as feed.

LANDSCAPING: ungainly hedge, although a shorter, variegated, ornamental variety exists.

LIVING-FENCE: lanky.

NURSE-PLANT: for young Cacao, Cola, etc. 43

DESCRIPTION: Large, woody or herbaceous, perennial shrub. Can grow 8 ft. (2.4 m) tall, or twice that. May drop leaves during droughts, but greens up again after a rain. Whitish to yellow-green flowers occasionally have a red tinge. Vigorous-growing.

LIFE SPAN: short lived.

ORIGIN: eastern South America & Central America.

CLIMATE: tropical lowlands.

PREFERS: deep, loose, rich, well drained sandy loam & full sun. Heavy feeder. For year-round leaves CASSAVA is planted closely, fertilized heavily & harvested monthly. Note that excessive fertility promotes greenery as opposed to roots. Grown in raised beds, ridges or flat ground.

TOLERATES: various soils, & once established CASSAVA can tolerate drought, sea-coasts & neglect.

INTOLERANT OF: cold conditions, wet feet & very shallow, rocky, or acid soil.

ASSOCIATES: can be interplanted with annuals.

ADVERSARIES: resistant to most diseases & pests, except for certain viruses.

WEEDY: some forms are weedy. Can escape cultivation & apparently can naturalized, but is not very persistent. Leans & roots. Easy to control. SEX: monoecious.

PROPAGATED BY: cuttings; 8 to 12 in. (20-30 cm) pieces of woody mid-stem can be stacked in the shade until buds emerge. Longer pieces can be placed vertically, 4 to 6 in. (10-15 cm) deep. Shorter pieces for horizontal placement are planted 4 in. (10 cm) deep. CoastalLowMid, ?/MesicDry

CHASTE TREE. Vitex agnus-castus. SEE: VITEX. In Permacopia III.I, the Weed Book, ☆ CHAYA Mayan Spinach, Tree Spinach, Spinach Tree. Cnidoscolus chayamansa. Euphorbiaceae (Spurge) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed & valuable food. Tender, young leaves & shoot-tips chopped & cooked as greens, in soups & stews, or whole for tamale wrappers. Finely textured & does not reduce much in size with cooking. Reportedly rich in vitamins, calcium, protein & iron. High yield & high quality.

☠️ TOXICITY: The toxic cyanide CHAYA contains is rendered harmless by cooking at least five minutes; cyanide inactivated. Well cooked leaves are safe to eat.

⚠️ CAUTION: most varieties have stinging hairs, which are also eliminated by cooking.

MATURITY: Within a few months of planting.

HARVESTING: Succulent branch-tips are snapped off when needed. If stinging hairs are present, gloves are warranted.

STORING & SHIPPING: CHAYA leaves wilt rapidly, thus do not store or transport well, although they could be dried.

APPLICATIONS: ANIMAL FEED?: Of doubtful value as a feed unless cooked.

LANDSCAPING: Thick hedge when pruned regularly.

LIVING-FENCE: Fast growing from large cuttings.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: The medicinal applications reported may be false.

DESCRIPTION: CHAYA is an attractive, mostly herbaceous, perennial shrub. Can grow 9 to 12 ft. (3-4 m) tall & about half that wide. Succulent stems. Large, dark-green, lobed, Maple-like leaves. Clusters of small white flowers. Day-length neutral. Fast growing. Roots are shallow, giving poor support in heavy rain or strong wind.

LIFE SPAN: about five years.

ORIGIN: Mexico & Central America.,

CLIMATE: Tropics & subtropics. Prefers wet, warm, lower elevations. CHAYA loves heat. Tolerates very dry, or very wet conditions, as well as intensely hot, humid summers. Even though plant handles drought, it will reduce yield. Foliage is intolerant of frost, but plant can regrow from roots.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Somewhat recently introduced to Hawaiʻi, but not common.

PREFERS: Moist, well drained soil, acid pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: most soil types & some cultivars may tolerate brief flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: prolonged flooding, in general.

PRUNING: Pruning encourages bushiness.

ASSOCIATES: As a fast growing shrub, CHAYA tends to dominate surrounding plants & requires frequent pruning.

ADVERSARIES: Typically pest & disease free. WEEDY?: Rarely, if ever, sets seed & therefore is probably not rampant, but discarded branches readily root.

DISADVANTAGES: The stinging hairs & toxic nature of the raw leaves.

REMARKS: This vegetable is very productive, nutritious & merits more attention. SEX: Monoecious; usually males, with a few females.

POLLINATION: ?

PROPAGATED BY: Easily reproduced from large cuttings, especially of mature wood. Plants with fewest irritating hairs are chosen. Planted right-side-up with leaf scars smiling. Soil is kept moist, not excessively wet.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow, WetMesicDry

SOME NOTED CULTIVARS: While ‘Chaya brava' has stinging hairs, ‘Chaya mansa' is free. Other varieties exist, but are little known.

CHAYOTE Pipinella, Chuchu, Chocho, Choko, Vegetable Pear, Christophine, Mirliton, Sayote. Sechium edule. Cucurbitaceae (Gourd) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Wrinkled, green, yellow-green, or white, Pear-shaped fruits. Sometimes a bit spiny, 4 to 8" (10-20 cm) long, containing one flat seed 1 to 2 in. (2.5-5 cm) long. Seed sometimes protrudes from one end. Young, tender fruits can be steamed, baked, stuffed, sautéed, stir-fried, frittered, made into soups & stews, casseroles, added to Apple pies, pickled, or eaten raw in salads when very young. Mature seed-kemels are delicious sautéed, stir- or deep fried. New leaves & tendrils provide excellent cooked greens. Contains iron, beta-carotene & many B vitamins, Smaller starchy tubers growing around the main rootstock, harvested at end of second year, are eaten baked, boiled, or fried. These tubers are the reason CHAYOTE is planted in most countries.

— scan page 129 —

BEARING: three to five months.

MATURITY: from flower to fruit in one month. Can bear year-round in warm wrk conditions.

STORING: fruits can last a few weeks if lightly wrapped & kept cool.

APPLICATIONS:

GROUND-COVER: CHAYOTE has successfully smothered patches of the rampant Lantana, then pigs can harvest the root, tilling.

SHADE: on roof or trellis.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Hairy, herbaceous, perennial vine. Vigorous vines can reach 40 ft. (12 m) or longer. Climbing or scrambling habit, Climbs by tendrils. Large heart-shaped or slightly lobed leaves. Inconspicuous whitish flowers bloom during shorter days in fal], Thick rootstock.

PREFERS: rich, moist soil, pH 6.0 to 8.0 & full sun, or part shade in very hot regions. Needs ample room, preferably with a trellis, fence, or arbor to climb. Benefits from being fed annually & mulched.

TOLERATES: acid soil.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding or high water-table.

ASSOCIATES: clambers over anything nearby.

ADVERSARIES: rare.

WEEDY: aggressive nature; caution - will suffocate trees. Sparingly naturalized. SEX: usually monoecious, but since some vines only have flowers of one sex, several may be planted to ensure pollination.

PROPAGATED BY: a sprouted fruit can be planted edgewise or horizontally, with narrow-end protruding slightly. Emerging shoot can be trimmed back to 1 or 2 in. (2.5-5 em). For fast growth CHAYOTEis planted early spring.

☠️ CHERRY

Vol II · scan p. 129

CHERRY Prunus species. Rosaceae (Rose) Family. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Esteemed food & ornamental. Fruits are eaten fresh raw, pitted for pies, muffins, pancakes, jams & jellies (pectin needed), canned, or dried. For other applications, seg: individual listings.

MATURITY: mid summer through fall.

HARVESTING: fruit are typically abundant. When plucking CHERRIES, care is taken to leave the stem (delays deterioration) without pulling off the fruit-spur it is attached to.

☠️ TOXICITY: Fresh seeds & wilted leaves contain cyanide & are poisonous if eaten. Because cooking destroys this toxin, there is no need to de-pit fruit in the beginning stages of jelly-making. APPLICATIONS,

IN GENERAL:

CONTAINER-GROWING: dwarfs.

LANDSCAPING: omamentals, screens, & dwarfs for foundations, hedges, or containers.

SHADE TREES: summer cover. DESCRIPTION,

IN GENERAL: Attractive, deciduous, small to medium trees. Most species have showy clusters of white flowers from spring to early summer.

CLIMATE: although most CHERRIES need many hours of chill, some low-chill species & varieties exist. Southern exposure ideal in cold climates. Intolerant of extremely hot summers.

PREFER: all CHERRIES need full sun.

ADVERSARIES: several pest possibilities, especially birds. Tree can be netted. Prone to gummosis. ORGANIC-

GROWING: gummosis remedy: working in at least 20 Ib. (9 kg) of compost under crown.

WEEDY: many forms can spread.

SEED-SAVING: pits cleaned.

PROPAGATED BY: budding, grafting, cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: semi-ripe- or hard-wood. Seeds need three months or more of cold, moist stratification. Germination: one to two months.

CILANTRO Coriander, Chinese Parsley, Mexican Parsley, Dhania, Yuen sai, Yuan sui. Coriandrum sativum. Apiaceae (Parsley) Family. Many cultivars exist, including green- or red-petioled, & larger-leafed-, early- & slower bolting varieties.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed herb. Piquant young leaves & tender shoots, fresh raw as a nutritious garnish, & in mixed salads, salsa, guacamole, soups & stews, stir-fries, Latin American- & Asian cuisine, chicken-, duck-, meat- & fish-dishes, or with Tomatillos, Tomatoes & Chilies, & in sauces or chutneys. To preserve flavor, CILANTRO is added at the end of cooking or directly before serving. Roots are often cooked in Thai dishes. Seeds become the spice CORIANDER.

MATURITY: harvest can start in thirty or forty days & plant matures in sixty.

STORING: lasts about two weeks in a refrigerator with roots in water & leaves covered with a bag. Leaves can be dried whole, or better, chopped & frozen.

APPLICATIONS:

BENEFICIAL INSECT HOST: Umbeliferous flowers attract beneficial insects. INSECT PEST REPELLENT.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: reported to assist the body in the elimination of mercury. 23%

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous annual. Can grow 1 to 3 ft. (30-90 cm) tali. Fragrant foliage & flowers. Umbels of white or sometimes purple flowers. Fast growing. Long slim taproot.

ORIGIN: south Europe, Mediterranean, Eurasia.

CLIMATE: grows best in cool weather; bolts quickly when hot.

PREFERS: moist, fertile or poor, light, well drained soil, alkaline pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: various soils & conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: seeds sprout poorly in heavy clay.

ADVERSARIES: pest free.

WEEDY: escapes & occasionally naturalized, but not thought invasive.

SEED-SAVING: seeds have a long life span under the right conditions.

PROPAGATED BY: easily by seeds. Soaked overnight & sown directly, % to 1 in. (1.25-2.5 cm) deep (depending on conditions), "Seeds" are actually a pod that can be gently cracked into two seeds prior to sowing. Transplant shock causes rapid bolting. For continuous harvest, can be successively planted every few weeks. Planted early spring or fall. Germination: seven to twenty-one days: darkness required.

Elevation / Rainfall: ?C/LowMidHigh, WetMesicDry
