☆🌳☠️ CITRUS

Vol II · scan p. 130 · book p. 48

☆ CITRUS Citrus, Fortunella & Poncirus species. Rutaceae (Citrus) Family. Many cultivars, hybrids & a few other species exist. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Ripe fruits are eaten fresh raw, in many dishes, or in juice, lemonade, wine, brandy & liqueurs. High in vitamin C. Rind as marmalade, or sugared, pickled, in liquors, or an essential oil, as well as a source of pectin. Leaves can be brewed as tea. SEE DETAILS UNDER INDIVIDUAL LISTINGS, FOLLOWING.

BEARING: Seedlings can yield in six to seven years; graftlings in three to four.

MATURITY: Most CITRUS fruit are harvested when mature & fully expanded, after a third to half of its rind shows its color. In some species, ripe fruit may hang on the tree for an extended time without loss of quality, although this increases their chances of being stung & may reduce next seasons’ yield.

STORING: Fruit hold up very well in a refrigerator, ideally at 35 to 40°F (2-5°C).

SHIPPING: Fruit transport easily. Refrigeration preserves vitamin C. APPLICATIONS,

IN GENERAL:

ANIMAL FEED: Excess fruit & some byproducts: peels, pulp-meal, dried pulp, CITRUS molasses, & seed-meal for livestock.

☠️ TOXICITY: Seed-meal contains limonin that is edible for ruminant animals, but poisonous to poultry & pigs.

BEE FORAGE: Nectar source.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Soil is allowed to dry out between watering. Scale can be wiped off with an alcohol-soaked swab.

LANDSCAPING: Specimens, hedges, entrance trees, espalier, bonsai, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications.

PERFUMES.

SHADE TREES: Excellent candidates.

WOOD: Hard, fine-grained & strong. Utilized for pestles, tool handles & other small objects.

🌳 GENERAL DESCRIPTION: CITRUS are small to mid-sized, evergreen trees. Thorny or not, depending on species & propagation method. Grafted trees have more branches & are less thorny; seedlings more likely to be thorny & have an upright, single trunk. All have fragrant flowers. Roots can grow 4 ft. (1.2 m) deep & reach twice the width of the crown.

ORIGIN: Eastern hemisphere.

GENERAL CLIMATE: Warm temperate zones, subtropics & tropics. CITRUS require a warm climate & a long growing season. Optimal temperature range is 65 to 90°F (18-32°C). The larger the difference between night & day temperatures, especially during ripening, the better the fruit. Although most species can tolerate frost, the fruit or flowers may die. Tolerates some drought during dormancy. Intolerant of harsh winds, & drought during growth period (depending on cultivar). Fruits may become dehydrated in drought. SEE: individual listings.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Most CITRUS thrive in Hawaiʻi. Some prefer wet, hot lowlands, while others thrive at mid- or higherelevations. ‘Heen Naran' as a rootstock has been recommended for Hawaiʻi by the U of H. PREFERENCES & CULTURE,

IN GENERAL: Most CITRUS prefer deep, moist, fertile, well drained, airy, sandy or loamy soil, pH to full sun. Respond to added humus & a nitrogen-/mineral-rich fertilizer provided every few months, or at the very least yearly. Sometimes CITRUS like to be mulched (but, SEE: ADVERSARIES, following regarding root-rot). Tolerate light shade in extreme heat, but this impairs fruiting.

INTOLERANT OF: lawns, flooding, poorly drained or salty soil & high alkalinity. Lawns are typically too wet & competitive.

PRUNING: Each species has special needs, but all need their water-shoots, crossing limbs & dead branches removed. Tree interior should be open enough to allow good air- flow & light. Lower branches tend to be most productive. After harvest, a light pruning is often beneficial. Heavy pruning tends to reduce yields because it stimulates vigorous new growth. If heavy pruning is needed, the trunk can be wrapped or painted to prevent sunburn.

— scan page 131 · book page 49 —

ASSOCIATES: Avocado, ANNONA species, Banana, Cacao, Coffee, Papaya, Calabash Tree, perennial gardens, etc.

ADVERSARIES: The pests & diseases of CITRUS are numerous, yet most do not get out of hand in small, diverse plantings. Advice from local experts is important. Possibilities include scale, scab, anthracnose, viruses, algal spot, gummosis & melanose. There are a few conditions of great severity, thus the grower must be alert. C/TRUS is susceptible to root-rot from Phytophthora. Where root-rot is present, mulch should be light or avoided altogether. Foot-rot can be caused by root injury during cultivation. Vectors for sooty-mold include white-flies, scale & aphids. Oleander, Nerium oleander & Pepper Tree, Schinus molle, both harbor black scale; avoid proximity.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidates when given good cultural care. Grafted plants generally have greater disease resistance. Gummosis remedy: gently working a couple of inches of compost into soil under tree. To kill slugs & snails, sprinkle on one of the safe iron-phosphate baits, like “Sluggo"". Sticky bands can prevent ants. WEEDY?: Not thought of as invasive, although some natural regeneration does occur, especially in SOUR ORANGES.

DISADVANTAGES: Trees are often thomy. Commercial production requires more care than many other fruit need.

REMARKS: Excellent yard trees. On small sites, dwarf rootstocks will create smaller trees. SEX: Hermaphroditic, maybe self incompatible. Often has polyembryonic seeds.

POLLINATION: Bees.

SEED-SAVING: Polyembryonic seeds have a greater chance of coming true. Cultivar seedlings have a tendency to have greater vigor, but generally do not run true, produce more thoms & are slower to fruit.

GENERAL PROPAGATION: Depends on species. Multiplied by seeds, cuttings, budding, grafting, air-layering & transplanted volunteers. Cuttings: semi-ripe pieces, dipped in rooting hormone & misted: summertime. New trees are planted so that the crown is at its original level. New CITRUS need wind & sun protection until becoming established.

SOME NOTABLE SPECIES:

BLOOD ORANGE. SEE: SWEET ORANGE, BLOOD. ☆ CALAMONDIN, Golden Lime, Chinese Orange, Panama Orange, Orangequat, Philippine Lime, Musk Lime, Kalamansi, Kalamunding, *Alani ‘lani ‘awa‘awa. Citrus mitis, syn. x Citrofortunella mitis, syn. Citrus reticulata x Fortunella species, syn. microcarpa, syn. C. mitis v. microcarpa, err.C. madurensis. A natural hybrid. Cultivars exist, including dwarfs.

EDIBILITIES: Small, fragrant, yellow to orange-red fruit nearly 2 in. (5 cm) wide, with a flattened base. Skin is thin, edible & easy to remove. Orange pulp is very tart & juicy, containing several small seeds. Fruit is generally too sour to eat raw, but it is often fried in curries, cooked in sauces, Southeast Asian cuisine, as a flavoring for fish or meat, made into breads, cakes, preserves, marmalades, chutney, or pickled. Juice for pies, gelatins, in teas, ades & wherever LEMON- or LIME-juice is called for. Juice is also an ink-stain remover & deodorant. Rind is a flavoring, pectin source, or can be preserved.

BEARING: cuttings can fruit in two years.

MATURITY: nearly year-round. Fruit is best when gathered while still green since quality drops when it's full ripe.

HARVESTING: fmuit-stem is clipped to prevent tearing tender peel.

STORING: lasts a couple of weeks if kept cool & humid.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING: bonsai, lanai, etc., in large pots.

LANDSCAPING: ornamental, entrances, hedges, screens, etc, MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Small, attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 3 to 25 ft. (.9-7.5 m) tall, depending on cultivar. Rounded crown. Few spines. Crushed leaves are aromatic. Fragrant white or yellow/orange flowers. Very deep tap-root.

ORIGIN: probably China or the Philippines.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics.

GROWN IN HAWATE: often grown near homes.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, well drained soil, slightly acid pH & full sun. Typically fertilized twice yearly.

TOLERATES: various soils & climates, including calcareous soils, frost & some drought (drought reduces yield).

INTOLERANT OF: harsh winds & poor drainage.

PRUNING: usually kept small & accessible.

ADVERSARIES: several possibilities, especially fruit flies & nematodes. Resists gummosis. SEX: hermaphroditic & self-fertile. No crossing needed.

PROPAGATED BY: fresh seeds (run true), cuttings & budding. Cuttings: leafy or not: constantly misted. Excellent rootstock for NAGAMI KUMQUAT & other small Citrus.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆ CITRON

☆ CITRON, Tipolo, Hadar, Kov-Yuan. Citrus medica, Several cultivars exist, including ‘Buddha's Hand.'

EDIBILITIES: Large, oblong, rounded or irregular fruit 4 to 12 in. (7.5-30 cm) long. Yellow rind is thick, bumpy or smooth & fragrant. Rind can be sliced for mixed salads, jellies, marmalades, fruit-bars, or made into syrup for flavoring. Rind can be also briefly blanched in hot water, or fermented in brine & candied for fruit-cakes, sweet-rolls, puddings, candies, cannoli, other desserts & liqueurs, etc. Tart or sweet pulp is usually seedy & dry; rarely eaten. Juice of some cultivars as a flavoring for various desserts & beverages.

BEARING: around three years.

MATURITY: when fruit-rind is destined to be candied the fruit is picked young, under 6 in. (15 cm) long.

APPLICATIONS:

FRAGRANCE: fruit is good as scenting. Rind can be dried to put with clothes. Essential oil for perfumes.

INSECT-REPELLENT: fragrant rind as a moth-repellent. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: dense, close grained, relatively hard: farming tools, walking-sticks, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Small evergreen tree or shrub. Can grow 15 ft. (4.5 m) tall. Thorny. Fragrant foliage. Aromatic white or pinkish flowers. Slow growth rate.

LIFE SPAN: around twenty-five years.

ORIGIN: not known for sure, but possibly India, Africa or Asia.

CLIMATE: tropics. Adapted to moderate climates.

PREFERS: well-aerated soil, slightly acid pH & full sun. Water-sprouts pruned off.

TOLERATES: various soils.

INTOLERANT OF: frost, drought, or extreme heat.

ADVERSARIES: those typical of most Citrus species.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are polyembryonic.

PROPAGATED BY: cuttings, or occasionally by budding, grafting & seeds, Cuttings: two to four year old branches with leaves left on, immediately placed into a moist medium misted. ?LowMid, WetMesic ☆ GRAPEFRUIT, Toronja. Citrus paradisi, syn. C. maxima x C. sinensis. A naturally occurring hybrid of SWEET ORANGE x

PUMMELO. Two forms, either with white- or pink-colored flesh & many cultivars of each exist, some being nearly seedless. U of H recommended cultivars include: ‘Nitta,' Marsh Seedless' & ‘Ruby Red.’

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed fruit. Large, round or a bit flattened, light-yellow, greenish, or pinkish fruit 6 in. (15 cm) or wider. Fruit have a thick or thin, fragrant rind surrounding juicy, tart & often pleasantly bitter pulp. Eaten fresh raw, or in fruit salads, puddings, jellies, preserves, marmalades, compotes, gelatins, canned, or as juice. ORANGE-replacement for many recipes. Rich in soluble fiber & pectin. Fruit is more flavorful at room temperature. Juice is an excellent liquid for poaching, marinades, sorbets or ice-creams, canned, frozen, vinegar or wine-making. Rind adds zest to baking & can be candied, or as an essential oil pectin source. Seed-oil is edible after processing & is a natural antibiotic.

BEARING: three years from grafting, five to six years from seed.

MATURITY: seven to eighteen months from flowering, depending on region & cultivar.

HARVESTING: may require ladders to clip or snap fruit stem.

STORING: fruits hold up well in vegetable drawer of refrigerator in plastic bags, ideally at 45°

F SHIPPING: stems are removed to prevent damage to other fruit.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: packing-waste is made into molasses for supplementing cattle feed.

FIREWOOD: trimmings & old trees. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: hard & close grained: household utensils, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 50 ft. (15 m) tall in time, but usually seen under half that. Rounded crown. Trunk is often fluted. Short flexible thorns. Fragrant white flowers. Generally vigorous.

ORIGIN: West Indies.

CLIMATE: warm subtropics. Thrives in warm or hot, wet, humid lowlands. Can only handle dry climates with irrigation, especially when young. Although GRAPEFRUIT does not need the low temperatures ORANGES do to develop color, most cultivars do require prolonged heat to ripen fruit & bring out richest flavor (twice as much as ORANGES).

PREFERS: well drained soil, pH 5.5 to 6.2 full sun. Fairly easy. Preferences & cultural requirements are much like SWEET ORANGE, although more space is needed. Requires free moving air. Although tree needs fertilization for highest production, excess nitrogen during fruit-ripening reduces quality.

TOLERATES: hotter, drier regions than SWEET ORANGE, many soils & frost. In poorly drained soil, trees can be planted on a mound. Tolerances depend also on cultivar & rootstock.

INTOLERANT OF: dry soil, while young.

PRUNING: dead or broken limbs & perhaps very low branches (in areas of high humidity) removed.

ADVERSARIES: typically quite resistant.

ORGANIC-GROWING: IPM is beneficial.

PROPAGATED BY: grafting, budding & seeds.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesicDry

"ALL my hurts, my garden spade can heal. Ww LEMON; Lemi. C, itrus limon, syn. C. limonia, syn. C. limonium, syn. C. meyeri, syn. C. pyriformis. Many cultivars & hybrids exist, including: ‘Ponderosa,’ ?C. mon x C. medica, ‘Kukane.' ‘Villa France,’ the productive tropical ‘Meyer ?C. limon x C. reticulata, the ‘Improved Meyer,’ & the huge, subtropical adapted Rough Lemon,'C. jambhiri. — scan page 133 · book page 51 —

EDIBILITIES: Fragrant, round or oval, light-yellow fruit are quite variable in size, 4 in. (10 cm) long. Pulp is tart & juicy. Degree of seediness depends on cultivar. Eaten as a garnish, or sliced & cooked with fish, soups & with tea. Juice for salad dressings, marinades, sauces, tarts & pies, puddings, many desserts, preserves, ice-cream, stain-remover, pharmaceutical applications, tea & ade, etc. Entire fruit is often sliced thin & cooked with fish. Rind is grated, or dried & ground as a flavoring, or can be candied, preserved. Rind is also a source of pectin & essential oil. Essential oil is a flavoring for juice, candy or in Moroccan cuisine. Flowers are made into LEMON-flower butter, or added to fritters, jams or ice-creams. Leaves can be dried as a tea flavoring.

MATURITY: picked when rind color changes & fruit has softened.

HARVESTING: fruit need careful handling to avoid oilspotting & are not gathered when wet.

STORING: long lasting if kept cool, but holds up best in sealed jars in a refrigerator.

SHIPPING: fruits are gathered green & "cured" by storing several weeks in 80% relative humidity at 60°F (15.5°C).

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Rind-oil can irritate skin & lips, if handled or eaten daily. 2. Daily ingestion can damage tooth enamel. 3. Sawdust of LEMON wood can irritate skin.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: dried rind for cattle fodder. CONTAINER-GROWING.

ESSENTIAL OIL: essential oil in soapshampoo-making & furniture polish.

LANDSCAPING: specimen, hedges, etc. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: dense, close grained & easily worked: small items, carving, etc., but

NOTE: TOXICITIES (#3), prior.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: LEMON is a smal), attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 20 ft. (6 m) tall. Some cultivars are very thorny, others nearly thomless. Nevertheless, most young twigs typically have sharp, long thors. Crushed leaves are fragrant. Lightly to strongly aromatic, white flowers with purple undersides. Generally vigorous.

ORIGIN: possibly India.

CLIMATE: thrives in cooler regions of the subtropics or in the tropical highlands.

PREFERS: heavy, well aerated, well drained soil, pH 5.5 to 6.5 & full sun. Can be thickly mulched; should be kept weed free. Needs to be regularly fertilized according to destiny of fruit & soil analysis. Can be fed with a foliar spray, or top dressing with compost/aged manure, etc. Fertilizers should include trace minerals.

PRUNING: often trained young & kept short. Periodically pruned of dead or awkward branches.

TOLERATES: sandy or poor soil & drought (drought reduces yield).

INTOLERANT OF: heavy freezes, harsh winds & herbicides.

ASSOCIATES: Cassava, Beans, Tannier, Pepper, Tomatoes, etc.

ADVERSARIES: many possibilities; choosing disease-resistant cultivars & practicing IPM is important.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds (generally run true), budding, grafting & large cuttings (especially Meyer).

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesic & Dry(if irrigated)

PROPAGATED BY: grafting, cuttings, air-layers & seeds.

☆🌳 TAHITIAN LIME

Vol II · scan p. 133 · book p. 51

☆ TAHITIAN LIME", Tahiti Lime, Persian Lime. Citrus aurantifolia cultivar, prev. C. latifolia. Possible hybrid of West INDIAN LIME x CITRON, or x LEMON. A few cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Rounded, light-yellow fruit 3 in. (7.5 cm) long. Pleasant, bitter/tart, juicy, green-yellow pulp is typically seedless. Edible as a garnish, or splashed over meats & fish, & excellent as pies (KEY LIME pie), jam, jelly, marmalade, preserved, pickled, beverages & juice (wherever LEMON juice is called for). Rx: antidote for Aroid irritation.

CAUTION: rind-oil, tree sap & thors can irritate.

HARVESTING: picked when weather is dry to prevent oil-spotting.

STORING: no curing needed. Fruit lasts around two months in refrigerator.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Small, attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 20 ft. (6 m) tall. Irregular rounded crown. Relatively thornless. Crushed leaves aromatic. Fragrant white flowers. Fairly vigorous.

ORIGIN: not yet known.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics.

PREFERS: moist, well drained soil. Due to continuous growth, they require regular fertilizing.

TOLERATES: more cold than

WEST INDIAN LIME.

ADVERSARIES: several possibilities.

PROPAGATED BY: cuttings, budding, grafting (easier than West Indian Lime’) & seeds (highly variable & rare). Cuttings: often successful under glass, in part shade. Air-layering is possible, although reportedly not as effective.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆🌳 WEST INDIAN LIME

Vol II · scan p. 133 · book p. 51

☆ WEST INDIAN LIME’, Key Lime, Mexican Lime, Bartender's Lime, Chinese Lime, Dalayap. Citrus aurantifolia cultivar, syn. C. lima, syn. C. acida, syn. Limonia aurantifolia. Several cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Round to elliptical, light-yellow fruits 2 in. (5 cm) wide. Typically smaller & seedier than TAHITIAN LIME. Pulp is very tart, juicy & fragrant. Edible as a garnish, or splashed over meats & fish, & excellent as pies (KEY LIME pie), jams, jellies, marmalades, preserved, pickled or as beverages. Rind a source of LIME-oil & citric acid. LIME-oil is a flavoring for icecreams, sherbets, beverages, various foods, candies, perfumes, etc. Leaves are chopped fine for Javanese cuisine.

BEARING: seedlings yield in three to six years.

MATURITY: six months from flowering, gathered when green skin lightens & fruit become a bit softer.

STORING: fruit lasts several weeks in refrigerator. Juice can be frozen.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: dried rind for cattle fodder. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

— scan page 134 · book page 52 —

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Small evergreen tree. Can grow 15 ft. (4.5 m) tall. Quite thorny, although spineless cultivars exist. Fragrant leaves. White flowers. Vigorous.

ORIGIN: India, Malaysia.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Thrives with warmth.

PREFERS: ample moisture, well drained sandy or gravelly soil, slightly acid or acid pH & fult sun. Fertilized with a cover crop/green manure, or a seaweed mulch (washed & dried).

PRUNING & TRAINING: trained when young, after that only water-sprouts & deadwood need be removed.

TOLERATES: many soils, & more drought than most Citrus species.

INTOLERANT OF: cold conditions & dense clays.

ADVERSARIES: basically pest free, although ants can bring in scale, & fungi can occur where conditions are excessively humid or wet.

WEEDY: has naturalized in warm countries.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds (generally run true), root-sprouts, air-layering, budding, grafting & cuttings. Cuttings: mature wood can be successful, but typically have weak root systems.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SEE ALSO: KAFFIR LIME. Citrus hystrix.

Citrus reticulata & C. reticulata var- Gelicigsa. Several classes exist, including: ‘Satsuma,’ ts oe an Dancy,’ Fairchild, 'Lee,' 'Wilking’ & 'Nova.’ EDIBU rime, Highly estocmed, Koundich orange red or yellow fruit 1% to 3 in. (4-7.5 cm) wide. Fruit have a depressed top & thin, loose rind. Degree of seediness depends on cultivar. Pulp is sweet, rich & juicy. Eaten fresh raw, or in fruit salads, mixed green salads, stuffing for poultry, preserved, on cakes, candy-making, gelatins, puddings, juice, canned, liqueurs, etc. Higher in vitamin A than most CITRUS. Rind, dried, is a tasty condiment, food-flavoring, medicinal, & essential oi] source. 🌳 DESCRIPTION: Small, attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 25 ft. (7.5 m) tall, in time, but usually less. Typically thorny, but many nearly thornless cultivars exist. White flowers. Slow growing, with some cultivars being more vigorous.

ORIGIN: Southeast Asia, Philippines.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Best flavor is developed with heat. Some classes (i.e. ‘Satsuma,’ etc.) & some cultivars can tolerate tropical heat & humidity, as well as drought.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: well adapted to mid-elevations & may be higher elevation candidate.

TOLERATES: salt & more frost than most CITRUS.

PRUNING: trained while young, then pruned only of its dead wood.

ADVERSARIES: several possibilities exist. SEX: although most are self-fertile, some cultivars require another variety nearby.

PROPAGATED BY: grafting & seeds (some run true).

☠️ sr PUMMELO

Vol II · scan p. 134 · book p. 52

sr PUMMELO, Shaddock, Jeruk Besar. Citrus grandis, syn. C. maxima, syn. C. decumana. Numerous cultivars exist, including those with excellent fruit, with various colors, sweet or sour pulp, or a dwarfish habit. U of H recommendations include: ‘Haiku B; 'Chandler, ‘Kao Pan,' ‘Pauthel,' ‘Diamond Head,' ‘Leslie’ & ‘Sakata,’ all having sweet, firm pulp.

EDIBILITIES: Very large, rounded, flattened, or Pear-shaped fruits 4 to 12 in. (10-30 cm) wide. Fruits have a thick, yellowish rind. Typically few, although degree of seediness depends on cultivar & crossing. Pulp is either somewhat sweet or sour & can be on the dry side. Fruit pulp is refreshing raw, in fruit salads, jams, preserves, marmalades or as juice. Peel-pith is made into marmalades, lightly parboiled for braised dishes, dried or candied.

BEARING: air-layers can fruit in two to three years; seedlings in five.

STORING: if kept from drying, the fruit last very well. Actually one to three months of storage can improve its flavor.

SHIPPING: fruit transport well due to thick rind.

☠️ TOXICITY: As is true with other Citrus species, rind oil can be irritating with prolonged exposure.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: hard, tough & close grained; tool handles, small objects, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. PUMMELO is the largest CITRUS. Can grow 50 ft. (15 m) tall, but usually seen less. May be thomy. Large, fragrant, cream-colored flowers. Vigorous.

ORIGYN: Southeast Asia & Malaysia.

CLIMATE: tropics. Some cultivars tolerate cold conditions.

GROWN IN HAWATIT: thrives in hot, wet, humid lowlands here.

PREFERS: fertile silt overlaying a humusy clay loam, slightly acid to neutral pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: heat & salty soil.

INTOLERANT OF: harsh winds.

ADVERSARIES: leaf miner & similar possibilities as SWEET ORANGE.

PROPAGATED BY: air-layering & budding.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow, WetMesicDry

🌳 SOUR ORANGE

Vol II · scan p. 134 · book p. 52

SOUR ORANGE, Seville Orange, Bitter Orange, Moli. Citrus aurantium. Several strains, varieties & cultivars exist, including thornless, smailer & disease-resistant ones.

EDIBILITIES: Fragrant, round or oval, red-orange fruits 3 in. (7.5 cm) wide. Seediness depends on cultivar. Pulp very tart, bitter, aromatic; typically too sour raw; added to salads, curries, chili, pies & tarts, cakes, beverages, ades, marmalades, preserved or candied. In Mexico the fruit is halved & eaten salted with chili paste. Juice is very good in marinades, sauces, as fish or meat flavoring, ades & in wine-making. Fragrant “Neroli” oil is distilled or expressed from flowers & is a flavoring for the liqueurs Cointreau, Grand Marnier, Curacao & other beverages, candies, ice-cream, etc. Rind is made into marmalade, "bouquet garni,” BITTER ORANGE-oil. BITTER ORANGE-oil is utilized as a flavoring for many foods, beverages, chewing gum, liqueurs, etc. Under developed fruit can be fried or made into pickles. Leaves are brewed as a tea. Flowers provide tea scent & perfume.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: leaves as fodder.

BEE FORAGE: nectar.

FRAGRANCE: flowers, & “Neroli” oil as perfume.

FIREWOOD.

LANDSCAPING: omamental, hedge (some cultivars), MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

SOAP: pounded leaves & fruit as a soap replacement.

WOOD: hard, dense, fine-grained & valuable. Utilized for turnery, cabinet-making, baseball bats, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 30 ft. (9 m) tall with 20 ft. (6 m) crown, though dwarfish cultivars exist. More upright, narrow crown than SWEET ORANGE. Degree of armoring depends on cultivar, but often has long thorns. Crushed foliage has a strong, acrid odor. Fragrant, white to light-green flowers. Vigorous. Deep tap-root.

LIFE SPAN: six hundred plus years.

ORIGIN: Southeast Asia.

CLIMATE: near tropics & subtropics.

PREFERS: moist, fertile soil, slightly acid to neutral pH full sun.

TOLERATES: most can accept various soils, drought, wetness, high water-table, brief frost, neglect & other harsh conditions.

ADVERSARIES: although the tree is a survivor, it can be subject to tristeza & other viruses, fungi & scab. Resists gummosis & foot-rot.

WEEDY: naturalized in many warm countries.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds (generally tue). Germination: three weeks. An important, vigorous & disease-resistant rootstock for other Citrus species.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

☆🌳☠️ SWEET ORANGE

Vol II · scan p. 135

☆ SWEET ORANGE, Common- durant. or Kona Orange, Laranja, Moli kai, Moli ‘aina, ‘Arani, Alani. Citrus sinensis, prev. C. rantium var. SINENSIS. Several types & many cultivars exist, some seedless, & dwarfs. SEE: SOME NOTABLE VARIETIES, following.

DIBILITIES: Highly esteemed fruit. Round, orange, yellowish-green or green fruit 2 to 4 in. (5-10 cm) wide. Smooth, adherent tind, & solid core. Degree of seediness depends on cultivar. Pulp is sweet & juicy & delicious eaten fresh raw, in fruit salads, gelatins & many other desserts, or with poultry & meats, as a gamish, candied (with peel), or dried for powdered food-flavoring. Juice, either fresh or frozen, as a beverage, for jellies, candy-making, sherbets & ice-creams, wine- & brandy-making, etc. Full sun & abundant heat during fruit maturation increases sweetness & juiciness. Various oils distilled or expressed from flowers, peels, leaves are utilized as aromatic & essential oils for flavoring & perfumes. Rind as marmalade, food-flavoring, candied & in cleaning products. Flowers are edible or as a tea. Leaves can be made into tea. Seeds are a source of oil for cooking & other products.

BEARING: budded trees can begin to yield at a younger age than seedlings, they also tend to have fewer thorns & seeds, be smaller & have less vigor. Can be alternate bearing.

MATURITY: for year-round harvest, early-, mid- & late-season varieties can be planted.

HARVESTING: fruit are clipped or snapped off. Most varieties store well on tree.

STORING: fruit last well if kept cool & humid. Juice freezes very well,

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Proximity to a flowering tree has caused respiratory irritation in many people. 2. Rind oil can irritate skin. 3. Saw-dust from wood can initiate an asthma attack,

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: pelleted pulp-residue from juice extraction for livestock. Seed-residue as partial cattle-feed.

BEE FORAGE: nectar.

FRAGRANCE: various distilled or expressed oils.

INSECTICIDE: limonene in peel.

LANDSCAPING: hedge, etc. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

OILS: perfumes, cleaning products, soap-making, etc. ROADSIDE & PARKING-LOT

TREE.

WOOD: hard, fine grained, but subject to termites: cabinetry, furniture, tumery, carving, walking sticks, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: SWEET ORANGE is an attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 25 ft. (7.5 m) tall, or twice that in time. Rounded canopy. Degree of thorniness depends on cultivar, but generally has few thorns. Aromatic white flowers. Typically slow growing, although some cultivars are quite vigorous. Even though fairly shallow rooted, its roots usually extend twice as wide as the canopy.

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: possibly southwest Asia, China &/or India.

CLIMATE: tropics, subtropics, or warm temperate zones. Although ORANGES require ample heat, their rind develops deepest color only where temperature drops below 60°F (15.5°C). ORANGES in hot, wet lowland tropics tend not to blossom well, & due to high temperature, rind may stay green even when fruit is good & ready to eat. Most cultivars are intolerant of excessive heat or cold.

GROWN IN HAWATLT: ORANGES grow from the lowlands to mid elevations depending on cultivar.

PREFERS: rich, moist, well drained, loamy or sandy soil, pH 5.5 to 7.2 & full sun. Care & weeding is needed, especially in youth. Benefits from mulch. Specific nutrients are given according to soil-tests, leaf-analysis & destiny of the fruit.

PRUNING: training is typically not needed. Water-sprouts & deadwood should be cut off & sealed, as well as those branches within 12 in. (30 cm) of ground. Harsh pruning can reduce blossoming, stimulate suckering, & spread diseases.

TOLERATES: many conditions, including brief frost. Tolerances depend on cultivar, thus it is wise to choose the best ones for your locale.

INFOLERANT OF: dry soil, neglect, harsh drying wind, long periods of cold weather, & its life is shortened when grown on heavy clay.

ADVERSARIES: fruit flies, scale, mites, & subject to gummosis fungus, foot-rot, some viruses. Mono-culture increases likelihood of adversaries.

ORGANIC-GROWING: excellent with resistant cultivars, healthy vigorous rootstock, diversity & IPM. Careful attention to plant- & soil- health can prevent many problems. SEX: probably self infertile & needs crossing pollination.

PROPAGATED BY: budding, grafting & seeds (variable). Seeds sprout well when fresh or refrigerated. Germination: three weeks.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

PARTIAL LISTING OF VARIETIES: ‘BLOOD ORANGES.' Many cultivars exist, with some being nearly seedless.

EDIBILITIES: Refreshing, reddish pulp. Eaten in fruit salads, sauces, marmalade, or as a garnish. Juice is very good in sauces, beverages, etc. Develops red pulp only in colder weather.

STORING & SHIPPING: some cultivars hold up well.

☆ CUCUMBER / KAʻUKAMA

Vol II · scan p. 136 · book p. 60

☆ CUCUMBER / KAʻUKAMA Cucumis sativus. Cucurbitaceae (Gourd) Family. Many cultivars, types, forms & resistant varieties exist.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient food. Long, crisp, refreshing fruits are eaten fresh raw, sliced in mixed salads (‘English’ varieties), cold soup (“aspic"), stews, as a cooked vegetable, sautéed, oil braised, marinated with onions & vinegar or yogurt, pickled (gherkin & dill pickle varieties), or as kimchee. Seed kernels can be eaten raw, roasted, or as a minor source of edible oil. New leaves & tender stems in mixed salads or as cooked greens.

MATURITY: two to four months. Fruits are best when picked while still young.

HARVESTING: continued picking can prolong production up to six months.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: over-mature fruits for livestock & chickens.

LANDSCAPING: bush forms for flower-gardens, climbing forms for trellis. MEDICINAL QUALIFIES.

PEST-REPELLENT: deters ants.

DESCRIPTION: Annual vine. Stems can grow 10 ft. 3 m) long. Sprawling, climbing, or bush habit. Climbs by tendrils. Yellow flowers. Fast growing. Extensive shallow roots. Some varieties are allelopathic.

ORIGIN: South Asia tropics, East Indies.

CLIMATE: tropics, to temperate zone summers. Ideal temperatures between 65 & 75°F (18-23° C.)

PREFERS: fertile, evenly moist, well drained, light, humusy soil, pH 5.5 to 7.5 & full sun or light shade. Heavy feeder. Responds to amending with aged manure or compost. Benefits from mulch & nitrogen feedings. Planted in "hills" or on a trellis, fence, or as an orchard groundcover. An east-west trellis orientation provides greatest sun. Constant water availability reduces bitterness.

TOLERATES: some varieties are more resistant to disease or drought.

INTOLERANT OF: sandy or heavy soil & wet feet.

PRUNING: tip-pinching encourages branching.

ASSOCIATES: benefits from being grown after a nitrogen-fixing crop.

ADVERSARIES: fruit flies & CUCUMBER-beetles. Powdery- or downy-mildew & anthracnose are common in cool, or excessively humid weather. CUCUMBER are said to be antagonistic to fragrant herbs & Potatoes.

ORGANIC-GROWING: resistant varieties are selected. Floating row-cover provides warmth & protection (highlands). Hard skinned varieties are more resistant to’ fruit flies.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize, but not invasive. SEX: monoecious.

POLLINATION: bees.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span can be three years.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown 1 in. (2.5cm) deep. Germination: about one week. Warmth is necessary; chilling soil with cool water should be avoided. Transplanting is not recommended since roots are so delicate. Benefits from being hilled up, once established.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

DAYLILY / LĪLIA PALAʻAI Hemerocallis flava. Hemerocallidaceae Liliaceae Alliaceae (Lily) Family. Many species & thousands of colorful hybrids exist, including dwarfs.

EDIBILITIES: Flowers, flower-buds & shoots may be eaten cooked, braised, as fritters, in "hot & sour soup," sautéed, meat dishes, as condiment, dried or pickled. Vegetable-like flavor varies from sweet to slightly bitter. Early shoots as an Asparagusreplacement. Next-day blooms are sliced diagonally for salads. Day-old or dried flowers, called “Kim choi" or "Huang hua ts'ai," are a meaty addition to soups & stews. Flowers are high in beta-carotene. Young tubers, harvested early spring, are tasty in salads, stews, cooked like Com. Older tubers can be eaten cooked.

⚠️ CAUTION: DAY LILY is diuretic & laxative, thus eaten only in moderation.

APPLICATIONS: EROSION CONTROL.

LANDSCAPING: ornamental, banks, borders, rockeries, ground-cover, pool- & streamsides, etc. Low in allergens. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous perennial. Foliage grows 2 ft. (.6 m) tall; flower-stalk 3 ft. (9 m). Fragrant, yellow or orange flowers; "Hemerocallis;" Greek for "beautiful for a day." Blooms nearly year-round. Clumping tuberous roots,

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: central Europe, temperate northern Asia.

CLIMATE: subtropics & temperate zones.

PREFERS: moist, average, well drained soil, slightly acid pH & either full sun (with after-noon shade in hot climates) or shade. Easy & adaptable. Thrives with mulch. Heavy fertilizing is best avoided.

TOLERATES: various conditions, including acid soil, heavy rains, frosty winters, full shade & some drought.

INTOLERANT OF: dry conditions.

ASSOCIATES: can be planted with Iris for successive blooms. Understoried with Marigold, Dill, etc.

ADVERSARIES: generally resistant. WEEDY?: although H. flava is only an occasional garden escapee, H. fulva & H., lilio-asphodelus are serious, invasive weeds.

PROPAGATED BY: divisions & seeds. Divided during cooler months, especially early spring, or if over-crowded, at least every few years. Seeds need over a month of cold, moist stratification. Germination: half to two months.

Vol II · scan p. 139 · book p. 63

☆ DURIAN Durio abethinus. Bombacaceae (Bombax) Family. Many varieties exist. Some non-odorous DURIANS exist, but are not preferred by DURIAN lovers.

EDIBILITIES: Thought to be the "King" of tropical fruits. Large, green, heavy, fetid fruit are covered with sharp spines. Fruit grow to 6 in. (15 cm) wide & twice that long & can weigh to 5 Ibs. (2.3 kg). Enjoying DURIAN is an “acquired taste." Rich nutritious pulp is eaten fresh chilled, or in sauces, custards, preserves, ice-creams, candies, paste, dried, salted, canned in syrup, or fermented. To open, gloves should be wom & fruit cut along one of the faint lines that run from top to bottom. Under-ripe fruit may be eaten in soups, or cooked whole as a vegetable with spices & Coconut-milk. Seed-covers (aril) are edible. Seeds have been eaten boiled, roasted, sliced & fried, or dried then boiled, but, SEE: TOXICITY, FOLLOWING. Young tender leaves, flower-petals, tender shoots are edible cooked.

BEARING: can begin fruiting in five years, but usually twice that.

MATURITY: about three to four months from fruit-set to ripening. Short summer season. Ripe when the seeds rattle & the fruit’s mid-section smells strong, but not sour.

HARVESTING: fruits fall when ripe.

STORING: fruit spoils very quickly at room temperature, although it can hold up several days in a refrigerator. Fruit may be fermented in a Palm-leaf wrap, & lasts as long as a year as “tempoya.”

SHIPPING: fresh fruit only rapidly, while frozen fruit transport well.

☠️ TOXICITY: seeds contain a poison that is said to cause difficulty in breathing.

APPLICATIONS:

FIREWOOD: dried rinds. MEDICINAL QUALITIES. Possible aphrodisiac. wINDBREAK: climate modification.

WOOD: lasting: construction, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Very large evergreen tree. Can grow 100 ft. (30 m) tall, but grafted trees rarely reach 40 ft. (12 m). Nocturnally aromatic flowers.

CLIMATE: needs warm, humid, tropical conditions year-round.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: on occasion.

INTOLERANT OF: wet feet.

ADVERSARIES: generally resistant, but root-rot, Grass-hoppers & Chinese Rosebeetles are possible.

WEEDY: can reseed, but not thought to be invasive. SEX: hermaphroditic. Cross-pollination is needed.

POLLINATION: possibly by bats, though tree can fruit where no bats reside.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are variable. Fresh seeds are cleaned before sowing. Seed life span is about one week.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds, budding & grafting. Germination: about one week. Low, WetMesic

L. nervosa. Sapotaceae (Sapodilla) Family. Varying types, qualities & cultivars exist. "Ross Sapote' is a high quality variety.

EDIBILITIES: Glossy yellow fruit 5 in. (12.5 em) long with a pointed end, thin skin, & one to five seeds. Pulp is soft, musky, sweet & very rich. Can also be sweet, dry & mealy, similar to a baked Sweet Potato. Eaten spooned fresh raw, or in fruit salads, frozen, quick baked with spices, puddings & custards, cupcakes, pies, pancakes, ice creams, sherbets, milk-shakes, jams, marmalades, butter, smoothies, dried & powdered, or frozen. Rich in carotene, niacin, with some vitamin C. Latex is "chicle’like.

BEARING: seedlings can yield in three to six years; graftlings sooner.

MATURITY: summer to fall. Itis difficult to judge the correct moment of maturity & picking too soon results in poor ripening. Harvesting fallen fruits each morning is the best option. Otherwise, fruit can be picked just before fully ripe & allowed to ripen a week at room temperature.

HARVESTING: fruit are clipped off tree so as not to tear delicate skin.

STORING: ripe fruit holds up well with refrigeration. Freezes well.

SHIPPING: transports well if picked firm.

APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: ornamental specimen. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

SHADE TREE: dense cover.

WOOD: dense, heavy, strong & rot-resistant: building, timber, furniture, etc.

ORIGIN: low elevation Central America.

CLIMATE: humid tropics.

LUCMO. Pouteria lucuma.

MIRACLE FRUIT. Synsepalum dulcificum, syn. Pouteria dulcifer. SAPOTE, MAMEY & GREEN. Pouteria species. ☆ EGGPLANT / LAHOPIPI Aubergine, Talong, Brinjal, Belingela, Mad Apple, Apples of Love. Solanum melongena. Solanaceae (Nightshade) Family. Many cultivars exist varying in form, size, color of fruit, level of disease resistance & adaptation. Dwarfs are available.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed. Shiny, round, long, oval, or Pear-shaped fruits. From 1 in. (2.5 cm) miniatures to 12 in. 30cm) "longs," with round fruited forms averaging 6 in. (15 cm) long. Although EGGPLANT skin is typically deep-purple, they also can be white, striped, yellow, or lavender. Excellent sweet, mild flavor, or sometimes somewhat bitter. High in potassium, low in sodium. Eaten baked, stuffed, fried, steamed, sautéed, broiled, grilled, roasted, mashed, curries, soups & stews, battered for tempera or frying, with other vegetables & meats, moussaka, ratatouille, EGGPLANT-caviar, sometimes raw, chutneys, preserves, marinated, pickled (baby EGGPLANT, small types), or dried. Delicious when brushed with oil, soy sauce & herbs, & baked, broiled, or grilled. Some cultivars have tenderer skin than others. Under ripe fruit is occasionally an ingredient in curries.

☠️ TOXICITY: Leaves of the Solanaceae Family often contain alkaloids & are not recommended for eating.

⚠️ CAUTION: Hairs on leaves & stems may be irritating to skin..

BEARING: Harvest can begin in two to three months (depending on cultivar), with fruiting period extending three to four months, or longer. Can continue to bear several years, if well tended, especially when grafted onto resistant rootstock.

MATURITY: Fruit are ready to pick when highly glossy, firm & some color has developed. Can be harvested from one third to full sized. Small, glossy, young fruit, with their smaller, softer seeds, are preferred to older ones.

HARVESTING: Fruit stem is cut. Regular harvesting prolongs production.

STORING: Stores a few days if wrapped tightly in plastic bags in a refrigerator. May also be dried, pickled, or preserved.

SHIPPING: Transports fairly well with careful handling.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: Borders, raised beds, herb & flower gardens, etc.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: EGGPLANT is an attractive, herbaceous, or somewhat shrub-like perennial. Can grow 3 to 6 ft. (.9-1.8 m) tall, though 10 in. (25 cm) dwarfs exist. EGGPLANT is occasionally spiny, but there are unarmed types. Leaves are green with purple highlights. Flowers amethyst & yellow. Rapid growing. Deep tap-root.

LIFE SPAN: around three years.

ORIGIN: Tropical Southeast Asia, or East India?

— scan page 141 · book page 65 —

CLIMATE: Tropics, subtropics, or temperate zone (summers). EGGPLANTS need a long, warm or hot growing season. Ideal temperature range is 70 to 85°F (21-29°C). If night temperatures fall below 70°F (21°C), cloches or floating row-cover can help keep plants warm. Tolerates high temperatures & high humidity. Some cultivars can handle drought well, but most need itrigation & mulch in dry condition. Intolerant of cool weather & frost.

GROWNIN HAWATLI: Very successfully, even year-round in many regions,

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: EGGPLANT needs ample space. Cultured as a Tomato would be. Prefers deep, moist, rich, light, well drained, humusy loam, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. Heavy feeder; thrives in beds deeply amended with aged manure or compost & benefits from side-dressing monthly. If cultivated, it is done only shallowly to prevent root damage. Benefits from mulch when seedlings are well established & soil has warmed sufficiently. Where cool, floating row-cover protects plants & increases warmth, thus enhancing production. When plants are over ft. (30 cm) tall, soil can be mounded up around base of stem. In dry conditions, young plants are watered once or twice a week. Later, the fruiting plants are given a heavy soaking twice or three times weekly.

TOLERATES: average garden soil.

INTOLERANT OF: prolonged flooding, as well as poorly drained soil, or wet clay,

PRUNING: Plant can be cut back to 1 ft. (30 cm) tall after first harvest, although some plants may subsequently die from disease. Benefits from fertilizing after pruning.

ASSOCIATES: Beans... & ?

ADVERSARIES: Possible pests include whiteflies, spider mites, aphids, leaf miners, flea-beetles, Rose-beetles & nematodes. Mildew, wilt, &/or fungus may be problematic where conditions are too wet, too humid, or overly crowded. To date there is no way to control bacterial wilt & no resistant varieties, thus infected sites must be avoided.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate in warm fertile conditions. Disease- & pest-resistant cultivars exist. EGGPLANT require at a least three year rotation from other Solanum, i.c.: Peppers, Potatoes, Tomatoes, etc.

WEEDY: Can escape & naturalize, but not considered a serious threat.

DISADVANTAGES: Plants can lodge. Some species allow the fruit to touch the ground, while others hold them in the air. Thoms call for vigilance when harvesting.

REMARKS: EGGPLANT is grafted onto wild Solanum forvum for nematode resistance. Tomato can be grafted onto EGGPLANT for its greater tolerance to excess water. sEX: Hermaphroditic & mostly self pollinated.

POLLINATION: ?

SEED-SAVING: For home plantings, varieties are isolated by 150 ft. (45 m); more for pure seed. Seed life span two years.

PROPAGATION: Seeds & occasionally cuttings. Seeds are soaked first, then covered % in. (6 mm) deep. Germination: one & a half to three weeks, ideally at 70 to 90°F (21-32°C). Beginning at two weeks, seedlings like to be fed liquid fertilizer weekly. Sown in flats in spring to transplant one & a half to two months later. For strong plants, transplanted when 3 in. (7.5 cm) tall into rich pots & then to the garden when twice that height. Planted at same level. Transplants benefit from starter solution. Cuttings: semi-ripe, compact, noded stem-pieces are best for disease-resistance, or strong axillary sprouts.

ENDIVE / ESCAROLE Cichorium endivia, Asteraceae (Sunflower) Family. Curly-, cut-, or broad-leafed & upright forms exist, with numerous cultivars of each. ‘Escarole' is broad-leafed, while 'Endive’ is curly. ‘Broad-leaved Batavian' is a self-blanching, rot-resistant variety. Curly ENDIVE is sometimes mistakenly called "Chicory."

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed greens. Large slightly bitter leaves have a robust flavor & are more nutritious than most Lettuce. Eaten fresh raw, or cooked, sautéed, in soups & stews, braised, pickled, or juiced. First-year roots may be sliced, dried, roasted & ground for a Coffee-additive. (Reported a caffeine antidote).

MATURITY: leaves are cut while young, especially during hot weather. 436

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous biennial or annual. Leafy rosette of 1 ft. (30 cm) stretches to 3 ft. (9 m) when flowering. Blue flowers.

ORIGIN: possibly the highlands of East India, Asia or the Mediterranean.

CLIMATE: temperate zones.

GROWN IN HA WATT: grows well here, especially in cool weather.

PREFERS: requires fertile, moist, well drained, humusy soil. Heavy feeder. Benefits from mulch for weed control & moisture retention.

TOLERATES: shade. Also accepts heat, but yields better in cool weather.

INTOLERANT OF: drought & poor soil.

PRUNING & TRAINING: can be "blanched" by tying up leaves to make a milder, though less nutritious leaf; blanched only two to three weeks during dry weather, since wetness causes rot of inner head.

ADVERSARIES: very resistant.

WEEDY: can naturalize, but not considered invasive.

PROPAGATED BY: direct seeding or transplanted. Seed is covered 1/3 in. (8 cm). Sown very early spring or fall. Germination: one week.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

⚠️Ⓦ GINGER / ʻAWAPUI PĀKĒ / ʻAWAPUHI ʻAI

Vol II · scan p. 143 · book p. 70

GINGER / ʻAWAPUI PĀKĒ / ~AWAPUHI‘AI Vegetable Ginger, Spice Ginger, Ginger Root, Edible Ginger, True Ginger, Jamaica Ginger, Keong, Sheng jiang (fresh rhizome), Gan jiang (dried rhizome). Zingiber officinale. Zingiberaceae (Ginger) Family. Types & races differ in level of fiber, pungency & quality of yield. Several varieties exist, including a dwarf. VEGETABLE- & SPICE-GINGERS are sometimes listed as different varieties.

SEVERAL TYPES: ‘Chinese': Large plant & rhizomes. Heavy yields, but less pungent than the Japanese type. ‘Chinese Yellow’: Smaller plant & rhizomes. Yellow rhizomes have a mild flavor. ‘Japanese’: Plant & rhizomes are smaller, but more pungent.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed spice, medicine & food. Fragrant underground stem has a tasty, spicy flavor. Skin is usually cleaned or scraped off. GINGER root may be eaten fresh raw or cooked with vegetables, fish & meats, as well as in stir-fries, soups & stews, Asian- & Eastern Indian cuisine, puddings, cakes, GINGER-cookies & -breads, Pumpkin pies, pastries, condiments, curry powders, chutneys, pickles, marmalades, preserves, crystallized, candied, pickled, beverages (GINGER-ale, -beer, or -wine), tea, or is a source of essential oil. Immature rhizomes, peeled, are eaten fresh raw in mixed salads, as a sweetmeat, or pickled, etc. Young, tender leaf-shoots are only somewhat pungent & edible cooked as greens, or pureed for dips & sauces.

⚠️ CAUTION: Caution is indicated regarding GINGER when there are conditions of “heat” in the stomach (i.e. ulcers, etc.). Large doses of GINGER in the beginning stages of pregnancy, are avoided, although in normal amounts the rhizome is a safe & proven remedy for moming sickness.

BEARING: Eight to ten months.

MATURITY: Ready to harvest after summer, as days shorten. For SPICE GINGER, the mature rhizomes are gathered when the foliage begins to yellow & die back, after the skin has toughened. For VEGETABLE GINGER, the slightly immature rhizomes are gathered while their skin remains tender, just after plants have flowered (if they do flower).

HARVESTING: Rhizomes are dug by hand with a garden fork, -O°O bar, or machinery. Rhizomes can be stored in the soil & dug as needed, but tend to deteriorate if left too long. New growth spoils the rhizomes. A ratoon crop may follow primary harvest.

PROCESSING: Immediately after digging & washing, the rhizomes are dried in a shady spot around two days to heal-over. With VEGETABLE GINGER, the rhizomes are separated into "hands," cleaned & sorted. The rhizomes of the SPICE variety are cleaned, cut into pieces, sorted & then dried for five to six days. Sometimes germination is suppressed by dipping the rhizome in boiling water first. Once dried, they can be milled to a powder, however this reduces the spice's potency. GINGER for preserving can be stored in brine before processing.

STORING: Roots are stored in a dry cool] spot. Can also be dried, powdered, or cut into pieces & canned, frozen, or preserved in vinegar, salt, or syrup. ‘

SHIPPING: Dried SPICE GINGER transports very well. VEGETABLE GINGER ships well, if kept cool.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Not appealing as animal feed, although pigs will eat it.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Needs to be well fed & watered.

LANDSCAPING: Shady edges, raised beds, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications. Rhizome & rhizome skin are important in Chinese Medicine. Massage-oil ingredient. Thought to be an aphrodisiac. Two pungent, reddish-root races that are purely medicinal exist.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, deciduous, herbaceous perennial. Can grow to 4 ft. (.3-1.2 m) tall. Slender stems. Foliage dies back in autumn. Flowers are yellow-green with a purple lip. GINGER rarely flowers & when they do, they seldom fruit. Thick, creeping, rhizomes, with slender, fiber-like roots just under soil’s surface.

ORIGIN: An ancient plant from either India, the Islands of the Pacific, or Southeast Asia.

CLIMATE: Tropics & subtropics. Thrives in hot, humid conditions. Intolerant of temperatures below 65°F (18°C), cold soil, dry conditions & intense sun. Rhizomes can rot in wet, cold conditions.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: GINGER, principally in the VEGETABLE form, is produced in quantity for local & export markets. The SPICE type is almost unknown in Hawaiʻi.

— scan page 144 · book page 71 —

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Easy to grow. Heavy feeder. Prefers moist, rich, loose, humusy, well drained loam, somewhat acid pH light shade or full sun. To encourage rapid growth, GINGER needs plenty of food, such as aged manure, compost, or manure-tea. Responds to amending & side-dressing. Mulched to control weeds, maintain moisture & nourish soil.

TOLERATES: some water-logging. Can be planted on ridges for better drainage.

INTOLERANT OF: sandy or gravelly soil. Hard soil can deform the rhizomes,

ASSOCIATES: Can be grown under the protective shade of Pigeon Pea, Hapu‘u, Camellia, Coffee, ‘Olena (Turmeric), Citrus or Coconut. Intercropped with Yams,

ADVERSARIES: Relatively free of pests, but susceptible to root-knot nematodes. GINGER is particularly sensitive to bacterial wilt, soil-bome disease that reduces yields & kills the plant.

CAUTION: the GINGER in Hawaiʻi is full of bacterial wilt & it is easy to introduce the disease with infected propaguls, tools, muddy boots, etc.

ORGANIC-GROWING: To avoid bacterial wilt disease it is necessary to plant only clean, disease-free rhizomes, & to sow only where GINGER has not grown for several years. Unfortunately it is difficult to be sure seed-pieces are disease-free.

WEEDY: Can escape & naturalize, especially the SPICE form. Soil infested by bacterial wilt keeps it in check. SEX: Hermaphroditic. Seldom produces seed.

SEED-SAVING: Approximately a forth to a third of the yearly harvest is saved each year.

PROPAGATION: Multiplied from pieces of rhizome. Sections are typically 1 to 2 in. (2.5-5 cm) long, each having several growth buds. Cut ends are allowed to dry superficially before planting. Placed 2 to 4 in. (5-10 cm) deep. Planting can be done at any time. Sprouts can emerge in about ten days. Most store-brought GINGER has been killed in hot water.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

ANOTHER NOTABLE SPECIES: vw» MIOGA, Japanese Ginger. Zingiber mioga.

EDIBILITIES: Rhizome is a flavoring in Japanese cuisine. Flower-bracts as a soup flavoring or sliced as a condiment.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous rhizomatic perennial. Can grow 3 ft. (.9 m) tall.

ORIGIN: Japan. GROWN IN

HAWAIʻI: on a small scale.

TOLERATES: colder conditions than Zingiber officinale. [WEEDY?]

PROPAGATED BY: rhizome pieces.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

SPAN: very long lived.

Dried seeds can be stratified first in warm, moist conditions for one to two months, followed by one to two months of cold, moist conditions. Seeds need light to sprout. Germination: one to two months at 70 to 75°F (21-24°C). ?/High, WetMesic/?

🌳☠️ GUAVA / KUAWA

Vol II · scan p. 145 · book p. 75

GUAVA / KUAWA Common Guava, Yellow Guava, Apple Guava, Lemon Guava, Pear Guava, Bayabas, Guayaba, Goiaba, Tuava, Kuawa Lemi. Psidium guajava, syn. P. cujavillus. Myrtaceae (Myrtle) Family. Several varieties & many cultivars exist, including seedless, dwarfs & a number with outstanding fruit.

EDIBILITIES: Economically important, but weedy. Fragrant, yellow, round or Pear-shaped fruits grow 1 to 4 in. (2.5-10 cm) or wider. Size, shape, color & flavor are highly variable & depend on cultivar. Yellow, ivory, or pink pulp varies from being creamy & smooth, to granular & coarse, & from sweet to tart. Some varieties are exceptionally tasty. Seed-ball can be large or small. Very high in vitamin C, with moderate amounts of vitamins A, B, calcium, iron & phosphorus. Eaten fresh raw, cooked for desserts, stewed, baked, pies, etc., as well as dried as slices & leathers, or frozen. Pulp (seeds removed) is eaten in fruit salads, jams & jellies, preserves, marmalades, pastes & purees, chutneys, GUAVA-butter, sherbets, juice & nectar, etc. Sometimes can be eaten skin, seeds & all. Tart, wild GUAVA are pectin-rich & excellent for jelly-making. Seeds are a source of an edible oil.

☠️ TOXICITY: Excess consumption of fruit can cause diarrhea. Large quantities of immature fruit are detrimental due to tannins. Leaves & bark are also very high in tannins.

BEARING: Can begin fruiting in two to three years. Vegetative cultivars can be highly productive.

MATURITY: Three to five months from flower to fruit. Fastest in warm weather. Although rain & temperature influence cycles, GUAVA can yield nearly year-round. Fruits best when harvested after they enlarge, just begin to yellow, but before full ripe. Fruit picked immature do not ripen well. Tree-ripened fruit have best flavor, though more susceptible to bird & insect damage.

HARVESTING: Fruit can be clipped or plucked from trees & must be handled gently.

STORING: After harvest, mature fruit will ripen in two to seven days. Ripe fruit can then last several days to a week at room temperature, & up to two weeks when refrigerated at 39 to 41°F (4-5°C). Lasting quality depends upon cultivar. Fruit with waxy skin hold up best. Fruit may be canned either stewed or as nectar or juice, & frozen either chopped or whole. Juice & fruit may be dehydrated.

SHIPPING: Fresh GUAVA are rarely transported far since they are so easily bruised & quick to decompose. To ship, the fruit can be harvested mature, but still under-ripe. Wrapped individually in tissue, layered with padding & kept at 45 to 55°F (7-13°C). GUAVA are usually shipped as a processed product, such as nectar or juice. 76 xs: (SEE! WEEDY, following. DO NOT INTRODUCE GUAVA TO GUAVA-FREE AREAS.)

— scan page 146 —

APTIMAL FEED. Young leaves & fruits as forage for cattle & pigs. (Although animals spread seeds). BEE FORAGE,

EARTHWORKS. Durable & lasting, but Weedy. Can be planted on berms.

FIREWOOD & CHARCOAL: Excellent.

LANDSCAPING: Omamental, hedge, or dense barrier (pruned low).

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications, but largely due to tannins.

SHADE TREE: Big, old trees can provide welcome shade. 7

WOOD: Hard, strong, close grained & lasting if not exposed to the elements. GUAVA wood decomposes when wet. Utilized for lumber, carpentry, engraving, turning, tool handles, poles, etc. Twigs for basketry, roasting quills, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: GUAVA is a small, evergreen tree or shrub. Can grow 6 to 35 ft. (2-10.5 m) tall, with a trunk to 10 in. (25 cm) thick. Although GUAVA has a single trunk, it's usually short, with branches forming near soil level, & often suckers near its base. Smooth peeling bark. Leathery leaves are fragrant when bruised. Clusters of slightly fragrant white flowers. Relatively fast growing. Shallow root system. Probably allelopathic; roots exude a substance that inhibits nearby plants (although not GRASSES),

LIFE SPAN: about fifteen productive years, although tree can live to forty.

ORIGIN: American tropics.. ded

CLIMATE: Tropics & subtropics. Highly adaptable to a variety of climates, dry, wet, or humid. Tolerates light frost & exten drought. Intolerant of prolonged freezing conditions, although GUAVA can regrow from its roots. Excessive water during ripening can cause fruit-splitting

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Introduced possibly early in the 1800's & now very common as an orchard & dooryard tree, & weed. Thrives from the coasts to the highlands.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Prefers rich, moist, well drained, heavy loam, pH 4.5 to 8.0 & full sun. Responds to quarterly feeding. Benefits from mutch, keeping it at least 6 in. (15 cm) from trunk.

TOLERATES: most soils, including heavy wet clay, sandy, gravelly or poor ones, some salt, temporary flooding & areas with high water-tables.

INTOLERANT OF: long term flooding.

PRUNING & TRAINING: GUAVA can be trained by allowing five to eight, strong, well placed limbs to grow after main trunk has achieved desired height. Because fruits are bome on new branches, GUAVA benefits from frequent pruning. Pruning is best done before the spring flush. Old branches also can be cut back to force new growth. Suckers & water-shoots are removed, especially from grafted & budded trees. Very low limbs may also be pruned off.

ASSOCIATES: ?

ADVERSARIES: Many pest & fungal problems are possible. Fruit flies have a notorious love of GUAVA, even before fruit ripen. Fruits are sometimes hardened by a fungus. Bird damage of ripe fruit is a serious problem. Tree succumbs to hot fires, but can resprout after a medium or low intensity burn.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Several somewhat fruit fly resistant varieties exist. Fallen fruit should be gathered & buried deeply, or anaerobically composted, to reduce infestation. Some very large fruited varieties can be bagged for protection. Providing adequate moisture at the beginning of fruit growth can reduce certain diseases. IPM is beneficial. WEEDY!: GUAVA belong to a remarkably weedy Family & Genus & are declared a Noxious Weed in many countries. GUAVA has become widely naturalized. "Sleeper weed.” Forms dense thickets. It is recommended NOT to introduce GUAVA to areas where they have not already invaded. GUAVA is difficult & expensive to eradicate. This tree can destroy pastures & is often found wild on grazing land, road edges, gulches, as well as fallow, disturbed, or barren land. Seeds are spread far & wide in bird- & other animal-droppings. Readily re-sprouts from cut stumps. Reportedly GUAVA may not have invaded Kaho olawe or Ni ihau; thus DO NOT plant them there.;

DISADVANTAGES: Weediness & the propensity of GUAVA fruit to host several serious fruit flies are drawbacks. SEX: Hermaphroditic. Either self-fertile or crossing. Most cultivars require a different variety nearby for pollination.

POLLINATION: Insects, largely honey-bees.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds run fairly true. Hand-pollination is an effective way of reducing seed variability. Although seed life span is about one year, fresh is best. Select cultivars must be propagated vegetatively to come absolutely true.

PROPAGATION: Budding, cuttings, air-layers, grafting, root-sprouts, root-cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: green to half-ripe wood, 4 to in. (6-12.5 mm) in diameter, are taken from new shoots. Growing tip, as well as two leaves are left on, & cutting is dipped in rooting-hormone, given bottom heat & misted. In hot, humid conditions, longer, larger cuttings have been successful, even without rooting-hormone. Air-layering is done in spring. Root-cuttings 6 in. (15 cm) long & % in. (1.25 cm) thick, are placed in moist medium. They are slow growing, taking up to a year before being large enough to transplant. Since trees from air-layers & cuttings do not tend to form a tap-root, thus blowing over easily, grafting & budding are preferred methods. Budding is the fastest & most cost effective propagation method. Seeds: sown % to % in. (.6-1.25 cm) deep. Germination: two to three weeks, up to two months. Scarification with boiling water or sulfuric acid speeds germination. Seedlings are susceptible to damping-off. Transplanted around six months.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow Mid, WetMesicDry

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed fruit. Tough skinned, green to maroon-black fruits 1 to 1% in. (2.5-4 cm) wide (depending on form.) Fruit grows singly or in small clusters on older branches & trunks (cauliflorus-habit.) Pulp is juicy, Grape-like, translucent & sweet to somewhat tart, or sometimes resinous & puckering. Eaten fresh raw & in pies, fruit-cakes, marmalades, jellies & jams (pectin needed), juices, ice-creams, wines, or liqueurs. Skin & seeds are discarded.

BEARING: while seedlings can begin fruiting in six to ten years; three years is possible with grafted trees.

MATURITY: from flower to fruit in one to two months. Ripens during warm months; April through July. Often bears more than once a year. Can bear nearly continuously if moist & warm enough. About one week after color changes, fruit can be taste-tested for readiness. Flavor declines rapidly after peak maturity.

HARVESTING: fruit should be plucked at least every other day.

STORING: fruit becomes bland & spoils rather quickly at room temperature, but can last two weeks in a refrigerator. Freezes well.

SHIPPING: holds up well with moderate care, especially when harvested somewhat immature.

☠️ TOXICITY: Astringent skins are high in tannin, thus excess consumption is avoided. When preserving, the tannin can be reduced by peeling most of the fruit.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: specimen, pruned hedge, topiary, etc. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WINDBREAK: closely spaced.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree or large shrub. Can grow 40 ft. (12 m) tall, but often seen half that. Upright habit. Dense foliage & branches. Fragrant white flowers. Flowering often occurs after a dormant or slow period, Relatively slow growing.

ORIGIN: Brazil.

CLIMATE: humid tropics & subtropics.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: frequently.

PREFERS: deep, fertile, moist, well drained soil, pH 5.0 to 7.0 & full sun or part shade. Needs plenty of room. Site should be well prepared to encourage early growth. Benefits from ample water & feeding until age four, then feeding may be reduced to encourage flowering. Fruiting trees again need regular fertilization to hold nitrogen at a moderate level, while still keeping leaves a light green. Excessive vegetative growth inhibits flowering & fruiting. Mulched to maintain moisture.

TOLERATES: various soils, including sandy or heavy, clay soil, various climates, wind, rain, flooding & full shade.

INTOLERANT OF: shade, salt air, drought, dry conditions & excess heat humidity.

PRUNING: pruned only for shaping, size reduction & easier access. Over-zealous pruning can encourage regression to non-fruiting stage.

ADVERSARIES: birds. Generaily disease resistant, except for a flower fungus rust in rainy seasons.

WEEDY: occasionally escaping cultivation, but probably not naturalized.

DISADVANTAGES: messy unharvested fruit. SEX: hermaphroditic & self-fertile. Parthenocarpic fruit do not need pollination. Crossing is said to increase fruiting.

POLLINATION: probably bees.

SEED-SAVING: seeds run true. Seeds are polyembryonic, with about four seedlings per seed. Seed life span is quite short.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds, cuttings, air-layering, grafting & inarching. Germination: three to six weeks. Propagation by vegetative means is difficult.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, WetMesic

🌿☠️Ⓦ JACK FRUIT & CHEMPEDAK

Vol II · scan p. 148 · book p. 80

JACK FRUIT & CHEMPEDAK Jak Fruit, Nangka. Artocarpus heterophyllus, syn. A. integrifolius. Moraceae (Fig) Family. Types & varieties vary widely in flavor, texture, latex content, hue, shape & age of bearing. Several named cultivars exist.

SEE ALSO: CHEMPEDAK, following.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed by many. One of the largest fruits known. Can grow 8 in. to 3 ft. (20-90 cm) long & 1% ft. (45 cm) wide & weigh from 10 to 110 Ibs. (4.5-50 kg). Yellow rind covered with short, thick, sharp, cone-like bumps. Quality is variable. The edible part of the fruit can be juicy & sweet, or dry & tart. High in carbohydrates & contains vitamin A & C. Young, unripe, but full grown fruit are excellent when boiled or cooked in stews, soups & curries, pickled, sliced & dried, or canned. Its quality is said to rival Breadfruit. Fully ripe unopened fruit have a strong, disagreeable aroma, but once opened, the whitish pulp may have a fruity fragrance. Ripe fruit can be cut into chunks, cored, then eaten raw or cooked, fried in curries, batter-fried, preserved, dried, or fermented. Rind is easier to cut off after cooking. “Rags," the juicy, golden arils around the seed of mature fruit, are thick, soft, & yielding with a flavor that varies from sweet & spicy to tart, & have a strong, spicy odor. “Rags” are eaten fresh raw as a dessert, or in fruit salads, soups, with Coconut milk, fried, added to main courses (especially with fish or Rice), or made into chutneys, ice-cream & other desserts, frozen for jam-making (“rags” are high in pectin), or preserved in syrup, dried, canned, or frozen. Large, nutritious, pale-brown seeds are similar to Chestnuts & edible roasted or boiled, then eaten as is, or fried, canned, ground into flour, or chopped & added to stews. Cooked seeds are high in carbohydrates & thought to be aphrodisiacal. Very young, tender leaves, shoots & immature male spikes are edible cooked, added to soups, stews, or curries. Rind is made into jelly.

☠️ TOXICITY: Overindulgence may result in digestive complaints. Ripe fruit has some laxative qualities. Unripe raw fruit is astringent & thought to be indigestible. Although raw seeds contain a strong trypsin inhibitor & are said to be indigestible, this can be remedied by roasting, baking or boiling.

STORING: KATUK does not store well. Short-term storage is possible if chilled. Can be frozen.

SHIPPING: Short distances only, unless frozen.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: Grown with nitrogen-fixing trees.

BIOMASS: KATUK produces large amounts of dry matter.

LANDSCAPING: Good slim, edible hedge, when regularly pruned.

LIVING-FENCE: Smail.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Known best for its tendency to reduce blood sugar.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: KATUK is a tall, lightly woody, perennial shrub. Can grow to 12 ft. (3.6 m) tall, but usually pruned lower. Sprawling, upright habit. Long stems tend to lodge due to their own heaviness. Understory plant. Small flowers sometimes mature into round, white pods containing three seeds. Pods dehisce when ripe. Either day-length neutral or blossoming during shorter days. Fast growing & vigorous in warm conditions. Produces a network of roots.

ORIGIN: South Asia, Bomeo.

CLIMATE: Thrives in hot, humid, tropical lowlands. Tolerates heavy rains, coastal conditions & some frost. Intolerant of drought freezing conditions. Does not do well in the highlands.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Frequently, but still not widely known.

PREFERS: Moist, rich, well drained soil, somewhat acid pH, & sun or part shade. Tip-growth is encouraged by regular watering, fertilizing, pinching, mulching & part shade. Fertilizer with both organic material & minerals.

TOLERATES: full sun, most soils, including acid or heavy ones, temporary flooding & neglect.

INTOLERANT OF: prolonged flooding.

PRUNING: KATUK is usually kept trimmed between 3 to 6 ft. (.9-2 m) tall. Plant tends to be awkward unless pruned often. Regular pruning or harvesting induces tender new shoots.

ASSOCIATES: KATUK is not very competitive, thus it can be grown with other crops, including nitrogen-fixing trees.

ADVERSARIES: Generally pest & disease free, except for slug & snail damage to seedlings (try "Sluggo"™),.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate.

WEEDY: Rarely, though KATUK can reseed. SEX: Monoecious. Plants bear many male & only a few female flowers.

PROPAGATED BY: Cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: part-woody, old or new material up to 12 in. G0 cm) long, each having a couple of nodes. After most of the leaves have been removed, cuttings can be planted directly in soil in a partly shady spot. Cuttings readily root, & while they grow slowly at first, they eventually become vigorous. Planted ideally during a rainy season. Seeds are sown no deeper than % in. (1.25 cm). Germination: irregular, up to three months..

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

KENAF Hemp-Leafed Hibiscus, Indian Hemp, Deccan Hemp, Bastard Jute. Hibiscus cannabinus. Malvaceae (Hibiscus) Family. Various forms, varieties & cultivars exist, including a wide range of adaptations. Frequently crosses.

EDIBILITIES: Important fiber plant with a few edibilities. Young tender leaves can be eaten as cooked greens or in soups. Flowers are edible cooked. Seeds may be eaten roasted, but are more often processed for an edible oil.

APPLICATIONS:

FIBER: bast is similar to Jute & is more rot resistant, but coarser & less flexible. Made into rope, cord, fish-net, coarse cloth, & is excellent for paper-making. Whiter color & less lignin calls for fewer chemicals & less energy to make paperpulp compared to wood fiber from trees.

HARVESTING: plants for fiber are cut before seed-set; at three to five months.

PROCESSING: stems are bundled, retted for one to two weeks, after which fiber is separated, washed & sun dried. OIL: oil from seeds for illumination, lubrication, paints, soap, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Woody & herbaceous, shrub-like perennial or annual. Can grow 18 ft. (5.4 m) tall. Large, red-centered, yellow flowers 6 in. (15cm) wide. Day-length sensitive. Taproot.

ORIGIN: eastern hemisphere tropics.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics.

PREFERS: fertile, humusy, well drained, medium or light soil, neutral pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: various conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: water-logging.

ADVERSARIES: several possibilities exist. Highly susceptible to root-knot nematodes.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize,

POLLINATION: self.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Germination: three to fifteen days or more; warmth beneficial. Seeds need light to sprout.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, MesicDry

☆ LANGSAT Lansone, Lanzon, Lansa, Bejetan. Lansium domesticum. Meliaceae (Mahogany) Family. The so-called WILD LANGSAT, var. pubescens, is also cultivated. Both have good quality fruits. Sweeter, smaller, seedless forms are highly valued.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed food. Clusters of around forty fruits 1 in. (2.5 cm) wide. Fruit have a thin, leathery, beige, yellowish to pink rind. Juicy pulp is fragrant & sweet/tart to acid. Pulp is eaten fresh raw, in fruit salads, cooked, pies, jellies, preserved, frozen (appearance & texture suffer, but taste remains), canned, dried, or made into wine & cordiais (sour varieties). Some varieties that are very high in latex can be dipped a few seconds in boiling water before peeling.

BEARING: seedlings can bear in ten to fifteen years; cuttings or graftlings in five years.

MATURITY: fruits typically ripen in tropical autumns. Ready to pick when color is at its deepest.

HARVESTING: entire cluster can be cut from tree.

STORING: quite perishable & lasts only a few days at room temperature. Can last in a refrigerator about two weeks.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Fruit skin, seeds & tree bark are poisonous. 2. Fruit rind is high in tannins.;;

APPLICATIONS:

INSECT-REPELLENT: fruit peel can be dried & burnt to repel mosquitoes, OF a8 an Incense for sick rooms.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES. SHADE TREE.

WOOD: dense, somewhat hard, lasting & strong: construction, small tools, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 50 ft. (15 m) tall. Climax tree. Symmetrical shape. Small yellow flowers can form directly on older limbs. Young trees grow quite slowly. Surface roots.

ORIGIN: Southeast Asia, Philippines.

CLIMATE: highly humid tropics.

GROWN IN HAWATIT: often.

PREFERS: deep, moist, fertile, well drained soil, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun (or part shade when young). Regular water & fertilizer enhances growth & production.

TOLERATES: shade, salt spray, some drought some wind.

INTOLERANT OF: alkaline soil, severe drought, intense sun, frost, wet feet or flooding.

ASSOCIATES: grown under COCONUT.
