☆🌿⚠️ LETTUCE / LEKUKE

Vol II · scan p. 152 · book p. 88

☆ LETTUCE / LEKUKE Lactuca sativa & others. Asteraceae (Sunflower) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed. Eaten fresh raw as salad greens, roll-ups, as well as in stir-fries, as boiled greens, or shteddeg sautéed or simmered with fresh baby Peas or Onion, & as a soup or stew addition, or stuffed like a Cabbage-roll. The deeper the green, the higher the nutrition. High in vitamins A & E.

⚠️ CAUTION: LETTUCE may contain trace amounts of lactucarium, a mild medicinal opiate.

MATURITY: Depends upon form & cultivar.

LOOSELEAF LETTUCES: twenty-five to sixty-five days.

COS LETTUCES: fifty to eighty-five days.

HEAD LETTUCES: fifty to ninety days. Harvest can begin with thinnings as soon as they are big enough to eat, Ali LETTUCE is better if gathered before they become bitter.

HARVESTING: Larger leaves of LOOSELEAF. or COS LEYTUCE can be gathered as needed, taking care not to damage growing point: cut-&-come-again greens. HEAD LETTUCE is typically allowed to form a firm head, then are cut entire. Head can be palpated for solidity, since appearance can be misleading.

STORING: LETTUCE can be stored unwashed in a plastic bag in a refrigerator. If chilled to just above 32°F (0°C) quickly after harvest, HEAD LETTUCE can store for a month. LEAF LETTUCE wilts quickly & is difficult to store or transport.

SHIPPING: Some forms & varieties of HEAD LETTUCE transport well refrigerated: "Big Boston,’ ‘Great Lakes,’ ‘Montello.'

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Rabbits relish the discarded leaves.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Excellent candidates.

LANDSCAPING: Many attractive forms & colors exist. Herb- & flower gardens, edges, raised beds, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Rich in nutrients. Cancer protection & other healing properties.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: LETTUCE are attractive herbaceous annuals. Leaves can grow 1 ft. (30 cm) tall, with plant stretching to 3 ft. (90 cm) when flowering. Often starts as a low growing, leafy rosette. Light yellow flowers on a tall upright stem. Tends to fiower (bolt) as the temperature rises. Typically day-length neutral, though short-day varieties exist. LETTUCE have a mass of shallow feeder roots while young, with taproot thickening & lengthening with age.

ORIGIN: Mediterranean region.

CLIMATE: Prefers warm or cool, moist, mid- or higher-elevations. Ideal temperature range is 60 to 65°F (15.5-18°C). Many cultivars tolerate lower elevations, especially in the cooler seasons, & under shade-cloth (20% to 45% coverage) or floating rowcover (highlands). Heat can cause faster maturation, bitterness, tip-burn, loose heading & early flowering. Some varieties tolerate more heat, especially the COS LETTUCES, whereas HEAD LETTUCES do not grow well at temperatures higher than 75°F (24°C). The LOOSELEAF LETTUCES fall somewhere in between. Intolerant of drought or dry conditions.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often & well.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: LETTUCE prefer moist, rich, light, well drained, moisture retentive, humusy loam, neutral or slightly acid pH 6.0 to 7.0, & part shade or full sun. Respond to soil deeply amended with aged manure or compost. Often grown under shade cloth or in greenhouses to provide needed coolness for head-formation, & protect the delicate leaves from direct sun & pounding rain. LETTUCE like careful, constant watering or misting. Benefit from being fed a few weeks after transplanting with liquid fish-emulsion, manure-tea, etc. Mulched to control weeds, conserve water & cool soil.

TOLERATES: various soils, including heavy to light soils & some alkaline soils.

INTOLERANT OF: poorly drained, strongly acid soils, or flooding.

ASSOCIATES: Often grown under the protective shade of other plants, including fruit trees, trellised vines, young Com, Eggplant, Peppers, Tomato, etc.

ADVERSARIES: With its short life cycle LETTUCE are usually free from serious pest problems, but can be bothered by leaf miners, cutworms, thrips, garden loppers, aphids, slugs, snails, etc. LETTUCE is sensitive to root-knot nematodes. Possible diseases include drop- & bottom-rot, tip-bum, spotted-wilt virus. Thrips spread spotted-wilt virus.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Resistant varieties are chosen, sowing only disease-free seed to prevent introducing mosaic virus. Drop- & bottom-rot can be reduced by watering early so foliage dries quickly & by going light on fertilizer. Garden sanitation is important. Leaf minered foliage is removed. Young plants can be collared to protect from cutworm. Toads’ diet is made up largely of cutworms. Raised beds can help protect plants from slugs or snails. A safe slug & snail bait is available now, made of iron-phosphate mixed with an attractant. WEEDY?: LETTUCE can spread by air-bome seeds, but is not hard to control.

DISADVANTAGES: Plants are quick to bolt in hot weather, or when stressed for water. SEX: Hermaphroditic. Self-fertile, with a small amount of crossing.

POLLINATION: Self-pollinated. Some crossing by insects.

SEED-SAVING: Summer heat promotes flowering. Sometimes HEAD LETTUCE needs to be pried open to allow the flower-stalk to arise. Mature seed-head can be shaken in a bag to capture seeds. Seed-fluff can be removed by stirring seed in a jar, then winnowing. Seed life span: can remain viable four to six years in cool, dry conditions at 50°F (10°C), with a 45 to 58% relative humidity. In moist, tropical conditions, even dried seed stored in an airtight container may last only six months. pROPAGATION: By seeds. Sown directly, or in flats of sterile, fine, rich starting medium. Sown % to % in. (6-12 mm) deep, or less. Transplanting delays maturation (which is good). Seed can also be broadcast or drilled on a finely prepared bed, covered lightly & watered very carefully. Germination: four to five days, with coolness & light being required. Seedlings tend to be delicate thus need protection from burning sun & torrential rains. Seedlings benefit from a starter solution at transplanting. LETTUCE does best if thinned ruthlessly after sprouting, never allowing leaves to touch. Can be sown successively every two to weeks for continuous harvest.

☆🌿⚠️☠️Ⓦ LILIKOʻI / PASSIONFRUIT / PASSIONFLOWER

Vol II · scan p. 154 · book p. 90

LILIKO‘I / PASSIONFRUIT / PASSIONFLOWER Passiflora species. Passifioraceae (Passion Flower) Family. Many species, hybrids & varieties exist. SEE: TWO NOTABLE SPECIES, following. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Most Passiflora species produce highly esteemed fruits. Fruits are round to oblong & 2 to 4 in. (5- 10 cm) or longer. Smooth skinned shell. Taste, color, shape, size & thickness of rind vary with species & variety. Generally containing juicy, fragrant, pleasantly tart pulp surrounding numerous edible seeds. Pulp is eaten fresh raw, in fruit salads, asa flavoring for many toppings, syrup, sauces, jellies (pectin needed) & jams, pie & cake fillings, frostings, ices, ice-creams & sherbets, juices, beverages, canned, frozen or fermented to wine. High in vitamins A & C. Seeds can be processed for an edible oil & are a small-scale source of industrial oil..

☠️ TOXICITIES: Foliage of all Passiflora species is poisonous to eat. Leaves, immature fruit, immature seeds & skin contain toxic cyanogenic glycoside & are dangerous to eat; caution around children. First-aid: vomiting induced & patient to doctor.

BEARING: Can begin fruiting in one to three years.

MATURITY: From flower to fruit about two months in summer, to three in winter. Mature when color changes. Best fruit color is achieved in full sun, with moderate temperatures. Although LILIKO‘! can yield fruit nearly year-round with enough water, they are most productive throughout the summer & fall.

HARVESTING: Depends on species & variety. YELLOW- & PURPLE LILIKO'I fruit usually drop & are picked up daily, or several times a week. During hot weather, even one day in the sun can burn fallen fruit. Vine can be shaken to dislodge fruit that would fall later during the hot time of that day. Mature fruits develop more color & flavor after they fall. Immaturely gathered fruit will not ripen well. Passiflora species are generally quite productive.

STORING: Fruit will keep a couple of weeks at room temperature & a month in a refrigerator in plastic bags. Ideal temperature range is between 41 to 45°F (5-7°C), preferably with high humidity. Fruit that is sunbumed need to be quickly processed to prevent decomposition & loss of quality. Fruit lasts well when frozen or freeze-dried.

SHIPPING: Fruit destined for long transport are often harvested before becoming full-ripe, being only lightly colored. Rubbing with a little petroleum jelly or wax, prevents shriveling & enhances appearance. Fruit are placed in boxes or lugs, as plastic bags tend to make the fruit sweat. If fruit are not transported immediately, they are stored on airy racks. For local markets, fruit are best harvested full-ripe & handled with care to avoid damaging its skin.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Chopped, dried rinds, with molasses, as fodder or silage for cattle or swine. Fruit; fodder for pigs & poultry.

LANDSCAPING: Screen, arbor or fence covering. Grown on walls, shed-roofs or water-tanks to deflect sun. Caution: vigorous vines outgrows allotted space. Needs regular pruning after two years of age. Foliage attract butterflies & their caterpillars.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Some.

SHADE: When grown on trellis or arbor, foliage can provide shade for an understory. Density depends on species & season.

🌿 GENERAL DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous & part-woody, perennial evergreens. Vine length depends typically is long. Climbs by spiraling tendrils, Large, handsome leaves. Showy, fragrant, purple & white flowers. Most species vigorous & rapid, especially YELLOW LILIKO'!. Shallow surface-roots.

LIFE SPAN: around three to eight productive years, depending on culture.

CLIMATE: Tropics & subtropics, depending on species. All LILIKO'! prefer warm or hot climates with high humidity, except perhaps PURPLE. Reportedly suited to similar conditions as Citrus. Cool temperatures, drought, excess heat, rain, or winds during blossoming lowers productivity. Deficient water reduces size of fruit. Intolerant of drought & strong winds.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often & sometimes too well. SEE: WEEDY, following.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Prefers rich, loose, moist, well drained, humusy clay or sandy loam, pH 5.5 to 7.5 & full sun. Bed should be amended a month ahead of planting, if possible. Thrives with regular, knowledgeable fertilization, including adequate nitrogen, potassium & minor elements. Mulch reduces weeds & retains water; mulch should not touch graft-union & must allow water to reach soil.

TOLERATES: many soils, including poor soil if well tended, also heavy or light soil, & a wide pH range.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage, prolonged flooding & excess acidity. Deep cultivation can damage roots & vine base.

— scan page 155 · book page 91 —

PRUNING & TRAINING: LILIKO"! vines need a strong trellis, arbor or fence 7 to 8' (2-2.4 m) or taller. When possible, trellis is placed at right angles to prevailing winds.

CAUTION: LILIKO'I vines can smother & kill even large trees. To train, one stem per plant is led up twine or a light stake to help it reach support wires. (Tying may be necessary at beginning, removing tie as stem swells.) Side-shoots are clipped until plant reaches wire. When finally supported by the wire, growing tip is pinched & two side-shoots are encouraged to grow laterally on wire. Limiting new lower side-shoots encourages wider coverage. Thereafter, side-shoots are draped over wire. Future pruning consists of cutting growth near the ground for easier access to fallen fruit, & thinning to allow good air-flow around trunk. After two years, yearly pruning encourages new growth, thus more flowers & fruits, & keeps vines within bounds. Excess branches are cut back to where they join another branch.

ASSOCIATES: Dense, choking growth will generally out-compete neighboring plants,

ADVERSARIES: Susceptibility to many pests & diseases make LILIKO' difficult to grow organically as a large-scale mono-crop. PURPLE LILIKO‘l is susceptible to fungal root diseases, often dies prematurely from diseases such as PASSION VINE wilt, Fusarium oxysporum f. passiflorae, etc. They tend to have a longer life when grafted onto resistant YELLOW LILIKO'l varieties. Excessive foliage & humid weather stimulates diseases of foliage & fruit. Nematodes: YELLOW LILIKO'S has greatest resistance to these pests. LILIKO*I are sometimes attractive to large caterpillars who are adapted to its poisonous foliage. Fruit is stung by fruit flies, although tough skin hampers their passage into the pulp: squeeze to test.

⚠️ CAUTION: Insecticidal spraying for fruit flies is dangerous to all animals & destroys beneficial insects, including pollinating bees. Insecticides also tend to promote mealy bug & scale infestation.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Organic culture is possible with well-grown, disease resistant stock & diversity. Most large monoplantations of LILIKO*I tend to be abandoned eventually due to disease.

WEEDY: These species are quite weedy & have often naturalized. The BANANA POKA, Passiflora mollissima, readily destroys ancient Koa forests. Weediness of certain tamer species can be controlled by picking up all fruits & disposing them where seeds cannot germinate & by giving a hard yearly pruning after two years of age. sEX: Hermaphroditic flowers are either self-compatible or not. (See individual listings.)

POLLINATION: Mostly by carpenter bees occasionally honeybees or wasps. Excess rain & overhead water destroys pollen; ground-level irrigation recommended.

SEED-SAVING: Seed from fully ripe fruit can be planted fresh, without pulp removed. However, to speed germination, fruit is allowed to sit two weeks, then mashed & left for two days. After that seed is wash & dried. Alternately, fresh seeds can be cleaned of pulp after three days of fermentation. Viable seeds remain at bottom when juice & pulp are poured off. Cleaned seeds can be dried in a shady spot, then stored sealed in a refrigerator, although this can delay germination. Seeds can be scarified with sandpaper. Seed life span: two to three months at 55°F (13°C).

PROPAGATED BY: Seeds, cuttings, layering, budding & grafting. Seed is soaked for one day, then broadcast on clean sand, pressed in, then lightly covered with sand 1/3 to 1/2 in. (8-12.5 mm) deep & watered regularly. Germination: two to four weeks at 70 to 75°F (21-24°O), for fresh seeds, otherwise three to twelve months. Cuttings: soft-, semi-ripe wood, or newly hardened vinetip (soft tip removed), around the thickness of a pencil, each with up to three nodes, treated with rooting-hormone. Grafting: other forms are often joined to the vigorous, disease-resistant YELLOW LILIKO'l rootstock. Seedlings, graftlings, or cuttings need protection from excess heat & wind. Young vegetatively propagated plants need humid or misted environment. Benefits from being transplanted into pots before final planting out. 7

TWO NOTABLE SPECIES:;: vw PURPLE LILIKO'I, Purple Passionfruit, Black Passionfruit(Australia), Purple Granadilla. Passiflora edulis f. edulis. 7 Many cultivars & a few bybrids exist. i.

EDIBILITIES: Round to oval, purple-green fruit 2 to 3 in. (5-7.5 cm) wide. Sweet to semi-tart, refreshing, juicy orange pulp (sweeter ret when ripe fruit is aged). Eaten fresh raw, or in pies & cakes, sauces, syrup, candy-making, sherbets & ice-creams, juices, or wine. Seeds are a source of an edible oil.

APPLICATIONS: CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: espalier-, arbor-, or trellis cover.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, perennial, mostly-evergreen vine. Stems can grow 65 ft. (20 m) long. Handsome, sometimes fragrant, white & purple flowers; open in the morning.

ORIGIN: South America.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Thrives in cooler elevations than the YELLOW LILIKO'T is suited to.

INTOLERANT OF: frost, when young.

ADVERSARIES: tends to be more susceptible to diseases than YELLOW LILIKO'l. Prone to nematodes, wilt, fungus & wind damage.

WEEDY: escaped & naturalized; possible serious pest. Rampant smothering vines. Found wild in forests, shrub-lands, trail edges, abandoned home sites, etc. SEX: hermaphroditic. Self-fertile & does not need hand-pollination.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: seeds & grafting.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☆ YELLOW LILIKO‘I, yellow Passionfruit, Liliko‘i melemele. Passiflora edulis f. flavicarpa, or possibly P. edulis X ligularis. Many intercrossing forms, hybrids & other cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Round to oblong, yellow or reddish fruit 3 in. (7.5 cm) wide. Pleasantly tart juicy pulp is eaten fresh raw, or as preserves, in ice-cream, as juices, etc. More productive than PURPLE LILIKO'I & higher in vitamin A.

BEARING: can begin fruiting in one year.

SHIPPING: well protected by tough skin.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Large, attractive, perennial vine. Stems can grow 65 ft. (20 m) or longer. Climbs by tendrils. Vigorous. Fragrant flowers; open in the afternoon. Does not form root-suckers.

ORIGIN: South America.

CLIMATE: thrives in tropical lowlands.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: introduced & cultivated here.

PREFERS: reportedly yields more fruit & is less attacked by insects & diseases when grown on a fall (alien) tree.

ENTOLERANT OF: cold conditions, frost, poorly drained, or excessively heavy soil.

ADVERSARIES: generally disease resistant, especially to nematodes & wilt.

WEEDY: escaped & naturalized; a serious pest. Found wild in forests & shrub-lands. SEX: hermaphroditic flowers are often self-sterile, thus crossing is needed. At least two plants (from same or different parents) can be trained together for maximum crossing.

POLLINATION: carpenter- & honey-bees (depending on flower style-type). Yields are increased by hand-pollinating (morning). Heavy rain during flowering reduces fruit-set.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: seeds & grafting. Birds often disperse the seeds.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

NOTE: Numerous other fruiting Passiflora species cxist.

TOLERATES: shade, various soils & conditions.

Vol II · scan p. 156

☆ MANGO, MANAKŌ oes Manga, Mangue. Mangifera indica, Anacardiaceae (Mango) Family. Several races & hundreds of varieties, cultivars & hybrids exist, including dwarfs. Fruit appearance & quality, as well as tree’s climatic adaptation vary significantly with the cultivar.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & highly esteemed. MANGO is called "King of the Fruits." Yellow, green, or reddish fruit from 3 to 8 in. (7.5-20 cm) long, with one large seed. Flesh varies from deliciously sweet, fragrant & juicy, to tart, stringy & resinous. Pulp is eaten fresh raw, or in fruit salads, stewed, in curries, pies, tarts, puddings & custards, jams & jellies, marmalades, conserves & preserves, relishes, chutneys & sauces (half-ripe), juice & nectar, gelatins, ice-creams & sherbets, pickled, dried, fruit-leather, canned, frozen, or fermented to vinegar or wine. High in vitamin A, moderate in vitamins C, G & K & others, some minerals, & insoluble dietary fiber. Low in fat & sodium. Frozen fruit can be made into sauces, mousses, ice-creams, beverages, etc. Seed kemel is a scarcity food when boiled, roasted, or dried & ground as a flour for breads & puddings, or processed for a solid fat. Fruit skin is a pectin source, but is high in dangerous tannins. Tender, young leaves of many varieties are edible cooked (but never eaten raw, nor in large quantities).

☠️ TOXICITY: Sap of leaves, bark, limbs, trunk & fruit (especially near rind), contains caustic properties that can cause skin irritation, blistering & swelling ("MANGO rash"). Around two out of a hundred people are allergic to the fruit. Pulp can cause a rash around lips & is toxic to some people. If you are sensitive to Poison Ivy, it is wise to be cautious around this tree & its fruit. Smoke from wood or leaves is irritating & can blister skin. While MANGOES are flowering, some people have eye irritation. Before preparing fruit, sap should be washed off. Kernels are high in tannins.

BEARING: Seedlings begin fruiting in five to ten years & graftlings in three to five years. Since one to two year-old graftlings are not usually strong enough to bear fruit, their flower-buds are typically removed. MANGO have a strong tendency towards alternate bearing (either whole tree, or some of the branches). Older trees of some varieties may cease to flower.

MATURITY: Typically three to five months from flowering to fruit, although faster cultivars exist. Climate, especially the amount of rainfall, affects time of maturity. Fruit typically mature late spring through autumn. To reduce pest & disease problems, fruit are best picked when full size & turning color, but not yet soft. The stem of fully expanded, mature fruit will readily snap with a slight tug. Test trials may help determine appropriate time. Ready to eat when stem end is fragrant; skin color is not a good indicator of npeness. When buying, avoid MANGO with black spotting or wrinkles (denoting stringy pulp.)

HARVESTING: To prevent bruising, fruit need to be picked before they drop. To avoid spurting caustic, staining sap, stem can be cut with clippers or a bagged picking-pole with attached cutter, leaving a 4 in. (10 cm) piece of stem on fruit. Fruit are kept in cool shade & handled with care to prevent bruising or skin blemishes. Before packing, stem can be clipped to % in. (6 mm) long. Since sap from cut stem burns the fruits! skin, too, fruit are washed after picking.

STORING / RIPENING: Maturely picked green fruit will ripen in one to two weeks at room temperature. Placing in paperbag speeds ripening. MANGO picked immature may never ripen well. Some cultivars hold up better than others. Typically, ripe fruit last two days to almost a week in refrigerator, especially if wrapped in paper & placed in the warmest part to avoid chill-damage. (Excess cold can blacken skin, although pulp usually remains good.) Temperature of 54 to 55°F (12-13°C) has been suggested, then raised to 65 to 76°F (18-24°C) for a few days to sweeten fruit before eating. MANGO pulp also stores well frozen (whole or sliced), dried, or canned. Slices, peeled can be frozen for a chilling treat. Ship. '; rown, but green & not yet soft. Some varieties can still develop good flavor

PING: For transporting, fruit are harvested fully 5 sported at temperatures no lower than 54°F (12°C). Fruit require careful when harvested two weeks before final maturation. 7 Treatment with vapor heat can eliminate fruit fly larvae. handling to prevent bruising, over-heating & anthracnose

APPLICATIONS:

— scan page 157 · book page 100 —

ANIMAL FEED: Fallen & excess fruit, as well as seed-kernels (soaked, dried & tannins removed) for partial feed for livestock, poultry & especially pigs. Seed-residue after soap-making for cattle.

TOXICITY: %6* although MANGO leaves can serve as q scarcity fodder, continual ingestion of foliage can be deadly.

BARRIER PLANT: MANGO can be pruned or shaped for a large barrier.

BEE FORAGE: Fair.

CLIMATE MODIFICATION: Hedgerow. DYE.

EROSION CONTROL: Roots can provide soil stabilization.

FERTILIZER: Seed-residue after soap-making enriches soil.. of.

FIREWOOD & CHARCOAL: Excellent charcoal & fair firewood, but CAUTION; smoke from wood or leaves is very irritating & can blister skin. MANGO is not burned as cooking-fuel, firewood, or refuse. GUM: A Gum Arabic-replacement & for repairing crockery.

LANDSCAPING: Ornamental, but, SEE: DISADVANTAGES, following.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications.

SACRED: Hindu.

SHADE TREE: Very dense canopy, but, SEE: DISADVANTAGES, following.

SOAP-MAKING: Seed-kernel fat.

WINDBREAK: MANGO is not generally susceptible to blow-over. Protection for Cacao & other small tree crops. woOoD: Moderately hard & dense, with a coarse, wavy grain. Salt-water seasoned or kiln-dried. Wood is not lasting in the ground, but holds up well in water. Unfortunately, MANGO wood is not easy to work into a finely finished product. Utilized for timber, construction, plywood, furniture, turnery, farm tools, boat-building, boxes, poles, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 30 to 130 ft. (9-40 m) tall. Height depends on cultivar, conditions & propagation technique. Climax tree. Short, thick trunk is often buttressed. Wide, dense crown in open areas, tall & narrow where closely planted. Long, narrow, glossy leaves, produced in flushes of copper-red or rose-colored new growth. Large terminal clusters of small, fragrant, pinkish or greenish-yellow flowers. Deep, strong tap-root, & wide spread surface feeders.

LIFE SPAN: vigorous & very long lived, three hundred productive years is possible.

ORIGIN: India & Southeast Asia.

CLIMATE: Tropics & warm subtropics. MANGO prefers a hot, monsoonal climate, with its distinct dry & wet periods. Thrives with 30 to 100 in. (750-2500 mm) annual rain during summer, with a dry period of several months during flowering & while fruits are small. MANGO reportedly grow to 1800 ft. (540 m) in elevation in Hawaiʻi, but they do better under 1200 ft. (360m). At higher elevations, fruiting is poor & there are more fungal problems. Tolerates heat, drought & drier areas if there is underground water. While most MANGO do not tolerate constant high humidity, some varieties are more resistant. Rain, fog, or heavy dew during flowering reduces fruiting. Cold weather at flowering may create many nubbins (small infertile fruit): a smallscale remedy is to remove first flowers to stimulate later blossoms. On a larger-scale, it would be wise to plant different varieties. Excessive wind can damage flowers, new growth & fruits. Intolerant of frost.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often & well.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Needs ample space. Some MANGO will cease fruiting where their branches touch other MANGO trees. Prefers deep, moist, average or fertile, well drained, mid- to light loam, pH 5.5 to 7.5 & full sun. Mulching retains water controls weeds. Fertilized every three to four months, if needed, but soil that is too moist or too rich favors vegetative growth over flowering & fruiting.

TOLERATES: temporary flooding better than most fruit trees, & poor, impervious, or shallow soil (if moist enough), & some salt-spray. Most varieties tolerate many soil types, if the weather is favorable.

INTOLERANT OF: continual water-logging, very alkaline soil, & salty water or soil.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Typically not trimmed at all until tree is four years old. Then trained to a good form. Thereafter MANGO is only pruned to remove dead, diseased, awkward, or weak growth, to correct shape & reduce height. Pruning is usually done after fruiting. Branches are strong & do not tend to break.

ASSOCIATES: Avo's, Breadfruit, Coconut, Cacao, ete. Intercropped while young with Pineapple, Papaya, vegetables, legumes, etc.

ADVERSARIES: MANGOES are susceptible to anthracnose (especially in wet, humid conditions), powdery mildew (especially in dry, cool months) & scab. Some varieties are more resistant to anthracnose. Generally resistant to root-rot. Attacked by several fruit flies, especially Oriental fruit fly. MANGO-midge & seed-weevil can both be problematic.

ORGANIC-GROWING: An excellent candidate, especially with the right varieties, good conditions & pest protection. Some varieties are more resistant to problems. Waxed, waterproof bags can protect fruit from insects & chaffing. Removing & destroying fallen fruit reduces fruit fly infestation..

WEEDY: MANGO has escaped & naturalized in many parts of the tropics. Mature trees are difficult to eliminate. MANGO can be a serious environmental weed.

DISADVANTAGES: 1. Because of the MANGO seed-weevil, exportation of fresh fruit to the continent from Hawaiʻi is currently(still?) prohibited. This has also been true to Japan, Australia & other areas, although regulations are changing. Processing is thus important in Hawaiʻi. 2. MANGO is a very large, dominating tree, with roots that crack foundations & dry surrounding soil. Needs adequate space as the trees may blow over in very high winds. 3. Heavy falling fruit.

REMARKS: Many varieties have particular deficiencies that may be locally important. Selecting the correct varieties for your region is critical. A test-trial is recommended before planting a large number of MANGO trees. SEX: Hermaphroditic & male flowers occur on each panicle. Many varieties are self-fertile. In some varieties, seeds are produced asexually (apogamic) with no pollination required.

POLLINATION: Various insects, especially flies & wasps, visit the blossoms & transfer pollen. Some self-pollination occurs. Although honey-bees are not especially fond of MANGO blossoms, bringing in bee-hives does tend to increase pollination. Dry weather stimulates blossoming. During flowering, low rainfall & low humidity are important for fruit-set. High humidity, heavy rain, or strong wind hinders flowering, pollination, as well as setting of fruit. sEED-

— scan page 158 · book page 101 —

SAVING: Seedlings of most of the polyembryonic seeds of Hawaiian, Philippine, Chinese, or Southeast Asian varieties tend to breed true to type. (Note: although seedlings arising from outer folds of polyembryonic seeds tend to come true, seediings coming from center tend towards being cross-bred & thus variable, but more vigorous). Monoembryonic seedlings from true sexual parents are typically highly variable. Seed life span: around one month. pROPAGATION: By seeds, grafting, budding, transplanted volunteers & tissue-culture. Air-layering & cuttings are not usually successful & both tend to have poor root-systems. When sowing seeds, the hull can be removed from seed-kernel, any weevil Jarva destroyed. Removing the hull also speeds germination. Seed is placed point up (or convex edge up), in sterile medium such as sand or peat, just under soil level, or a forth sticking above. Germination: when lightly mulched & kept moist, warm & shaded, seeds may sprout in one to six weeks, with an average of three weeks. Grafted trees tend to be smaller & more easily managed than seedlings. Cuttings: leafy wood is pre-ringed, treated & kept misted. MANGO are not easy to transplant. Roots must be kept constantly moist,

OTED CULTIVARS: Because cuitivars & names vary, itis beneficial to seek local guidance for improved, locally adapted, resistant varieties. Popular cultivars for home plantings include; "White Pirie,’ ‘Hayden, 'Keitt, ‘Julie’ (dwarf), ‘Ah Ping,’ 'Kurashige,’ etc. Check with the U of H College of Tropical Agriculture & Human Resources for their extensive variety listings.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesicDry

NOTE: Many other Mangifera species exist, offering edible, although inferior fruit,

☆ MANGOSTEEN

Vol II · scan p. 158 · book p. 101

☆ MANGOSTEEN Mangostan, Mangusta, Men-gu. Garcinia mangostana. Clusiaceae (Mangosteen) Family.

EDIBILITIES: The esteemed "Queen of the Fruits." Round fruit 3 in. (7.5 cm) wide, with thick, reddish-purple rind. White, threesided pulp sections are juicy, delicately sweet & tart. Meltingly delectable fresh raw, in jams (seed discarded), preserves (seeds included), or frozen. Skin can be cut through around girth, fruit twisted & half of rind can be lifted off to expose pulp segments.

CAUTION: rind-juice stains. Seeds are edible raw, roasted, or boiled.

BEARING: seedlings in six to fifteen years. Worth the wait. Can fruit for a hundred years, though it peaks at half that.

MATURITY: fruit are ready when a bit soft & full-colored, but before they turn blue-black or dark purple. Best if allowed to tree-ripen, as fruit do not ripen well after being picked. High variation in fruiting season & volume.

HARVESTING: fruit are hand- or pole-picked avoiding dropping.

STORING: fruit lasts a few days at room temperature, several weeks at 50°F (10°C). Can be wrapped in paper & placed in warmest part of refrigerator to avoid chill-damage. Entire fruit can be frozen.

SHIPPING: thick rind permits successful shipping. Picked somewhat under-ripe, tissue-paper wrapped, boxed, chilled & delivered quickly.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: non-fruiting trees: wood is hard, dense: building, handles, pounders, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Very attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 80 ft. (25 m) tall, but usually seen half that. Leaves leathery. Showy, multi-colored flowers. Slow growing. Tap-root.

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: Southeast Asia.

CLIMATE: tropics with hot, humid weather year-round. GROWN IN HAWATI': not often grown here & only occasionally successful.

PREFERS: apparently requires deep, well-watered, fertile loam or clay soil, acid pH & full sun. Does best with close, fresh ground-water moving 6 ft. (1.8m) below surface. Benefits from mulch & ample annual applications of composted manure. Challenging. Needs ample space.

TOLERATES: occasional brief, light frost & dry air, but needs constant ground water.

INTOLERANT OF: excessively dry or cool climates, salt, harsh winds, drought, & limey, alkaline soil.

PRUNING: inner branches can be pruned.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, except for fungal diseases. The thick fruit-rind is high in tannins & quite resistant to insects.

WEEDY: can naturalize. SEX: female. Male trees are unknown. The "seeds" are produced apomictically & are actually embryos, needing no fertilization.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span is one week or less. The largest seeds are selected.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds, inarching (sometimes successful), approach-grafting & budding. Germination: two to four weeks. Prefers a peat moss or other acid starting mix. Plant has weak roots, especially the first couple of years. Transplanting can be damaging, therefore direct seeding in deeply cultivated soil is more often successful. Then, the entire root-ball can be transplanted after around two to three years, or when 6 to 8 ft. (1.8-2.4 m) tall, into a well manured planting hole. Given 50%, or denser, shade for several years until established. Hardened off to full sun gradually. Can be inarched on Gambage rootstock.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, WetMesic

MAPLE, JAPANESE

MAPLE, JAPANESE Ash Leaved Maple, Box Elder Maple. Acer palmatum. Aceraceae (Maple) Family. Many named selections exist, including weeping & dwarf forms. Upright forms tend to be more vigorous & sturdy.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING: bonsai.

LANDSCAPING: omamental specimen, groves, hedge, screen, etc.

ROADSIDE & PARKING-LOT TREE. SHADE TREE.

🌿Ⓦ OKRA

Vol II · scan p. 161 · book p. 110

OKRA Gumbo, Lady's Finger. Abelmoschus esculentus, syn. Hibiscus esculentus.Malvaceae (Hibiscus) Family. Forms exist, incl. dwarfs, green-, white- & red pods,

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed & nutritious foods. Tapered pods can vary in size & shape, but are generally four-, to many sided, or cylindrical. Tender, immature pods have a thick, mucilaginous texture after cooking. Eaten boiled, steamed, in gumbo's, soups stews, gravies, sautéed, braised, fried as slices, chilled for salads, as a sauce thickener, or pickled similar to Capers. High in minerals, vitamin A & fiber. Mature green pods can be cooked for their seeds. Young leaves, flowers, buds & flower-calyces have an agreeable sour flavor & are boiled as vegetables. Dried seeds are edible boiled, as well as extracted for oil or protein, or ground & mixed with water, then precipitated as a vegetable-cheese, tofu, or tempeh, or pickled. Seeds can also be milled & sifted to a flour, or washed, roasted & ground for a tasty Coffee-adulterant. TOXICITY?: It was formerly thought the seeds contained poisonous gossypol. Current evidence states that the substance is not gossypol & is not poisonous.

MATURITY: Pods mature in one & a half to three months, depending on cultivar. Tender, half-grown pods can be harvested every few days at stage desired. Usually picked when still pale green, under 3 in. (7.5 cm) long, while tips still can be easily snapped off seeds being around half size. Best on the forth day after blossoming. Pods of most cultivars tend to toughen if left too long.

HARVESTING: Pods are cut from their stems. Daily harvest prolongs yield. OKRA can produce for two months or longer.

STORING: To hold over for more than a day & prevent over-heating in closed containers, pods can spread thinly on a tray & moistened as needed. At room temperature pods can last around three days. OKRA can also be stored in a refrigerator a couple days in a paper bag or wrapped in a towel & put in a plastic bag; unwashed, as moisture causes sliminess. Cooked OKRA lasts a few days im frig if covered tightly. Holds well up to a week at 32°F (0°C). Pods can also be frozen, canned, or dried (as slices or strung as halves). Leaves & pods can be dried & powdered for longer storage.

SHIPPING: Fresh pods do not ship well as they are tender & easily damaged.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING.

ANIMAL FEED.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Even one plant in a large container can be worth the effort.

FIBER: Green stems are a source of a low-quality fiber for cordage, weaving, basketry, etc., but excellent quality paper.

FIREWOOD: Dried stems can be burnt as fuel.

EROSION CONTROL: For fast coverage of loose soil.

GROUND-COVER: OKRA makes a tall, rapidly growing ground-cover.

HEDGE: Fast growing summer fence.

LANDSCAPING: Ornamental cultivars are utilized for borders, backgrounds, etc.

LIVING-TRELLIS: Fast, but temporary.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Several important applications.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: OKRA is an attractive, slightly woody, long lived herbaceous annual, or somewhat perennial shrub. Can grow 2 to ft. tall, depending on cultivar. Upright or branching habit. Plant &/or pods are sometimes spiny. Large, palmatelylobed leaves. Large yellow flowers, with deep red throats mature into pods. Pods contain spherical seeds 3/16 in. (5 mm) wide. Mature seed-pods dehisce lengthwise. A few cultivars are less sensitive to day-length than most. Although it is usually difficult to produce OKRA during the winter months, there is a species-hybrid African form (from ECHO) that yields during shorter days. Robust, fast growing plant.

ORIGIN: African, Indian or Asian tropics.

CLIMATE: Grown throughout the tropics, subtropics & the temperate zones. OKRA is easy to grow in hot climates with long sunny days. Ideal temperature range between 70 to 85°F (21-29°C). Tolerates tropical lowlands. Most cultivars tolerate drought heat quite well. Intolerant of cold conditions.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: OKRA is grown here, but is not well known for its many other applications.

PREFERS: Moist, rich, well drained, humusy loam, pH 5.0 to 8.0 & full sun. Needs ample room. Plants yield much higher if beds are fertilized with compost or aged manure, allowing bed to rest before being planted. Although OKRA benefits from at least one feeding, excess food encourages foliage instead of pods. Thrives in similar conditions as Cucumbers, Com or Melons. Benefits from muich.

TOLERATES: most soils.

INTOLERANT OF: shade, poor drainage & flooding.

ASSOCIATES: Louise Riotte, in Carrots Love Tomatoes, says she plants her OKRA with rows of Sweet Bell Peppers on the shady side & Eggplant on the sunny side.

ADVERSARIES: Although OKRA is generally pest resistant, it is very sensitive to root-knot nematodes.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Rotation is necessary. Disease-resistant cultivars exist.

WEEDY: Can naturalize, but not thought invasive.

DISADVANTAGES: OKRA needs careful, regular attention to keep in production.

REMARKS: OKRA can be a prolific food & multipurpose plant. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Partially self-pollinated & also cross-pollinated by bees.

SEED-SAVING: In tropical conditions, seeds need to be stored under refrigeration, in a sealed container.

PROPAGATED BY: Seeds. After soil has warmed, days lengthening, water is available, soil loosened & fertilized. Seeds tend to rot if cold & wet. Greater chance of sprouting if seeds are washed with dish-soap, soaked for twelve to twenty-four hours, & drained before sowing. Seeds are sown 3/8 to 3/4 in. (1-2 cm) deep (deepest in loose soil). Often sown on hills. Germination: only few days, if warm. When heavy soil crusts over during pounding rain, sprouting can be hampered. Difficult to transplant.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesicDry

FEW NOTABLE CULTIVARS: ‘Clemson Spineless' & ‘Perkins Spineless.' Old cultivars, well adapted to tropical conditions. ‘African Okra.’ Can yield during short days. Tolerates dry conditions.

SEE ALSO: EDIBLE HIBISCUS. Abelmoschus manihot.

🌿☠️Ⓦ ONION & RELATIVES / ʻAKAʻAKAI & others

Vol II · scan p. 162

ONION & RELATIVES / ʻAKAʻAKAI & others Allium species. Altiaceae (Onion) Family.

GENERAL EDIBILITIES: Ancient, popular, pungent foods, Ail parts of these species are edible either raw or cooked. Numerous applications. SEE: INDIVIDUAL LISTINGS, following.

☠️ TOXICITY: In large quantities, ONION & other Allium species contain alkaloids that are toxic to dogs & possibly humans, but rarely will either eat enough to cause symptoms.

SEE ALSO: CAUTIONS, under GARLIC.

STORING & SHIPPING: Dehydrated COMMON ONION slices, flakes &/or powder are long-lasting & less costly to ship. GREEN ONION & others can be chopped & dehydrated. Cured bulbs of GARLIC store & ship very well.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Although ONIONS & byproducts can serve as livestock feed, they can taint milk & cheese in dairy cows. SEE

ALSO: TOXICITY, prior.

GUILDS: Pest repellent.

LANDSCAPING: Many attractive species for beds, borders, edges, omamentals, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications. af

GENERAL DESCRIPTION: In general, ONIONS are herbaceous perennials, or biennials, with some being grown as annuals or biennials. Long, flattened, round, hollow, or solid leaves arise from bulbs, tillers, or rhizomes. In time, a compact head of flowers may arise, usually followed by seeds. COMMON ONIONS are influenced by day-length (needing fifteen or more hours of daylight). Northern types don't tend to bulb in tropical or subtropical conditions; appropriate short-day or medium-day length varieties are necessary. Shallow roots.

GENERAL CLIMATE: While most ONIONS originated in the north temperate zone, they are now commonplace in the tropics as well. Most varieties of COMMON ONION can be challenging to grow in tropical conditions, but there are shorter-day cultivars & other adaptable species. Tolerates winter cool, or frost. Intolerant of dry conditions.

GROWNIN HAWALI: ONION & their relatives have all been introduced to Hawaiʻi & are appreciated as condiment & food. Because of their popularity & difficulty in growing, the local COMMON ONIONS are pricey. There is considerable experience in Hawaiʻi with these plants & local information is highly desirable. PREFERENCES & CULTURE,

IN GENERAL: Culture of the ONION relatives is somewhat distinct according to species. Growing COMMON ONION requires careful attention to detail. The plot must be kept well weeded &/or mulched. In general, they prefer —rich, moist, loose, humusy, well drained soil, neutral or slightly acid pH & full sun or part shade. Typically benefit from amending with aged manure or compost, & regular fertilization.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding.

ADVERSARIES: All ONION relatives have several pests possibilities, including aphids, thrips, leaf miners, & a small fly-larvae (ONION moth) in the bulbs. ONIONS are also sensitive to nematodes & are intolerant of competition from weeds. Diseases include purple blotch, rust, & soft-rot bacteria.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Problems may be prevented by planting only species & cultivars suited to your area, by conditioning the soil with humusy compost, by practicing crop-rotation, good garden sanitation, & by planting ONION throughout garden instead of in pest-inviting rows. Radishes can be planted as a trap crop for ONION-maggots & are destroyed once infested. Mature bulbs are harvested & air-dried before they are attacked by pests.

WEEDY: Many species can reseed & naturalize. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Sticky pollen is transported by honey-bees & other insects.

SEED-SAVING: Cross-pollination may be avoided by separating varieties & species by 100 ft. 30 m) or more.

GENERAL PROPAGATION: Grown from seeds, small bulbs (sets), bulbils, or clump division.

SOME NOTABLE SPECIES: (Note: there are many more species; some more valued than others.)

BULBING ONION. Allium cepa. SEE: COMMON ONION.

BUNCHING ONION. Adium fistulosum. SEE: JAPANESE BUNCHING ONION.

CHIVE. Allium species: CHIVE, Chives, Cive. Allium schoenoprasum. Many varieties & cultivars exist, including dwarfs.

They are eaten as condiment, chopped fine & added (fresh or dried) to mixed salads, salad dressings, butters, cheeses, including cream cheese & sour cream, baked Potatoes, cream- & Potato soups, stews, sauces & gravies, omelettes, casseroles, egg-, cheese-, chicken- & vegetable-dishes, on sandwiches & as a gamish. Flowers, divided into florets, are added to cheese-, egg-, fish-dishes as garnish.

ADVERSARIES: generally free of problems, with some cultivars being more resistant than others, WEEDY?: somewhat, since it can spread slowly or occasionally self-seed, but it is not difficult to control. PROPAGATEp By. division, offshoots, or seeds. Sown directly or to transplant. Divided every few years. ?7LowMidHigh, WetMesic COMMON ONION, Bulbing Onion, ‘Aka‘akai, “Aka‘a kai kt ka nia. Allium cepa Cepa Group, syn. A. cepa var. cepa. Many varieties & cultivars exist, including yellow-, white- & red-skinned types, as well as PEARL ONIONS. Most are round, although other shapes exist. Short-day varieties suggested by the U of H include the mild Tropical Ace hybrid," "Yellow Granex hybrid,’ ‘Excel.’ Early Texas Grano 502' & Yellow Bermuda Medium-day varieties include ‘Amber Express,’ "Ely Harvest hybrid,’ "San Joaquin,’ & ‘Pronto-S hybrid’ Hot varieties include ‘Red Creole' & 'Awahia.’...

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed vegetable. Bulbs are pungent whether mature Or immature. Eaten as a seasoning, condiment, vegetable, as well as in innumerable applications in cooking & preserving. Hotter ONIONS are cooked, sautéed for pasta or pizza, fried, blanched whole, soups, peeled, stuffed & baked, in sauces, pickled (brine or vinegar), or dried. Milder ONIONS can be eaten fresh raw, & in all the above. High in vitamin C. Degree of pungency depends on variety, cultivar & soil sulfur content (higher sulfur equals more pungent flavor). Young plants can be harvested, beginning in three to five weeks, as thinnings: called GREEN ONIONS, SPRING ONIONS, SCALLIONS, or BUNCHING ONIONS. They are eaten fresh raw or in salads. Mature leaves are strong, but edible (milder when cooked) as in soups & stews. Pungent seeds are pungent.

MATURITY: three to six months or longer (depending on cultivar & propagation method), When a quarter or half of the plants' foliage has withered & fallen, the leaves of the rest are bent over, & bulbs are gathered a couple days later.

HARVESTING: bulbs are pulled from ground & left on soil surface for half a day, with foliage protecting them, to begin curing & drying in the air & sun.

CURING: bulbs can be cured with attached leaves, or tops & roots can be cut to within ¥% to in. (1.25-2.5 cm) of bulb, soil residue cleaned, but not washed. Bulbs are then spread thinly in a cool, shaded, ventilated shed for five to ten days. Curing is complete when bulbs are hard & neck is firm. Thick-necked bulbs do not cure or store well.

STORING: certain cultivars store better than others. Dried, cured bulbs can hold up weil for several months or longer (less in tropics). Bulbs last best if placed in airy containers such as net bags, Citrus crates, etc. Stored in a dark, dry, cool, well-ventilated spot, but not in refrigerator (unless cut). Ideal: 75% humidity & between 76 to 86°F (24.5-30°C), or at 32°F ONIONS can sprout if stored below 65°F (18°C), above 32°F (0°C). Bulbs are not particularly sensitive to light. Hot ONIONS generally store longer than mild varieties. Can also be heat- or freeze-dried.

SHIPPING: dried, cured bulbs tolerate transport & fairly rough treatment.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous biennial, sometimes cultured as an annual. Can grow 3 ft. (.9 m) tall. Emits a strong aroma when any part is crushed. Greenish-white flowers. Photoperiodic: all COMMON ONIONS are day-length sensitive & begin bulb formation during long summer days, although cultivars now exist that can form bulbs during the short-, medium-, or long days. ONIONS have shallow roots, with one primary root & many adventitious laterals.

ORIGIN: Middle East, West Asia.

CLIMATE: most cultivars tend to form bulbs during warm weather, then bolt when temperatures drop, if bulbs have become sufficiently large. Ideal temperature range is 55 to 75°F (13-24°C), Foliage grows well in cool conditions, then hot, dry weather is best to form, mature & cure bulbs.

GROWN IN HAWALE: although most bulb ONIONS can be difficult to grow here, several excellent adapted varieties are available.

PREFERS: deep, moist, fertile, well drained, light, humusy loam, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun. Responds to soil amended with compost or aged-manure, especially to correct sandy or clay soil. Although excess nitrogen (which inhibits bulb-formation) is avoided, ample potassium & phosphors is necessary. Needs to be kept well weeded, but is cultivated only gently to avoid damaging roots.

TOLERATES: a variety of climates, acidity down to 5.5 pH & very light shade.

INTOLERANT OF: very light or very heavy soil, gravel soil, dry soil, excess rainfall in the humid lowlands, flooding & drought.

ASSOCIATES: Cabbage & its relatives, & rotated after Corn or Carrots.

ADVERSARIES: a variety of problems are possible including thrips, downy mildew, ONION root-maggot, soft-rot, etc.

ORGANIC-GROWING: ONION-maggot can be trapped with Radish. To help prevent soft-rot, water can be withheld when bulbs have finished growing & tops start to fall over.

DISADVANTAGES: in the tropics, ONION seed often just produce small GREEN ONIONS but no bulbs.

POLLINATION: bees & other insects. SEED-

SAVING: crossing of cultivars readily occurs: for pure seed, cultivars are separated by at least 4 mile (.4k), or the plants are bagged. Bulbs destined for seed-production in the tropics need to be stratified at 40 to 50°F (4.5-10°C) for two months before planting out, otherwise they will not flower. Seed life span: under one year; best in dry, cool storage.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds sets (small bulbs). Sets around a dime in size tend to have good vigor, but are not easy to find in Hawaiʻi. Set is buried upright, to in. cm) deep, tamped well & watered. A starter solution speeds growth. Seed takes longer to grow, but can be planted very early spring & allows for greater diversity of varieties. Seeds: drilled or covered with 4% to % in. (1.25-2 cm) of fine compost. Germination: two to three weeks. Need to be thinned well.

Elevation / Rainfall: MidHigh, ?Mesic

GARLIC & RELATIVES. Allium species +:

⚠️ COMMON GARLIC

Vol II · scan p. 164 · book p. 113

COMMON GARLIC, Clove Garlic, Clown's Treacle, “Aka’akei pilau. A finan sativum. Many cultivars exist. Common types, the pungent SPANISH GARLIC with small, purplish heads, & the mild ITALIAN g ARLIC with larger, white heads. There are also the TOP. SETTING GARLIC types, AHium sativum Ophioscorodon group, which create bulbs & bulbils, eer,;

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed culinary & medicinal plant. Bulbs are a pungent, odorous condiment. Eaten in salad dressings, soups & stews, baked, broiled, roasted, sautéed, or added to season many foods, especially Mediterranean-, Italian-, Chinese- & East Indian-dishes. Bulbs can be crushed with the flat of a broad knife to release flavor & ease peeling. Long, moist cooking, as in braising or stewing, mellows the flavor. Roasting brings out a nuttiness. Flowers, leaves & young shoots have a mild flavor & are eaten in mixed salads, soups & stews, omelettes, etc. Flower stalks are eaten as a seasoning. Seeds are edible as is, or sprouted.

MATURITY: four to eight months. Bulbs are ready to harvest when leafy tops start to yellow & fall over.

HARVESTING: entire plant, with bulbs attached, is pulled from the ground. Roots are trimmed off, loose parts of sheath are removed, then bulbs are air dried in the shade. Stems can be braided & hung in a dry, airy spot to cure a few weeks. Bulbs can also be field cured in dry conditions.

STORING: cultivars vary in lasting qualities. Best in a cool, dry, dark, airy spot, but not refrigerated. Can also be tied as bunches, plaited as ropes, or stored loose, lasting from four to twelve months. Bulbs can be dried as granules or powder,

⚠️ CAUTIONS: 1, Although large medicinal quantities are avoided while pregnant, normal cooking amounts are O.K. 2. Babies usually find GARLIC-flavored breast-milk unpalatable. 3. GARLIC can be upsetting to the stomach.

NOTE: chewing on Parsley can help reduce the odor somewhat.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous perennial. Can grow 2 ft. (60 cm) tall. Flattened leaves 1 in. (2.5 cm) wide. Pinkish flowers. Fairly shallow, adventitious roots.

ORIGIN: Eurasia & the Mediterranean.

CLIMATE: favors temperate regions. Needs a long, hot, dry season to form & mature bulbs, as in a Mediterranean climate. Ideal temperature range of 55 to 75°F (13-24°C). GROWN IN HAWATI?: not well adapted here: most cultivars will not bulb in the tropics.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, light, well drained soil, pH to full sun. Cultured like COMMON ONION. Responds to soil amended with aged-manure or compost, & monthly feeding of manure-tea or fish-emulsion. Usually irrigated. Mulched to control weeds & retain moisture.

TOLERATES: various soils & frost.

INTOLERANT OF: poor soil.

PRUNING: woody flower stalks are trimmed off to promote multiple cloves.

ASSOCIATES: GARLIC has insect-repellent qualities; good companion plant.

ADVERSARIES: typical ONION enemies & other pests are possible. To prevent mold or stains, water is reduced near date of maturity.

WEEDY: GARLIC can persist & sometimes becomes an annoying weed. Spreads by bulbs & aerial bulblets (piant rarely sets seeds).

SEED-SAVING: generally seedless, but hand-pollination can create viable seeds. SEX: hermaphroditic.

PROPAGATED BY: sets, cloves, aerial bulbs & seeds. Bulbs aged before sowing: need a dormant period at 45°F (7°C) for four to five months. Separated cloves are sown base down, to 2 in. (2.5-5cm) deep.

Elevation / Rainfall: ?High, Mesic

🌳☠️Ⓦ PAPAYA / MĪKANA / HĒʻĪ

Vol II · scan p. 167 · book p. 125

PAPAYA / MĪKANA / HĒʻĪ ay Papaw, Melon Pawpaw, ree Melon, Papaia, Milikana. mea ty Carica papaya. Caricaceae (Papaya) Family. Varieties differ in form of tree & fruit. Natural dwarts alsoexist sy

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed & nutritious. Yellow, yellow-green, reddish, or orange fruit can grow to 20 in. (15-50 cm) long, depending on age & variety. Ripe pulp is finely textured, juicy & either: very sweet or bland. Peeled or cut in half, de-seeded, & eaten fresh raw, as a dessert fruit (a splashof == Citrus or Liliko’i juice enhances flavor), in fruit salads, stews, jellies, jams, marmalades, chutney, pies,; candied, ice-cream, juice or nectar, pickled, dried or frozen. Sweetness is affected by variety, time of harvest, degree of pollination (more seeds equals more flavor), hours of sun, & potassium availability. Fresh, ripe pulp contains vitamins A, B, C, G, sugar, retinene (an antioxidant), calcium, iron & other nutrients. Green fruit is edible cooked as a vegetable (then chilled for salads), or baked, in soups, sauces, Young leaves can be eatey ies, preserves, candies, canned, pickled, or fermented as a sauerkraut. SEE: TOXI; ollowilB° ' ’ cooked as a vegetable, or crashed & wrapped overnight around meat as a tenderizer, or dried, older leaves edible aS a boiled vegetable (bitterness can be reduced & alkaloids rendered harmless by changing cooking water at least twice). Male flower clusters are edible, but bitter unless cooked in several water changes. Seeds edible fresh or dried as a condiment, or in salad-dressings, & a possible oil source (industrial & edible.) Green fruit & leaves are high in enzymes. The milky latex is extracted & dried as a meat tenderizer, etc.

— scan page 168 · book page 126 —

☠️ TOXICITIES: Unripe, raw fruit is not edible until cooked, due to latex & papain. Contact with the caustic latex (sap) should be avoided, especially around eyes. Sap contains the protein digesters papain & chymopapain, & an alkaloid named carpaine. Fruit can accumulate nitrates & phosphorus where fertilization is excessive. Leaves need to be cooked before eating to remove dangerous alkaloids. Tea from dried leaves is purgative & is not routinely consumed. Flower pollen has caused extreme respiratory complaints in sensitive people, creating subsequent reactions to the fruit & all other parts of the plant. Overeating fruit may cause stomach pains. Fruit is mildly laxative.

BEARING: PAPAYA can begin to bear under one year..

MATURITY: From flower to fruit in four to nine months, depending on variety. Time to ripening is longer in cool seasons. For home eating, fruit can be picked when a third yellow (or orange). Allowing fruit to fully pen on tree apparently does nothing to improve its taste, but does increase danger of insect & bird damage.

HARVESTING: Fruit for home eating can be twisted free, but for commercial purposes, stems are cut with a sharp knife or clippers to prevent damage. Hard to reach fruits may be removed with a picking-pole. Note: glasses, gloves & long sleeves can protect skin from burning sap.

STORING: Fruit that are harvested when they just begin to color will develop good taste a few days at room temperature. Peak summer flavor occurs when rind becomes 80% colored; in winter months, better flavor develops when fruit is harvested when 50% colored. Ripe fruit lasts only a couple of days, even refrigerated. Ripening can be hastened by scaring the rind’s surface with a fork. Partly colored fruit can be held as long as two weeks in a refrigerator. Fruit is susceptible to chill-damage. Can also be preserved, canned, pickled, juiced, dried or frozen.

SHIPPING: PAPAYA is handled only minimally & with great care to prevent bruising, scratching, or contact with burning latex. Gloves are recommended to protect both the picker & the fruit. Shipped one-layer thick in padded containers. Fruit to be shipped in the summer are best harvested when just beginning to show color. Ideal storing or shipping temperature is between 50 60°F (10 to 15.5°C), with 90% relative humidity. Chilling below 50°F (10°C) fosters skin-rot, prevents full ripening, & reduces flavor & sweetness. Fruits from hermaphroditic plants tend to be longer & have thicker, firmer pulp, thus tolerating shipping better than the rounder, thinner pulped fruits of female plants..

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: In multiple cropping systems.

ANIMAL FEED: Fruits are eaten by livestock.

FIBER: Bark as rope fiber.

LANDSCAPING: PAPAYA plants can provide a tropical ambiance.

LEI-MAKING: Small, tubular male blossoms may be strung into lei.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: PAPAYA has many important medicinal applications. Papain has numerous utilizations. Caution: sap is caustic. A few seeds are eaten with the fruit for their beneficial properties.

STAIN-REMOVER: Papain juice removes blood & fat stains.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Tall, attractive, herbaceous, tree-like perennial. Can grow 7 to 35 ft. (2-10 m) tall, depending on variety & conditions. Pioneer species. Single, upright stem is soft & mostly hollow. Although PAPAYA is typically unbranched, occasionally the trunk will divide into limbs, especially when topped or injured. Large, palmately lobed leaves grow in a spiral cluster at the crown. Each leaf lives four to six months. Caustic, milky sap. Slightly aromatic, ivory, or light yellow flowers. Fast growing. Short tap-root, with wide spreading, shallow, lateral roots.

LIFE SPAN: PAPAYA is typically productive for only three to four years, although can continue fruiting for twenty-five years, depending on variety & culture.

ORIGIN: Western hemisphere tropics, probably Southern Mexico & Central America.

CLIMATE: Tropics & subtropics. Prefers even, ample moisture & heat. Tolerates some drought & light frost. Intolerant of hot, dry conditions, severe drought, strong wind, frost & cold.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often & well. PAPAYA is well adapted to Hawaiʻi especially in low- & mid-elevations. Although PAPAYA will bear in the highlands, fruit tends to lack sweetness & flavor.

PREFERENCES: Rich, fairly deep, moist, well drained, porous, humusy, clay-loam, pH 6.0 to 6.5 & full sun. Requires excellent drainage; can be planted on slopes or mounds, if necessary. Needs protection from damaging winds. Benefits from abundant potassium & calcium. Young plants need adequate water & balanced fertilizer, where needed, including the minor elements. (But, SEE: TOXICITY, prior, regarding accumulation of nitrites & phosphorus), Excessively rich soil makes for abundant vegetation, but low quality fruit. Cultivation is avoided since it damages roots. Mulching preserves water, reduces weeds, protects & cools the soil, & reduces root-knot nematode damage.

TOLERATES: various soils, including heavy ones, light soils if well watered, brief flooding & coastal conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: shallow, poor, very acid, or sandy soil, poor drainage (especially in heavy soil), flooding for more than two days & weed competition.

PRUNING: PAPAYA is pruned only to remove its broken or dead leaves, & suckers that may form below the blossoms. Crowded fruit may be thinned to good advantage. Older, vigorous trees that have grown too tall can be cut back to one to three ft. (30-90 cm) tall in early summer, with stump being covered to keep out water. After a month, the strongest sprout (or two to three sprouts) is secured & the remaining sprouts removed. During a summer growing season, when the sprouts are well established, the stump remaining above the sprouts can be trimmed at an angle. Even though the fruits grown on suckers tend to be smaller, the entire branch can break off due to their combined weight.

ASSOCIATES: Avocado, Banana, Citrus, Coconut, PAPAYA may be grown in multiple cropping systems with small vegetables, Pineapple, etc. Can be intercropped with Kukui, conveniently dying out as Kukui matures. Or, PAPAYA plots may be renewed every few years by rotating with other plants.

— scan page 169 —

ADVERSARIES: PAPAYA are susceptible to viral & fungal diseases, including the devastating aphid- no gransinitted "Ringspot" virus. Fruit are usually attacked by fruit flies & birds. Plant susceptible to ee pematodes. In overly wet conditions, root-rot is common. Ripe fruit are also susceptible to rot. PAPAYA eer: suffer from weed competition. They are readily killed by herbicide spray-drift.

ORGANIC-GROWING: PAPAYA is an excellent candidate, especially with resistant varieties, clean, homegrown seed, favorable growing conditions, good management, including IPM, & removing fallen, invested fruits. The incidence of "Ring-spot" & other diseases might be reduced by enriching the soil with fo. compost & other organic material, by planting resistant varieties (i-c.: 'Cariflora,' etc.) Also by maintaining sterilized seedbeds (& isolating the seedling areas from old, mature plantings), by planting in well drained soil, & by practicing croprotation. Ladybugs will devour disease transmitting aphids. Neem may help. Amending with humus, & mulching well, may inhibit harmful nematodes. Fruit fly & bird damage are best controlled by early harvest of fruits, or bagging

WEEDY: Persistent, escaped & sparsely naturalized. Occasionally found wild in dry to moist lowlands, especially in regrowth forests & barrens. Wild fruit typically quite small. Wild trees usually eradicated to prevent cross-pollination, pests, & diseases.

DISADVANTAGES: Chemical-assisted mono-cropping of PAPAYA is a recipe for pestilence & disease.

REMARKS: The high cost of labor & land typically makes mono-cropped PAPAYA unprofitable as an agri-business, but it is yaluable in polycultures & other diverse home plantings. PAPAYA tends to be dioecious, with unisexual flowers on separate female & male trees, but its sex is not stable. Sex can be determined when plants begin to flower at six months of age, or earlier. There are three or more forms: female, male & hermaphroditic. Male flowers are found in long clusters, while large-fruiting females are solitary or in small clusters near the trunk. Male flowers sometimes produce slim fruit. Hermaphroditic trees do not need a male tree to make fruit. Environment, including cultural techniques, change of season, & tree-age, can alter a trees' sex. Poor growing conditions can create sterility in hermaphroditic trees. Topped male trees have reportedly become female, but they may have been changing their sex then anyway. Sex may also temporarily change in high summer heat. With dioecious trees, one male tree needed for every ten to twenty females. Dioecious female trees are more productive & have greater cold tolerance.

POLLINATION: PAPAYA tend to cross-pollinate via insects & wind. Heavy or prolonged rain hampers pollination. There are also times when males are not shedding much pollen. Hand-pollination improves fruit-quality & fruit-set, especially during rain, & is also done for breeding purpose. Best time to hand-pollinate is just after blossoms open.

SEED-SAVING: If the PAPAYA is dioecious, the seeds are selected from a superior tree. If hermaphroditic, seeds are selected from the plumpest, longest fruit. Seeds from inbred hermaphroditic plants will produce almost identical offspring. Jelly-like seedcovering (aril) can be rubbed off between a cloth & hand, then seeds can be washed, drained & spread to dry on paper. Fresh seed is reportedly dormant & needs to be aged about six months before sowing. Stored dry, sealed in ajar. Seed life span: two to three years, or longer if refrigerated.

PROPAGATION: By seeds, cuttings, air-layering, grafting & tissue culture. Seeds can be planted directly in the field, but need careful tending. Directly sown seed usually makes for a straighter, deeper tap-root, earlier fruiting & a more vigorous, productive plant. Or, three to five seeds can be sown on sterile starting medium & covered 4 to % in. (6-18 mm) deep with clean, coarse sand, vermiculite, etc. Germination: two to five weeks. Germination is quickest when the aril is washed off seed before they are dried. Seedlings like to be placed where they wiil get moming sun & afternoon shade, or in a partly shaded spot. Although the medium is kept moist until the seeds sprout, allowing the seedbed to dry afterwards & providing good ventilation will reduce damping-off. To prevent plant-stunting, seedlings are moved to full sun before cotyledons shrink & turn brown. Fast, constant growth should be maintained. In dry conditions, seedlings are watered at four to five day intervals & provided with some shade, if necessary. Three select seedlings are ultimately thinned to one plant of the preferred sex. Unwanted plants are cut at soil-level rather than pulled up. Seedlings can be planted out when one & a half to two months old. Plants are often placed slightly high, since excessive settling can cause stem-rot. Cuttings: side-shoots (induced or spontaneous) 1 to 3 ft. 30-90 cm) long, taken midsummer. (A simple test is available to identify Genetically Modified genes.) Cuttings are kept wet & cool until placed in coarse sand to root. All but its tip & one large leaf are removed (rot can be prevented by letting the other leafstalks fall on their own). Adequate, continual moisture & a weekly foliar feeding are beneficial. Cuttings are hardened-off in a shade-house before planting out. Roots cuttings are hand-watered to soak & settle the starting medium when transplanting, continuing watering for a month, twice a week. During a rainy season, rooted cuttings can be planted in a trench 6 in. (15 cm) deep, gradually mounding up soil to 12 in. (30 cm) deep as they grow; this supports the plant & provides some wind protection.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE VARIETIES & CULTIVARS: Note: many other worthy cultivars exist. 'Cariflora.' Small fruit; f to 1% Ibs. (.45-.7 kg). half female & half male. A somewhat virus resistant variety from Florida. ‘Kaymia,' X-77. Yellow-orange, very sweet fruit. Prolific dwarf. ‘Solo.’ Varieties exist, including: ‘Malaysia Exotica,’ a Hawaiian Solo/Malaysian cross. Smaller excellent fruit. Only female & hermaphroditic plants, thus every tree yields fruit if pollinated by hermaphroditic parent. Resistance to fruit-rot, but susceptible to viruses. ‘Dwarf Solo.’ Bears good fruit in regions with abundant rain. ‘Kapoho Solo,' ‘Puna Solo.' Tolerates wet conditions. ‘Sunrise Solo,' 'Strawberry Papaya.’ Bears small fruit with sweet, delicious reddish pulp. Precocious. Waimanalo Solo,' 'Solo Line 77,’ Bears large, sweet, high quality, long-lasting fruit on hermaphroditic plants. Female plants reportedly have a rough appearance. Good for regions with lower rainfall.

BABACO, Mountain Papaya, Chamburo, Bush Melon of the Andes. Carica pentegona, syn. C. pentandra, or Carica species crosses. Several cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed fruit with an unique tropical flavor. Mostly seedless, yellow fruits to 12 in. (30 cm) long, weighing up to 10 Ibs kg). Said to be better than C. pubescens. Eaten fresh raw (including skin of some cultivars), honey-glazed, in salads, cooked, cakes, puddings, stewed, sauces, jams & preserves, sorbets, or as a Pineapple-replacement in cooking. Diced or halved fruit is often sprinkled with a sweetener, wrapped up & refrigerated for several hours. Generally very high in papain.

BEARING: beginning in less than twelve or up to eighteen months. Bears late spring to frost, in temperate climates.

APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: tropical-looking ornamental.

PAPAYA. Single trunked.

TOLERATES: cool weather & brief freeze.

INTOLERANT OF: wet feet, poor soil-aeration, & strong winds which can topple fruit-laden trees.

Ⓦ PARSLEY

Vol II · scan p. 171 · book p. 129

PARSLEY Perejil (Spanish). Petroselinum crispum Hortense Group, syn. P. sativum, syn. Carum petroselinum, syn. Apium crispum, & P. carum. Apiaceae (prev. Umbellifereae) (Parsley) Family. Several groups, forms & many varieties exist, including dwarfs.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed & nutritious. Leafs & stems have a strong, slightly bitter flavor. Eaten fresh raw, or in mixed salads & in cooking (fresh or dried). PARSLEY brings out the flavor in soups, stews, sauces, vegetable-, meat- & fish dishes, omelettes, tabouli, casseroles, stuffings, Potatoes, marinades, & as a gamish. High in vitamins A, B's & C, also rich in calcium, phosphorus, iron & other minerals, as well as a fair amount of protein. Roots have a sweet flavor & are eaten fresh raw, boiled, or dried (as a seasoning). Seeds have been utilized as a flavoring & a source of medicinal oil, but are needlessly risky to eat.

LTOXICITY: Seeds are toxic in large quantities.

MATURITY: Sixty-five to ninety days, depending on cultivar. A light, first harvest in one & a half months is possible.

BEARING: Y ear-round.

HARVESTING: Cut-&-come-again greens. Outer leaves can be removed as needed, clipping or snapping off stems at their bases, being careful not to damage the growing crown.

STORING: Leaves, preferably with their entire stem intact, can be stored in plastic bags in a refrigerator. Alternately, stems can be removed & leaves dried untl crisp in a dry, shaded, airy location, or a tukewarm oven. Dried PARSLEY can then be stored in an air-tight container in a dark spot. Roots need a Jonger drying time,

SHIPPING: Transports well if carefully packaged & refrigerated.

APPLICATIONS:

BENEFICIAL INSECT HOST: Flowers feed pest-predators.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Can be grown indoors on a window sill, or in a window box, etc.

COVER CROP: Deep tap-roots retrieve buried minerals.

DYNAMIC ACCUMULATOR: Collects calcium, iron, magnesium & potassium.

LANDSCAPING: PARSLEY is handsome in borders, edges & as fill.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Important properties.

NO-TILL GARDENING: Excellent, long-lasting candidate.

DESCRIPTION: PARSLEY is an attractive, herbaceous biennial, or slightly perennial, often grown as an annual. Can grow 6 in. to ft. (15-90 cm) or taller, depending on cultivar. Rosette habit. Yellow-green flower umbels on a 3 ft. (.9 m) stem may arise in its second year. Generally vigorous. Thick, Parsnip-like tap-root 2 to 4 ft. (.6-1.2 m) deep.

ORIGIN: Southern Europe, eastern Mediterranean region.

CLIMATE: Subtropics, cool tropics & temperate zones. Tolerances depend on cultivar. Not well adapted to hot tropics, & does not live long in equatorial conditions. Can be planted in containers & protected from intense heat. Rarely flowers where warm.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Heavy feeder. Prefers deep, moist, fertile, well drained soil, slightly acid pH & part shade or full sun. Responds to amending with compost & aged manure. Side-dressed with sifted compost. Flower-stalk is cut off at its base to promote further leafing.

INTOLERANT OF: fast-drying, excessively alkaline soil & poor drainage.

ADVERSARIES: Basically pest free. Seemingly unbothered by vog. PARSLEY-worm is the larval stage of the beautiful black swallowtail butterfly. Root-rot can occur in excessively wet soil.

WEEDY: PARSLEY can reseed, escape & naturalize in wet areas, including stream & loi edges. Not hard to control.

REMARKS: PARSLEY is a valuable, long-lasting plant in fertile, well drained soil. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Wind or insects.

SEED-SAVING: Aged seeds reportedly germinate better than freshly gathered seeds.

PROPAGATION: Seeds are sown directly or in flats to transplant. Covered 4% in. (6 mm) deep. Germination: fairly slow & erratic, three to four weeks. A twenty-four hour soak in lukewarm water speeds sprouting. Seed of the fast sprouting RADISH can be mixed with PARSLEY seed as markers. When the PARSLEY seedlings have around six leaves they can be transplanted, avoiding damage to their sensitive young tap-roots.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic
