EDIBILITIES:

GARDEN PEAS: Highly esteemed vegetable. Immature, tender, shelled green seeds are eaten fresh raw in mixed salads, or steamed, boiled, or sautéed. High in vitamins A, C, B's & E; larger-seeded, late varieties contain less vitamin C than the smaller, early varieties. Sugar in seed starts turning to starch within two hours of harvest.

EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS: Highly esteemed. Young tender pods are delicious fresh raw, or in stir-fries, many Asian dishes, omelettes, or frozen. Seeds can be allowed to mature for “shelled PEAS.”

FIELD PEAS: Ripe, mature, shelled & dried seeds, either whole or split, are eaten cooked, in soups, stews, pureed, ground to flour, tempeh, sprouted, roasted for a Coffee-replacement, canned, or frozen. High in protein & starch.

PEA SHOOTS: Cooked in Chinese cuisine such as chow mein, or noodle dishes. All

PEAS: Young tender leaves, succulent shoots & leafy tendrils are edible as cooked vegetables, or in stir fries, etc.

MATURITY: fifty to eighty-five days depending on cultivar & conditions.

BEARING: Spring & summer, or nearly year-round in cool conditions.

MATURITY & HARVESTING:

GARDEN PEAS: Gathered immature or mature, as desired.

EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS: Usually gathered young & tender, around five to seven days after blossoming, before seeds begin to swell, although most cultivars can stay tender & sweet even when larger, with formed seeds. Often stringless. Yield is usually best if pods are gathered when under half grown. Daily harvest is needed since pods form so quickly.

FIELD PEAS: Gathered mature or immature.

PEA SHOOTS: Shoots are harvested when only 4 to 5 in. (10-12.5 cm) tall. Flowers kept pinched. Prostrate plants.

NOTE: All PEA plants will cease production if seeds are allowed to mature.

STORING: PEAS last well frozen or canned. Dried seeds are long lasting. EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS can be frozen or dried.

SHIPPING: Dried, frozen or canned PEAS transport well. Fresh EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS don't, unless chilled & treated with care.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Dried, ripe seeds, whole or split for livestock. Plants as hay or silage. PEAS are also grown as forage.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Dwarf varieties.

GREEN MANURE: Certain cultivars of FIELD PEAS.

LANDSCAPING: Some cultivars have attractive &/or fragrant flowers. Dwarfs are suited to garden edges, flower boxes, roof-gardening.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, nitrogen-fixing annuals. Can grow from 8 in. (20 cm) dwarfs to vines 6 ft. (1.8 m) or taller. Vine, bush, or prostrate habit. Climbing by tendrils. Attractive white, pink or purple flowers, sometimes fragrant. Day-length sensitive: reportedly varieties 'Alaska' & 'Surprise' are short-day adapted. GARDEN PEA pods dehisce their seeds. EDIBLE- PODDED PEAS are indehiscent. Certain cultivars are more prolific than others. Fast growing. Although roots are not vigorous, tap-root can grow 3 ft. (.9 m) deep, soil permitting, with slim lateral roots.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

— scan page 173 · book page 131 —

UATE: Temperate zones, subtropics & highland tropics. Prefers cool or warm, humid weather. Temperature range of 55 to 65°F (13-18°C) is ideal for good yield. In tropical regions PEAS can be grown in the highlands, or during lowland winter. Tolerances depends upon cultivar & can include resistance to drought, heat & cold. PEA plants tend to mature too rapidly in hot climates. Roots can be kept cooler with a heavy organic mulch. EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS are more adapted to warmer conditions than GARDEN- or FIELD PEAS, & there are varieties well adapted to lowland gardens. Generally all PEAS are intolerant of drought, especially while pods are filling.

GROWN IN HAWATLI: EDIBLE-PODDED PEAS grow very well here. pREFERENCES: Prefers well drained, moisture-retentive, light, humusy soil, near neutral pH (5.5 to 7.5) & full sun. Benefits from amending with potassium & phosphorus, compost, & side-dressing when young. PEAS require constant moisture.

TOLERATES: part shade.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly acid or strongly alkaline pH, water-logging, & poor drainage. (

RAINING: Although bush & dwarf types do not require trellising, vining varieties certainly do. Trellis can be provided by twiggy, roughly barked brush pushed into the ground between rows, or by securely staked, fine-meshed chicken-wire, or other trellis 4 to 6 ft. (1.2-1.8 m) tall. Supports put in place before planting so tendrils have something to easily grab onto.

ASSOCIATES: Trellised vines shed their lower leaves, allowing interplanting of shade-tolerant plants. PEAS grown as a hay field are often interplanted with cereals.

ADVERSARIES: Pests possibilities can include white-flies, aphids, leaf miners, cutworms, pod-borers & mites, although these are typically not severe. PEAS are also susceptible to damping-off, root-rot & root-knot nematodes. Where rain is heavy, diseases such as leaf-spot, fungus & powdery mildew can be problematic. Where viruses are a problem, growing PEAS near Alfalfa, Clover or Vetch is avoided. Viruses may be spread by aphids. Cold-adapted PEAS are more susceptible to diseases when grown in warm regions.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidates with the right variety & conditions. Disease resistant cultivars may be found for your locale. PEAS should only be planted in clean soil. Crop-rotation with an unrelated species is essential. Watering only at soil level helps prevent mildew on leaves. Ladybugs will devour aphids.

WEEDY: PEAS can reseed.

DISADVANTAGES: GARDEN PEAS & FIELD PEAS are not as prolific in tropical regions. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Self-fertilized.

SEED-SAVING: "caution in saving seed... in order to avoid Ascochyta blight which is seed borne.” (7)

PROPAGATED BY: Direct seeding. Seeds soaked overnight. Sown 1 to 14 in. (2.5-3.75 em) deep; shallow in heavy, wet, or cool soil, & deep in light, drier, or warmer soil. The sweeter the seed, the more wrinkled & shrunken it is. Sweet-seeded varieties tequire warmer, drier soil to prevent rot. Normally soil is moistened before sowing, then not again until seedlings emerge. Germination: a few days. Rain-induced soil crusting on heavy soil can prevent germination; may be avoided by improving soil's tilth by amending with organic material &/or aged-manure, & by applying a very light mulch. For best germination & prolonged yield, rather than planting successively, different cultivars with varying maturity dates can be sown at the same time.

INOCULATION: When planting in new soil, soaked seeds are inoculated before sowing.

Elevation / Rainfall: Low(some varieties)/MidHigh, WetMesic

🌿☠️Ⓦ PEPPERS / NĪOI

Vol II · scan p. 175 · book p. 135

PEPPERS / NĪOI NĪOI PEPA, NIOJ PUHA‘UHA‘U (SWEET PEPPER), NĪOI KAMAKAHALA (round, red fruit), NĪOI LOLOA (long, narrow fruit). Capsicum species. Solanaceae (Nightshade) Family. Many varieties & cultivars of each. Other species are cultivated elsewhere in the world. SWEET PEPPERS, Capsicum annuum; typically annuals, with a perennial tendency, mild fruit, usually borne singly. HOT PEPPERS, Capsicum frutescens; typically perennials with pungent fruit, usually borne in clusters.

GENERAL EDIBILITIES: Ancient & highly esteemed foods. Yellow, green, red, white, purple, lavender, or black fruits, hot or not, & seeds discarded or not. Eaten fresh raw, or in mixed salads, cooked, sautéed, stir-fried, in Rice- or pasta dishes, broiled, roasted (puréed roasted PEPPERS for soups & sauces), stews, chili, stuffed, in curry powders, as garnish, condiment, pickled, or dried. Important sources of vitamins A & C. Pungency is mostly produced in the thin, inner suture, or placenta, to which the seeds are attached. Young, tender leaves & tender shoot-tips are fairly high in protein & are edible as cooked greens, or in soups, stews, or roasted in oil.

☠️ TOXICITY: Many PEPPERS produce the irritating substance capsaicin. Capsaicin is medicinal & addictive.

SEE ALSO: TOXICITIES, under CAYENNE.

BEARING: Two to three months or longer to first fruit, depending on variety.

MATURITY: One month from flower to fruit.. Maturity is noted when fruits' skin becomes glossy & waxy. Vitamin C is highest if fruit is harvested when red (or other mature color) rather than green. Hot PEPPERS are harvested when they are full-ripe, not green. Immaturely harvested PEPPERS become limp & shriveled. As fruit in varying degree of ripeness may grow on a plant at any one time, it is harvested every few days. Harvest period can continue for three months, or longer, when the plant is well tended.

HARVESTING: PEPPERS are clipped from plant, leaving at least 4 in. (1.25 cm) of stem attached.

STORING: PEPPERS can hold up well several weeks in plastic bags in the refrigerator, especially in the crisper drawer. Can be dried whole, or dried & ground for future applications. Solar-drying can take from three days to two weeks, depending on weather & size of pieces. PEPPERS can also be pickled. a

SHIPPING: The tender flesh of PEPPERS is easily damaged. Refrigeration during transport is normal.

APPLICATIONS:

— scan page 176 · book page 136 —

CONTAINER-GROWING: Some varieties are appropriate.

INSECTICIDE: Homemade hot PEPPER-spray or -dust for many garden pests. Room fumigation: a spoonful of CHILI PEPPERS can be smoldered in a heavy iron pan (leaving room until air is clear!)

LANDSCAPING: Edible omamental & variegated varieties exist for a low temporary hedge, background planting, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Especially CAYENNE.

🌿 GENERAL DESCRIPTION: PEPPERS are attractive, herbaceous, or slightly woody, evergreen perennials. Often grown as annuals in cold climates. Can grow from 6 in. to 8 ft. (15 cm - 2.4 m) tall, depending on variety. Bush habit. White, lavender, or greenish flowers. Varieties differ in color, size & form. Fruit have a hollow interior with numerous seeds. Fruit is indehiscent. Capsicum annuum grows more quickly than C. frutescens. Sturdy tap-root with many branching laterals reaching 3 ft. (.9 m) deep as wide.

LIFE SPAN: two or three years.

ORIGIN: American tropics.

CLIMATE: HOT PEPPER types thrive in warm or hot, sunny, sheltered locations, with temperatures between 70 & 85°F (21-29°C). SWEET PEPPER types like cooler temperatures between 65 & 75°F (18-24°C). Although all PEPPERS need sun during fruiting for best color & uniformity of ripening, excessive sun or heat can hamper SWEET PEPPER fruit-set & actually burn the fruit. In hot seasons, plants can be spaced closer so foliage can provide shade for the fruit. PEPPERS rarely fruit when temperatures go over 90°F (32°C). Although early cultivars exist, they all typically need a prolonged growing season. PEPPERS do best with rainfall between 25 to 50 in. (625-1250 mm) annually. Heavy rain or excessively cloudy conditions can hamper fruit-set, prevent proper coloring, & cause fruit-rot or other diseases, Cultivars with varying tolerances exist. Intolerant of severe drought.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often & well.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: PEPPERS prefer rich or average, light, well drained, loamy soil, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun. Responds to thorough amending with compost or aged-manure, greensand, rock phosphate, etc. While plants are actively growing, they are watered deeply, but infrequently. Consistency & frequency in watering becomes more important when bearing begins. Mulching thickly retards weeds, maintains moisture & coolness. Mulch kept away from stem. Plants respond well to topdressing 2 couple of times as plants are growing (before setting fruits starts), then plant is fertilized only lightly to maintain production. Note: excessive nitrogen can result in blossom-drop. Cultivated only shallowly due to danger of damaging roots.

TOLERATES: various soils if well drained.

INTOLERANT OF: weed competition & even brief water-logging or flooding.

PRUNING: One month old seedlings can be topped to promote branching.

ASSOCIATES: Growing PEPPERS with other plants reportedly gives them some protection from pests & diseases.

ADVERSARIES: Under home gardening conditions, numerous pests & diseases are possible, but seldom a severe problem. Pest possibilities include white-flies, leaf miners, aphids, PEPPER-weevil, mites & nematodes. Typically PEPPERS are not stung by fruit flies. Disease possibilities include bacterial leaf-spot, mosaic, anthracnose, late-blight, Cercespora leaf-spot & biossom endrot. Viral-mosaic & leaf-cur] can be serious in tropical climates: vectors are probably thrips, aphids, host weeds, & contaminated hands, -gloves & -equipment. Blossom end-rot can be caused by lack of water. Sun can scald fruit.

ORGANIC-GROWING: PEPPER production is highly successful with the choice of adapted varieties, good culture, & a diversity of other species nearby. Mosaic prevention: weed- & insect-control & careful garden sanitation. It is also important to wash hands tools before contacting healthy plants. In soil where bacterial wilt is problematic, all members of the Solanaceae Family should be avoided for at least five years. Crop rotation is very important to avoid mites & viruses. Nearby Peach, Alfalfa & wild Solanums can host diseases & pests.

WEEDY: Capsicum frutescens can be dispersed by birds & is naturalized in many tropical countries.

REMARKS: The more primitive hot types are easier to grow than SWEET PEPPERS. SEX: Hermaphroditic.

POLLINATION: Self- & cross-pollinated by bees & ants.

SEED-SAVING: No isolation is necessary. Seed life span: two to five years.

PROPAGATION: Grown from seeds. Although seeds can be sown directly, it is better to start in containers for later transplanting. Seeds covered 4 in. (6 mm) deep. Sown spring & beginning of summer in cool highlands; end of autumn or winter in lowlands. Although kept moist until sprouting, it is important to avoid over-watering after, especially if weather is cloudy or damp. Germination: one to three weeks: soaking seeds a few hours before sowing may improve germination. Seedlings benefit from being lightly fertilized weekly after they attain two weeks of age. Usually big enough to transplant in one & a half to two months. Seedlings are handled with care to avoid breaking or stunting their tap-root. Fertilized at transplanting with a startersolution. Seedlings are thinned well & kept weed-free.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, MesicDry

SOME NOTABLE VARIETIES: Most taxonomists separate the principle varieties into two species, Capsicum annuum & C. frutescens. number of types exist: abbreviatum - wrinkled fruit. acuminatum - chilies. cerasiforme - cherries. ‘vy. conoides - cones, including TABASCO. grossum, or Grossum Group - sweet peppers & paprika. vy. longum - long peppers.

CAYENNE, Capsicum. Capsicum frutescens variety, syn.C. minimum. Many varieties & cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Very hot fruits 1 in. (25mm) long. Red, ripe PEPPERS can be de-seeded, dried, ground, mixed with flour & yeast, baked, then ground into the spice of commerce. CAYENNE heats up curries, sauces, chili powder, & such bland foods as eggs & Rice, etc. Leaves are edible steamed as greens, or in soups & stews.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Large amounts of CAYENNE should be avoided during pregnancy & breast-feeding. 2. Seeds are removed as they can be toxic. 3. Excessive amounts can irritate kidneys, liver & intestines. 4. Can be addictive. 5. After handling fresh CAYENNE PEPPERS, touching eyes, mucous membranes, or cuts should be avoided. 6. Prolonged compresses can blister skin.

☆ PERSIMMON Diospyros species. Ebenaceae (Ebony) Family. Many varieties, strains & cultivars of each species exist, including dwarfs.

TWO SPECIES: ORIENTAL PERSEIMMON, Japanese Persimmon, Korean Persimmon, Tamopan, cope, Kaki, Diospyros kaki. Larger fruit than AMERICAN PERSIMMON. “e f - Two types: Both types are adapted to subtropics or warm-temperate climates, OR Puckering, astringent types that can only be eaten when very soft. These types Nota -_ tolerate cooler climates than non-astringent. Although they tend to be sweet & re colorful in hot climates, they can have inferior texture & often produce black areas. oy ee BON Non-astringent types are edible when still crisp & firm. Although cold-adapted ee om cultivars exist, these types typically do not do as well in temperate climates. Some re + ae cultivars tolerate frost well. oo AMERICAN PERSIMMON, Diospyros virginiana. All varieties are astringent until very ripe & soft. Adapted to temperate climates, depending on cultivar. Spreading, suckering habit; not appropriate for Hawaiʻi.

EDIBILITIES: Round, squarish, or cone-shaped yellow or red fruit 4 in. (10 cm) wide with thin, tough, shiny skin. Ripe flesh is sweet, delicious & nutritious, although some cultivars are better than others. Some cultivars are seedless. Eaten fresh raw (nonastringent types, or very ripe astringent types), or sliced for mixed salads (non-astringent forms), in many desserts including pancakes, pies, cakes, tarts, puddings, mousses, cookies, PERSIMMON-bread, jam, marmalade, gelatin, fudge, milk-shakes & ice-cream. Pulp can also be pureed as a sauce or topping, a molasses source, as well as dried, frozen, or fermented into wine, vinegar, or beer. Leaves of ORIENTAL PERSIMMON have been pickled with Radishes. AMERICAN PERSIMMON leaves can be made into a Sassafras-like tea. Fruit peel can be dried & powdered for a sweetener. Seeds have been roasted for a Coffee-replacement.

CAUTION: Eating too many PERSIMMONS can cause intestinal compaction due to excess fiber forming "bezoars." In Israel, this problem has been reduced by drying the fruits first.

BEARING: PERSIMMONS can begin bearing in three to six years, depending on cultivar. Typically productive. Many cultivars tend towards alternate bearing. Yield varies, depending on growing conditions, cultural techniques & cultivar.

MATURITY: Long fruiting season. Fruits ripen from late summer into winter, depending on cultivar. Non-astringent fruit are harvested while still firm & allowed to ripen indoors. All AMERICAN PERSIMMON & astringent types of ORIENTAL PERSIMMONS need to become very soft before they can be eaten. They can also be harvested as softness begins, but are then more susceptible to pests.

HARVESTING: Ideally, fruit are clipped from tree to avoid damage. Most cultivars hold their fruit well.

STORING: Non-astringent fruits last up to two weeks at room temperature, or as long as four months at 30 to 34°F (-1.0 to 1.0°C), with a 85 to 90% relative humidity. Astringent types don't last as long. Whole fruit can be blanched, peeled, wrapped separately, placed in the freezer, or frozen as pulp. Can readily be dried. Certain ORIENTAL PERSIMMON cultivars become as, or more palatable than dried Figs & are called Chinese Figs. Ripe fruits can be stewed, flattened & dried, or sliced thickly & dried.

SHIPPING: Excellent candidate when wrapped in tissue, placed in Peach boxes & refrigerated. Fruit is easily damaged when soft. Some cultivars ship better than others. Non-astringent types tend to be harder when harvested & thus hold up better.

APPLICATIONS:.

ANIMAL FEED: Fruit is excellent as forage for pigs, cows, cattle, horses & mules. Livestock, including goats & sheep, do not tend to eat leaves, thus it can be planted in pastures.

BEE FORAGE.

EROSION CONTROL: Holds shallow soil well.

— scan page 178 · book page 138 —

LANDSCAPING: Handsome, ornamental specimen for Japanese gardens, espalier, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITEES.

SHADE TREE: Dense summer cover.

WOOD: Valuabie timber, related to Ebony. Wood is hard, heavy, close-grained, shock resistant, stable & finishes smoothly, although can be odorous. Made into weaving shuttles, golf club heads, shoe-lasts, plane stocks, inlays, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive deciduous trees. Seedlings can grow 30 to 60 ft. 9-18 m) pe tali, while grafted trees are shorter. AMERICAN PERSIMMON tend to be taller than * t

ORIENTAL PERSIMMON. Typically have an upright habit, but usually trained to a Pe rounded, lower crown. Dark, shiny foliage turns to rich autumn-colors, depending rs, ae. on cultivar. Yellow-green or whitish flowers form on new growing twigs in spring- ‘ ee time. Usually slow growing, although faster cultivars exist. Deep tap-root & Oty N cous oo extensive shallow, lateral & adventitious roots, which can form suckers in nan —

AMERICAN PERSIMMON.

LIFE SPAN: twenty-five years, or longer. neta

ORIGINS:

ORIENTAL PERSIMMON: eastern Asia, Himalayas, northern India.

AMERICAN PERSIMMON: south & east USA.

CLIMATE: Tropical highlands, subtropics, or temperate zones, depending on species & cultivar. Some cultivars tolerate drought. PERSIMMON tolerate wet or dry climates, high or low humidity, & some wind. The colder the winter, the higher the yield. Said to be unproductive in lowland tropics. AMERICAN PERSIMMON needs 100 to 500 chill-hours, depending on cultivar. Intolerant of strong winds (damages fruit).

GROWN IN HAWAPT: Often & well.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: PERSIMMONS are easy to grow, but need ample room. They prefer moist, moderately rich, well drained, clay-loam, pH 5.0 to 6.5 & full sun. Mulched to retain moisture & suppress weeds. Although timely, balanced fertilizing is needed to keep tree healthy (including micronutrients), excessive spring growth & excess nitrogen can cause fruit-drop.

TOLERATES: many soil types & conditions, including sandy, clayey, mucky, infertile, eroded, or shallow soil & some flooding. AMERICAN PERSIMMON can tolerate part shade, while the ORIENTAL species prefer full sun. Intolerant of poor drainage (although the AMERICAN PERSIMMONS are more tolerant of wet feet & heavy soil).

PRUNING & TRAINING: Varies with cultivar & management needs. Young trees are trained to a sturdy, rounded, well-branched shape. Thereafter, only dead wood, crowded, or crossed branches need to be removed. Can be trained onto a tall trellis or as an espalier. Older or over-bearing trees can be cut back hard to rejuvenate. Some cultivars, especially of AMERICAN PERSIMMON, tend to form thickets unless suckers are removed yearly. Thinning of fruit enhances fruit-size, reduces over-production &/or tendency to bear biennially.

ASSOCIATES: Food crops are said to grow close to PERSIMMON trees.

ADVERSARIES: Although resistant to most pests & diseases, young trees can be damaged by mealy bug. PERSIMMON are susceptible to root-knot nematodes. ORIENTAL PERSIMMON tends towards crown-rot in poorly drained soil, while AMERICAN PERSIMMON is tolerant. Fruit flies & birds may attack tree-ripened fruit. Anthracnose & fungus can be serious. PERSIMMONS generally do not grow well in lawns due to Grass competition.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent with right conditions & cultivars. Certain cultivars resist anthracnose.

WEEDY: AMERICAN PERSIMMON can reach out by root suckers to cover an acre!; not appropriate for planting in Hawaiʻi. ORIENTAL PERSIMMON is well behaved.

DISADVANTAGES: Tends to drop frit if food or water lacking, or nitrogen in excessive. Deep roots make transplanting difficult. SEX: ORIENTAL PERSIMMONS are generally dioecious, requiring a pollinator, but sometimes have hermaphroditic flowers & do not require a pollinator. AMERICAN PERSIMMONS are typically dioecious & self-sterile. Need for cross-pollination depends upon cultivar. One male tree for every eight females.

POLLINATION BY: Bees & other insects. Pollinating insects can visit over er long distances. Pollination is hampered by excess rain, or dry, hot weather during flowering.

SEED-SAVING: Seeds tend to be variable & are grown mostly for rootstocks.

PROPAGATION: Grafting, budding, cuttings, suckers & seeds. Seeds can be sown directly or in pots. Seedlings are difficult to transplant due to their long, non-fibrous tap-root. Best grown in long, skinny containers at first, then moved to larger pots. Because of this long tap-root & its transplanting difficulty, only young nursery trees are purchased. Trees need to be kept well watered until well established. D. virginiana as a rootstock tolerates water-logged soil & is more vigorous than rootstocks of D. kaki, The later can also be grafted to the wild D. lotus. L?/MidHigh, WetMesicDry (depending on species & cultivar)

SOME ORIENTAL PERSIMMON CULTIVARS: Astringent Types: Better suited to colder climates. Only palatable when very ripe. ‘Hachiya.’ Large, seedless fruit. Popular for drying. Often vigorous & can be productive. ‘Okada.' Astringent until fully ripe & soft. Reliable fruiting in lower elevations in Hawaiʻi. Typically seedless or almost so. 'Saijo.' Small, long fruit with a delicious sweet flavor. ‘Sheng.’ Medium, very tasty fruit when ripe. Good for drying. Open, irregular, dwarf tree. Mid vigor. Benefits from a pollinator. ‘Tanenashi.' Mid-sized, cone-shaped fruit. Sweet & seedless. Early. Vigorous. Can be alternate bearing. Non-astringent Types: Better suited to subtropics. ‘Fuyugaki,' ‘Fuyu.’ Mid- to large fruit, sweet when ripe or not. Nearly seedless. Productive. Stores & ships well. Vigorous. Popular. ‘Hyakume.’ Large, flattish fruit, non-astringent, spicy fruit. Stores & ships well. ‘Yiro." Large, squarish fruit of excellent quality. Stores & ships well. Self-pollinating. Resistant to anthracnose. Popular in Japan. 'Surga.’ Large, very sweet fruit. Nearly seedless. Annual. Well suited to warm climates. ‘Triumph.’ Large astringent fruit. Reportedly fruits well where winters' are mild. Pollinators include: ‘Gailey,’ astringent, & 'Shogatsu,' non-astringent.

☠️Ⓦ PIGEON PEA / PĪNŪNŪ

Vol II · scan p. 179

PIGEON PEA / PĪNŪNŪ Katjang, Dahl, No-eye Pea, Red Gram, Gandul, Congo Peas, Cardis, Kadios, Cadios. Cajanus cajan, syn.C. flavus, syn. C. indicus, syn. Cytisus cajan. Fabaceae (Bean) Family. Two recognized varieties & many cultivars exist, including long-podded, sweeter seeded ones.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed. Higher in vitamins A & C than Garden Peas. Young, tender, fresh seeds are eaten shelled & cooked like Peas, or in dishes with Rice. Mature, but still green seeds are higher in nutrients & more digestible than dried seed & eaten cooked. Mature dried seeds are high in protein & are eaten split or whole as a cooked pulse, dhal (split), or in soups, curries, or ground for flour, sprouted, or fermented. Very tender, under-ripe pods can be cooked as a vegetable, or in soups, stews & curries. Leaves & young, tender shoots are high in protein & edible cooked as greens (with a strong, spicy aroma, unique flavor & abundant fiber).

☠️ TOXICITY: Any anti-nutritive qualities in PIGEON PEAS are eliminated by cooking.

BEARING: Original cultivars bloom only in the shorter days of fal] & winter. Some newer day-length neutral cultivars are available. Early cultivars begin to pod in three months, reaching maturity in five or six. Later types take nine months to.a year.

MATURITY: Maturity depends upon application. Harvested green or ripe, as desired.

HARVESTING: Individual pods can be gathered at desired stage of ripeness. Or, entire plant can be dried & threshed.

STORING: Green seeds can be frozen (fully mature) or canned (while still tender). Dried seeds last very well.

SHIPPING: Immature pods need protection from heat & drying. Mature seeds store & ship well, especially if protected against insects with Neem or Bay leaves,

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: An important species in many semi-arid locales.

ANIMAL FEED: PIGEON PEAS were extensively grown in Hawaiʻi for hay, pasturage & silage. Foliage, pods & ground seeds are relished by farm animals, including cattle, cows, horses, pigs, fowl, goats, rabbits, etc.

BIOMASS & MULCH MATERIAL: Accepts coppicing for a couple of years when cut between 6 in. to 5 ft. (15 om - 1.5 m) tall, but this reduces its vigor. Stump does not regrow when cut to ground.

EROSION CONTROL: Good on loose, bare, or eroded land.

FIBER: Basketry & thatching.

FIREWOOD: Woody stalks & plant residue are fast burning & abundant, but tend to be moist & lack density.

GREEN MANURE & COVER CROP: Harvested before plants grow too tall & woody. Excellent for resting & rejuvenating Pineapple, Cassava, Corn, or Papaya fields, etc. Decomposes in about three months.

LANDSCAPING: Temporary hedge, while other plants are taking hold.

LIVING-FENCE: Temporary.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

NURSE PLANT: Fast growing protection for Vanilla, Cacao, Coffee, Ginger, various vegetables, or herbs.

WINDBREAK: Excellent, small, temporary barrier. —

DESCRIPTION: PIGEON PEA is an attractive, woody, weakly perennial, mostly evergreen, nitrogen-fixing shrub. Often grown as an annual. Can grow 3 to 15 ft. (.9-4.5 m) tall, & around 7 ft. (2 m) wide, depending on cultivar & conditions. Pioneer species. Form, flowering-period & seed-type varies widely with cultivar. Trifoliate leaves. Can lose much of its foliage during jong droughts. Clusters of yellow to orange flowers mature into short pods with two to eight seeds. Most varieties are adapted to short-days but day-neutral varieties have been developed. The tall, late types yield only during short-days; the early dwarf cultivars can produce all year. Does not tend to shatter its seed unless pods are left too long on the plant. Slow growing at first, fast once established. Long lateral roots & deep tap-root which mines buried nutrients & water.

LIFE SPAN: up to twelve years, but productive for no more than three to five.

ORIGIN: Southern Asia, tropical Africa, East Indies, India, or Malaysia. -

CLIMATE: Widely adapted in the tropics & subtropics, although not in wet areas. Likes it warm or hot. Grows best with an annual rainfall between 20 & 80 in. (500-2000 mm). Tolerates harsh conditions, including dry areas, drought & heat (once established), brief flooding, & moderate humidity. Generally intolerant of very wet conditions, water-logging, prolonged flooding, frost, although cultivars vary widely in adaptabilities.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Introduced to the islands, probably with very early settlers. Can grow up 3000 ft. (900 m) in elevation in dry or semi-arid locales.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Easy & needs little care. Prefers moist, fertile, well drained loam, pH 5.0 to 8.0 & full sun.

TOLERATES: various soils & adverse conditions, including somewhat salty, sandy, alkaline, acid, or impoverished soils.

INTOLERANT OF: strongly acid, or very salty soil.

PRUNING: Responds to being periodically cut back & fed. Not pruned during flowering or fruiting.

ASSOCIATES: Since PIGEON PEA is non-competitive during its first year, it can be interplanted with Papaya, Cor, Sorghum, Cowpea, Sesame, Millet & other cereals, etc.

SEE ALSO: GREEN MANURE, COVER CROP, & NURSE PLANT, prior.

ADVERSARIES: Although plants are rarely bothered, insect infestation of pods is a common problem. Somewhat nematode resistant. Intolerant of weed competition.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Easy.

WEEDY: PIGEON PEA occasionally escapes & sometimes naturalizes, but is not considered to be rampant. Found wild on disturbed ground; Sugarcane land, road edges & pasture-lands. Easy to remove once spent.

— scan page 180 —

REMARKS: PIGEON PEA will grow in hot, dry tropical regions where Garden Peas cannot. Competes well with some weeds, but not with Grasses. Varieties side by side readily cross-pollinate, SEX: Hermaphroditic. Mostly self-pollinating, but crossing does occ¥.

POLLINATION: Insects, including bees. Pollination is hampered by rain. Can be hand-pollinated.

SEED-SAVING: Open-pollinated cultivars. Seed life span: at least five years.

PROPAGATED BY: Typically by seeds, but cuttings are successful, too. Sown directly (broadcast or drilled), % in. (1.25 em) deep, Although tap-root makes transplanting difficult, it is possible with careful handling. Germination: about a week: soaking seeds over night speeds germination, but is not necessary. Preferably planted in spring.

INOCULATION: Inoculation with COWPEA rhizobia is sometimes beneficial.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow Mid, MesicDry

SEE ALSO: SIBEREAN PEASHRUB. Caragana arborescens.

🌳☠️ PILI NUT

Vol II · scan p. 180

PILI NUT Javanese Almond, Canarium ovatum. Burseraceae (Torchwood) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Obiong, almost black fruit 2% to 3 in. (6-7.5 cm) long, contain a nearly triangular kernel inside a thick, stony shell. Kernel is tasty, oil- & protein-rich, nutritious & easier to digest than most nuts. Kernel is edible raw (in small amounts), or roasted lightly, & in candies, cookies, nut-brittle, puddings, ice-creams, preserves, as a nut-butter, nut-milk, Chocolate additive, or as an edible oi! source. Fruit pulp is edible boiled (flavored with salt &/or vinegar), in preserves, or as source of edible oil when pressed. Soaking fruit in hot water until pulp separates makes it easier to remove.

BEARING: trees can begin bearing in five or more years & by then they are fairly large. Trees may take ten years before they produce substantial yields.

MATURITY: commonly bears during autumn, but potentially year-round.

HARVESTING: nuts are gathered from the ground. For fresh pulp, fruits are harvested directly from the tree.

STORING & SHIPPING: dried nuts can be easily stored & transported.

☠️ TOXICITY: Uncooked seeds in quantities, are purgative. Seed coat must be totally removed, otherwise it causes diarrhea.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: pigs love the fallen fruits.

FIBER: shells for decorations & potting medium. FIREWOOD &

CHARCOAL: wood good, shells burn well. LANDSCAPING.

RESIN: trunk tapped for its resinous sap; vamish, ink, etc.

SHADE: dense cover.

WENDBREAK: tall, effective buffer.

WOOD: very good timber.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: PILI NUT is an attractive, evergreen tree. Can grow 65 ft. (20 m) or taller. Upright habit. Dark green, pinnately compound leaves. Large clusters of small, fragrant, whitish flowers. Slow growing at first, then rapid.

ORIGIN: Indonesia, Philippines, East Indies, east Asia.

CLIMATE: prefers the hot, humid tropics, with alternately wet & dry seasons. Tolerates wet conditions, as well as long, dry seasons, seasonal drought. Intolerant of severe drought, cold, & even light frosts. GROWN IN HAWAFT!: introduced & though uncommon, it is a promising tree for nut production in hot, humid regions. Very good seedling trees have been identified.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, soil, acid or neutral pH & full sun or partial shade. Needs ample room. For fastest growth, tree is fed & watered moderately & kept well weeded. Needs wind protection. Often grown as ati understory tree in its homelands.

TOLERATES: heavy, acid soils & flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: higher elevations.

ASSOCIATES: intercropping would be beneficial until the trees mature. Generally grown in a grove, with their mature shade being too heavy for most other crops.

ADVERSARIES: probably no serious pests or diseases in Hawaiʻi.

ORGANIC-GROWING: an excellent candidate. WEEDY?

DISADVANTAGES: unless a reliable variety is found, one takes a chance.

REMARKS: select, high-quality, grafted varieties are needed. Existing seedling trees vary in productivity & quality. SEX: dioecious. Male trees are needed for pollination.

POLLINATION: bees & other insects.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are highly variable. Seed life span is short. Seedling trees vary considerably in quantity & quality of nuts, as well as bearing season. Seeds may be occasionally be available through the U of H Ag. Extension Service.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds & sometimes by air-layering, budding, grafting. Germination: four to six weeks. Although cracking the nut-shell speeds sprouting, it often kills the embryo.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow/?, WetMesic

Vol II · scan p. 181 · book p. 145

POMEGRANATE / POMEIKALANA / POMEKELANE Granado, Chinese Apple, Shih liu, Limoni, Pomelaiki. Punica granatum. Punicaceae (Pomegranate) Family. Many varieties & cultivars exist, including dwarfs, & those with seedless fruits.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed & ancient food. Leathery-skinned fruit 2% to 5 in. (6-12.5 em) wide. Skin color differs with variety. Juicy, refreshing, pulp-sacks are embedded in a bitter, spongy membrane (desideratum). Pulp-sacs are sweet to somewhat tart, depending on variety. Eaten fresh raw, or in fruit- & mixed salads, stuffings, many desserts, dried, or made into juice. POMEGRANATE-juice for beverages, soups, sauces, marinades, chutneys, jellies, desserts, including cakes, pastries, ice-creams, grenadine syrup, ices, frozen, wine, etc. Fruit can be broken open under water, skimming of desideratum. Dried seeds may be utilized as a seasoning in chutneys, dhal, stuffings & other foods. Leaves are reportedly eaten boiled (in moderation).

BEARING: one to three years.

MATURITY: late summer to fall, depending on cultivar. Ripens around six months after flowering. Ready when tapping the fruit produces a "metallic" noise. While fruit should be picked before over-ripe to avoid splitting, it is also true that immature fruit will not ripen post-harvest.

HARVESTING: gathered by cutting stem close to fruit.

STORING: fruit last two to three weeks at room temperature, & many months if kept cool & dry. In fact, flavor is enhanced by aging.

SHIPPING: handles transport well if tissue wrapped, cushioned & kept cool.

☠️ TOXICITY: Leaves, bark, desideratum, rind & immature fruit are very high in tannins.

APPLICATIONS: ALLEY-CROPPING.

ANIMAL FEED: excess fruit for livestock, including cattle & camels, BEE FORAGE.

CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: ornamental, hedge, cottage gardens, espalier, etc., or trained to a tree-form.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

SACRED: possibly the "Apple" in the Garden of Eden (or Quince).

WINDBREAK: only somewhat wind-tolerant, but a good inner-edge species.

WOOD: small & very hard: crafts, walking sticks, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Small, attractive tree or shrub. Can grow 3 to 30 ft. (9-9 m) tall, depending on cultivar. Tends to be a shrub with arching branches, unless trained. Somewhat spiny branches. Glossy foliage. Nearly evergreen in warmer climates. Striking red, orange, pink, to white flowers in spring.

LIFE SPAN: very long lived.

ORIGIN: Himalayas to east Mediterranean.

CLIMATE: tropics to warm-temperate zones. Chill-hours needed: 100 to 200. Thrives in a dry climate. Needs dry heat to ripen fruit.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: occasionally.

PREFERS: average or rich, deep, well drained loam, ample ground moisture for good production, slightly acid pH & full sun. Fairly easy to grow, needing less fertilizer than most fruits. Fed after harvest in autumn again in spring, before new growth. While the tree needs protection from strong winds, it also requires good air-circulation.

TOLERATES: extreme drought, frost, brackish irrigation water, poor drainage, & various soils, including heavy-, light-, alkaline-, or rocky soils. Some cultivars tolerate poor, thin soil.

INTOLERANT OF: high humidity, shade, strong wind & lawns.

PRUNING: trained during first three years to a stocky ‘tree-shape with numerous, short limbs. After that only the basal suckers,

🌳Ⓦ PUMPKIN & SQUASH / PALAʻAI / PU / IPUPU

Vol II · scan p. 182 · book p. 148

PUMPKIN & SQUASH / PALAʻAI / PU / IPUPU Cucurbita species. Cucurbitaceae (Gourd) Family. Approximately twenty-five Cucurbita species exist, with four being especially important. a ae ” ae Many varieties & cultivars of each species exist. There is much confusion as to names. ° Vig

GENERAL EDIBILITIES: Important multipurpose foods. ia " SEE: SOME NOTABLE SPECIES, VARIETIES & CULTIVARS, following. “sal aw WINTER SQUASH or

PUMPKIN: These firm-skinned, round or pear-shaped fruits are P green, brown, or sometimes becoming yellow-orange as they ripen. Their thick yellow flesh surrounds a cavity filled with many flat seeds held by a loose web of tissue. Sizes range from tiny to huge. High nutritional content, but specific vitamins minerals vary with species & cultivar. PUMPKINS are typically coarser, stronger flavored & more often baked or made into pies. There is no exact difference between PUMPKINS & WINTER SQUASH. Mature fruit are eaten baked, roasted, mashed, in soups & stews, cakes, puddings, custards, pancakes, pies, jams, pureed, etc. Young, tender fruits are eaten boiled, steamed, fried, stuffed, added to other vegetable-, meat- & fish- dishes, pies, puddings, etc. Tender shoot tips, tendrils & young leaves are delicious as cooked greens, or stir-fried, cooled for salads, added to other vegetable- & fish dishes, etc. Flowers (especially the prolific male blossoms) & buds are edible cooked, added to other foods, stir-fries, pastas, frittered, puddings, sandwich filling, stuffed, or can be dried. Seeds contain high quality protein & oil, with some cultivars having less hull. Seeds are tasty raw, roasted, parched, sprouted, ground into a meal, or as an oil source. To prepare seeds, rinse off membrane & dry on paper towels. Seeds can then be spread one layer thick on an ungreased cookie sheet & baked thirty minutes in a preheated 300°F (150°C) oven.

SUMMER SQUASH: These are generally harvested young & eaten raw (in mixed salads), or cooked, fried, stuffed, grated for breads, etc. Some cultivars can mature into WINTER SQUASH, while others just become bland with age.

BEARING: SUMMER SQUASH can be ready to gather in around forty-five to sixty days, depending on variety & cultivar. PUMPKIN & WINTER SQUASH mature in eighty to one hundred & twenty days, or longer, depending.

MATURITY: PUMPKIN & WINTER SQUASH are either harvested when young as a "SUMMER SQUASH," or left to mature, depending on cultivar & applications. Hard-shelled SQUASH for storing are best if harvested after plant-stem has browned & begun to dry & harden. SUMMER SQUASH are picked when half-grown or smaller, while seeds are still soft.

HARVESTING: Harvest WINTER SQUASH or PUMPKIN for storing when "ground spot" turns from white to a creamy gold & rinds are hard. Stem is cut, leaving 3 to 4 in. (7.5-10 cm) on PUMPKINS. PUMPKINS without their stem do not store as well. Bruising or scratching needs to be avoided. Fleshy stermmed squash can be cut off the vine with 1 to 2 in. (2.5-5 cm) of stem remaining. The fruit of some SUMMER SQUASH cultivars separate from their stems more easily than others. Many species have profuse & bristly stems, making harvest somewhat difficult bare-handed.

— scan page 183 · book page 149 —

CURING: Mature, undamaged, cleaned & dried PUMPKIN & WINTER SQUASH can be cured a few days up to one or two weeks in a warm, dry environment; ideally at 75 to 85°F (24-29°C). Curing hardens rind & allows cuts or scraps to heal. sTORING: After curing they will store several months in a well ventilated, dry spot, with a temperature range of 40 to 55°F (5- 13°C), with 50% to 80% humidity. Rubbing with a vegetable oil helps prevent drying during storage. Stored in a single layer, not stacked. Inspected often, with condensation or mold wiped off during cold weather, remove softened squash. Intolerant of dampness, high humidity, or poor air circulation. Plastic or paper bags tend to be intolerable damp. Most varieties improve in flavor with age. Can also be dried, canned, or cooked & frozen. SUMMER SQUASH store best refrigerated. Leaves, flowers & seeds last well dried, too

SHIPPING: PUMPKIN & WINTER SQUASH ship well. Some cultivars of SUMMER SQUASH transport better than others.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: Can be grown very well as a crop either in the alleys, or within the hedge.

ANIMAL FEED: Both fruit & foliage are readily eaten by livestock.

GROUND-COVER: Vines can provide a fast, temporary cover.

LANDSCAPING: Ground-cover, arbor, or fence-covering, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Seeds.

SHADE: Many SQUASH species provide temporary cover when grown on a trellis or arbor.

🌳 GENERAL DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, annual or somewhat perennial vines. Stems can grow 3 to 18! (,9-3.6 m) long, depending on species, variety, cultivar & conditions. Trailing, climbing, or bush habit. Some species & cultivars have fewer irritating spines on leaves & stems. Large leaves. Large yellow flowers. WINTER SQUASH are slower growing than SUMMER

SQUASH. WINTER SQUASH also produce a more compact, dense fruit, are more likely to root at the stem nodes, & show more of perennial tendency. Although roots are typically shallow, they can reach 6' (1.8 m) deep & three times that wide, soil pemnitting. Stems often form roots at their nodes.

ORIGIN: Western hemisphere tropics.

GENERAL CLIMATE: Grown throughout the hot tropics, subtropics & temperate zone summers. General temperature range of 65 to 75°F (18-24°C). Cucurbita moschata are more tolerant of hot conditions. C. pepo & C. maxima are more tolerant of cool. They prefer medium or light rainfall. Most of the “improved” northem types do not grow well in constantly wet tropical conditions. While some cultivars tolerate excess rainfall, occasional flooding & drought, most do not. Moisture is necessary, especially as fruit start to set. Intolerant of frost & harsh wind.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Common in gardens & smali farms. Several better varieties are available & are becoming more widely planted. There are a few varieties adapted to hot, humid lowland conditions. Grown year-round here. PREFERENCES & CULTURE,

IN GENERAL: Vining types need ample space. All are heavy feeders. These species prefer rich, moist, well drained, humusy loam, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun. Likes ample potassium & fertilizer. They benefit from well prepared beds, amended with compost or aged-manure. Only light cultivation is recommended, if at all, since shallow roots are easily damaged. They respond to monthly feeding. Mulching suppresses weeds & retains soil moisture.

TOLERATES: sandy soil, pH 5.5 to 8.0 & shade. While most species & varieties can tolerate heavy or poor soils if well managed, many do not.

INTOLERANT OF: poor-drainage, infertility, competition & strongly acid soil.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Vines benefit from trellising. Pinching back vine-tips encourages fruiting, controls rampancy, & provides excellent cooked greens. Excess fruit can be pinched off, leaving one or two fruit to ripen. Large PUMPKINS are turned weekly for best shape & uniform color.

ASSOCIATES: SQUASH are typically strong, dominant plants that tend to clamber over other plants, but they are frequently interplanted with Corn.

ADVERSARIES: Cucurbita species have a wide variety of pests & diseases. Downy mildew, powdery mildew, mosaic viruses, damping-off, fruit fly, Cucumber-beetle, & nematodes may be problematic in tropics. Other possible pests include leaf miner, white flies, cutworm, aphid, & Melon-fly. Growing Potatoes nearby is said to be detrimental.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidates with right cultivars, fast growing conditions, clean soil, & garden sanitation. Fruit fly damage can be reduced when vines are allowed to run into tall grasses, or fruit is bagged or covered with floating row-cover. Certain weeds host the serious mosaic viruses. Some pests can be discouraged by lightly dusting stems & leaves with fine woodashes, especially at the plant's base.

WEEDY: Rarely escapes & naturalizes. Not difficult to control.

DISADVANTAGES: Vines have a tendency to cover large areas. Nevertheless, TROPICAL PUMPKIN can be one of the most efficient food producers in the tropics, if fully utilized. SEX: Monoecious. Prolific male flowers are followed by female flowers if the conditions are right.

POLLINATION: Bees & other insects. Hand pollination increases fruit-set & size. This is best done in the early moming. Caution: pollinating honey bees are highly susceptible to insecticides.

SEED.

SAVING: Cultivars within a species will readily cross. Isolation of 1000 ft. G00 m) or greater, or hand-pollinating & bagging is required for pure seed. Crossing between species is very rare. Seed life span: four years is possible.

PROPAGATION: Seeds, cuttings & ground-layering. Typically three to five seeds are sown in hills, thinned to one or two plants. Sown ¥, to 2 in. (1.25-5 em) deep (depending on seed size), in warm soil. Germination: one week to ten days. Cuttings: can be rooted in advance by covering young nodes with soil & maintaining moisture. Can be planted year-round, but in most places the best yield will be in a hot, dry season.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, MesicDry

SOME NOTABLE SPECIES,

VARIETIES & CULTIVARS: Large PUMPKIN cultivars suggested by the U of H for Hawaiʻi include: ‘Jack O’ Lantern,’ Big Max' & 'Big Tom.' ☆ SEMINOLE PUMPKIN

Vol II · scan p. 184 · book p. 1

☆ SEMINOLE PUMPKIN, Tropical Pumpkin. A semi-wild Cucurbita moschata cultivar. Readily crosses.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed food. Mature fruit typically a dull, mottled orange. Eaten boiled, steamed, baked, as pies, etc. High in nutrients. Young fruit are boiled like a SUMMER SQUASH or mashed. Tender vine-tips, with small leaves & tendrils are tasty & nutritious as boiled greens. Male flowers can be eaten steamed, egg-battered & fried or deep-fried. Seeds separate cleanly from pulp. Seeds are high in protein & unsaturated oil, & are probably the most nutritious part of the entire plant. Seeds are eaten raw, toasted, or ground into a meal, as an oil source, or dried for later soaking, then frying or roasting.

STORING: hard-shelled, mature fruit last well, as do solar-dried slices..

DESCRIPTION: Trailing or climbing vine. Can grow 30 ft. (.9 m) long. Vigorous rooting at nodes keeps plant growing & producing.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, loamy soil, slightly acid pH. Benefits from amending, including a tiny bit of wood ashes.

TOLERATES: heavy rains, hot, humid tropics, as well as drought.

TRAINING: vine appreciates a trellis to climb.

ADVERSARIES: disease & insect resistant.

POLLINATION: hand-pollinating in early morning will increase yield. CoastalLowMidHigh, Mesic;

☆ RAMBUTAN Rambotang, Rambustan, "Hairy Lychee," Shao tzu, Val thieu. Nephelium lappaceum, syn. Eephoria nephelium, syn. Dimocarpus crinita. Sapindaceae (Soapberry) Family, Many diverse varieties, cultivars & forms exist. The best ones are 'freestone’ & have small seeds.

EDIBILITIES: Fruit from better cultivars are highly esteemed. Clusters of greenish to yellow, orange, or red fruit 3 in. (7.5 cm) long, covered with soft tubercles. Pulp can be juicy & mild, sweet, tart, or very tart. Peeled & eaten fresh raw, stewed, in compotes, jams, jellies & preserves, or canned. In some ‘freestone' cultivars, the papery testa surrounding the seed needs to be removed. Seeds can be eaten roasted, boiled, or a source of edible oil.

BEARING: seedlings around five years, graftlings in two to three years.

MATURITY: fruit are ready when plump, fully colored & tasty. Fruit do not ripen post-harvest. Production varies with the year. Ripening varies with cultivar, but often during autumn or winter,

HARVESTING: entire fruit cluster can be cut from tree, later separating individual fruit, leaving some stem attached. Needs to be cooled quickly after harvest. STORING &

SHIPPING: fruits need to be handled with care as their soft spines bruise easily. Fruit generally deteriorate within a few days at room temperature. Some varieties hold up well, especially when kept cool & humid, as in a plastic bag in the drawer of a refrigerator. Temperatures between 59 & 68°F (15-20°C) are ideal.

☠️ TOXICITY: Raw seeds are probably poisonous, if chewed & eaten.

APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: omamental. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

WOOD: too valuable to fell, but hard & strong if well cured: building, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree. Related to Lychee. Can grow 80 ft. (24m) or taller, but grafted trees are often half that. Wide, dense crown.

ORIGIN: Southeast Asian archipelago, Malaysia.

CLIMATE: hot, wet, humid tropics, preferably with a dry period to promote flowering. Most varieties like the daily mean temperature continually close to 82°F (28°C). GROWN IN

HAWAIPI: occasionally.

PREFERS: deep, moist, fertile, well drained, humusy foam, slightly to somewhat acid pH & full sun. Needs ample space, as well as nitrogen, & potassium (esp. while fruiting).

TOLERATES: various soil types & warmer climates than Lychee. More tolerant of sun & dry areas than Pulasan, though less fruitful in dry soil.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage, prolonged drought, harsh winds, cold, excessive fertilizer, & salty or alkaline conditions.

PRUNING: ultimate size, shape & strength can be enhanced by early, cautious training. After which, only dead wood, water-shoots, & excessive inner branches are removed.

ADVERSARIES: often resistant.

WEEDY: may reseed. SEX: dioecious. Some varieties are self-fertile though fruiting is enhanced by a male tree of another variety.

POLLINATION: bees (& 2)

SEED-SAVING: vegetative or asexual propagation is suggested, as seedlings vary in quality & quantity of fruit, as well as sex. Seed life span: cleaned, fresh seeds can last up to four weeks in moist sphagnum, sawdust, or charcoal (pulp-juice retards germination).

PROPAGATED BY: inarching, budding, airlayering, grafting, cuttings (possibly), & seeds. Seed sown rounded side up 1 in. (2.5 cm) deep, in sterile potting mix. Seeds can be sown directly in field & later staked for budding. Dislikes having roots cut during transplanting. Germination: one to three weeks. CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

ROSE / LOKE

Vol II · scan p. 186 · book p. 155

ROSE / LOKE Rosa species. Rosaceae (Rose) Family. Numerous species, varieties, hybrids & cultivars exist. EDIBILITIES,

IN GENERAL: Berry-like fruits ("hips") are tart, tasty & high in vitamin C. Edible fresh raw, or as jams. Flower petals vary in flavor, but are generally sweet. When flowers are bitter, whitish petal bases are removed. Petals are eaten in salads, pastries & cakes, jams, jellies, syrups, tea (dried or fresh), wine, or as a garnish for miso soup. Tender, young, red leaves & shoots can be eaten fresh raw, or parboiled & cooked as greens, sautéed, in soups, or as a condiment. APPLICATIONS,

IN GENERAL: CONTAINER-GROWING.

FLORAL ARRANGEMENTS: lasting if cut late in the afternoon.

LANDSCAPING: specimen, accent, hedges, borders, barriers trained on fences, trellises, arbors, etc. MEDICINAL QUALITIES. DESCRIPTION,

IN GENERAL: Thorny perennials. Size depends upon species & cultivar. ROSES have been on the planet at least 40 million years. Evergreen or deciduous. Most species are thorny. Attractive, often scented flowers vary widely in form & color. Surface- & deep tap-roots.

CLIMATE: temperate zones & subtropics.

PREFER: porous, fertile, well drained soil, slightly acid pH (5.0 to 6.0) & full sun. Heavy feeders. Respond weil to a settled bed that has been deeply amended with aged manure & organic matter. Other possible additions include bone-meal, compost & leaf mold. Benefit from regular feeding. ROSES require good air-circulation. Plants need deep, weekly watering in dry weather, but wetting leaves should be avoided. Benefits from mulch, especially in dry, hot weather.

TOLERATE: winter cold.

INTOLERANT OF: poor-drainage of air or water, high humidity, harsh winds & root-competition.

PRUNING: except for removal of oldest canes & dead wood, pruning varies with type.

ASSOCIATES: Allium species.

ADVERSARIES: Chinese- & Japanese- ROSE-beetles are fond of the tender types. Fungusdiseases are common from stagnant, humid air &/or unsanitary growing conditions.

ORGANIC-GROWING: although ROSES can be bothered by a variety of problems, prevention & care reduce the damage. This includes proper location & bed-preparation, wind-protection, appropriate watering, mulch, timely feeding & pruning, & planting suitable, resistant varieties. To prevent many fungal conditions, soil surface should be cleaned in spring, allowing sun to bake it for a month before a summer mutch is applied.

WEEDY: many species can escape & naturalize. Can be serious environmental weeds. Good candidates for containergrowing.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are variable & often return to species form.

PROPAGATED BY: grafting, cuttings, budding, ground-layering, root-suckers & seeds. Cuttings: half ripe wood, or hardwood cuttings in fall, & softwood in summer. Seeds need light to sprout. Germination: erratically from one to twelve months or more, at 55°F (13°C).

FIVE TYPES OF ROSES:

BEDDING ROSES: Borders, beds, low fences. Grow under 3 ft. (.9 m) tall. Specific pruning needs. CLIMBING ROSES, Loke-hihi: Actually, they lean rather than climb. Two types: Ramblers, which are tall & vigorous reaching over 30 ft. (9 m) tall. Canes are cut back to ground level after yearly blooming, to restrain their unruly growth & encourage new flowering buds.: Large-flowered Climbers or Climbing hardy 'perpetuals' that are slower & lower growing.

NOTE: Both climbing types can be trained to “climb” on trellises, walls, arbors, arches, or fences. Vines need tying on smooth surfaces. Allowing ample space between support & building walls permits air-circulation & maintenance. Can spread by running root-suckers.

CREEPING ROSES: Trailing habit. Small flowers.

LANDSCAPING: ground-, wall-, or bank-cover. SHRUB- or

BUSH ROSES: New shrub ROSES that have been breed for compactness. Large ROSE-hips. Can spread by root-suckers. TREE- or

STANDARD ROSES: Trained from SHRUB- or BEDDING ROSES.

LANDSCAPING: specimens, accents, etc.

RYE / CEREAL RYE / HUAPALAOA ʻELEʻELE Secale cereale. Poaceae (Grass) Family. Many cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Important staple food. Grain is made into flour for breads, as well as sprouted, fermented to beverages, or roasted for a Coffee-replacement. Not as nutritious as many other grains. Sprouted grain for salads, or ground for an Essene-type bread.

NOTE: Wheat contains phytates that tie up iron, but adding 15% RYE to recipes buffers & keeps the iron available. On the US continent, most RYE is made into whiskey.

MATURITY: mid-summer if sown in autumn.

☠️ TOXICITY: Beware of poisonous ergot (Claviceps purpurea) infestation.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: pasture.

COVER CROP: WINTER RYE for weed suppression.

GREEN MANURE: autumn or winter sown WINTER RYE, turned under in springtime. Older growth can be tough, so it is best to incorporated when under 9 in. (22.5 cm) tall.

LANDSCAPING: WINTER RYE mowed for lawns or paths. MULCH MATERIAL. ROTATIONAL PLANTING.

SOIL-RENOVATION: far reaching roots create-, bind- & protect soil, & foliage die-back provides muich.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, tufted annual or sometimes biennial Grass. Can grow 1% to 7 ft. (45 cm - 2 m) tall, depending on cultivar. Fast growing. Extensive roots.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

CLIMATE: temperate zones. Adaptable. Some varieties grow best during winter. GROWN IN HAWALT introduced & cultivated here.

PREFERS: full sun.

TOLERATES: acid or slightly alkaline soil, light or heavy soil, heat & drought.

ASSOCIATES: Wheat, Pansy & Bachelor's Buttons, or as an intercrop.

WEEDY: has escaped; occasionally found growing in corrals, being spread in horse feed. Can establish itself in pasture- & range lands, roadedges, & barren areas. Volunteer RYE is serious weed in Wheat fields. SEX: cross-pollinated.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span is long.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown autumn or winter, as weather cools. Covered % in. (18 mm) deep. Germination: two to three days.

INOCULATION: Azotobacter reportedly beneficial.

Elevation / Rainfall: High, Mesic

☆ GARDEN SAGE, Broadleaf-, Dalmatian-, or Blue Sage. Salvia officinalis. Many forms, cultivars & varieties exist.

Pungent foliage, dried or fresh, can be added to salads & dressings, sauces, cheeses, soups & stews, pesto, omelettes, soufflés, vegetable dishes, stuffings, poultry-, egg-, cheese-, seafood- & meat dishes, or as a tea. ☆☠️ SPINACH / ʻINIKA

Vol II · scan p. 191 · book p. 167

☆ SPINACH / ‘Inika Horen-so Spinacia oleracea. Chenopodiaceae (Goosefoot) Family. Two forms exist: crumple-leafed 'Savoy' & smooth ‘Oriental’ forms. Many cultivars exist, including ‘Low Acid,’ disease-resistant, some slow bolting.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed. Delicious nutritious as cooked greens, or pureed, sautéed, in soups, quiches, pastas, souffiés, omelettes, & occasionally eaten in a wilted salad. High in protein, minerals & vitamins A, C & E. Seeds may be sprouted for mixed salads.

MATURITY: three weeks to two months, depending on cultivar.

HARVESTING: entire plant is cut to the ground. Washed gently, but thoroughly, just before cooking.

STORING: holds up best in a plastic bag in the refrigerator with a moist paper-towel in the bag, or frozen (some varieties freeze better than others).

☠️ TOXICITY: Laves of most cultivars are very high in oxalic acid; can be broken down by cooking & discarding the cooking water & avoiding over consumption. Oxalic acid robs calcium & iron from the body.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous annual. Can grow 8 in. (20 cm) tall. Fast growing.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

CLIMATE: subtropics temperate zones. Thrives in cool, moist conditions, with an ideal temperature range of 60 to 65°F (15-18°C). Heat & long days stimulates bolting.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: thrives in the highlands.

PREFERS: fertile, humusy, well drained, well-dug soil, near neutral pH (6.0 to 7.0) & full sun. Responds to added compost or rotted manure. Calcium, if needed, should be added after the nitrogen amending. Mulching conserves moisture, suppresses weeds & provides food for the plants.

TOLERATES: some salt & some frost.

INTOLERANT OF: drought, intense sun, tropical lowlands, & acid soil.

ADVERSARIES: leaf miner.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize, but not considered invasive.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Sown under in. (1.25 cm) of fine compost. Germination: about two weeks; coolness is beneficial. Sown in successive weekly plantings for continuous supply. L?/MidHigh, WetMesic

☆ SPINACH GREENS, PERENNIAL Various Genera & Families. ☆ swt? NEW ZEALAND SPINACH, Botany Bay Greens. Tetragonia expansa, syn. T. tetragonioides, syn. Demidovia tetragonioides. Aizoaceae (Carpetweed) Family. Varieties exist.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed vegetable. Succulent leaves & tips as cooked greens, or in stir-fries, quiches, creamed, etc. Not recommended raw. High in iron, calcium, phosphorous, folic acid & other vitamins.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous, evergreen perennial. Stems can grow 3 ft, (.9 m) tall & 5 ft. (1.5m) long. Either Indigenous or naturalized. Trailing ground-cover. Thick, soft, triangular leaves. Inconspicuous, green-yellow flowers mature into homed fruit. Fast growing.

LIFE SPAN: several years.

ORIGIN: New Zealand, Australia & Asia.

CLIMATE: subtropics & warm temperate zones. Ideal temperature 60 to 75°F (15-24°C),

GROWN IN HAWATIT: frequently.

PREFERS: fertile, sandy loam, neutral or slightly acid pH (6.0 to 6.8) & full sun. Thrives in a deeply dug bed with compost or well-rotted manure. Benefits from being fed a couple times a year. Mulching prevents drip-splash. Flourishes with deep regular water.

TOLERATES: drought, heat, intense sun, salt spray, sandy areas, or part shade in intensely sunny tropics, & some cool, damp conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding, & hot, dry summers.

PRUNING: trellised or tied on chicken-wire, etc. Pinching encourages branching.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, although drip-splash encourages molds & other diseases. Drier soil surface discourages stem rot.

WEEDY: often self-seeding & sometimes spreading, but not terribly aggressive. Occasionally found wild by the sea.

NOTE: other weedy Tetragonia species exist. SEX: hermaphroditic.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds & cuttings. Cuttings: root easily in sand. Germination: quite irregular; twenty-four hour hot-water soak beneficial.

CLEANER: sour fruits are high in potassium oxalate that removes rust stains & tarnish, or is a metal polish. CONTAINER-GROWING. HEDGEROW.

LANDSCAPING. MEDICINAL QUALITIES. ROADSIDE & PARKING-LOT TREE. SHADE TREE.

WINDBREAK: windresistant, once established.

WOOD: dense & somewhat hard: furniture, building, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Attractive, somewhat deciduous tree. Can grow 30 ft. (9 m) tall. Open rounded canopy. Foliage folds up at night. Pinkish to white flowers. Slow growing. Non-aggressive roots.

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: Ceylon, China, Moluccas & possibly Malaysia.

CLIMATE: warm, humid tropics & subtropics.

GROWN IN HAWATIT: frequently grown here.

PREFERS: deep, moist, fertile, well drained clay-loam, slightly acid pH (5.5 to 6.5) & full sun. Easy. Quality & productivity are enhanced with ample growing room, plenty of sunshine, wind protection, regular light feedings (quartesly), & constant moisture.

— scan page 193 · book page 169 —

TOLERATES: various soils, part shade (while young), & some wind (when mature) & temporary drought.

INTOLERANT OF: strong, or harsh drying winds, shade, flooding, frost, wet feet, alkalinity, & prolonged drought.

PRUNING & TRAINING: initially trained to shape, thereafter pruned only to open, or to maintain hedgerow. Fruiting clusters & smaller fruit can be thinned, leaving three to four to a clump.

ADVERSARIES: rarely bothered, except by fruit flies.

WEEDY: can escape. SEX: usually selffertile, though crossing improves harvest.

POLLINATION: insects, including bees.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are quite variabie. Seed life span is only a few days.

PROPAGATED BY: very fresh seeds, air-layering, inarching, grafting & budding. Seeds are often sown in a peat moss medium. Germination: one to three weeks, depending on season. Tender seedlings require gentle handling & shelter from wind.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

SEE ALSO: BILIMBI. Averrhoa bilimbi.

🌿☠️Ⓦ STRAWBERRY

Vol II · scan p. 193 · book p. 169

STRAWBERRY Garden Strawberry, Pineapple Strawberry. Fragaria x ananassd, syn. F, chiloensis x F. virginiana, x F. vesca, x F. moschata, & x P. elatior, & others. Rosaceae (Rose) Family. A number of other species, many hybrids & a multitude of cultivars exist, including low-chill.

TWO TYPES: "EVERBEARING" STRAWBERRIES, A.K.A. “Perpetual Strawberries”: Many day-length neutral cultivars exist, with nearly year-round production in cool tropical regions. "MAIN CROP" STRAWBERRIES, A.K.A. “June-bearing Strawberries”: Vigorous, high quality, heavy bearing ptants 7!; that tend to produce one heavy crop a year in spring. Numerous early-, mid- or jate-season cultivars exist.. vos

EDIBILITIES: Popular & highly esteemed, red, white, or yellowish fruit. Sweet, tart, juicy fruit are a. delicious fresh raw, stewed, as well as in pies, cakes, tarts, pastries, ice-creams, jams, jellies, preserves, ne a oe dried, or made into wine. Size, flavor, firmness, etc., depend upon heredity, fertility, & exposure. Young ns fresh leaves can be eaten in mixed salads, soups, or as a tea (dried or fresh). Stems & stalks are edible.

☠️ TOXICITY: Leaves contain tannin.

BEARING: Can begin a few months after sets establish. Some bear almost year-round, others bear one main crop yearly.

MATURITY: Ideally, fruit are left to ripen on the plant. If pests & transport are issues, fruit can be harvested in its greenwhite/pinking stage & ripened for two days at 85°F (29°C). Fruit does not develop color well at 55°F (13°C) & under.

HARVESTING: To protect fruit & plants, fruit stems are clipped, leaving a bit attached. Regular picking twice or three times a week extends fruiting.

STORING: Most cultivars freeze (preferably in glass) or dry well. Long lasting as jam, jelly, or preserves.

SHIPPING: Some cultivars tolerate transport well, if fruit is kept cool & handled with care. Others are too soft to ship.

APPLICATIONS:

BEE FORAGE.

BERM PLANT: Yes, but does not tolerate flooding.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Many "EVERBEARING" types are excellent for hanging baskets, sills, cold-frames, barrels, etc.

DYNAMIC ACCUMULATOR: Leaves are said to collect iron.

INDICATOR PLANT: Spontaneous WILD STRAWBERRIES denote acid soil.

LANDSCAPING: Edible ground-cover, but can be invasive. SEE: WEEDY, following.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: Many applications.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous evergreen perennial. Can grow 6 to 12 in. (15-30 cm) tall, depending on variety. Numerous runners can quickly colonize soil, forming a mat. White flowers. Day-length sensitive; neutral varieties are better adapted to short, tropical days. Shallow rhizomatic roots.

LIFE SPAN: three to six years.

ORIGIN: Temperate World.

CLIMATE: Thrives in cool, moist conditions. Typically needs 200 to 300 chill-hours; ‘Fern’ is a low-chill variety. Tolerates light shade in hot climates. Resists light frost. Generally intolerant of drought (resistant cultivars exist) & strong wind.

GROWN INHAWATII: Although most STRAWBERRIES prefer growing above 3000 ft. (900 m) elevation in the tropics, some cultivars can grow lower; Fragaria chiloensis var. ananassa is grown successfully in Hawaiʻi as low as 300 ft. (90 m).

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: STRAWBERRIES prefer moist, fertile, well drained, humusy loam, pH 5.0 to 5.5 & full sun. Excess nitrogen encourages foliage instead of fruit. Preferably fertilized after harvest to avoid fruit rot. Appropriate mulch conserves water, suppresses weeds, adds humus, reduces fruit rot & keeps berries from getting soiled; shredded leaves, wood-shavings, straw, stones, etc., or ideally, Pine-needles.

TOLERATES: light shade, & some cultivars can grow in poor soil, although the yield will be reduced.

INTOLERANT OF: weed-competition, poor-drainage, flooding, & dry, salty, or alkaline soil. Can be planted on mounds for better drainage.

PRUNING & TRAINING: On "MAIN CROP" STRAWBERRIES, the first year blossoms are removed one or two times a week to strengthen the mother plant. “Daughter” runners need to be thinned regularly to prevent rampancy. On "EVERBEARING" types, the first year blossoms are pinched only until mid summer, allowing a late summer & autumn crop to fruit.

ASSOCIATES: Planted among vegetables or flowers, especially Lettuce, Spinach, Onion, Bush Bean, Soybean, Sage, Borage.

ADVERSARIES: Although resistant cultivars exist, STRAWBERRIES are susceptible to mildew, verticillium wilt, red stele (root-rot), leaf-spot, viral diseases, nematodes & fruit-rot. Aphids often spread diseases. Slugs, snails, beetles, etc., relish the fruit. Floating row-cover at night may help prevent Rose-beetle attack. Diseases can be reduced by not wetting the leaves during watering. It is important to avoid growing STRAWBERRIES near Cabbage Family members.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate with resistant cultivars, right climate, good cultural practices & protection.

— scan page 194 · book page 170 —

WEEDY: Escaped & naturalized. Sometimes found wild in forest clearings, farmlands, shaded road edges, especially the whitefruited form. Spread by runners & seeds. Dispersed by birds, feral pigs, etc.

REMARKS: STRAWBERRY is called "Humi nascentia fraga" (child of the soil), by Virgil. SEX: Hermaphroditic. Generally self-fruitful.

POLLINATION: Most cultivars are self-pollinating.

SEED-SAVING: Open-pollinated cultivars exist. Seed life span is probably not more than a year.

PROPAGATION: Grown by divisions, offsets or seeds. Diseased or damaged parts are removed from new bare-root plants, New plants need to be protected from drying, direct sun, or excess wetness. Roots are spread evenly on a smali mound in deep, halffilled holes, then backfilled. Care is taken to avoid both covering the crown or planting too shallowly. New plants benefit from protection full sun for several days, then given daily water for a couple of weeks until established. Seeds are sown on top of moist starting mix, gently tamped & placed in the shade. Covering with plastic or glass helps maintain high humidity. Seedlings are gradually hardened off when sprouting begins. Germination: around one to four weeks.

Elevation / Rainfall: Low/(some cultivars)/MidHigh, WetMesic

SOME NOTABLE SPECIES: Many cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed. Small, very flavorful, red, white, ivory or yellow fruit are delicious in all applications previously noted. High in pectin.

MATURITY: nearly year-round.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING: most cultivars.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive perennial. Can grow 6 to 10 in. (15-25 cm) tall. Non-running. Generally vigorous. Easy to grow. Most cultivars grow well in either full sun or part shade.

ADVERSARIES: birds are less tempted by the yellow- or white-fruited forms.

ORGANIC-GROWING: disease-resistant cultivars exist.

WEEDY: even though this species does not spread by stolons, it readily naturalizes.

PROPAGATED BY: divisions or seeds.
