🌿Ⓦ SUNFLOWER / PUA NĀNĀ LĀ

Vol II · scan p. 194 · book p. 170

SUNFLOWER / PUA NĀNĀ LĀ Common Sunflower, Cultivated Sunflower, Pua nana 1a ("flower looking at the sun"), Nanaia. Helianthus annuus variety macrocarpus. Asteraceae (Sunflower) Family. Cultivars vary highly regarding climatic suitabilities, size, timing, etc.

SEE ALSO: JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE, following.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed foods. Tasty hulled seeds are eaten raw, or tossed in oil & roasted until golden, boiled, in soups or stews, ground into flour or meal for seedcakes or breads, or SUNFLOWER-butter, roasted as a Coffee-replacement, sprouted, or as source of oil. Nutritious, highly digestible seeds are rich in protein, oil, vitamins & minerals. SUNFLOWER-seed oil is high in beneficial linoleic acid & lecithin. Oil is eaten on salads, in cooking, as margarine or shortening. It's said that when grown in cool conditions, or when seeds ripen slowly, linoleic acid is favored over oleic acid. Unopened flower buds & small, underdeveloped side flowers are esteemed when cooked like an Artichoke (buttered & seasoned). Tubers of some varieties are edible (

SEE ALSO: JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE, foliowing). Hulls can be roasted for a Coffee-replacement. TOXICITY?: None.

BEARING: From two to five months, depending on cultivar, with an average of four. ‘Sunspot,' ‘Progress’ & ‘Dwarf Russian' mature in 60, 63 & 68 days, respectively.

MATURITY: SUNFLOWER seed-heads are ready to gather when seeds loosen, but before they scatter or the birds start on them. Ideally, seed-heads are harvested when fully mature & dry. Wet weather can spoil the seeds.

HARVESTING: Seed-heads are cut from their stems, leaving 12 in. (30 cm) piece remaining. They are hung to dry in a warm, ventilated spot until seeds are dry enough to drop out of their sockets. Dried heads are easily threshed by rubbing two together, face to face. Commercially, threshed seeds are dried to a moisture level less than 12%.

NOTE: Corona grain-mills can be adapted with hard-rubber disks to ease hulling of seeds.

STORING & SHIPPING: Dried seeds store & transport well in their shells, in air-tight containers. Deshelled seeds & seed-oil require vacuum sealing or refrigeration. Dried, vacuum-sealed seeds transport very well.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: SUNFLOWER seeds are a nutritious feed for livestock, including cattle, horses, sheep, pigs, rabbits, poultry & cage-birds, etc. Whole seed-heads can be given to larger animals. Leaves & empty seed-heads are good as fodder. Entire plant, when harvested before the flowers open, is excellent as fresh fodder, or can be made into silage. Seedcake residue from oilextraction is high in protein. Hulls are utilized as a filler for feed-cakes & meal.

— scan page 195 · book page 17 —

BEE FORAGE: Nectar & pollen source.

BENEFICIAL INSECT HOST: Flowers of most of the members of this Family feed helpful insects.

COMPOST-MATERIAL: Spent stalks & seed-heads.

COVER CROP: SUNFLOWER can be harvested before flowering as a green fodder or biomass source. DYE: Flowers. Hulls of the cultivar 'Hopi Black Dye.’

DYNAMIC ACCUMULATOR: Husks & stalks are high in potassium.

FIBER: Stems are made into a fine silky fiber. Inner stem fiber is excelient for paper-making.

FIREWOOD: Stems of certain cultivars.

GREEN MANURE: Widely adapted.

BULLS: Animal bedding.

LANDSCAPING: Tall varieties, with attractive blossoms for backgrounds, borders, wind buffers, screens, mass plantings, vertical gardening, etc. Omamental species exist grown for their cut-flowers: doubles, red & banded fiowers, or variegated.

MULCH MATERIAL: Spent stems & hulls. OIL: Semi-drying oil. Salad-dressing, cooking, illumination, lubricant, soap-making, paints & varnish, etc.

SACRED: The Incas revered SUNFLOWER as an embodiment of the Sun.

STATE FLOWER: Kansas.

TOBACCO-REPLACEMENT: The leaf, when dried carefully, can be smoked.

WATER-PUMPS: SUNFLOWERS utilize a great deal of water, helping to dry a wet area.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: SUNFLOWERS are tall, handsome, herbaceous annuals. Can grow 2 to 15 ft. (.6-4.5 m) or taller, depending on variety & conditions. Upright habit. Rough, unbranched stalks. Large, hairy, spade- or heart-shaped leaves. Showy flowers have yellow rays & reddish-purple/brown centers, can grow over 12 in. (30 cm) wide & mature into large seed-heads. Flowers track daily course of the sun: heliotropic. Rapid growing. Strong tap root & wide spread surface feeders. Reportedly allelopathic; chemicals in roots & leaves retard most other plants & are said to suppress nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

ORIGIN: Western North America from Mexico to Canada.

CLIMATE: Temperate zones through subtropics. Although grown principally in hot regions of the temperate zones, SUNFLOWERS are widely adapted. Plants do require long, sunny days, & a hot, dry spell in order to mature their seed-heads. Tolerates heat, drought & light frost. Intolerant of wet tropical conditions & heavy frost. GROWN IN HAWATLL A few varieties are outstanding here in hotter, drier mid- & upper elevations, occasionally lowlands.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Heavy feeder. Prefers deep, slightly moist, rich, loose, well drained soil, pH 6.0 to 8.0 & full sun. Needs wind-protection. Benefits from a deeply dug bed, amended with compost or aged manure, granite dust, rock phosphate, etc. Sweetened where too acid. SUNFLOWERS are sensitive to a lack of boron.

TOLERATES: various soils, including fairly poor ones.

INTOLERANT OF: heavy-, waterlogged-, or strongly acid soil.

TRAINING: Tying to stakes can help prevent lodging in windier sites, although this is labor intensive. A few stalks can be carefully looped together for support. Some cultivars resist lodging.

ASSOCIATES: SUNFLOWERS are said to improve soil when moderately intercropped. They can provide shade & wind protection when planted with other plants, such as Lettuce & Cucumbers. Can be grown among Corn with beneficial effects, as well as helping prevent Jodging. Tal! cultivars can be suitable as a living-trellis for Beans, although both will compete for space & light. (

SEE ALSO: allelopatby at the end of the DESCRIPTION).

ADVERSARIES: Wet cool condition can promote gray mold. Stem-rot, downy mildew & rust can also be problematic. Rodents & birds relish the seed-heads. Leaves are chewed by insects. Dislikes growing near Grasses.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent. Maturing seed-heads may be protected with bird-netting or floating row-cover

WEEDY: Has naturalized on the continent, appearing wild along road-edges, open bottomiands, grass- & pasture-lands, & barren areas. Can be a Noxious environmental weed. Very sparingly naturalized in Hawaiʻi. SUNFLOWERS have been found in the saddle between Mauna Kea & Mauna Loa. Wild forms have smaller flowers. SEX: Disk flowers are hermaphroditic, while ray flowers are sterile.

POLLINATION: Insects, especially bees, & long tongued flies. Cultivars are sometimes self-compatible. They may hybridize with other compatible varieties.

SEED-SAVING: Suitable seeds are solidly filled out. Seed life span: a few years if dried & air-tight in a cool, dry spot.

PROPAGATION: By seeds. Sown directly 4 to % in. (1.25-2 cm) deep, in fine soil. Germination: one to two weeks at 75 to 85°F (24-29°C), otherwise up to three weeks. Planted early in the season while the days are lengthening. Produces stronger plants when thinned well. Can be grafted onto the perennial JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE.

INOCULATION: SUNFLOWERS are reported to benefit from Azotobacter.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, Mesic (with dry weather during seed-maturing)

THREE MAJOR TYPES & THEIR CULTIVARS: Giant Types: 6 to 15 ft. (1.8-4.5 m) tall. Late harvest. Produces heads over 12 in. (30 cm) wide, with large seeds. Seeds are fairly low in oil, & so afe often utilized as snack food, rather than oil source, especially the cultivar ‘Mammoth Russian.’ These plants require more moisture than the smaller cultivars. Semi-dwarf Types: 4! to 6 ft. (1.3-1.8 m) tall. Early harvest. Mid-sized heads & seeds, fairly rich in oil: ‘Progress,’ ‘Jupiter, ‘Pole Star,’ & 'Rostov' (reportedly tolerates rain & wind.) Dwarf Types: ! to 4% ft (.3-1.3 m) tall. Early harvest. Head 6 in. (15 cm) wide & small seeds, richest in oi}: ‘Sunrise,’ ‘Sunspot,' 'Advance.' Tolerates very dry conditions. These smaller seeded types, with some exceptions, are primarily grown as an oil, protein-meal, & sprouting-sceds, rather than as a snack food.

NOTE: Many other Helianthus species & hybrids exist.

ANOTHER NOTABLE SPECIES:

JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE

Vol II · scan p. 195 · book p. 17

JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE, Sunchoke, Sun Root, Sunflower Artichoke, Girasole, Girosol, Topinambour. Helianthus tuberosus. The name said to come from the Italian "Girasoli Articocco" ("Sunflower Artichoke"). Many various colored varieties, dwarfs & cultivars exist, including those with smoother, easier to clean tubers. Although "Sunchoke" was originally the label given to a cross of SUNFLOWER & JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE, a potential sugar plant, now it has replaced the name JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE in some areas.

— scan page 196 · book page 172 —

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed food. Tubers are moist, sweet & nutty. Eaten peeled either fresh raw (grated for mixed salads), or boiled, baked, fried, in soups, pureed, casseroles, pies, Artichoke spaghetti, pickied, or roasted for a Coffee-replacement, etc. Also tubers are a source of alcohol (industrial). High in minerals, vitamins & inulin (a diabetic-safe carbohydrate), low in fat & starch.

HARVESTING: tubers can be dug as needed.

STORING: tubers do not store well; last best when kept cool, humid, soaking briefly in water each day.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: tubers, leaves, flowers & upper stalks for livestock & poultry forage or fodder. BENEFICIAL

INSECT HOST.

COMPOST-MATERIAL: tops.

LANDSCAPING: temporary hedge or screen, ornamental, back borders, etc.

SOIL RECLAMATION: roots break up dense soil.

WINDBREAK: garden windscreen.

DESCRIPTION: Tall, attractive, herbaceous perennial. Usually grown as an annual. Can grow 5 to 12 ft. (1.5-3.6 m) tall. Thick rough leaves are narrower than SUNFLOWER. Yellow flowers 3 in. (7.5 cm) wide. Vigorous & productive.

ORIGIN: North America.

PREFERS: rich, light, moist soii, pH 6.0 to 7.0 & full sun or light-shade. Easy to grow. Needs ample space. Responds to amending with manure or compost. Benefits from thick mulch.

TOLERATES: various climates & soils, including poor ones, drought & heat.

INTOLERANT OF: low wetlands.

ASSOCIATES: good companion to Corn, as well as sheltering plant for lowgrowing species. Probably alietopathic to some plants.

ADVERSARIES: basically pest & disease free.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize. Can be a Noxious environmental weed, or casual. To keep in check, all tubers are removed at harvest.

PROPAGATED BY: tubers or root-sections. Slightly dried tuber pieces, each with an "eye," are sown 3 to 4 in. (7.5-10 cm) deep.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesicDry

☠️ SUNN HEMP

Vol II · scan p. 196 · book p. 172

SUNN HEMP Sun Hemp, Sann Hemp, Sand Hemp, “Tropic Sun." Crotalaria juncea & C. ochroleuca. Fabaceae (Bean) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Although SUNN HEMP'S primary importance is as a green manure & fiber plant, the leaves & flowers are said to be edible. While plant is believed to be non-poisonous, the seeds are questionable.

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1, Seeds may contain poisons. 2. Ventilation is required when storing seed where people or animals may reside. 3. Many Crotalaria species are poisonous to eat.

APPLICATIONS:

ALLEY-CROPPING: temporary. Accepts coppicing & can be cut as low as 12 in. G0 cm).

ANIMAL FEED: leaves & dry stalks as fodder for livestock, but only with CAUTION; potentially harmful in large amounts, with seeds probably being poisonous. COVER CROP. EROSION CONTROL.

FIBER: stronger & longer lasting than Jute, but not as strong as Hemp: bast fiber for sacks, rope, cordage, twine, fish-nets, camo-nets, rope sandals, shoe-soles, paper, etc.

HARVESTING FIBER: plant is pulled from the ground or cut at three to three & a half months. Bundled, retted, beaten & washed.

GREEN MANURE: as an ancient & important green manure. For quickest decomposition, plants are turned in after two to two & a half months or just as flowering begins.

INSECTICIDAL PROPERTIES: a substance in the roots is thought to deter soil-borne nematodes. MULCH

MATERIAL.

ROTATIONAL PLANTING: for Com & other heavy feeders. SONL-CONSERVATION. WEED-SUPPRESSION.

WOOD: farm tools, pulp, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Deciduous, nitrogen-fixing, annual shrub. Can grow 10 ft. (3 m) tall. Generally single-stemmed & upright. Medium density canopy. Attractive yellow-gold flowers mature into smal] rattling pods (indehiscent). Long vigorous tap-root & laterals. Fast growing.

ORIGIN: African tropics.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Needs warmth. Seed-set is better during short days.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: frequently.

PREFERS: well drained, light or medium soil, alkaline or acid pH, & full sun. Can grow vigorously even on hard, clayey, wet soil, but light, well drained, loamy soil makes for finer fiber.

TOLERATES: monsoonal climates, some drought, as well as frost, & most soils, including those somewhat salty or alkaline.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage & strongly acid soil.

ASSOCIATES: interplanted, for cut mulch, with Citrus, Banana, Coconut, etc.

SEE ALSO: ROTATIONAL PLANTING, prior.

ADVERSARIES: anthracnose, wilt, borers & root nematodes are possible. Resistant to Witchweed, Stiga species.

WEEDY: both species can escape & naturalize. Many weedy Crotaria species exist. Can become tough hard to manage if stands are allowed to grow tall. SEX: crossing is required.

POLLINATION: by a large bee species.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds. Seeds are broadcast & covered '4 in. (1.25 cm) deep. Seeds can be mixed with rough sand before sowing. Thick sowings can delay woodiness, & produce better green manure & fiber. Thinner sowings for seed-production. Germination: quick, usually all at the same time. Seedlings require gentle handling.

INOCULATION: Cowpea rhizobia usually improves nitrogen-fixation, but is not always needed,

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, MesicDry

SEE ALSO: CROTALARIA. Crotalaria species. In

🌳⚠️ TAHITIAN CHESTNUT -

Vol II · scan p. 196 · book p. 172

TAHITIAN CHESTNUT - Polynesian Chestnut, Kayam, Rata, IVI, IH1, MAPE. Inocarpus edulis, syn. I. fagifer. Fabaceae (Bean) Family.

EDIBILITIES: An important food on some islands of the South Pacific; minor elsewhere. Flattish, thick-walled, egg-shaped seedpod contains one seed 3 in. (75 mm) long. Fruit is difficult to open until it is cooked. Soft, tasty kernel is edible raw, or better yet, boiled, roasted, or baked in the pod. Pods roasted in a fire make nut-extraction easier, after which nuts can be boiled. Cooked nuts can be mashed for greater digestibility. Grated nuts can be cooked in breads, flat-cakes, puddings, etc.

MATURITY: seed-pods turn yellow-orange at maturity.

HARVESTING: fallen pods.

STORING: shelf-life only a few weeks.

SHIPPING: fresh fruits ship well.

— scan page 197 · book page 173 —

⚠️ CAUTION: Even though nuts are (tasty, they may not be very digestible & moderation is suggested.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: foliage for livestock & pods for pigs.

FIREWOOD: good. MEDICINAL QUALITIES. SHADE

TREE.

WOOD: fair, except for it's tendency to buttress.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: Large, evergreen, nitrogen-fixing tree. Can grow 50 ft. (15 m) or taller. Spreading crown. Fluted, buttressed trunk with age. Dense canopy. Clusters of small, white flowers. Slow growing.

ORIGIN: probably Malaysia, then spreading to South Pacific.

CLIMATE: widely adapted in the hot, humid tropics.

GROWN IN HAWATLT: in the lowlands.

PREFERS: moist, somewhat heavy soil, slightly acid pH & full sun.

TOLERATES: various soils, including some salinity.

ADVERSARIES: unknown.

WEEDY: sometimes found naturalized along streams & coastal regions throughout Polynesia.

DISADVANTAGES: large size, sparse production, & weediness. SEX: hermaphroditic.

SEED-SAVING: short seed life span.

PROPAGATED BY: fresh seeds.

INOCULATION: mycomrhizal association is suspected; TAHITIAN CHESTNUT'S slow establishment may signify its need for a particular bacteria.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

TAHITIAN TARO

TAHITIAN TARO, Xanthosonta brasiliense. SEE: BELEMBE.

☠️ TAMARIND / WĪ / WĪʻAWAʻAWA

Vol II · scan p. 197 · book p. 173

TAMARIND / WI / wrAWA‘AWA Wil, Sampalok, Indian Date. Tamarindus indica, syn. T. indicus, syn. T. officinalis, syn. T. occidentalis. Fabaceae (Bean) Family, Caesalpiniaceae (Senna) Subfamily. Superior & sweeter varieties exist.

EDIBILITIES: Mature, velvety, brittle shelled, bulging pods 2 to 8 in. (5-20 cm) long & 1 in. (2.5 cm) wide. Pods contain a thick layer of tasty, sticky, sweet-sour pulp. Pulp is eaten fresh raw, or in curries, chutneys, zesty sauces, jams, jellies, preserves & sweetmeats. Also made into flavorful syrup for many applications; ice-creams & sherbets, beverages, beer, wine, etc. Pulp high in carbohydrates (mostly sugar), tartaric-, citric- & acetic- acid, several B vitamins, vitamin C, pectin, minerals (including calcium, phosphorus & iron), & some protein & fiber. Young, tart, tender pods in soups, stews & other dishes. Young leaves & flowers are pleasantly sour & edible fresh raw in mixed salads, or in soups, stews, curries, or with bland vegetabies, etc. Seedlings under 12 in. (30 cm) tall, can be cooked as a vegetable, or in curries. Seeds can serve as a starch- & protein-rich scarcity food. They are edible boiled, fried, roasted, or ground as Coffee-replacement, flour, & a source of a gum or pectin, or a palatable oil. The outer papery seed-shell can be removed by soaking roasted or boiled seeds. Bark as a masticatory, but high in tannin.

☠️ TOXICITY: Pulp is laxative, cooling, may be purgative, & due to tartaric acid, it can disturb digestion if eaten in excess.

BEARING: Graftlings or cuttings can begin fruiting in three to four years. Seedlings can fruit in four to twelve years, depending upon location. Trees may remain highly productive over fifty years.

MATURITY: TAMARIND pods mature in summer. Skin of pods turns brittle as it ripens. Pods may be left to dehydrate on tree for up to half a year, in dry conditions.

HARVESTING: For immediate applications, pods can be pulled, leaving its long fiber on the tree. Mature fruit usually fall sooner or later. Branches can be shaken to free the ripe pods, but they should not be beaten with poles since this tends to damage new flowers & foliage. For transport, entire stalk can be clipped off, handling brittle pods with care.

STORING: Pods last weil refrigerated. Pulp can be preserved in sugar or salt, or sun dried for storage or transport. Steaming the blocks of pulp before solar-drying lengthens storage period. Processing techniques vary with country.

SHIPPING: Dried or preserved pulp transports well.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Foliage, shoots, pods & ground seeds for livestock. But, SEE: DISADVANTAGES, following.

BARRIER TREE: TAMARIND can become a large tree, if the soil is adequate.

BEE FORAGE: Slightly tart honey.

CLEANER: Very ripe pulp, when mixed with salt water, can clean copper, brass & silver.

CONTAINER-GROWING: Forty gallon pots or larger. TAMARIND has attractive bark for bonsai.

EROSION CONTROL: Deep roots hold soil.

FIBER: A poor quality fiber can be obtained from the bark of youthful trees.

FIREWOOD & CHARCOAL: Intensely hot firewood & charcoal. Trees are rarely cut down, but are topped for fuel. Although TAMARIND tolerates coppicing, it recovers only slowly.

LANDSCAPING: Omamental. Leaf-litter can be a nuisance. Tree can be pruned smaller.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

MULCH: Leaves. OIL: Semi-drying oil for illumination & vamish. —

ROADSIDE & PARKING-LOT TREE: Good candidate.

SACRED: TAMARIND is sacred to many.

SHADE TREE: Excellent coverage.

SOIL-CONSERVATION & -STABILIZATION: Deep roots hold soil, fi

Vol II · scan p. 197 · book p. 173

SOIL-CONSERVATION & -STABILIZATION: Deep roots hold soil, fix nitrogen & retrieve deep nutrients,

STARCH: Seeds can be a source of sizing for paper, cloth, etc.

WINDBREAK: Large, older trees provide excellent wind protection.

WOOD: Dense, durable, strong, flexible heart-wood; polishes well, resists insects, but not large & not easily worked. Valued for furniture, wall paneling, tool handles, mortars & pestles, etc.

DESCRIPTION: TAMARIND is an attractive, evergreen, nitrogen-fixing tree. Can grow 80 to 100 ft. (24-30 m) in deep soil in its homeland, but in Hawaiʻi it does not tend to grow so tall. Stout trunk, which often twists with age. Typically single trunked. Dense, half-domed crown. Graceful, flexible branches droop nearly to the ground. Feathery, bright-green foliage close up at night. Tree can briefly lose its leaves in extremely dry, hot weather. Small, hanging racemes of yellow, red- or orange-streaked flowers mature into indehiscent pods. Fairly slow growing where dry, but fast where soil is moist & deep. Tap-root. LIFE

— scan page 198 · book page 174 —

SPAN: two hundred years or longer.

ORIGIN: Africa.

CLIMATE: Prefers hot, lowland & coastal tropics. Also grows in dry land forests, semi-arid, hot savanna conditions, subtropics, monsoonal climates & even temperate maritime locales. Requires dry conditions during fruiting. Tolerates drought, salt spray & high winds.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often.

PREFERS: Deep, moist, fertile, well drained, light or medium soil, pH 5.5 to 7.0 & full sun.

TOLERATES: a variety of soils, including poor, alkaline, salty, sandy, or shallow soil.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding.

ASSOCIATES: Few species can grow beneath TAMARIND'S dense shade. In its homeland, it is found near Baobab.

ADVERSARIES: Insect pests are a common problem in other countries. [Here?] Fire sensitive.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Small-scale; most fruit are harvested from neglected or wild trees.

WEEDY: Escapes & naturalizes in favorable spots. Can be a serious environmental pest, but reportedly seldom weedy here.

DISADVANTAGES: It is said that TAMARIND leaves have a “corrosive effect" when they've dropped onto damp fabric, fur, or hair, is therefore not a good tree underwhich to sleep or shelter a horse. SEX: Hermaphroditic. A pollinator is sometimes necessary. Little is known of its self-incompatibility.

POLLINATION: Probably insect pollinated.

SEED-SAVING: Seed can be kept a year or more under dry conditions.

PROPAGATION: By seeds, off-shoots, cuttings, air-layering, budding & grafting. Seeds can be sown directly or transplanted. Seeds may need scarification & soaking. Germination: about one week.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow, Wet(seasonal)/MesicDry

Ⓦ TANNIER

Vol II · scan p. 198 · book p. 174

TANNIER Yautia, Tannia, Indian Kale, Cocoyam, Malanga blanca. Xanthosoma sagittifolium, X. atrovirens, & X. violaceum. Araceae (Arum) Family. Many varieties exist, varying in yield, cooking time, flavor, weediness, etc

EDIBILITIES: Important & ancient food. Tubers are peeled & cooked by boiling, roasting, baking, or fried as chips, fritters, pureed for soups, stews, pancakes, or grated for starch extraction. High in carbohydrates, fair in vitamins & minerals, with some protein. Tubers are drier & more nutritious than regular Potatoes. Starch grains are much larger than Taro & not as easy to digest. Young, tender, un-furled leaf (preferred), young leaves, stems & petioles peeled are acrid when undercooked, but excellent after prolonged cooking, & in soups & stews.

NOTE: irritating acids can be neutralized with the juice of a tart Citrus species.

MATURITY: eight to eleven months.

HARVESTING: soil is dug from around plant base & mature, side corms can be removed, after which the soil is filled in again, allowing plant to continue producing. Side corms are harvested; large main one too acrid. Wild forms are of little value.

STORING: can last a few weeks in dry, airy conditions, or a bit longer in a cool, humid spot

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: a rare application. CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: omamental.

NURSE PLANT: lateral shade for young Cacao plants, etc. 43+

DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous perennial, similar to Taro. Can grow 6 ft. (1.8 m) tall. Large arrow-shaped leaves. Light green flower spathe can appear, but the plant rarely flowers or sets seed.

ORIGIN: West Indies & American tropics.

CLIMATE: warn, humid tropics.

PREFERS: deep, moist, fertile, humusy soil, acid pH & full sun or filtered shade. Responds to aged manure or compost. Benefits from mulch. Like Taro, TANNIER requires a lengthy growing period & ample water, but is easier to grow than Taro.

ASSOCIATES: inter-cropped with Lemon, or other tall crops that give partial shade. Short-term, rainy-season crop.

TOLERATES: heavy clay soil & light shade.

INTOLERANT OF: dry soil.

ADVERSARIES: basically free.

WEEDY: all these species can escape & naturalize. Wild forms are Noxious, environmental sleeper weeds in wet areas. SEX: monoecious.

POLLINATION: flies.

PROPAGATED BY: corm tops & pieces & cormels. Pieces with at least one eye.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMid, Wet

NOTE: Other Xanthosoma species with edible tubers exist.

SEE ALSO: ʻAPE, COMMON. Xanthosoma species.

☆ TEA / KI / WAIKi Cha, Tsia, Chia. Cr, Camellia sinensis, syn. Thea sinensis, syn. C. thea. a oe Theaceae (Tea) Family. 1000+ known varieties, hybrids & cultivars exist. a E Mf ie Two basic types: ye: ‘a oy ‘Assam,’ Camellia sinensis var. assamica. Generally taller & better suited to the tropics. nan ci Ye 'Chinese Teas,’ C. sinensis var. bohea. Smaller & more adapted to temperate zones. a ae

EDIBILITIES: Ancient, esteemed beverage & medicine. Tender leaves require knowledgeable & careful Sg curing. Cured leaves are brewed as tea, preserved, fermented to a beverage, or for powdered 'green' TEA in candies, etc. Fruits are the source of a non-drying, TEA-seed oil. Flowers in tempera.

— scan page 199 · book page 175 —

BEARING: begins to yield in two years, quickening in three, then at four or five the plant can be harvested every couple of weeks for about six years. After that it is cut back to stimulate new shoots.

HARVESTING: young, tender ieaves are nipped off or sheared. Leaves are steam-heated immediately, then cooled & rolled for GREEN TEA, or wilted (withered), rolled, oxidized (enzymatic processing), & dried for OOLONG or BLACK TEAS. Great attention to detail & cleanliness in growing & processing is needed to produce a quality leaf. Producing TEA is best leamed by apprenticeship, not solely from the literature. TEA

BREWING: during the first couple of minutes of brewing, the caffeine infuses, a minute or so later the color, finally at four or five minutes the flavor arrives, & then after six minutes the astringent tannin-like compounds start to be released.

☠️ TOXICITY: TEA is high in caffeine. Over-steeped TEA contains dangerous tannin-like compounds.

APPLICATIONS: COMPOST- or

MULCH MATERIAL: nitrogen-rich grounds. CONTAINER-GROWING.

LANDSCAPING: ornamental, low, dense screen or hedge, borders, lawns, & foundation planting.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: powerful antioxidant effects, especially with the semi-oxidized GREEN & OOLONG TEAS.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive evergreen tree or shrub. Can grow 15 to 50 ft. (4.5-15 m) tall, though plants are usually kept pruned under ft. 1.5m). Upright, rounded, bushy habit. Small, leathery, Camellia-like foliage. White or pink-tinged, aromatic, autumn flowers mature into hard, dehiscent fruit-capsules. Growth-speed depends on variety & presence of mycorrhiza. Tap- & Sateralroots with mycorrhizal association.

LIFE SPAN: one hundred years is possible, but thirty more likely.

ORIGIN: China, India.

CLIMATE: will grow in the warm temperate zones, but thrives in humid, warm, tropical highlands, as well as subtropics. Thrives with sunny mornings, afternoon clouds & cool, misty nights.)

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: more frequently lately & there is a thriving TEA society here.

PREFERS: deep, moist, friable, wel] drained, humusy soil, acid pH (4.5 to 6.0) & full sun. Benefits from regular rain, cool roots, & wind shelter. Grows in heavy or very light soil when moist & well drained. Will grow where Bracken, Dissotis species, & Albizia species thrive. TEA plants appreciate added compost or well-aged manure. Mulch helps keep soil cool, moist & weed-free. Planting too deep should be avoided. Close spacing seems to produce denser, more uniform plants. Cultivation can damage surface-roots.

TOLERATES: some frost (certain varieties) & some shade. There are varieties that resist drought.

INTOLERANT OF: excess rainfall, poorly drained-, salty-, neutral- or alkaline soil, & deficiencies in nutrients such as copper, sulfur &/or aluminum.

PRUNING: trimming stimulates a new flush of tender leaves. Readily accepts pruning best during dormancy.

ASSOCIATES: a nitrogen-fixing cover crop can provide fertilizer & reduce weeds.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, though many fungal, viral & other diseases & pests including nematodes are possible, especially when mono-cropped. Red spider mites can be a problem. Finding disease resistant cultivars are very important.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize, but not considered invasive. SEX: hermaphroditic & mostly self-incompatible.

POLLINATION: insects.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are variable. Seed are generally gathered from ‘select’ vegetatively propagated trees that are allowed to flower. Seed life span is very short; fresh seed is planted within three days or stored properly until a wet season.

PROPAGATED BY: grafting, budding, layering, cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: nodal, semi-ripe wood or stem-tips. Seeds are soaked in warm water for one to two days, then sown in. (2.5 cm) deep, with hilium down. Seeds may benefit from one to two months of cold, moist stratification. Germination: one to three months at 70 to 75°C (21-24°C).

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, WetMesic

☠️ THYME

Vol II · scan p. 199 · book p. 175

THYME Thymus & Lippia species. Sixty plus species exist. Lamiaceae & Verbenaceae (Mint & Verbena) Families. Numerous types, varieties, crosses & cultivars exist, including upright & prostrate forms.

PARTIAL LISTING: COMMON THYME, Garden Thyme, English Thyme, German Thyme, Winter Thyme, Kaima. Thymus vulgaris.

EDIBILITIES: Leaves & flowering tops have a warm, tangy, strongly pungent, Clove-like flavor. Added sparingly, fresh or dried, to salads & dressings, soups, stews & chowders, vegetables, casseroles, ragout, guacamole, pastas, sauces, cheeses, stuffings, gravies, Bean-, egg-, cheese-, seafood-, poultry-~ & meat dishes, paté, French- & Mediterranean cuisine, bakery items, vinegars, marinades, pickles, vegetable juices, garnish, essential oil, or as a tea. Accepts long cooking & blends flavors well. Essential oi! from leaves.

MATURITY: leaves are gathered as flowers start opening.

HARVESTING: cut to within 2 in. (5 cm) of ground. Drying; hung or laid on trays in a warm, dark, well-ventilated spot.

STORING: maintains flavor well if thoroughly dried, stripped from stems & stored airtight.

— scan page 200 · book page 176 —

☠️ TOXICITIES: 1. Although large amounts should be avoided during pregnancy since THYME is a uterine stimulant, regular cooking quantities are O.K. 2. Excessive consumption can be poisonous & over-stimulate the thyroid glands. 3. Essential oil can Iritate Mucous membranes unless diluted.

APPLICATIONS: BEE FORAGE.

CONTAINER-GROWING: terra cotta important to allow roots to breathe.

ESSENTIAL OI: Steam-distilled from leaves as a medicinal & as a flavoring for medicines, tooth-pastes, & perfumery.

FAIRY HOST: a bed of THYME for the Fairies. INSECT-REPELLENT.

LANDSCAPING: ground-cover for rocky hillsides, borders, edging, mounding, or as small hedge if kept trimmed.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: the THYMES are powerful antioxidants.

DESCRIPTION: Small, attractive, woody, evergreen perennial. Branches can reach 6 to 12 in. (15-30 cm) tall, depending on variety. Shrub-like or occasionally prostrate habit. Downy, deep-green, aromatic leaves. Minute white or violet flowers. Vigorous.

ORIGIN: southern Europe, western Mediterranean.

CLIMATE: warm, mild conditions. The hotter the climate, the stronger the flavor.

PREFERS: warm, rich or average, moist, well drained, light, rocky or sandy soil, alkaline pH & full sun or very light shade. Needs to be kept well weeded. A stone mulch is ideal.

TOLERATES: poor, dry soil.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize.

PROPAGATED BY: cuttings, crown division, ground-layering, or seeds. Cuttings: rooted in sand, under glass. Seeds sown early spring. Drilled directly, 4 in. (6 mm) deep, or started in a partially shaded, moist, warm spot, then transplanted. Germination: twenty-one to thirty days or longer. Seeds life span: several years or longer. Renewed every few years to prevent woodiness.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, MesicDry

🌿Ⓦ TOMATILLO

Vol II · scan p. 201 · book p. 177

TOMATILLO Husk Tomato, Maya Husk Tomato, Mexican Husk Tomato, Mexican Ground Cherry, Tomate Verde. Physalis ixocarpa, syn. P. aequata. Solanaceae (Nightshade) Family. Various strains & cultivars exist.

EDIBILITIES: Rounded, green, yellow to reddish fruit 2 to 3 in. (5-7.5 cm) wide, surrounded by a papery calyx. Pulp varies from sweet when ripe, tart when green, or can be bland. Eaten fresh raw (ripe), in mixed salads or guacamole, roasted for satsa (especially salsa verde), or as a cooked sauce (harvested young), with meat, in soups, baked, stewed, fried, in Chili-reilenos, tacos, etc., culties, pies, jams, marmalades, or canned.

MATURITY: fifty-five to seventy-five days.

HARVESTING: fallen fruit are gathered daily or picked. Can be prolific. Fruit are dried in their husks a few weeks.

STORING: lasts months in their husks if kept dry & cool, one layer deep. Or, whole plant can be hung upside-down in a dry spot. Fruit, husks removed, can be frozen.

APPLICATIONS: MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous & part-woody annual. Can grow 5 ft. (1.5 m) tall, but often sprawls lower & wider. Yellow, browncentered flowers.

ORIGIN: Mexico & South America.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics.

GROWN IN HAWATLT: occasionally.

PREFERS: rich, loamy, moist, average soil, slightly acid pH & full sun. Easy to grow where Tomatoes prosper.

TOLERATES: various soils & mild drought.

INTOLERANT OF: excess water & shade.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, except for possible damage by cutworms, caterpillars, etc.

WEEDY: can escape & naturalize; quarantine weed, SEX: hermaphroditic & selfincompatible. Requires crossing.

SEED-SAVING: seed life span can be three years.

PROPAGATED BY: seeds, cuttings & divisions. Seeds need light to sprout. Sown no deeper than ¥ in. (1.25 cm). Germination: two to four weeks at 70 to 75°F (21- 24°C). LowMidHigh, Mesic

NOTE: WILD TOMATILLO, Purple Groundcherry, Physalis philadelphica; edible fruits, but highly weedy nature.

SEE ALSO: GROUND CHERRY. Physalis pubescens.

🌿☠️Ⓦ TOMATO / ʻŌHIʻA LOMI

Vol II · scan p. 201 · book p. 177

TOMATO / ʻŌHIʻA LOMI Common Tomato, Tomatl, Pommes d'amours, Love Apple, Camatis, Kamatis, ~Ohi*a haole. Lycopersicon esculentum, syn. L. lycopersicum, syn. L. esculentum v. commune, syn. Solanum lycopersicum. Solanaceae (Nightshade) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Popular, esteemed food nearly world-wide. Red to yellow, small to large, juicy ripe fruit are eaten fresh raw, or in salads, on sandwiches, as well as cooked or processed in many ways & in numerous dishes, including soups & stews, stuffed, broiled, ketchup, paste, sauce, spaghetti, puree, conserves, cakes, juice, powder, or dried, etc. Ripe fruit are high in carotene, lycopene (red fruit), vitamins C, A & B, potassium, important minerals, & contain some fiber. Highest vitamin C content occurs in fruit exposed to the most sun. Low in sodium, protein & fat. Varieties differ in the level of nutrients. Immature green fruit are eaten stewed, roasted, fried, in pies, marmalades, relishes, or pickled. Dried fruit is delicious when marinated in Olive-oil & utilized in many gourmet recipes, or can be made into a flour for thickening & flavoring many foods, breads, desserts, etc. Seeds are a source of a semi-drying oil for salad oil, margarine, as well as soap manufacturing.

☠️ TOXICITY: Although foliage tends to be poisonous very young leaves are eaten as a condiment in Southeast Asia.

NOTE: consumption of TOMATOES, as well as Potatoes, Eggplant, Peppers & other member of the Solanaceae Family might be a causal factor in one kind of arthritis.

BEARING: Forty-eight to ninety days, depending on cultivar & conditions. Earliest harvests when grown in light soil.

MATURITY: TOMATOES can be harvested & cooked green, but better results are had by harvesting as the first yellow or pink color begins to appear. The very best fruits are harvested three-fourths to full-ripe. Can be ripened indoors on a well lit window-sill, but not in direct sunlight. Will ripen faster in a brown bag with a piece of ripe fruit in with it. Harvest period of "old fashioned" indeterminate varieties can last two to three months, while "modern" determinate varieties harvested over two to three weeks.

HARVESTING: Fruit are simply plucked from the vine, being careful not to damage the plant's tender stems. Typically harvested twice or thrice weekly.

STORING: Stored at room temperature, out of direct sun. Green, mature TOMATOES, individually wrapped in paper & layered in boxes, ripen slowly in a warm place, & last very well at 50 to 60°F (10-15.5°C). TOMATOES are excellent canned, juiced, or dried. Certain cultivars are better than others for these applications.

SHIPPING: For Jocal markets, TOMATOES are harvested as they start to color. For long distance, fruit can be picked at full maturity, but still green (difficult; usually resulting in many immature green fruit). Packed in stiff, airy containers.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: Seedcake residue for livestock.

COMPOST-MATERIAL: Spent, disease-free vines can be put into the compost pile. Note: seeds will not be killed even by the hottest of composts, thus they are often boiled first.

— scan page 202 · book page 178 —

CONTAINER-GROWING: Certain cultivars as ‘Tiny Tim,’ 'Pixie hybrid,’ & ‘Healani,’ suitable for hanging baskets, tubs, or window boxes. Need support & daily watering when fruit have begun to set. TOMATOES successful in hydroponics.

FERTILIZER: Seedcake residue.

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Popular herbaceous perennial. Can grow 3 to 15 ft. (.9-4.5 m) tall, depending on variety. Sprawling & vine-like, or upright, bush habit. Clammy odorous foliage. Yellow flowers. Day-length neutral. There are two types of

TOMATO: determinate & indeterminate. Determinate varieties are most suitable for commercial production as they are smaller, faster, more productive, & do not need their vines supported. Determinate vines stop growing when they reach their maximum size, then they ripen their fruit al] at once before dying back. Indeterminate varieties better suited for home gardening since they continue to grow & produce for a longer time. Indeterminate vines are larger & do better if supported. Fast growing. Sturdy tap-root, with fibrous lateral & adventitious roots. TOMATOES have somewhat allelopathic root exudates.

LIFE SPAN: under one year.

ORIGIN: American tropics, but exact origins are still uncertain.

CLIMATE: Tropics, subtropics & temperate zones. TOMATOES prefer long, hot days in the range 68 to 80°F (20-27°C) range, & cool nights between 50 to 70°F (10-21°C). Day & night temperatures, as well as, diurnal variations affect fruiting. A night temperature reaching 64°F (18°C) is reportedly cnitical for fruit-set. CHERRY-, PLUM- & ROMA TOMATO set fruit better in lowland tropics than the larger types. TOMATOES in very hot tropical regions can be rather flavorless & somewhat coarse, or may be damaged by sun. TOMATOES may be a good green-house candidate. Many heat-, humidity- & drought-tolerant varieties exist. TOMATOES do best with light, regular rainfall. Cloudy weather & heavy rains reduce yields & promote diseases. Intolerant of dry conditions & drought (in general) & frost.

GROWN IN HAWALIE: TOMATOES are often grown here. Adapted, disease resistant cultivars have been developed, including Hawaiian hybrids. There are a multitude of varieties bred for nearly every location. Although TOMATOES will grow at all elevations & seasons in Hawaiʻi where there is sufficient but not excessive moisture, they are severely limited by fruit fly infestation. “Windshield survey".

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Heavy feeder. Prefer moist, light, fertile, well drained, humusy soil, slightly acid or neutral pH (5.5 to full sun. Responds to deep, thorough amending with compost, well-aged manure, calcium, greensand, rock phosphate, rock-dust, etc. Lime or dolomite can be added to raise soil pH. Vigorous growth should be encouraged throughout the lifecycle by feeding regularly. Be aware, though, that excess nitrogen can stimulate foliage in preference to fruiting, cause blossomend rot, as well as puffy fruit. TOMATOES require good air-circulation. Needs ample phosphorus, but little or no potassium. Ratio NPK said to be 2-4-1. Mulching retains soil moisture, provides nutrients & suppresses weeds.

TOLERATES: various soils.

INTOLERANT OF: flooding & poor-drainage.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Vines of indeterminate varieties thrive when trained to climb stakes, wooden frames, wire cages, or other trellis 4 to 5 ft. (1.2-1.5 m) tall. Stems can be tied with strips of soft material, raffia, etc. The strip is first tied tightly firmly to the stake & then loosely around the stem. Side-shoots can be pinched to encourage one or two main shoots, resulting in larger fruit being held higher above soil-level. This also allows better air-flow & greater exposure to sun-light. Thereafter, pruning or topping only reduces fruit production.

ASSOCIATES: Polyculturing with other crops (of the same or a smaller size) can reduce disease & insect problems.

ADVERSARIES: TOMATOES are subject to many diseases & pests, especially fruit flies, white-flies, leaf miners, as well as vanous bacterial & viral infections. Problems depend on season, weather, soil, location, cultural practices & degree of resistance or susceptibility. Soggy, poorly drained soil, or inadequate air movement promotes fungal leaf-blight, stunting, bacterial wilt, fruitrot & other diseases. Letters after cultivar names indicate its resistance: N = Nematodes, T= Tobacco mosaic virus, V = Verticillium wilt, F1 & F2 = Fusarium wilt races 1 & 2. Unwashed Tobacco smokers’ hands readily spread the Tobacco mosaic virus. TOMATOES are susceptible to root-knot nematode. Fruits in contact with bare soil often rot. It is best to plant TOMATOES only where other Solanaceae have not grown, including Potato, Eggplant, Peppers, etc., & Okra. Said to repel & be repelled by Brassica species. Dislikes Fennel, Com, Potatoes & Apricot. TOMATO vines are tender, easily damaged, & readily become diseased if handled roughly, especially when wet.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Healthier soil creates more resistant plants. Keys to successful organic production are: suitable variety, correct timing, appropriate location, diversity, disease-free propaguls, crop-rotation & good cultural technique. Fruit fly infestation may be prevented by netting or bagging (cloth or paper bags) individual fruit or clusters, by floating row-cover, or by growing in screen- or green houses. Leaf-eating caterpillars can be hand picked. Other pests may be deterred with a hot Pepper spray to which a drop of soap is added. Leaf miner can be controlled by removing affected leaves, & with floating row-cover. Preferably, TOMATOES are watered early in the day & deeply, keeping stems & foliage as dry as possible by watering only at soil-level. For a more flood-tolerant plant, TOMATO can be grafted onto Eggplant & Wild Eggplant, Solanum torvom.

WEEDY: Can escape & naturalize. Can be an serious environmental weed. Small, feral TOMATOES are occasionally found in ditches & other disturbed ground. Wild Tomatoes are edible, washed, but careful with unintentional seed dispersal.

REMARKS: In tropical areas, three crops per year is possible. SEX: Seif-fertile, hermaphroditic flowers.

POLLINATION: Self-pollinated & occasionally crossing by bumble- & other solitary-bees.

SEED-SAVING: Being generally non-crossing, isolation is usually not needed. Vigorous, productive, high quality, open-pollinated plants with healthy colored leaves are best selected. Their fruit are allowed to ripen beyond eating stage, but not to the point of decay. On a small scale, seeds may be squeezed from fruit, washed free of pulp & dried. On a larger scale, fruit can be mashed, water added, & fermented a few days 70°F (21°C). The good seed settles to bottom & the rest is poured off. Then the seeds are washed in fresh water & spread thinly on paper to shade dry. Seed life span: clean, dry seed can remain vital to three or four years if kept in an air-tight vessel, in a cool, dry spot (Jess in tropical conditions).

PROPAGATION: By seeds, cuttings & grafting. Seeds are sown no deeper than ¥% in. (1.25 mm), in carefully prepared nursery beds, or in flats of a well drained, fine, loose sterile medium. Germination: one to one & a half weeks, with an ideal temperature of 70°F (21°C). Bottom watering (one or two times daily) reduces damping-off. When first or second true leaves have formed on early varieties, they can be transplanted to 3 in. (7.5 em) pots & grown until 6 to 8 in. (15-20 cm) tall before final planting out. Late varieties can be transplanted directly from nursery to garden, with their stem buried at least two-thirds of its length. Direct seeding is successful in some locales if they are provided with twice daily watering until germination, & then protected from hard rain until becoming well established. Keeping seedlings cool promotes a healthy stockiness, then they should be gradually exposed to heat before planting out. Seedling tap-root is easily damaged. Transplant shock can be prevented by careful handling of the roots, by planting deeply, & by applying compost, manure tea, or starter-solution at transplanting. Yield is highest when constant, vigorous growth is maintained. Volunteers can be quite productive. Sown late winter or early spring when warm enough. Grafting rootstock possibilities include Tree Tomato, Potato, some Solanum species, Eggplant, Tobacco, & others.

— scan page 203 · book page 179 —

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMidHigh, WetMesicDry (depending on cultivar)

SOME NOTABLE CULTIVARS: Numerous varieties & cultivars exist, with large variations in size, shape, color, taste, applications, nutrient content, maturity date, growth habit & Resistant varieties suggested by the U of H include: ‘Healani,’ ‘Puunui,' ‘Anahu’ & ‘Kalohi.'

🌳 TONKA BEAN

Vol II · scan p. 203 · book p. 179

TONKA BEAN Dipteryx odorata, syn. Coumarouna odorata. Fabaceae (Bean) Family. Several types exist, including a dwarf.

EDIBILITIES: Pods reach 2 in. (5 cm) long & contain a single aromatic seed. Shelled & cured TONKA BEANS have a Vanilla- or new-mown-grass scent (coumarin). Utilized to flavor Tobacco, candies, ice-cream, liqueurs, perfumery & soaps.

MATURITY: can begin to bear in two years, in ideal conditions, otherwise seven to ten years. Tends to alternate bearing.

HARVESTING: fallen fruits are gathered.

PROCESSING: fruits are sun dried several days, then the seed is opened by cracking its seam with a hammer, after which the kernels are dried in the shade.

CURING: kernels are soaked a few days in 45 to 65% alcohol or strong -rum, then dried in the shade about a week.

APPLICATIONS: FRAGRANCE.

INSECT-REPELLENT: aromatic seeds are placed in drawers & closets as pest repellent & in sachets, potpourri, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: a source of coumarin. Sap from bark is a source of "Kino."

WOOD: very strong, hard, lasting timber.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: TONKA BEAN is an evergreen tree. Can grow 130 ft. (40 m) tall, although a dwarf exists. Trunk can reach 3 ft. (.9 wide. Clusters of small, white, or rose-pink flowers mature into indehiscent pods. Short, but vigorous taproot, deeper anchor roots & thick mat of surface feeders.

ORIGIN: South America.

CLIMATE: thrives in tropical, forested river-banks.

PREFERS: moist, fertile, well drained, humusy soil & partial shade.

TOLERATES: fairly poor soil.

INTOLERANT OF: poor drainage.

PRUNING: branching is encouraged by topping trees when 6 ft. (1.8 m) tall. Staked to train.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, except for fruit bats. [WEEDY?]

PROPAGATED BY: seeds (variable), cuttings, air-layering, budding & grafting. Seeds are sown directly beside a training stake, in containers, or in nurseries. Planted out at around two months, or when two true leaves have formed. Germination: three to fourteen days when de-shelled, or four to six weeks if whole fruit is planted. Difficult to transplant if too large. Can be shaded until 6 ft. (1.8 m) tall with nurse plants such as Pigeon Pea, Banana, Cassava, etc.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLow, WetMesic

NOTE: Dipteryx oppositifolia, D. rosea & D. puncata are other sources of coumarin.

zw) UDO Oudo, Tu-huo, Japanese Asparagus, Spikenard. Aralia cordata. Araliaceae (Ginseng) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed food. Young, tender stalks can be eaten in salads (peeled, sliced thinly, & soaked one hour in ice water before serving), Or soups (pre-cooked in several changes of salted water). Root can be eaten like Salsify.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous perennial. Can grow 6 ft. (1.8 m) tall. Clusters of white flowers mature into small purple fruits.

INTOLERANT OF: harsh winds. [(WEEDY7}

Ⓦ UNG-TSOI

UNG-TSOI Ung-choi, Ong-tsai, Ong choy, Kang Kong, Enstai, Engtsai, Swamp Cabbage, Water Convolvulus, Water Spinach, Creeping Swamp Morning Glory, Balangeg. Ipomea aquatica, syn.I. reptans, syn. Ipomoea reptans, syn. Convolvulus reptans. Convolvulaceae (Morning Glory) Family. Several varieties exist, including lush, paddy forms, or smailer-leafed, upland forms.

EDIBILITIES: Esteemed food. Young leaves & tender tips have a mild, bland flavor. Eaten fresh raw in salads (tips), or cooked as greens, sautéed, stir-fried, cooked with fish & other dishes, in soups & stews, or sambals. High in protein, vitamin A, iron & other minerals. Tender stems can be pickled. Roots are edible cooked.

MATURITY: one to two months, depending on culture. Quicker in paddies.

HARVESTING: new shoots are cut weekly. Regular harvesting encourages branching & tender new shoots. Alternately, at two months, the entire plant can be harvested.

APPLICATIONS:

ANIMAL FEED: vines for pigs, cattle & fish. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Attractive herbaceous vine. Grows under 1 ft. (30 cm) tall & over 12 ft. 3.6 m) long. Creeping, trailing, or floating aquatic habit. Succulent, soft or hollow stems. Purple or occasionally white flowers mature into seeded capsules. Day-length sensitive; flowers as the days shorten.

ORIGIN: tropical Australasia & Africa.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. GROWN IN

HAWAIʻI: often & well.

PREFERS: rich, humusy, constantly damp soil, or fertile ponds, acid pH & full sun. Responds to monthly feeding. Grows lushly in well fertilized, humusy soil. Needs to be kept well weeded, or the weeds repressed by flooding as in paddy culture. In paddies, slowly flowing water is important.

TOLERATES: flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: drought.

PRUNING & TRAINING: vines can be trellised.

ADVERSARIES: basically free, but mites, white-flies, & white rust are possible.

ORGANIC-GROWING: fewer problems occur with appropriate management. Replanted in new spot if pests & diseases have accumulated, or when current bed is exhausted. Either way, every two or three years the plants are routinely replanted.

WEEDY: escaped & sparsely naturalized. Wild forms, & sometimes cultivated escapees, are found in wet & swampy lowlands in lo*i, ponds, pools & water courses. UNG-TSOI is considered a Noxious environmental weed & shipping of any part of the plant is not permitted to the continent.

SEED-SAVING: long seed life span.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: 1 ft. (30 cm) long, planted into damp soil or mud & kept moist. Seeds are scarified &/or soaked one day. Sown directly on moist, loose soil, or to transplant. Germination: one to three weeks at 70 to 75F (21-24°C). Seeds do not germinate well under water.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, Wet

☆ VANILLA / WANILA

Vol II · scan p. 204

☆ VANILLA / WANILA on Vanilla fragrans, V. planifolia, & others. Orchidaceae (Orchid) Family. Various forms exist.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & highly esteemed.

VANILLA BEANS: cylindrical yellowish-green, pod-like fruits grow 4 to 10 in. (10-25 cm) long. Cured for flavoring for many foods & drinks including custards, cakes, baked goods, candies, ice-creams, puddings, syrups, Cacao, beverages, yogurt, etc. Flavor varies with location, soil, climate, elevation, pollination, time of harvest, as well as cultural & curing techniques.

NOTE: Artificial! VANILLA is an inferior flavoring made from paper-mill wastes or from certain coniferous trees, from coal-tar extract, or Clove-oil eugenol. Contains the same principle flavoring component but not the important minor ones.

BEARING: Can begin flowering at two to three years of age, reaching maximum yield in seven to eight years.

MATURITY: Pods mature six to nine months after pollination. Full-sized pods are picked shortly before full ripeness, when their tips turn yellow. Fully ripe pods tend to split open on the vine.

HARVESTING: Pods can be snapped or cut off by hand.

CURING: After pods are slightly shriveled, within a week of harvest, they are best cured by being repeatedly sweated & dried for several weeks, then sun-drying on mats afew months. After that they can be conditioned in bins up to half a year. During this aging, the pods tum dark brown & become frosted with fragrant vanillin crystals. (SEE: Pursglove, Tropical Crops, for processing details.) Speedier processes do exist. VANILLA-extract is made by mashing steeping cured beans in brandy.

— scan page 205 · book page 182 —

APPLICATIONS:

LANDSCAPING: Attractive vine. An omamental, striped-leaf form also exists.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES: VANILLA is thought to be stimulating & aphrodisiacal.

TOILETRIES: Perfumery, soaps, lotions, etc.

DESCRIPTION: Handsome, herbaceous perennial vine. Can climb 30 to 50 ft. (9-15 m) tall, but usually kept much less. Succulent stems & fleshy leaves. Clusters of waxy, aromatic, yellow-green, spring flowers mature into dehiscent pods. Daylength neutral. Fast growing in good conditions. Adventitious aerial roots & branched, humus-layer roots. Mycorrhizal association is noted.

LIFE SPAN: seven to forty productive years is possible.

ORIGIN: Tropical Central- & South America.

CLIMATE: Needs a hot, humid climate. In its home lands, VANILLA is found climbing in wet, low elevation forests. Thrives with ten months of frequent, gentle rains, then two drier months to encourage spring blossoming. Tolerates excess rain during vinegrowth, but not during pod-ripening. Intolerant of prolonged drought.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: Often. Can grow successfully to 2000 ft. (600 m) elevation here.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: VANILLA prefers light, loose, moist, humusy, adequately drained, acidic soil & light shade. Can be planted on mounds. Needs wind protection. Mulching with organic matter retains soil moisture & restrains weeds. Cultivating is generally avoided due to its easily damaged, superficial root system.

TOLERATES: temporary flooding.

INTOLERANT OF: full sun, full shade & water-logged soil.

PRUNING & TRAINING: Requires trellis, trees, shrubs, or posts, etc., to climb on. Usually trained to a reasonable harvesting & pollinating height. Straight, well-formed pods are encouraged by allowing vines to climb & then droop over its support. Weakor old stems can be pruned back after harvest.

ASSOCIATES: Can be grown on trees that are fast growing, strong, prunable, with thin shade, & low, accessible branches for vines to climb. Possible species include Mother of Cacao, Bauhinias, Annato, Coffee, Calabash Tree, Erythrinas, Orchid Trees, Pandanus, etc., or, while young, Corn.

ADVERSARIES: Anthracnose can be problematic where there is excessive rain, or shade, poorly drained soil, or when planted too closely. Damage by mildew, root-rot, slugs & snails is also possible.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Excellent candidate in the right conditions.

WEEDY: V. planifolia can escape & naturalize.

DISADVANTAGES: Labor intensive & low returns, economically speaking, but worth it in the right place. SEX: [hermaphroditic?]

POLLINATION: Certain bees & by hummingbirds. In many countries, hand-pollination is necessary. Hand pollination is best done during sunny mornings, after a rain. When successful fertilization has occurred, the flower stays on the vine. Fortunately, in Hawaiʻi VANILLA have developed fruit without hand-pollination.

PROPAGATION: By cuttings & only rarely by seeds. Stems readily root at their nodes. Cuttings: as long as 3 to 12 ft. (.9-3.6 m) long can fruit in one to two years, while 1 ft. 30cm) cuttings bear in three to four years. Cuttings may last up to two weeks before planting if kept cool & shaded. VANILLA is usually propagated directly, in its final location, but it can also be started in nurseries. Young stems are tied to a support until aerial-roots have a good hold.

Elevation / Rainfall: CoastalLowMid, WetMesic

☆🌿 WATER CHESTNUT / ULU KAI

Vol II · scan p. 206 · book p. 185

☆ WATER CHESTNUT / uLuKal Chinese Water Chestnut, Spike Rush, Waternut, Pi-tsi, Ma-tai, Pip wai, Kohekohe. Eleocharis dulcis, syn. E. tuberosa. Cyperaceae (Sedge) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Highly esteemed. Somewhat spherical corms grow ¥ to 1% in. (1.25-4 cm) wide, & are covered by thin, brown leaf-bases. Sweet, crisp, nutty corms, peeled or not, sliced or whole, are eaten fresh raw (young corms), boiled, roasted, baked, stir-fried, in Chinese cuisine, pounded into cakes, or dried. Dried, powdered corm is utilized as a soup- or sauce thickener & as a Crisp coating for deep-frying.

TURITY: Ready to harvest in autumn, when the shoots begin to die back. Harvest season can last six months or more.

HARVESTING: Corms are dug, separated & washed.

STORING: Comms have good keeping qualities when refrigerated between 50 to 55°F (10-13°C), or kept in moist, cool mud. Fresh edible corms should not be allowed to dry. Pounded corm-cakes can last two weeks. Can be sun dried or canned.

SHIPPING: Dried or canned corms ship well.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING: SEE: LANDSCAPING.

FIBER: Dried stems for weaving baskets, mats, hats, etc.

LANDSCAPING: A water loving plant for downspout-gardens, tubs, bogs, ponds, etc.

MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

PONDSCAPING: High value aquaculture,

🌿 DESCRIPTION: Attractive, herbaceous, perennial bog plant. Often grown as an annual. Can grow to 3 ft. (3-9 m) tall. Upright, cylindrical, non-jointed, blunt tipped shoots arise from a common center below water. Deciduous leaves die back; plant over-winters as corms. Late in the season it can produce compact heads of minuscule flowers. Long day-length plant.

ORIGIN: India & subtropical Asia.

CLIMATE: Tropics, subtropics or warmer temperate zones. Grows in warm or hot regions. Intolerant of dry conditions.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: While not common, the WATER CHESTNUT is occasionally seen in Hawaiʻi.

PREFERENCES & CULTURE: Easy to grow in rich, muddy soil, & a constant cover of water, such as in bogs, lo*i, ponds, tubs & other stil] waters. Grows in paddy-cultures, much like wetland Kalo (Taro). Responds to Periodic feeding.

ASSOCIATES: Can be grown in paddies with Rice, or Taro, etc.

ADVERSARIES: Few pests or diseases.

ORGANIC-GROWING: Can be grown organically if water purity is maintained. WEEDY?: Although other Eleocharis are weedy in damp areas in Hawaiʻi, this species apparently has not naturalized.

PROPAGATION: Corms are submerged below the surface of the water. Normally propagated very early spring. CoastalLow Mid, Water

SEE ALSO: TRAPA NUT, a "Water Chesmut." Trapa species. In Permacopia III., the Weed Book.

⚠️Ⓦ WATER CRESS / LĒKŌ

Vol II · scan p. 206 · book p. 185

WATER CRESS / LĒKŌ Nasturtium officinale. Brassicaceae (Mustard) Family. An almost sterile hybrid of N. officinale x N. microphyllum is also cultivated for its greens.

EDIBILITIES: Popular, esteemed & nutritious. High yield-per-effort ratio. Tasty, tangy leaves & tender shoots are eaten fresh raw (but, SEE: CAUTION, following) in mixed salads, on sandwiches, or cooked as greens, blanched, in soups, omelettes, purees, as a blended spread (with butter added), or as a gamish. High in vitamins A & C, minerals & protein. Seeds may be sprouted & eaten. fresh in salads, or ground whole for a Mustard-like condiment.

MATURITY: about fifty days.

HARVESTING: mature leaves are gathered as needed. Continuous harvest encourages branching.

⚠️ CAUTION: Harvesting leaves from plants grown in contaminated water should be avoided, or else the leaves should be cooked weil to kill parasites!.

APPLICATIONS:

CONTAINER-GROWING: can be grown in pots set in water, indoors or out. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

DESCRIPTION: Herbaceous, aquatic, evergreen perennial. Grows in fresh water. Plants grow 15 in. (8 cm) tall, with stems 24 in. (60 cm) long. Stems are low growing, ascending, or trailing in water, readily rooting at their nodes. Clusters of tiny, white flowers mature into small pods.

LIFE SPAN: clump can live indefinitely.

ORIGIN: Eurasia.

CLIMATE: tropics to temperate zones.

GROWN IN HAWATLE: often cultivated here.

PREFERS: fresh, clean, cool, gently moving, shallow water, humusy soil, alkaline pH & part shade. Thrives on leaf mold & abundant calcium. In paddy culture, periodic flooding helps control weeds.

TOLERATES: full sun when grown in water, as well as heavy shade, flooding, & frost.

INTOLERANT OF: excess warmth & dryness.

ADVERSARIES: basically free.

WEEDY: escaped & commonly naturalized. WATER CRESS is a serious river weed in some regions of the world. Found wild in creeks, gentle streams & wet ground.

PROPAGATED & SPREAD BY: cuttings & seeds. Cuttings: rooted in water or sand, or placed directly into wet soil. Seeds are sown in containers to transplant & require constant moisture. Seeds need darkness to sprout.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, Wet/Water

NOTE: Wild WATER CRESS is sometimes confused with the similar, but poisonous Fool's Cress, or with Marshwort. (here?)

SEE ALSO: PĀʻIHI. Nasturtium sarmentosum. in i)

🌳 WHITE SAPOTE

Vol II · scan p. 207 · book p. 187

WHITE SAPOTE White Sapota, Casimiroa, Zapote Blanco, Abache, Matasano, Cochiztzapotl, Mexican Apple. Casimiroa edulis. Rutaceae (Citrus) Family. Diverse varieties & cultivars exist, including those with superior fruit, as well as semi-dwarfs.

EDIBILITIES: Ancient & esteemed food. But, SEE: TOXICITIES, following. Round, egg-shaped, flattened, yellow or green, thin skinned fruits reaching 3 to 5 in. (7.5-12.5 cm) wide. Sweet, juicy, delicious pulp is slightly resinous, buttery, custard-like & typically nutty. Fruit is peeled thickly or pulp spooned out. Pulp is eaten fresh raw, or in fruit salads, pies, ice creams, sherbets, milk shakes, or as jellies, marmalades, & pulp can also be frozen or dried as fruit-leather. High in vitamins, proteins, carbohydrates & other nutrients. Fruit pulp tends to be more bitter when grown in colder climates. The large, smooth seeds are discarded, as they are poisonous to eat.

BEARING: seedlings fruit in about five years; grafted trees in three.

MATURITY: ready to test-harvest when color changes & fruit are ripe, but still firm. WHITE SAPOTE can be prolific, with some cultivars bearing twice a year, although others bearing heavily every other year.

HARVESTING: gathered by clipping, leaving a piece of stem on fruit. Fruit softens & sweetens in three to fourteen days. Ready to eat when stern-piece falls off.

STORING: fruit need to be handled with care. Very perishable at room temperature, but can last weeks in a refrigerator at temperatures above 40°F (5°C).

SHIPPING: thin skin of mature fruit is easily damaged, therefore long-lasting varieties should be selected, & fruit picked several weeks early while still green & hard, Fruit are wrapped separately, boxed & refrigerated. Early picking reduces flavor quality of most, but not all cultivars.

TOXICITIES: 1. Raw seeds are bitter & deadly. 2. As an Aboriginal name for this tree means “kill health,” caution is recommended. 3. Also known as "sleep-producing sapote."

APPLICATIONS:

BEE FORAGE: pollen from some varieties. HEDGEROW.

LANDSCAPING: ornamental. Abundant fruit-drop can be raked up, or the tree can be planted over a chicken yard. MEDICINAL QUALITIES.

NURSE TREE: for Coffee, etc.

WOOD: somewhat strong & dense, but not long-lasting: building, furniture, etc.

🌳 DESCRIPTION: WHITE SAPOTE is an attractive evergreen tree. Can grow 60 ft. (18 m) tall, but usually kept half that. Climax species. Wide round crown. Fragrant glossy leaves. Can sporadically shed its leaves during winter, after a frost, or during a drought. Panicles of smali, whitish or yellow-green flowers. Fast growing & usually vigorous in good conditions.

LIFE SPAN: long lived.

ORIGIN: highlands of tropical Central & South America & Mexico.

CLIMATE: tropics & subtropics. Thrives in cool climates, with abundant summer heat, & is said to grow where Lemons prosper.

GROWN IN HAWAIʻI: occasionally.

PREFERS: deep, moist, well drained, average or rich, light soil, pH 5.5 to 6.5 & full sun. Low effort-per-yield. Benefits from being fertilized like Citrus, or Peach, although lighter on the nitrogen.

TOLERATES: various soils, some drought (once established), frost, some wind, & salty or calcareous conditions.

INTOLERANT OF: heavy rain, poor drainage & strong winds.

PRUNING: tips & terminal-bud can be pinched to maintain a low, wide, convenient size. Thereafter, only rampant shoots & low or awkward branches are removed. Fruiting is reduced if pruning is too severe. Fruit can be thinned to increase quality & size.

ADVERSARIES: WHITE SAPOTE are generally free of problems, except for fruit fly attack of sweet, tree-ripened fruit.

WEEDY: can naturalize. SEX: functionally female flowers or hermaphroditic. Mate is needed for most 'select' varieties.

POLLINATION: bees & other insects.

SEED-SAVING: seeds are highly variable. Seed life span is very short, thus they are cleaned & planted quickly before they dry.

PROPAGATED BY: very fresh seeds, air-layering, budding & grafting. Seeds are sown under 1 in. (2.5 cm) of soil. Germination: about one month, if warm enough. Young plants need to be protected from windburn. Transplanted to final site when 2 to 5 ft. (.6-1.5 m) tall. Young plants benefit from being headed-back to encourage low branching.

Elevation / Rainfall: LowMidHigh, MesicDry

SEE ALSO: BLACK SAPOTE. Diospyros digyna.

YACON Strawberry Jicama, Bolivia Sunroot, Liacon Polymnia sonchifolia. Asteraceae (Sunflower) Family.

EDIBILITIES: Minor food. Reddish or purplish tubers are crisp, juicy & sweet. Eaten fresh raw, when well grown, or in mixed salads (sliced, shredded), cooked, stir-fried, in soups & stews, or as juice (grated & squeezed). Sweeter, but not as crisp when suncured. TOLERATES: heavy rain, acid soil & part shade.

INTOLERANT OF: very hot conditions & drought.
