Glossary (Volume I)

Acid Soil: Soi] mat has a pH lower than 7.0. While most plants grow well in slightly acid soil {pH 6.0 to 7.0}, some plants prefer very acid conditions, such as AZALEA & BLUEBERRY. Compare Alkaline soil. SEE ALSO: pH.

Adventitious: Roots growing from the stem, rather than from the root stalk.

Aerial: Adventitious roots or tubers that form above the ground.

Ahupua'a: A wedge-shaped division of land from the sea to the mountain tip, usually including a river, its valley, & extending to the ridges.

Air-layering: Rootin:: Ss g a branch in peat-moss for subsequent separation & planting.

AKA: Also Known As. P 8

Alien plants: Species that are neither Indigenous nor Endemig

Alkaline soil: Sweet, or basic soil that has a:.. AKA: Foreign, or Exotic species. PH higher than we a s POMEG & JUTUBE, but most do not. SEE ALSO: pH cS) 70. Some plants thrive in alkalinity, such a MEGRANATE Alley ie The practice of growing alternating rows of plants with main crops to provide a nearby source of nitrogen-

Allelopathic: fy ulation, mulch, biomass, compost, etc, microorganje'® book, those plants whose roots, leaves, or exudates inhibit the growth of other nearby plants or Anaerobic compo stin, TRONWOOD, FAYA TREE, for example. 8: Decomposition of organic materials without oxygen: sealed plastic bags, under water, etc. Ann we tants that Can flower & make seeds within one season or year. E.g.: LETTUCE, CORN, SQUASH. Compare: Biennial Tennial.

Beneficial insects: SEE: Pest predators.

Biennial: Plants that produce foliage {food-storing organs} the first year, then flower, seed, & die the second. E.g.: CARROTS, PARSLEY, GOBO. Compare: Annual & Perennial.

Bio-control/ Biological control: The practice of keeping plant adversaries or weeds in check by utilizing the natural propensities of insects or other organisms, or mechanical controls. Bio-control includes predatory & parasitizing, & other beneficial sects, fungus, diseases, etc., who are imported & introduced. Caution: Bio-control is a young & often risky science. SEE

ALSO: IPM, & Pest predator.

Biomass: Living plant material when considered as a total mass,

Bisexual: SEE: Hermaphroditic.

Bolt: When annual plants form a flower-stalk & produce seed.

Bonsai: The art of training & pruning branches & roots to create a unique miniature.

Broadcasting: Scattering seeds, fertilizer, etc., over the surface of the soil. Often raked in.

Budding: A propagation technique where a ‘select’ bud is grafted onto a vigorous root-stock.

Buttressed: Thickened tree-base that provides added support to the trunk. E.g.: BANYAN, KAPOK. C: Degrees Centigrade. {C = F - 32 divided by 1.8}. Compare: F {Fahrenheit}.

Calyx: Green, outer, leaf-like whorl of sepals that protect a flower-bud.

Canopy: The top layer of a forest

Catch-crop: Plants grown after a main crop to absorb surplus nutrients that would other-wise be lost or not suitable for the next crop, or to produce something after a main crop.

Chill-hours / Chilling requirement: A dormant period consisting of a certain number of hours below 45F {7C} to initiate blossoming. Number of hours can vary from 100 to 2000. E.g.: APPLES...

Chlorosis: A systemic condition of reduced chlorophyll, resulting in a plant's newest leaves becoming yellow or blanched. Usually caused by a deficiency of particular minerals, such as iron, nitrogen, magnesium, zinc, or by parasites, drought, insufficient light, or herbicides.

Climax species: A stable stage in an association of plant species well adjusted to their environment.

Compost: Decomposed organic materials.

Coppicing: Frequent, heavy pruning that yields biomass, thatching, firewood, poles, etc. Compare: Pollarding.

Corm: Round, swollen, non-scaly, underground root-stock & food-storage organ from which emerges leaves, flowers & roots.

Compare: Tuber.

Cover-crop: Plants grown to prevent erosion & to accumulate nutrients, including humus. Typically incorporated into the soil, or cut as mulch, rather than harvested. E.g.: COWPEAS... SEE ALSO: Green-manure.

Cultivar: A named plant variety. Usually in lower case, surrounded by single quotation marks: °......

Cutting: A piece of plant branch, stem, root, rhizome, leaf, etc., that is rooted to produce new plants.

Damping-off: A disease usually caused by various fungi, that creates rot in seeds or seedlings at, or close to, the soil level resulting in their wilting or death. Typically occurs in damp, over-crowded conditions, or in garden soil {as opposed to a sterile medium}, or in seeds planted too deeply.

Day-length sensitive plants: Plants who flower according to day-light hours, being either short-day or long-day.

Day-neutral plants: Plants who can flower regardless of lengths of day & night.

Deciduous: The yearly dropping of leaves. E.g.: APPLE, WILIWILI, ʻŌLENA. Plants can be winter- or summer-deciduous. Some plants only occasionally loose their leaves, as during severe droughts. Compare: Evergreen.

Dehiscent: Mature seed-cases that open to release their seeds or spores. Compare: Indehiscent.

Dioecious: Unisexual species having female & male flowers on separate plants. Compare: Monoecious.

Disturbed ground: Soil that has been exposed by natural forces such as land-slides, fire, lava flows, etc., or by human intervention as in over-grazing, logging, bull-dozing, fire, etc. lve 9 pivision: A propagation technique utilizing sections of root-masses, or corms, bulbs, offsets, etc- jnage: The ability, or lack thereof, of water to pass through soil.;. pght tolerant / Drought resistant: Plants that can withstand lack of water for varying lengths of ume, OF those that have low water needs. E.g.: FIG, POMEGRANATE. CACTUS. Conditions such as age of plant, soil structure, exposure, slope, etc., can effect the ability of a plant to withstand drought. SEE ALSO: XERISCAPING. pwarf: A small, compact version of a plant.

Endemic plants: Species that have evolved to become unique to an area..

Entropic: A measure of the unavailability or degradation of energy or matter. Compare: Synergism.

Epiphyte: Plants which grow on plants, rocks, or other substrates, but obtain their nutrients & water from air & rain, as opposed to being a parasite. E.g.: CATTLEYA ORCHIDS, & some FERNS. Compare: TERRESTRIAL, or PARASITIC.

Espalier: A plant that is trained to grow on a flat plane as a building, fence, trellis, or other support. This practice conserves space & provides protection for the plant. Some popular candidates: APPLE, CITRUS, GARDENIA. Pp P P pia.

Evergreen: Plants which do not lose all their leaves at once, thereby remaining in foliage year-round. E.g.: ʻŌHIʻA, ʻŌLAPA, KĀWAʻU. Compare: Deciduous....: - Ajien-

Exotic: Plants introduced from a foreign place, not native to a region or country. AKA: Ali " Degrees Fahrenheit. (F = 1.8C + 32}. Compare: C {Centig eneric grouping of plants with characteristics or properties

F mnily: A taxonomic division after "Order" & before "Genus." As; jon.. - pre roots: ‘A mass of fine, spreading roots that emerge from a plant's base. These roots are usually of the same thickness, bear slimmer lateral roots, & are found mostly in the top layers of soil.

Fire-enhanced: Plants that add fuel to, or otherwise help spread a fire, then grow back quickly in its wake, making a larger, hotter fire next time. E.g-: MOLASSES GRASS, EUCALYPTUS, etc. a; rdant / Fire-bre: Moisture-retentive, or low-fuel plants that can form a line-of-defense against fire. Fire-retardant / rir light polyester cloth placed over plants providing protection from sun, heavy rain, insects, birds, sulfuric ing row-cover:.;; sae etc., as well a8 creating a Warmer micro-climate-

Fodder: Plants or grains, etc., that are fed to livestock. Fee ce Eaton iti elias ht ar preyel oo & absorbed bya plan's eaves

Forage: Plants that are grazed OF browsed by livestock.

Freestone: A fruit in which the stone does not adhere to the pulp.

Friable: Soil that has a loose, airy, easily crumbled structure. AKA: Good tilth.

Frond: The leaf of a FERN, etc.

Fruit: A mature berry or capsule containing a seed or seeds.

Genus: A taxonomic division ranking before species, & after Family. The related grouping of species with characteristics or properties in common. While Genus names are capitalized, species names are not. The scientific name of a plant is the Genus & species names.

Grafting: A method of uniting a ‘select’ plant's- shoot, twig, or bud {scion} onto an established rootstock, aligned cambium to cambium.

Green-manure: Plants grown to enrich soil by being incorporated while in their soft-, green-, nitrogen-rich state. Soil thus amended has more available nutrients, humus, a greater ability to hold water, etc. SEE ALSO: Cover-crop.

Ground-cover: Plants grown to blanket the soil in order to suppress weeds, protect & improve soil, check erosion, supply mulch, create an even appearance, etc.

Ground-layering: A propagation technique of securing a nicked branch into the ground until it has grown enough roots to withstand being separated from its mother-plant.

Guild: 1. An association of plants who are to some degree dependent on each other. 2. A beneficial grouping of interacting plants. E.g.: a heavy feeder, with a nitrogen-fixer, near a pest-repeller.

Habit: A plants' characteristic external form, or style of growth.

Habitat: The site or environment favored by a particular species.

Harden off: The process of adjusting a plant from being adapted to sheltered environment to an open site by gradually increasing its exposure over a period of a week or longer to minimize shock.

HCN: Hydrocyanic acid.

Hedgerow: A line of shrubs or trees on the edge of, or separating a field.

Herbaceous: Plants with soft, green tissues, having no woody fibers. E.g.: GINGER, BANANA, ONIONS.

Herbicide: Chemical utilized to inhibit or kill plants. Some are absorbed by the leaves, others by roots. While some kill many species, others are more selective. Dangerous toxins.

Hermaphroditic: Having both male & female organs in one flower.

Humus: Partially decomposed organic matter from plants & animals. An important ingredient in healthy soil that improves soil structure, water-retention, & fertility. Humus can be lost through erosion, leaching, sun-burn, over-cropping, etc.

Hybrid: Offspring that are the result of crossing different parents. Rather than breeding true, seeds from hybrid plants regress to previous parentage. Compare: Open-pollinated.

Indehiscent: Seed-cases, fruit, etc., that stay closed when they mature. E.g.: CORN. Compare: Dehiscent.

Indicator plant: Species that favor certain environmental circumstances, showing by their presence the nature of that habitat. E.g.: PLANTAIN denotes compacted soil, spontaneous wild STRAWBERRIES denote acid conditions.

Indigenous: In Hawaiʻi, these are species which have colonized the islands without the help of humans, but are still the same as their sisters & brothers elsewhere. Compare: Alien, Endemic, & Introduced.

Inflorescence: A flower cluster.

Introduced plants: Species that are brought into a region by humans, intentionally or not. jeM: Integrated Pest Management. The practice of protecting plants by coordinated treatments of various kinds. The first step is planting well adapted, resistant species & keeping them healthy through good stewardship. Other important components include solarizing the soil, garden sanitation, floating row-cover, trap-plants, host plants, low-impact controls, appropriate ming, etc. Carefully monitored & timed bio-controls are sometimes introduced. “Pest-management" has recently Superseded “pest-control" which implies eradication.

Layering: Generally mean air-layering, but, SEE ALSO: Ground-layering.

Lee-ward / Lee side: The side that is protected from the wind. Usually dry. Compare: Windward.

Loam: Mellow, friable soil made up of a variable mix of humus, sand, clay & silt. Loam is usually well-drained & non- compacting.

Lodging / Lodge: The tendency of a plant to fall over due to wind, rain, shallow roots, weak stems, heavy heads, etc.

Long-day plant: Species that will not flower unless the length of daylight is greater than 12 hours.

Mesic: Reasonably moist rainfall regime between 48" to 100" {1200-2500mm} annually,

Micro-climate: A small region that has a climate different from the surrounding area. This effect can be caused or created by Mic soonutrienn cOreaks, buildings, hills, valleys, etc. Mono-cropping. The minor mineral elements needed by plants, such as zinc, iron, manganese, etc.

Monoecious: », Lhe practice of planting only one species in an area. Compare: Polyculture. Monoembryonio, “Ue male, or hermaphroditic flowers on every plant. Compare: Dioecious..

Mon otypic: A. When a sexually pollinated seed creates a single seedling. E.g.: AVOCADO. Compare: Polyembryonic. * 4 8rouping that is composed of plants of a single species.

Mother trees: A tree selected to propagate from, whether by seeds or other means.

Mulch: A protective layer placed on the soil surface. Organic mulch can suppress weeds, increase water-retention, add nutrients, moderate soil temperature, & provide a favorable habitat for beneficial soil organisms. Mulch is kept @ least 6" {15cm} away from tree trunks. Inorganic mulches protect & warm soil, but add nothing.

Naturalized: An Introduced plant that has managed to flourish & is able to compete with existing plants without assistance from humans. E.g.: IRONWOOD, CHRISTMAS BERRY, EUCALYPTUS,,

Nitrogen fixing: The transformation of atmospheric nitrogen into organic nitrogen-rich elements in the soil, by means of root- nodulal rhizobia bacteroids & other organisms.

Node: The somewhat swollen segment on a plant stem or root where buds or roots typically emerge.

Noxious: Plants with unruly, toxic, harmful, distasteful, or otherwise irritating characteristics.

NPK: Nitrogen {N}, Phosphorous {P}, & Potassium {K}.

Nurse trees / Nurse crops: Species grown to protect & nourish crop plants, providing shade, green-manure, nitrogen-fixation, Open polligeed pore OF CACAO, ERYTHRINA species, etc, naturally by ins Species seeds that breed identical to their parents & can be replanted again & again. Pollinated Oreani ae €cts, wind, etc. Compare: Hybrid. 7 galic growing: A method of gardening or farming resulting in safe, nutritious foods, etc., utilizing only organic fertilizers, amendments, as well as natural disease & pests controls {management}.

Palmate: Leaves with spreading, finger-like lobes arising from a central, palm-like point.

Parasite: A plant or micro-organism that grows on, or in, its host & gains nourishment from it. Compare: Epiphyte.

Perennial: Plants that grow three years or longer. E.g.: ASPARAGUS, GINGER, WATER CHESTNUT. Compare: Annuals & Biennials.

Perfect flower: A flower containing al] functional sexes. Same as Hermaphroditic.

Permaculture: Designs for sustainable living.

Pest: An annoying, destructive, or otherwise non-beneficial insect, animal, bird, plant, etc.

Pest-predator: Beneficial insects or vertebrates who attack, or feed on pest insects or -plants. E.g.: Ladybugs, Lacewings, Praying Mantis, etc. SEE ALSO: IPM.

Pest-predator plant: A plant that feeds or provides a habitat for beneficial insects. E.g.: the flowers of various Umbelliferous plants such as CARROTS & PARSLEY.

Petiole: A leaf-stem or leaf-stalk. pH: The acidity, alkalinity, or neutrality of soil. The measure of the activity or concentration of electrically charged hydrogen molecules {ions}. On a logarithmic scale of 0 to 14, with 0 being acid, 14 being alkaline, & neutral @ 7. Acid soils have less hydrogen. Dry climates typically more alkaline, while rainy ones more acid.

Photoperiodism: The effect on growth & flowering exerted by the alternating length of days & nights. SEE ALSO: DAYLENGTH SENSITIVE.

Photosensitizing: Becoming more susceptible to the sun's radiance. Usually affecting skin & eyes.

Pioneer: Species colonizing bare soil, initiating a more favorable environment for successive plants.

Pollarding: A pruning technique where a tree' is shortened drastically & subsequently pruned each year during a dormant season. This procedure creates a dense cluster of new branches for fuel, fiber, mulch, screen, etc.

Pollination: When pollen from the male stamens is placed on the female stigma. Achieved by gravity, wind, insects {especially bees}, as well as bats, birds, etc., or by hand.

Polyculture: The practice of growing a healthy diversity of species together. Compare: Mono-cropping.

Polyembryonic: Seeds with a number of embryos wrapped together inside its seed-coat. Usually produced asexually & resulting in a number of seedlings from one seed. E.g.: MANGO & CITRUS.

Propagation: The multiplying of plants.

Propaguls: The plant part utilized for propagation: seeds, divisions, cuttings, scions, layers, etc.

Progyny: When the female part of the flower matures before the male's pollen is produced.

Protandry: When the male pollen matures before the female is receptive. E.g.: ‘BMS CHERRIES.

Pulp: The moist flesh of a fruit or stem. Q.V.: "Which see."

Ramified: Branched.

Rampant plants: Species with aggressive, invasive, weedy natures..

Retted: A method of soaking a pliant {E.g. FLAX, etc.} to soften & separate fibers from woody tissues.

Rhizobija: Soil-borne bacteria who create symbiotic root-nodule bacteroids on plants' roots & are able to convert gaseous nitrogen & make it available for nutrition to the plant.

Rhizome: A long, often thick, modified stem that sends out roots, buds, or aerial shoots from its nodes. Rhizomes typically grow horizontally, either under or along the soil surface. E.g.: many GRASSES, SWEET POTATOES, etc.

Root-nodules: Small, root swellings created by symbiotic, nitrogen-fixing rhizobia. Often occurring in legumes.

Rootstock: The roots & stem base of a plant on which a scion is grafted.

Rosette: A tight, circular or spiraled teaf- or flower-cluster. Common first year form of a biennial plant.

Row-cover: SEE: Floating row-cover.

Runner: A slim, creepin g stem emerging from a plant's base that sends out roots at its nodes & produces a new plant at its tip. E.g.: KUKUYI GRASS. STRAWBERRY, etc. SEE ALSO: Stolon..;;

Scarification: Softening a hard seed-coat or breaking seed-dormancy by either soaking, nicking, sanding, scraping, tumbling, or chemically treating a seed.

Cion: A section of stem, shoot, or bud, that is grafted onto an established root-stock. Self-compatible / Self-fertile / Self-pollinating: All refer to a plant that can pollinate itself without a nearby mate. E.g.: BEANS, etc,

Self-in compatible / Self-ste rile: Apia van nee be fertilized by its own pollen, needing pollen from a different plant or variety to produce fruit. a th, ” T

Shade tree: A tree that provides shelter from the sun. SEE ALSO: Nurse Tree.

Sheet-mulching: Applying layers of mulch over weeds, including a weed-suppressing layer {such as cardboard or newspaper}, a high-nitrogen green layer, & a brown, high-carbon top layer.

Shelter belt: A planting of trees or shrubs to create a buffer from strong winds or storms, resulting in a protected micro-climate for plants or animals.

Short-day plant: Species that can flower only when day-lengths are short {under 12 hours}.

Shrub: A woody plant typically under 30' {9m} tall, that has multiple branches arising from ground level, or near it, rather than a single trunk. Compare: Herbaceous & Tree.

Soil pH: SEE: pH.

Soil test: Analysis of various aspects of soils that can include pH, nutrients, or contaminants.

Species: A genetically similar plant grouping that can breed true. Taxonomic division ranking before "variety," & after "Genus."

Specimen: A shrub, tree, or large plant that makes a conspicuous, attractive contribution to a setting.

Stolon: A stem that emerges from a plant's base, sending out adventitious roots at its nodes, often creating new plants. E.g.: STRAWBERRIES, MORNING GLORY. SEE ALSO: Runner.:

Strand plants: Species that grow close to the ocean. Although these shore plants can live where splashed by salt-spray, they can't generally tolerate inundation by high tides.

Stratification: A method of breaking dormancy of seeds, or other plant propaguls. Time & temperature depends upon species. Cold, moist @ 40F {5C}. Warm, moist @ 70F-75F {21-24C}.

Subtropics: Climates that border on the Tropics where it does not reliably frost each winter.

Succulent: A soft, juicy, fleshy plant, designed for moisture conservation. E.g.: ALOE, CACTUS.

Sucker: A plant shoot arising from roots, or from above or underground stems. E.g.: BAMBOO, NEEM, many GRASSES. On grafted plants, a sucker is new growth emerging from the rootstock instead of the grafted part, & is typically removed. Syn. / Synonym: The same as, but replaced by.

Synergism: When the cooperation among independent elements or agents has an outcome greater than the sum of the effect of each element or agent acting independently. Compare: Entropic.

Tannins: Astringent complex compounds of tannic acid & other phenolics found in plants that are utilized in tanning, as well as in the manufacture of ink, dye, & medicine. Ingesting excess tannins has been linked to cancer. Contained in COFFEE, CAROB, etc.

Surface roots: Feeder roots that usually lie within the upper 1' or 1 1/2' {30-45cm} of the soil surface, through which the plant absorbs the largest part of its moisture & nutrients. BAMBOO & AVOCADO have only feeder roots & no tap-root.

Tap-root: A strong, centered, sometimes swollen, but tapering, main root that moves directly downward from a plants’ crown, having also small lateral roots. Tap-rooted plants typically have more drought-resistance, are well anchored, but are harder to transplant.

Temperate Zone: The two regions on the planet found between the Tropics of Cancer, or Tropics Capricorn, & the Arctic, or Antarctic circles, respectively. SEE ALSO: Tropics & Subtropics.

Terrestrial: Rooted to the earth. Compare: Epiphyte.

Thinning: Reducing the number of excess branches, immature fruits on an overbearing tree, or the number of seedlings in a bed. This permits better ventilation, sun exposure, or gives the rest a better chance at growing large.

Toddy: Sap from a number of PALM species that is drunk either in its fresh state, or fermented.

Top-dressing: Applying fertilizer, or other organic materials, to the soil surface.

Trap-crop: Plant species grown near a crop to entice pests away. These plants are disposed of when fully infested.

Tree: Long-lived, woody plant with well-delineated trunk topped by crown of branches & foliage. Compare: Shrub, & Herbaceous.

Trellis: A supporting framework, lattice, structure, plant, or tree for a plant to climb on.

Tropics: The equator-hugging region on the planet that lies between 23.5 degrees North or South, where the over-head sun tums back after the equinoxes. The only region of the earth where the sun can be directly over-head.

True: A plant whose seed will grow up to be similar or identical to its parent. Compare: Hybrid. quber: A swollen food storage area of a modified, usually underground stem, with the ability to create a new plant from its growth buds. E.g.: POTATO & DAHLIA. Compare: Corm, Rhizome. ungulates: Herbivorous, hoofed, & often horned mammals, including such grazers & browsers as cattle, cows, goats, etc.

UniseXual: Having either female or male organs, but not both. Variety / Var.: 1. A recognized kind of plant of a given species. 2. A taxonomic subdivision ranking before ‘cultivar,’ & after SP ecles." A plant that is in some way different from its ancestral species, either artificially or naturally produced through selection or jsojation. Compare: Cultivar. weed: A Plant that is out of place or unwanted. Specifically, a highly competitive, precocious, or rank plant that crowds out its more valued neighbors & is not easy to control. Weeds can range from being nearly innocuous to being highly invasive.

Weed control: Ground-covers, mulches, shading, solarization, landscaping fabrics, etc.

Wind-dispersed: The carrying of seeds, fruits, pollen, or spores on moving air.

Wind-ward: The side facing the wind. Compare: Leeward. eriscaping: Growing plants that are desi gned for & adapted to areas with a limited supply of water, low humidity, or droughts.
